en: Oṃ. The Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, together with the commentary composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya.
Now begins the sixth maṇḍala.
In the sixth maṇḍala of the Bhāradvāja [family], there are six anuvākas.
In that [maṇḍala], there are fifteen sūktas in the first anuvāka.
Among them, the first sūkta, consisting of thirteen verses, begins with “tvaṃ hyagne.”
Because it is stated in the *Anukramaṇī*: “O Agni, you indeed, as the son of Bṛhaspati, [are] Bharadvāja; he saw the sixth maṇḍala,” that very Bharadvāja is the seer (*ṛṣi*) who saw the maṇḍala.
By the rule regarding unspecified cases, the meter is Triṣṭubh.
By the rule regarding the beginning of the maṇḍalas, the deity is Agni.
This *manotā-sūkta* is to be recited by the Maitrāvaruṇa when the five portions of the oblation are being cut.
It is stated in the Sūtra: “He recites, ‘O Agni, you indeed are the first... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.6).
In the morning litany (*prātaranuvāka*) during a rite dedicated to Agni, this set of six hymns beginning with this one is used in the Triṣṭubh meter, with the exception of the second.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Agni, you indeed are the first... [Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13]; one should extract the second of the six verses. The first [verse] is employed at the *upākaraṇa* (commencement);
however, the Sūtra has already been stated in the preceding mantra.
For you, O Agni, are the first inventor of prayers, the wondrous invoker who brings forth inspired thoughts;
you, O bull, have made your power invincible, so that every force may be overcome by your might.
For you, O Agni, were the first inventor of this prayer; you, O wonder-worker, became the Hotṛ-priest. You, O bull, made that power invincible, so that it might prevail over every opposing force. 1.

O Agni, you are the first among the gods—the foremost, the most excellent, or the one who exists from the beginning—for you are indeed the *manotā* of the gods; that is, you are such that the minds (*manas*) of the gods are bound (*uta*) or connected to you.
The word "indeed" (*hi*) serves to indicate the well-known authority of the Brāhmaṇa texts, such as: "Agni is the *manotā* of all *manotās*; all *manotās* converge in him" (AiB 2.10).
O *dasma*, O wonderful one, you have become, or are, the *hotṛ*, the invoker of the gods, for this sacred thought (*dhī*), for this ritual act.
O Bull, you who rain down desires, you have made that power and strength—which is difficult to overcome and difficult for even a great being to master—accessible from all sides.
For what purpose?
To enable everyone to prevail, that is, to overcome every powerful enemy.

1. Jha-ta-na-bha-ra-paśī | Then you, the most worshipful one, sat down as the sacrificer in the station of Niḷa, being the subduer of enemies. Toward you, the first, men desiring the gods and seeking great wealth have followed in pursuit.

Then sit down, O Hotṛ, you who are most skilled in sacrifice, at the place of Iḷā, providing nourishment as one worthy of praise. Toward you, the first, the men seeking the gods have followed, discerning you for the sake of great wealth.

Now, O Agni, you who are the most excellent sacrificer (*yajīyān*), acting as the *hotṛ*—the performer of the oblation—have sat down (*nyasīdaḥ*) in the place (*pade*) of *iḷ*, that is, upon the altar characterized by the earth.
What were you doing?
Desiring food (*iṣayan*) consisting of the animal sacrifice, the *puroḍāśa* cake, and so forth, while being worthy of praise (*īḍyaḥ*).

Men—the leaders, human beings performing the office of priests—first of all, before other deities, desiring you as their god and seeking their own selves, following after you, the great one, for the sake of great wealth, knowing you or making you known through praise, went after you in former times.
As one who moves surrounded by many obstacles, they have followed thee, O wakeful one, toward thy wealth—
this bright, beautiful, vast, and fatty one, shining forevermore.
As if surrounded by many troops, they have followed thee, ever-watchful, as thou goest—Agni, the radiant, the visible, the great, the one possessed of fatness, shining forever. || 3 ||

"As if by a path" (*vṛteva mārgeṇa*); the word "as if" (*iva*) is used here in the sense of "presently. By a path situated between the two worlds, [he was followed] by many, that is, numerous, *vasavyas*, i.e., *vasus*.

The suffix is a *taddhita* affix with a reflexive meaning (*svārthika*). Along with those suitable for the dwellings of the sacrificers (*yajamāna*), they follow you as you go—“*anugman*” means they go after you;
the sacrificers enjoy [your presence].
What are they like?
The meaning is that they are those who, being watchful, bestow *rayiḥ*—that is, wealth—upon you, O God. How are you described? It is said as follows:

[He saw] Agni, shining and bright-colored, distinguished by qualities such as slaying [the foe], beautiful to behold, vast, possessing a splendid form, and blazing at all times throughout every season.
Entering the station of the god with playful joy, those seeking glory have attained perfect renown;
they have even assumed names worthy of sacrifice, and they delight in your auspicious aspect.

Seeking glory, they have attained the step of the god, his joy, and his splendor; they have won unimpaired renown and have even assumed names worthy of sacrifice. They have delighted in your auspicious appearance.

The ancient sacrificers, desiring food (*śravasyavaḥ*), going with reverence (*namasā*)—whether by means of oblation or hymn—to the station (*padam*) of the shining god Agni, namely the *āhavanīya* place, have repeatedly obtained everywhere-renowned, unimpaired food (*śravo amṛktam*) that cannot be obstructed by others. O Agni, they take delight in your auspicious aspect (*bhadrāyām saṃdṛśi*), which is the cause of their pleasure. 1. (Note: *kha*-āhavanīya-sthānam; *ga-śa*-āhavanīyādi-sthānam)

2. They do not cause [the sounds] *kha*, *gha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ya*, *ra*, and *ṛ* to resound; they delight [in them]. They have assumed—or maintain—the names worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiya*), that is, suitable for sacrifice, such as "Vaiśvānara" and "Jātavedas";
or alternatively, they have assumed the hymns (*stotra*) which are the means of bowing down.
The peoples on earth increase thee; both kinds of wealth of men belong to thee.
Thou art known as the savior in the crossing over, and thou hast become the father and mother of mortals in their dwelling.

The peoples on earth magnify you; both kinds of wealth belonging to men belong to you. You have become the protector, the one to be recognized in the crossing over; you are the father and the mother, the true seat of human beings. 5.
O Agni, the human *ṛtvij*s—those who perform the rites upon the earth characterized as the sacrificial altar—increase you; they cause you to grow.

Both kinds of wealth belonging to the people—the sacrificers—namely, those consisting of both domestic animals (*paśu*) and wild beasts (*apaśu*), increase you for your sake, O *ṛtvij*s such as the *adhvaryu* and others.
Alternatively, they increase you so that they may obtain both kinds of wealth, such as cattle and the like, for the sake of their people, their sons, and so forth.

O you who cross over, O Vagvan, we—possessing good intellect (*sudhyaḥ*), desiring happiness (*sumnāyavaḥ*), and longing for the divine (*devyantaḥ*)—pray to you, such a one of great majesty (*mahānubhāva*), the praiseworthy (*stutya*), with our hymns; that is to say, we praise you. We implore you. (The meaning is "we praise.")
O Vagnu, while shining—shining with what?
With great, resplendent *vṛcana* (brilliant) energy—you led us, the subjects (*viśaḥ*), the worshippers, to heaven (*divaḥ*). You caused us to go to the celestial realm.
Or rather, the connection is: "By means of the reddish sun, lead [him] to heaven";
that is to say, by way of the path of the sun.

The sage of the people, the lord of the eternal clans, the subduer, the bull among men— Agni, the purifier, who impels those seeking his favor, who shines as the sovereign of riches, the one worthy of worship.

The sage of the people, the lord of the eternal tribes, the subduer, the bull of the nations, the one who seeks the advance of men, the impeller, the purifier, Agni, ruling over riches, worthy of worship. 8.

We praise Agni—the lord and master of the eternal and constant clans characterized by the priests and the sacrificers; the seer who perceives all things; the destroyer of enemies; the showerer of desires; the one who moves toward the people, the singers, and men; the one who provides food and makes it accessible; the purifier; the one who advances, shines, and illuminates; the one who is to be sacrificed to for the sake of obtaining wealth. (This is the remainder of the verse.)
O Agni, that mortal who has sacrificed and performed worship, who has attained the offering of oblations through kindling wood—
he who understands the invocation with prostrations, he, protected by you, receives all desirable things.

Homage! O Agni, the mortal who has sacrificed and labored, who has attained your gift of oblations through kindling—whosoever understands the offering with prostrations, he, aided by you, gains all desirable things. ||9||
"O Agni, the mortal sacrificer worships you with seed;
he has labored and he praises you.
Since "śaśamānaḥ" is listed among the words for acts of praise in Nirukta 3.14.22, this [term] also denotes an act of praise.
That sacrificer, by means of your fuel-stick (*samidh*), accomplishes the offering of the oblation (*havyadāti*) through the gift of the sacrificial food (*havis*).
Furthermore, that sacrificer, with obeisances (*namas*) and hymns of praise (*stuti*), fully knows—that is, he offers—the oblation (*āhuti*) characterized by clarified butter and other substances.
This is the meaning.
The sacrificer, protected by you and favored by you, wins and holds all desirable riches.
To you, the great one, let us offer great worship with prostrations, with these kindled logs, and with oblations;
O Son of Strength, with our songs upon the sacrificial altar, may we strive to abide in your auspicious favor.

To him—*ūm*!—to thee, the great one, we shall offer worship with greatness, with prostrations, O Agni, with fuel and with oblations. O Son of Strength, with our songs upon the sacrificial altar, may we strive to abide in thy auspicious favor. 10.
Maṇḍala 6, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 1, Verse 5:
O Agni, for this great [purpose] of thine, we shall perform great service unto thee; by what means? This is what is being asked.

The connection is as follows: "With salutations (*namobhiḥ*), that is, with acts of homage, or with fuel-sticks (*samidhā*), and also with oblations (*havyaiḥ*), O Son of Strength (*sahasaḥ sūno*), upon the altar (*vedī*), we shall worship you with songs (*gībhiḥ*), that is, hymns of praise, and with recitations (*ukthaiḥ*).
Furthermore, may we strive to attain (*ā yatema*) your auspicious favor (*sumatī*), that is, your beautiful disposition of grace."
The meaning is "may we become."

O Agni, who with your radiance have filled the two worlds, you who are renowned for your fame and are a conqueror through your glories— shine forth far and wide among us with great, enduring, and abundant riches.

O King, you who have extended the two worlds with your light; may we, through our devotion to you, obtain in abundance many glories and riches at the beginning. For in you, O possessor of many boons, there are many treasures at the beginning for the one who honors you, O King. At the beginning, in abundance, through devotion to you, O King, may we obtain riches. For indeed, O possessor of many boons, many treasures are in you at the beginning; they are bestowed upon you, O King. 13. ā | yaḥ | ta॒na॒thu | roda̭sī iti | vi | bhāsā̭ | śrava̭ḥ | purūṇya̭gre | puruthā | tvā॒yā | va॒sūni̭ | rāja̭n | sutā̭ | te | a॒śyāma̭ | purūṇi̭ | hi | tve | puru'vā॒ra | sa॒nti | a॒gre | va॒su | vi॒dhatḙ | rāja̭n | tve | iti || 13 || May we, through our devotion to you, obtain in abundance many glories and riches at the beginning, O King, you who have extended the two worlds with your light. For in you, O possessor of many boons, there are many treasures at the beginning for the one who honors you, O King. At the beginning, in abundance, through devotion to you, O King, may we obtain riches. For indeed, O possessor of many boons, many treasures are in you at the beginning; they are bestowed upon you, O King.

O King Agni, may we attain—may we pervade, or may we enjoy—your many (*purūṇi*) riches (*vasūni*), which are manifold (*puruthā*) in form, such as cattle, horses, and so forth; [we do this] for the sake of wealth (*vasutāyai*), that is, for the state of possessing wealth (*vasumattvāya*).
Here, Bharatasvāmin took *vasutāt* as a single word ending in the locative case, while Bhaṭṭabhāskaramiśra also took it as a single word ending in the vocative case.

O King Agni, you who possess many boons and are worthy of praise by many heroes; in you, who are resplendent, there are many riches—numerous treasures—which ought to be given to me, who serves and attends upon you.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of the heart,
may Vidyātīrthamaheśvara bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Fourth Book in the Commentary on the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial throne of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious Emperor, Supreme Lord, and promoter of the Vedic path.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the fifth book begins.
In the first anuvāka of the fifth maṇḍala, which consists of six anuvākas, there are fifteen hymns (*sūktas*).
Among them, the second hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "tvaṃ hi," belongs to Bharadvāja and is addressed to Agni.
There is another *śakvarī* consisting of fifty-six syllables, with the first ten being *anuṣṭubh*s.
For it is stated in sequence: “You [O Agni] indeed [consist of] eleven *anuṣṭubh*s, ending with a *śakvarī*.
In the *prātaranuvāka*, during the *āprī* rite, this hymn is employed in the *anuṣṭubh* meter, excluding the final verse.
For it is stated: "Thou indeed, O Agni, who hast been born as the Hotṛ for the sacrificer" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13).
And this [hymn] is to be recited in the Āśvina-śastra, because it is extended by analogy according to the rule of the Prātaranuvāka.
For Agni, on the second day of the Dvirātra sacrifice, this very hymn is the Ājya-śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "For you are indeed possessed of dominion; thus [is] the clarified butter" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 10.2).

For you, O Agni, like Mitra, protect the glory of the lord of the dwelling; O Vasu, you who dwell among all people, you nourish renown as if it were prosperity. You indeed, O Agni, like Mitra, protect the glory of the master of the house; O Vasu, you who are far-seeing among men, you foster renown as if it were abundance.
O Agni, for you indeed— you yourself— pervade the *kṣaita*, that is,
the dry wood associated with *kṣiti* (dwelling or decay);
endowed with that, you go toward the glory and the food characterized by the oblation from all sides.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Like Mitra"—Mitra being the one who presides over the day (1. kha reads *abhi* while jha, na, bha read *atipasi*).

Mitra is a god; for he is indeed [the friend]. Or rather, *yaśas* is a name for the house. *Kṣetavat*: *kṣeta* means a dwelling, namely food characterized by the oblation. Like a person who has become a friend, you fly toward the sacrificer’s house which is endowed with that [food]. Or rather, the root *pat* signifies the act of ruling; you rule (*patyase*) over such a place here. For this reason, O *vicarṣaṇe*—O special beholder of all—O *vaso*, O dweller, you [cause] *śravaḥ*—the food worthy of being heard of—which belongs to the sacrificer’s house, as it were; and the word *na* here has the sense of "also. You nourish and increase the prosperity that consists of the effects of that food.
For verily the upholders of the people invoke you with sacrifices;
to you the prize-winning steed, free from malice, traversing the mid-air, goes—he who belongs to all people.
For indeed, the upholders of the people praise you with sacrifices and with songs; to you the prize-winning steed, free from harm, goes, traversing the mid-air and encompassing all people. 2.

O Agni, for indeed, O sustainer of the people, men—those who move across the earth—praise and laud you with sacrifices, with the means of sacrifice, with oblations, and with songs of praise. Moreover, you are the prize; "vāja" signifies movement or attainment.
The sun, possessing that [light], goes toward you; it enters you—this is the meaning.
And so it is heard in scripture: “Verily, the sun enters the fire at evening; therefore, fire is seen from afar” (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.1.29).

And the word *vājin* is heard in some places as denoting the sun: "Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya—they are indeed the *vājins*" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.6.3.9), and "Vāyu together with the sun is the *vājī*" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.7.8).
Of what nature is this *vājī*?
He is *avṛka*, free from harmers, and *rajastūr*, one who traverses the mid-region.
"Water" here refers to dust;
he is the impeller of that which has the characteristic of rain.
Or alternatively:
A crosser and goer of the worlds of the atmosphere, he is the observer of all, the beholder of everything.
In unison, the men of heaven kindle you, the banner of the sacrifice,
when the mortal folk, seeking favor, offer oblations to you in the rite.
In unison, the men of heaven kindle you, the banner of the sacrifice, when this mortal folk, seeking favor, invokes you at the rite.

O Agni, you who are well-pleased—those men, the leaders and officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), who are likewise well-pleased and delighted together with you, kindle you, the banner and indicator of the sacrifice, at the praise of heaven; that is to say, they enkindle you when that human being—the son of Manu, the sacrificer or the *hotṛ* priest—born for the sake of the rite, desiring happiness (*sumna*) for himself, invokes you in the sacrifice which is free from injury and transgression. That is the meaning.
Mortals strive with prayer for the sake of that most bountiful one;
through the aid of the lofty heaven, he crosses over his enemies as if over distress.
He prospers—the mortal who, with devotion, strives for you, the bounteous giver; through your protection, he overcomes the enmity of the great heaven and crosses over distress. 4.
1. Desiring good fortune.
May he prosper.
May that sacrificer prosper; O Agni, for you who are of beautiful gifts—that is, for you who bestow excellent gifts.
The fourth case ending is used in the sense of "intended for slaughter."
Through the thought associated with you, the mortal— the sacrificer subject to death— who exerts himself (*śaśamate*) or,
alternatively, who praises (*śamati*), becomes tranquil (*śāmyati*).

Being engaged in ritual action for your sake, that sacrificer praises you; through your aid—that is, your protection and strength—belonging to you, the great and radiant heaven, he crosses over his enemies, those who hate him, as one passes beyond the "aṃhas," which is like a striking sin.

O Agni, that mortal who attains your offering with fuel as his sharpened weapon, he prospers in a dwelling rich in offspring and endowed with a hundred-year lifespan. 5. *Samidhā yaḥ te āhutim niśitim martyo naśat | vayāvantaṃ sa puṣyati kṣayam agne śatāyuṣam || 5 ||*

O Agni, that mortal— meaning a human being— who, together with the *samidh*, the fuel that serves as the cause for kindling, should reach (*naśat*) your sharpened, refined, and mantra-consecrated oblation;
[the root] *naśati* has the sense of pervading—
that sacrificer, the human being, [reaches] one who possesses offspring.
The branches are characterized by sons, grandsons, and so forth.
Endowed with these, he nourishes, sustains, and causes to flourish his home—which possesses a hundred-year lifespan or, alternatively, which lasts for a long time;
the meaning is that he remains there for a long duration.

Your brilliant smoke rises to heaven, bright and far-extended; like the sun, O Purifier, you shine with light, for you are a trembling flame. 6. *Your* (*tveṣas*) *brilliant* (*te*) *smoke* (*dhūmaḥ*) *rises* (*ṛṇvāti*) *to heaven* (*divi*), being *bright* (*śukraḥ*) and *far-extended* (*ātataḥ*). For like the *sun* (*sūraḥ*), O *Purifier* (*pāvaka*), you *shine* (*rocase*) *with light* (*kṛpā*), for you are a *trembling* (*dhūtā*) [flame]. 6.

O Agni, your brilliant, pure, or radiant smoke, being spread across the sky—the intermediate space—proceeds as it transforms into the form of clouds. Moreover, O purifying Agni, like the sun (sūra), you shine indeed with a luster that illuminates when you are praised with hymns capable of winning favor.

For now you are indeed to be envied by all; you are our dear guest, delightful like an aged man in his home, like a son who protects the noble one. 7. For now... indeed... by all... you are... to be envied... dear... our guest... delightful... like an aged man in his home... like a son... who protects the noble one. 7.

Moreover, O Agni, among all creatures you are indeed worthy of praise and honor. For this reason—*hi* being used in the sense of "because"—you are our guest (*atithi*). This is a *luptopama* (elliptical simile), meaning you are as dear as a guest. Or alternatively: [1] *gha* means "connected with"; [2] *ta* means "mortal"; [3] *na* means "does not cease"; [4] *ga* means "of that which is pervaded"; [5] *kha* means "he wards off evil" (or *bha-ya* means "he crosses over evil"); [6] having made it small and consecrated it, and becoming one who goes swiftly to carry the oblation (*havis*), you are dear to us.
Likewise, like an ancient city, you are worn with age, an aged and venerable teacher; and like a king, you are delightful or worthy of being approached.
Furthermore, like a son, you are to be sought for refuge—you are to be protected and guarded by the sacrificers.
This is a metaphorical expression for the future.
Or rather, this is a qualification of the "son" (*sūnu*):
he goes by means of what is characterized by knowledge, austerity, and ritual action; thus it is *śrayāya*.
The suffix *āya* is an *auṇādika* suffix added to the root *yā*.
As in the word *spṛhayāyya*;
or else, *śrayayāyya* means one who has attained three births.
Three births are recorded in tradition: "The first birth is from the mother; the second is from the tying of the *mauñjī* [sacred grass girdle]."
"The third [birth] is from the initiation for sacrifice; thus three births are recorded" (Manu Smṛti 2.169).
Like such a son, you are *raṇva*, that is, delightful.

For by your power, O Agni, you have conquered in the wooden vessel like a prize-winning steed; like one who traverses all around, you are the self-sustaining master of the house, like a restless courser, a vigorous infant. 8. By your power, indeed, in the wooden vat, O Agni, you conquer like a prize-winning steed; like one who goes around, you are the self-dependent master of the home, like a restless courser, a youngling. 8.
O Agni, by your power (*kratvā*)—that is, by the act consisting of friction—you, who exist within the wooden vessel (*droṇe*), namely the fire-drill (*araṇyām*), are indeed manifested (*ajayase*).
Likewise, like a vigorous steed (*vājī na*) that is full of motion, you are active;
for *kṛti* is a name for action.
He is the performer of rites such as the carrying of oblations.
Just as he carries a person, so too the carrying of oblations constitutes the similarity between Agni and a chariot.
Likewise, like the wind that moves everywhere—just as one who goes about everywhere in the form of forest fires and the like—you are *svadhā*.
This is another name for it. You are food and you are *gaya*—that is, a house;
the meaning is that you are both.
Moreover, though you are but a child, a mere infant, you will move crookedly here and there like a noble steed—a horse of high breed that is difficult to control;
this is the form derived from the root *hvrī*, meaning "to be crooked."
In the Kārīrī sacrifice, "tvaṃ tyā" is the optional *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for the covering of the cart-pole.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Or [the verses] 'tvaṃ tyā cidacyutā' and 'dhāmante viśvaṃ bhuvanamadhiśritam'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.13).

O Agni, you [devour] even those things that are immovable, as a beast [devours] grass; for your imperishable power, O ageless one, rends the trees into shreds. 9. You—those very things—even the immovable, O Agni, like a beast in a pasture; for that which is your abode, O ageless one, the trees rend into shreds. 9.
O Agni, you [overcame] those very obstacles;
the word *cit* (even) has the same meaning as *api* (also) and is displaced in its position [in the verse].
They were *acyutā*, that is, immovable—indeed, impossible even to cause to tremble.
The word "exists" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like a beast let loose upon pasture," that is, like a beast upon grass.
Just as it consumes everything, so do you burn logs of wood and other materials in a mere moment; this is the meaning. O *ajara*, ageless Agni, *yat* means "of which."
The elision of the genitive case ending is by the rule "supāṃ suluk."

O Śikva, those who cut down, destroy, or consume your blazing domains (dhāma)—your splendors (tejāṃsi), which are desirable (vananīya) and worthy of being resorted to (saṃbhajanīya), namely the forests (araṇyāni)—you [should act] toward them; thus is the connection with the preceding.
The particle "ha" is for the purpose of completing the meter.
1. Kha-na-bha-ra: he who is to be praised;
2. Ta-ya-jase: for the sake of sacrifice;
3. Na-dhā-mā: the foundation.

For you, O Agni, go as the Hotṛ-priest into the home of the people who perform the sacrifice; bring prosperity to all, and enjoy the oblation, O Aṅgiras. For you, O Agni, go as the Hotṛ-priest into the home of the people who desire to undertake the sacrifice (adhvara); since you seek praise or the oblations, therefore, O Agni, protector of the people, make the sacrificers recipients of prosperity. And having done so, O Aṅgiras—O Agni endowed with the qualities of movement and so forth, or whose form is like a limb—enjoy our oblation.
O God, Agni, great as Mitra, speak for us to the gods; speak well of us to Heaven and Earth.
Grant us prosperity and a secure dwelling from heaven. May we overcome hostilities, distresses, and difficulties; may we cross over them, may we cross over by your protection.
O Agni, that sacrificer indeed dwells— he resides;
the meaning is that he shall live for a long time.
What kind of sacrificer is he?
He is a guardian of *ṛta*, the protector of the sacrifice; he is born of *ṛta*, having come into existence for the sake of the sacrifice.
And having dwelt there, desiring the gods for himself—that sacrificer—attains (*naśate*) the wide, expansive light known as the Sun.
O radiant Agni, you who are well-pleased with Mitra and Varuṇa—

where the nominative case is used in the sense of the instrumental— you protect (pāsi) that sacrificer from distress (aṃhas), that is, from sin, by means of the sacrifice (yajñasya), which is the instrument for performing the rite; such is the connection with the preceding verse.

He has sacrificed with sacrifices, he has labored with acts of service; he has given gifts to Agni, whose doors are prosperous. Even so, the favor of the glorious ones does not fail him; neither the curse nor the assault reaches him.

He has sacrificed with sacrifices; he has labored with ritual services. To him whose wealth prospers, O Agni, he has indeed offered gifts. Even so, the displeasure of the glorious ones does not reach that mortal, nor does distress, nor does destruction. 2.
The sacrificer who offers oblations to Agni—whose desirable wealth (*vara*) is abundant and prosperous—has sacrificed with all sacrifices;
likewise, through his ritual acts such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, he has become tranquil.
The meaning is that by means of the sacrifice to Agni, he obtains every fruit.
Moreover, the failure to obtain (*arjuṣṭi*) sons who are glorious among the glorious does not at all reach that sacrificer;
the meaning is that he certainly possesses sons.
Likewise, evil (*aṃhas*) does not reach that mortal man.
Likewise, he does not encounter that which is the cause of misfortune, namely harmful intent, nor does he encounter harm itself.
Whose appearance is like that of the sun, whose sight drives away the waters; when he approaches in his brilliance, his thoughts are terrifying.
Like a neighing steed, he is the winner of spoils at night; wherever he dwells, he is the joyous one born of the forest.

The sun—whose vision is stainless, whose appearance is terrifying as it moves toward the glowing one—is your thought; like booty from a neighing steed, he has come at the end of this night. Wherever he dwells, delightful in the forest, he is born of the woods.
The sight of that Agni is stainless, like the sun of the hero;
O Agni, as your flame, the sustainer, blazes forth,
it moves everywhere, being terrible and inspiring fear.
This Agni, who [is like] the *śurudhaḥ*— meaning the cows that restrain (*rudh*) sorrow (*śucaḥ*) accompanied by neighing (*heṣasvat*),
and [who is like] the night (*aktuḥ*); for *aktuḥ* is a name for night— and by that [name], a wanderer such as a *rākṣasa* is indicated therein.
The ellipsis implies that she gives herself to the *rākṣasa*s and others.

This very one, the "dwelling" (*vasati*), who serves as the abode for all, being "born in the forest" (*vanajā*)—that is, arising in the wilderness—is "delightful" (*raṇva*) in some place or other, such as a mountain peak.
Even his fierce form is great; with his mouth he devours like a horse controlled by the bit.
Stretching out his tongue like a boat, he consumes the wood like a swift runner, burning it up.
Even his fierce form is great; with his mouth he devours like a horse controlled by the reins. Stretching out his tongue like a joint, he, like a smelter, melts the wood as he consumes it. 4.
1. He destroys Kha, Jha, Na, Bha, and Ra. 2. He is the destroyer of the pride of Ta. 3. He is like Ya, the sun. 4. Kha, Gha, Bha, and Na are not for the sake of meaning.
Before this [word], *ema* refers to the path that serves as the means of going; it is *tigma*, sharp, because it is impossible to touch.
And its *varpha*, its form, *mahi*, great and abundant, *bhasat*, shines.
The verbal root *bhas* belongs to the meaning of "threatening" and "shining."
What kind of fire is it?
Like a horse (*aśva*), it is *yamānaḥ*—restraining or consuming grass and other fuel with its *āsā*, that is, its mouth;
likewise, it is like an axe (*paraśu*).
Just as an axe, casting its own edge upon wood, so too [the fire], licking its own tongue and casting its flame upon trees, shrubs, and the like,
burns— that is, consumes— the wood;
it is a *draviṇ*, a drainer, a maker of heaven.
Just as it melts gold and other such substances, so too does it melt the entire forest;
the meaning is that it reduces everything that has taken form to ashes.
He has indeed placed it here; he has sharpened his brilliance like the edge of a blade of iron.
He, whose splendor is variegated and radiant, has struck down the one who was difficult to overcome, as a swift arrow destroys its mark.

Like a bowstring being drawn back, let him take aim; sharpen your brilliance like the edge of an axe. He of wondrous splendor moves as a steward, swift-moving and leaping like a goat that is difficult to catch. || 5 ||
That fire, indeed, like an archer, having taken aim (*pratidhāya*), fixes its own flame;
that is to say, just as an archer fits an arrow toward a target, so too does he fix his flame.
And having aimed, being about to shoot—that is, about to cast forth the flame—he sharpens his own brilliance, making it keen.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"not the edge of iron.
Just as one who wishes to cast [an iron tool] sharpens the edge of an axe made of iron, so it is here.

Having sharpened [his brilliance], he shines with variegated splendor; he whose course is manifold, who is unassailable by day or night, who approaches like a bird, who is difficult to approach, who sits upon trees, and whose feet are capable of swift flight—being such as this, Agni exists; this is the connection with what precedes.
Like a bellowing bull, he clothes himself in rays; with his flame, the great friend roars.
He who is indeed the immortal one, red-hued by night and by day, who [protects] men by day.

He, like a singer, clothes himself in the rays of light; he, the great friend of Mitra, roars with his flame. He who is ruddy by night and ruddy by day, the immortal one, [protects] men—yea, the ruddy one by day, [protects] men. 6.
This Agni is like a singer worthy of praise; like the sun, he clothes himself in blazing flames.
Thus, as a friend providing light favorable to all, he roars intensely with his fiery luster.
He, this Agni, who at night is ruddy as he rises, impels men toward their respective duties as if by day.
Furthermore, the word *yat* (which) is a filler (*pūraka*).

Likewise, *amartyaḥ* means "immortal," possessing the nature of not dying; *aruṣaḥ* means "ascending" or "free from anger. That *agniḥ* (fire), by means of its shining (*divā*) splendor, impels the *nṛn*—the leaders or the rays—is to be connected with the preceding [sentence].
Or else:
This Agni, who at night (*naktaṃ*) during the evening (*rātrau*) mounts the rising dawn (*abhiruṣaḥ*), and who is the deathless fire that unites the gods—the leaders (*netṝn*)—with oblations;
the repetition of "the men" (*nṛn*) by day is for the sake of emphasis.
1. Of that which has gone; 2. casting away the *ta*;
3. the *jvālā* [flame] consisting of *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, *śa*, and *'*, does not exist.

Like the roar of heaven when it bestows gifts, his, the bull, the radiant one, has roared among the plants; like heat with its swift flight, he who goes with his path has joined the two worlds, the well-mated pair, with wealth in their home. 7. Like the roar of heaven when it bestows gifts, his, the bull, the radiant one, has roared among the plants; like heat with its swift flight, he who goes with his path has joined the two worlds, the well-mated pair, with wealth in their home. 7.
Like the roar of the blazing sun as it spreads its rays,
a great sound has issued forth from the front of this Agni.
This very point he explains:
The bull, the augmenter of desires, that blazing Agni, when the plants were being consumed, roared loudly;

he who moves about with a glowing, flickering, and radiant energy that is like a flame leaping here and there—he, Agni, subduing our enemies, fills the two worlds, Heaven and Earth, which possess excellent spouses, with wealth or treasure.

He who, with his supporting or yoked hymns, has shone forth like lightning with his own powers; or he who, like the *Ṛbhu*, fashioned the host of the Maruts—he, the fierce and impetuous one, has shone. With his supporting ones. Or. He. With yoked ones. Hymns. Like lightning. He has shone twice. With his own. Powers. Or. The host. Of the Maruts. He. Who. Fashioned. Like the *Ṛbhu*. Fierce. Impetuous. Has shone. 8.

Agni goes forth with his rays—which are like horses fit for bearing, like yoke-horses that are yoked by themselves, and like flames worthy of worship—and he shines like lightning with his own drying powers, his own splendors.
And he, like the host or the strength of the Maruts, fashions [all things], making them thin, sharpening everything;
that is to say, he dries it up.
Thus, like the sun, this one shines widely, brilliant and radiant; impetuous and displaying his speed, he flashes and illuminates.
The fourth hymn, beginning with “yathā hotaḥ,” consists of a Ṛc; it is the seer Bharadvāja’s composition, in the Triṣṭubh metre, and is dedicated to Agni.
It is introduced by the words “yathā hotaḥ.
Its application (viniyoga) has been prescribed for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āgnimāruta Śastra.

Just as I, O Hotṛ, son of strength, sacrifice with offerings at the divine assembly of man, so today, O Agni, desiring them, do thou sacrifice to the desiring gods for us equally and together in this common rite. Just as, O Hotṛ, at the divine assembly of man, I sacrifice with offerings, O son of strength—so now, O Agni, desiring them, sacrifice to the desiring gods for us equally and together in this common rite.

He is the one who brings the gods hither, the invoker of the gods, O Son of Strength, Son of Power; by whatever means or manner the mind of Manu—that is, of Prajāpati the sacrificer—is directed toward the *devatātā*, [meaning] the sacrifice (*yajña*);
at that sacrifice, in the *devatātā*, you shall sacrifice with sacrifices, that is, with the oblations which are the means for the sacrificer.

O Agni, desiring them yourself, sacrifice today at this sacrifice to our equals—the gods such as Indra who are like the sun—and to the gods who desire to be sacrificed, being yourself one who desires them; sacrifice quickly and equally.
Or else, "samana" refers to the sacrifice, for it is in this [sacrifice] that the gods are considered equal.
The word "in that" (tasmin) is to be supplied [to complete the sense].

May he, the radiant one, grant us sight; may he, who is worthy of praise, bestow wealth upon us as we strive for it. He who is the life of all, the immortal among mortals, the Jātavedas who has become our protector.

May he, Agni, shining far and wide like the eye from the dwelling, the worshipful ordainer, grant us delight—he who is all-enlivening, the immortal among mortals, who has become the guest brought near, Jātavedas. 2.

May that Agni—who is like the sun, the illuminator of the day, shining forth as the "Vibhāvā" (the one who shines pre-eminently), and the "Vedhas" (the one to be known or attained by all)—bestow upon us "vandāru" (praiseworthy) "canaḥ" (food); that is to say, may he grant it to us.

He who is Agni—possessing all life (*viśvāyuḥ*), complete in all limbs, or the cause of life for all; *amṛta*, deathless; *atithi*, the ever-moving guest for the purpose of carrying the oblation; *jātavedas*, the knower of all that is born, or the possessor of innate wealth—who, being such, has arisen among mortals, among human sacrificers, at the time of dawn (*upaḥ*) for the sake of the Agnihotra and other rites—he [is the one referred to]. This is the connection with what precedes.
Whose majesty the heavens admire, who clothes himself in splendors like the bright sun—
he, the purifier, ageless and far-reaching, has shattered even the ancient bonds of the serpent.

Whose formidable power the heavens do not surpass, who clothes himself in splendors like the bright sun—he, the ageless purifier, who sends forth his light. He takes heed even of the ancient deeds of the axle. 3.
"No," it is said; and it has been stated: "The word *sam* is used in the sense of comparison" (*Nirukta* 7.31).

"The heavens"—the illuminators—"of that Agni whose *abhvam* (great deed) they praise," that Agni, "like the sun"—as bright as the sun—is "bright" (*śukra*), meaning white in form; he "clothes himself" (*vaste*) in "food," that is, in light-rays and splendors.

And he who is "unaging" (*ajara*), devoid of old age, the "purifier" (*pāvaka*)—the fire capable of consuming everything—"pervades" (*vinoti*) all things with his light; he, moreover, "destroys" (*śikṣathat*) the "ancient" (*pūrvyāṇi*) "cities" (*purī*) of even the "formless" (*abhvasya*), such as Rākṣasas and others, whose nature is to pervade. The verbal root is *ṛth*, meaning "to injure."
For you have grown strong, O Son; by your very birth, Agni has established the race.
As such, bestowing vigor upon us, grant us strength, like a king dwelling among those who live in abundance.

For you have grown strong, O Son of Agni; here you have established your seat. By his very birth, Agni has made the path straight. As such, bestow strength upon us for the winning of vigor. Like a king who has conquered, you dwell within the two worlds.

1. *ta*—just so; 2. *ta*—he thinks; 3. *śa*—that which has arisen above from what was not; 4. *gha-śa*—white in color; 5. *ta-ya-ya*—he impels; 6. *śa-so*—this is Agni. O *sūno*, son of strength (*sahasaḥ*), or rather, [from the root] *pū* "to impel."
O Agni, you are indeed the impeller of all and worthy of praise. The latter quarter-verse is composed in the third person:
Agni, sitting (*asat*)—that is, settling—among the choice foods (*agrāsatsu*), the sacrificial offerings, for the purpose of accepting them, is by his very birth, by his nature, a path (*ajma*).
This is a name for the house;
he makes the house for the sacrificers.
O Agni, giver of strength—that is, of food—such as you are, bestow strength upon us. Give it to me.
Likewise, like a king, conquer our enemies.
For all these purposes, dwell—that is, reside—within (*antaḥ*), in the middle of our own house, which is free from wolves and other such harmful beings.
He who, like Vāyu, does not abandon his kingdom during the nights, even when he is oppressed by Varuṇa’s power—
he who has overcome the sight of the fourth [state], who is not cast down, and who is offered as a libation from that which falls.
He who eats the food of Varuṇa—may Vāyu not go toward him; he eats the nights. O Puruhūta, he who pierces your fourfold commands with his arrows shall fall like one sacrificed. 5.
That Agni who sharpens—that is, polishes and makes keen—his own brilliance, which wards off the obstructing darkness;
and who eats—that is, consumes—the food consisting of oblations offered by the sacrificers. (The verbal root *tija* means "to sharpen.")
And thus it is heard in scripture: “Agni, indeed, is the eater of food and the lord of food” (AiB 1.8). That Agni is “Vāyu,” that is, like Vāyu; he is the “Rāṣṭrī.
This is a name for the Lord.
*Rāṣṭra* means a kingdom; one who possesses that is *rāṣṭrin*.
Just as Vāyu, by his own majesty, rules over everything, so too is he.
The meaning is that he is the Lord of all.
Being such, he "passes through" (atyeti) the "nights" (aktūn);
the meaning is that he overcomes the darkness of night.
And by your grace, may we overcome him—that person who is hostile (*arāti*) toward you, toward the oblations being offered and presented to you.
[The lengthening of the vowel is Vedic.
Or alternatively: [the text continues].
We point you toward the enemies, those who do not give wealth;
we shall strike down that person who is hostile to us as we declare the names of our detractors.
And you, O swift-moving one, [be our protector] against him.
Like a noble horse when urged on, become the slayer of the attacking enemies who fall upon you from the front, having singled them out one by one.
This is the form of the root *hṛ* in the sense of harming.
Like the sun with its radiant beams, you have overspread both heaven and earth with your light;
brilliant and anointed with splendor, he has led us beyond the darkness, bursting forth like the son of Uśij with his flame.

Like the sun with its radiant rays, O Agni, you have spread across both worlds with your light. Brilliant and anointed with splendor, he leads us beyond the darkness; like the son of Uśij, he rends the gloom with his flame.

O Agni, you have spread out and specially overspread the two worlds, Heaven and Earth, with your radiance—that is, with your light. Therein lies the illustration: like Sūrya with his brilliant, powerful, and worshipful rays (arka). Just as Sūrya spreads them out, so do you. The second half-verse is composed in the third person: *panman*. That in which one moves is the supreme path (*parama*). In that [path], [you act] like Auśija; for the Uśijas—

1. By that very nature. 2. O you who possess power (*ūrjasan*)! 3. You dwell in *gha*, *ga*, and *śa*; you protect (*nivarmāsi*); you are the dwelling place (*nivāsa*). 4. You rule over all (*sarvam īṣṭe*) in *kha*, *jha*, *bha*, and *ra*; you rule over all in *gha*, *ta*, and *śa*. 5. [You rule] over the givers (*dātṛn*) in *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, *ya*, and *ra*. 6. From the other than the one who harms (*hisaka*), [you protect]; from those who harm (*hisakān*) who fall upon us (*patataḥ*), or who attack (*abhipatataḥ*).
The praisers (*stotāraḥ*) are those who praise most excellently. Those connected to him are the *Uśijas* and Sūrya.

Like him, Agni—who is devoted by his flame and splendor, who is well-instructed, and for that very reason wonderful and worthy of admiration—drives away, that is, he leads around and causes to recede from every direction, the nocturnal darknesses, the thick glooms of night.
This is the meaning: he turns them back from every quarter of the compass.
For we choose you, the most delightful one, with our hymns; may you hear our great prayer.
Like Indra, no deity equals you in might; the most heroic men satisfy you with their bounty.

For we choose you, the most resonant one, with the flames of our hymns; hear us greatly, O Agni! No deity fills you with power as Indra does, nor do the most heroic men fill you with bounty like Vāyu. 7.

O Agni, we choose you, the most delightful one, who are joined with hymns of praise—those worthy of worship, worthy of adoration, and consisting of radiant flames. Or rather, we honor you by means of hymns of praise that are worthy of worship, praiseworthy, and composed of light; therefore, hear our great hymn.
O Agni, the most heroic among men, the best leaders of hymns, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*),

with their vigor and strength, satisfy you— the one who goes to Vāyu, or rather, the one endowed with vigor like Vāyu— with wealth characterized by oblations, just as they satisfy Indra, the divine self among the gods.
From the word *devatā*, there is elision (*luk*) of the second case ending by the rule “*supāṃ suluk*.”

Now, O Agni, do thou lead us safely by paths free from enemies to the ways of wealth; grant those blessings to our patrons and to the singer. May we rejoice for a hundred winters, blessed with heroic sons.

Now, O Agni, with thy safe paths, lead us toward wealth; O Lord of the Earth, grant those blessings to our patrons and to the singer. May we rejoice for a hundred winters, blessed with heroic sons. 8.
O Agni, lead us by paths free from thieves and robbers; swiftly bring us to wealth and prosperity with well-being and security;
and deliver us from distress and sin.

Fulfill us with those paths characterized by longing, which are well-known and should be granted by you to the wise who offer praise. Grant me, who am singing and praising, those very blessings—those joys and comforts.
And may we, possessing heroic sons, live for a hundred winters—that is, for a hundred years. "Vīrāḥ" refers to sons and others who are born through heroic power.
Being endowed with excellent sons, grandsons, and so forth, may we rejoice and be filled with delight.
The fifth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with “huve vaḥ,” is the ṛṣi Bharadvāja’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is dedicated to Agni.
Thus it is enumerated: “huve vaḥ sasa. It is employed in the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra.

1. *kha-bha-ya-aktaḥ* is *siktaḥ*. 2. *ta-athavā*. 3. *ta-valayuktam*. 4. *ta-sumnāni tā tāni* does not exist [in this version]. 5. *ta-śobhanaputrādisahitāḥ*. 6. *kha-jha-ta-na-bha-ya-ra-madema modema*. 7. *gha-hṛṣyema*; *ta-hṛṣyāmaḥ*.

I invoke for you the Son of Strength, the youthful one, whose speech is free from malice, who is most active when approached with prayers; he, the wise one, who bestows all desirable riches—he who is rich in boons and bountiful. I invoke for you the Son of Strength, the youthful one, whose speech is free from malice, who is most active when approached with prayers; he, the wise one, who bestows all desirable riches—he who is rich in boons and bountiful.
O Agni, [we call upon] you with protection;
the plural number is used by way of grammatical transposition (vyatyaya). We [call upon] you with *matibhiḥ*—that is, with hymns worthy of contemplation (*mananīya*).
"I invoke; how [do I invoke him]?
As the son, the offspring, of Sahas, of strength."
For fire is born when churned with force.

[He is] "young," meaning eternally fresh, or one who mixes the fruit [of the sacrifice]; "one whose speech is not injurious"—that is, such a person in whom excellent, praise-worthy speech is employed that ought not to be harmed.

The youngest (*yaviṣṭham*), meaning exceedingly youthful; the most wise (*pracetāḥ*), meaning possessed of excellent knowledge; the one with many boons (*puruvāraḥ*), meaning desired and honored by many; the non-deceitful (*adruk*) toward the sacrificers—such is Agni, who impels (*invati*) all desirable (*viśvavārāṇi*), much-longed-for, and praiseworthy riches (*draviṇāni*) [toward the worshippers]. That is to say, he bestows them upon those who offer praise.
The connection with the preceding phrase is "I invoke you."

In you, O many-faced Hotṛ, the worshipful ones have brought their treasures at evening and at dawn; in you, the purifier, they have gathered all blessings, as all beings rest upon the earth. tve iti | vastūni | puru'anīka | hotaḥ | doṣaḥ | vastoḥ | ā | īrire | yajñiyāsaḥ | kṣāma'iva | viśvā | bhuvanāni | yasmin | sam | saubhagāni | dadhire | pāvake || 2 ||

O Agni, you of unprecedented form and many flames, at your invocation by the gods, both by night (*idāpā*) and by day (*vastoḥ*), the worshipful sacrificers (*yajñiyāsaḥ*), worthy of sacrifice, have offered (*erire*) and presented before you the sacrificial substances (*vastūni*) characterized as oblations.
This is the meaning: they offer them.

In that purifying fire (*pāvake*), like the earth (*kṣāmāiva*), all beings (*viśvā bhuvanāni*)—all created things—have together established (*saṃ dadhire*) their fortunes (*saubhagāni*) and riches; the gods have properly deposited them therein.
"In the fire they deposited the desirable wealth" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.1.1); such is the Brāhmaṇa. "In that he praises" is to be connected with what precedes.

From of old, you have sat upon these [fires]; by your power, you have become the charioteer of desirable things. From there, O wise Jātavedas, you bestow riches in succession upon the one who serves you. tvaṃ viśva pradivaḥ sīda āsu | ṛtvā rathīr abhavo vāryāṇām | ata inoṣi vidhate cikitvo vyānuṣag jātavedo vastūni || 3 || You have sat upon these from all eternity; by your power, you became the charioteer of desirable things. From there, O wise Jātavedas, you bestow riches in succession upon the one who serves you.
O Agni,
from of old—
you have sat down, you are seated, among these ancient lineages and among all these visible creatures of the primordial time.
You exist as the Vaiśvānara self;
likewise, by your own action (*ṛtva*), you are the non-injurer of those who are worthy of being chosen (*avāryāṇām varaṇīyānām*).
2. From that, towards [it]. 3. Its own nature. Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa.
Ṛgveda 3.3.

You have become the charioteer of riches, the impeller who brings them to the sacrificers. For this reason, O wise Jātavedas, Agni, knower of all living beings, you bestow treasures upon the worshipper who serves you; you send forth various riches continuously and in an unceasing stream.
In the Pravargya rite, the verse "yo naḥ sanuṣyaḥ" is prescribed;
and it is stated in the Sūtra: "The verses 'yo naḥ sanuṣyo abhidāsat', 'agne bhava no agne sumanāḥ', and 'upetau' are prescribed" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.6).

O Agni, whoever from afar seeks to harm us, or whoever from nearby would act as an enemy, O you who are great as a friend—burn him with your own ageless, bull-like flames; most fiercely burning, burn him with your heat as one possessed of power.

O Agni, whoever attacks us from afar, or whoever, being close at hand, seeks to harm us, O thou who art great as Mitra—burn him with thy own ageless, bull-like flames; O most scorching one, burn him with thy heat, for thou art full of fervor. 4.
O Agni, whatever enemy, being hidden— *sanutyaḥ* is a name for that which is concealed— dwells in a remote place and seeks to consume us, oppresses, or harms us; [may he be overcome].

And he who, being *antaraḥ* (an insider), O *mitramahaḥ* (O Agni of friendly luster, or O Agni who magnifies friends), would *vanuṣyāt* (seek to harm)—burn him, O *tapiṣṭha* (most heating) Agni, with your *tapas* (heat/energy), you who are *tapasvān* (full of energy), by means of your own, inherent, and unique *ajaraibhiḥ* (undecaying) *vṛṣabhaiḥ* (bulls/rain-showering causes of rain). Burn him with your heat!
O Son of Strength, that mortal who honors you with sacrifice, with fuel, and with hymns— O Immortal One, he, the wise among mortals, shines forth with wealth, splendor, and renown.
He who, O Son of Greatness, has worshipped you with sacrifice, with fuel, with hymns, and with songs—he, the wise one among mortals, O Immortal, shines forth with wealth, splendor, and renown. 5.
O Son of Strength, for him— the sacrificer who serves you with sacrifice,
and who [serves] with fuel, that is, with the means of kindling— [you are present].

And he who serves with *ukthas*—the ritual recitations—and with *arkas*—praiseworthy hymns of praise—he, O immortal Agni, free from the law of death, that sacrificer, being possessed of superior knowledge (*pracetāḥ*) among mortals, shines forth preeminently with wealth, with splendor, with fame, and with renown.
O Agni, perform that deed for us; as one who is powerful, overcome our adversaries with your might.
Since you are praised with words radiant through the days, enjoy this; grant the prayer of the singer.

Do that, O Agni, being impelled; overcome the rivals swiftly with your power, O powerful one! When you are addressed with words by the people, enjoy that which is worthy of praise; let the singer's prayer resound. 6.
1. Devoid of known [obstacles].
2. By means of those things that have become the causes for known rain.
O Agni, being thus impelled and sent forth, do you quickly perform that; do it!
To the question "What is that?", he says:
O powerful one, you who possess strength, overcome and destroy with force—the *spṛdhaḥ*, those who are contending—by means of your power capable of subduing others, or by your splendor;
with *dyubhiḥ*, with shining lights or splendors; and with *abhiḥ*, with words in the form of hymns, you are praised (*yacchaṃsi*) when you are lauded.
The meaning is: that hymn which is composed by the praisers with you in view—that hymn of the singer, which is to be proclaimed, I consider worthy of my mind; please accept and enjoy it.

For the offering of a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kāma, the verse beginning with "aśyāma" is the *yājyā*. This is also stated in the Sūtra: "With 'aśyāma taṃ kāmamagne tavotī' for Kāma" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.10).

May we obtain that desire, O Agni, through your protection; may we obtain wealth, O Wealthy One, consisting of excellent heroes. May we obtain strength, seeking strength; may we obtain your undecaying and ageless glory. 7. May we obtain. That. Desire. O Agni. Through your. Protection. May we obtain. Wealth. O Wealthy One. Consisting of excellent heroes. May we obtain. Strength. Toward. Seeking strength. May we obtain. Glory. O Undecaying One. Ageless. Your. 7.
O Agni, through your *ūti*—that is, through your protection—may we attain (*aśyāma*) that desire.
He explains that very desire:
O *rayivaḥ*, O Agni rich in wealth, may we attain (*aśyāma*) wealth (*rayi*) consisting of excellent sons and other blessings.
Likewise, seeking booty (*vāja*)—desiring booty from you—may we obtain and attain the booty given by you, facing toward it directly.
O ageless (*ajara*) Agni, free from decay, may we obtain and attain your own ageless, undecaying, radiant glory (*dyumna*).
The sixth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with “pra navyasā,” is the seer Bharadvāja’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and is dedicated to Agni.
It is listed under the heading “pra navyasā.
Its application (viniyoga) has been stated for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina Śastra.

Seeking a path and protection through sacrifice with a new [hymn], he goes toward the Son of Strength; he approaches the divine Hotṛ, who rends the forest, whose path is black, who is radiant, and who comes for the feast. With a new [hymn], seeking a path and protection through sacrifice, he goes toward the Son of Strength; rending the forest, [he approaches] the one of black path, the radiant one—the divine Hotṛ—for the feast. He goes toward him. 1.

Desiring *gātu*—whether meaning that which is to be approached, praised, or the protection of food—the worshipper, seeking aid from Agni, the son of strength (*sahasaḥ sūnum*), proceeds with a newer, more recent sacrifice; being thus prepared, he goes forth toward him with intensity.
What kind of Agni?

One by whom the forest is shattered—that is, cut down or consumed by fire—one whose path is black, whose track is dark, who is radiant and white-hued, the invoker (*hotā*) and sacrificer (*yaṣṭā*), divine, existing in heaven, who is to be sought through the desirable sacrifice (*vītī*).

1. O Knower, you overcome others. 2. O Knower, you are praised. 3. O Knower, with your newness, you are ever-renewing (or, for the one who is most youthful). 4. *Gha*-suffix: *nirddhadham*; *Śa*-suffix: *yuktaṃ nirddhadham*.

O Most Youthful One, dwelling in the luminous realm, roar aloud with your unaging, thundering [flames] toward those who have taken refuge in you—You, the Purifier, who, being most abundant, go forth toward many broad [spaces], increasing in power.

He, the youngest, the purifier, who is most abundant, Agni, as he goes along, follows those who have taken refuge [in him], who are spread out, who dwell in the luminous realm, with his unaging, thundering [flames]—he who is most extensive, following after many broad [spaces] as he manifests himself. 2.
That fire, shining white, exists with a white color. It is the *tanyatu*, the producer of sound, situated in the *rocana*.
The *rocana* is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), so called because the planets, stars, and other celestial bodies shine within it.
Stationed there, joined with flames that are ageless—meaning devoid of decay—and roaring exceedingly, making a great sound; or [joined] with reins, he is the most youthful (*yaviṣṭha*).

That purifying fire (*pāvaka*), being most abundant (*purutama*) and exceedingly copious, as it consumes many (*purūṇi*) broad (*pṛthūni*) and massive logs, follows after them, pursuing them; such is its manner of proceeding—this is the connection with what precedes.
If there is mutual contact between the Gārhapatya and other fires, an oblation must be performed for Agni Vivici;
in that rite, "vi te" is the invitatory verse (anuvākyā). (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.13)
Thy flames, O pure Agni, impelled by the wind and spreading in all directions, move along, pure themselves;
they, the fiercely devouring, divine, and newly born, boldly strike down and shatter the forests.
O Agni, your flames, impelled by the wind, all-pervading, pure and bright, move forth; they, the divine ones with many eyes, the Navagvas, boldly strike down the forests as they break them apart. 3.
O pure, purified, or radiant Agni, your flames—impelled by the wind, bright and stainless—move forth in every direction, spreading everywhere.
Touching many pieces of wood, those divine rays, belonging to the shining fire in heaven and possessing a new course, consume the forests;
that is, they burn them.
What were they doing?
Breaking through the forests with bold, defiant energy, they were shattering them.
Those bright, pure, and radiant steeds of yours, O Radiant One, who, when let loose, shave the earth; then, having been loosened, he shines widely, moving across the ridges of the speckled earth.

Those bright, pure, and radiant ones who, like horses with loosened manes, shave the earth; then the glowing one shines forth widely over the ridges of the speckled mountain, driving away the darkness.

O you who are radiant, O shining one: those pure and beautiful flames of yours which are bright and blazing shave the earth—the ground—meaning they burn the herbs and trees that stand in place of hair. "Agni gives the hair of the earth."

1. *tan-bhavan* is the vessel (*bhājana*). 2. It is not a *anuvākyā*. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "vi te viśvagvātajūtāso agne tvāmame mānuṣīrīḻate viśaḥ" (RV 1.65.4). 3. Regarding *kha-jha-bha-ya-vanā vanāni*, there is another Vedic citation (*nigama*):
"te raśmayo vibhītāsaḥ vimuktā aśvā iva itastato gacchanti" (the remaining sense is that those rays, having been released, go here and there like horses).

Now at this time, your whirling mass of flames, moving about upon the back—that is, above—the earth of various forms, reaching toward the high ridges such as mountain peaks, and spreading its own food, shines forth extensively and preeminently over the wide expanse.
The tongue of the bull, fighting for cattle, falls like a released thunderbolt;
like the destruction of a hero rushing forth, the terrible, difficult-to-restrain [flame] consumes the forests.

Halfway, the tongue falls forward; like the thunderbolt released by a bull fighting for cattle, like the consuming fury of a hero in his onset, the terrible Agni, difficult to approach, devours the forests. 5.
Moreover, the tongue—the flame—of the showering Agni flies forth repeatedly with great force;
therein lies the comparison: it is like a thunderbolt being hurled by one who fights for cattle.

When the cattle had been carried off by the Asuras, Indra, fighting for the recovery of the cattle (*goṣuyud*), was like a thunderbolt being hurled, as if utterly consuming them. Likewise, just as the binding of a hero— a man endowed with valor— is difficult for others to withstand when he is engaged in combat, so too the *kṣāti*, the flame, of Agni is impossible to endure.
The term *kṣiti* is derived from the root *kṣi* (to perish) with the suffix *ktin* in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), meaning "that in which herbs and trees are destroyed and consumed."
Moreover, the formidable and terrifying fire, difficult to restrain and impossible for others to check, consumes—that is, burns—the forests;
for here the root *day* signifies "to burn."
With your light, O great one, you have boldly stretched out the terrestrial expanses at your rising;
with your powers, drive away fears, and being a conqueror, burn up the rivals who seek to overcome us.

With your radiance, you have boldly spread out the earthly expanses of the great impeller. Drive away our fears with your powers; as one who conquers, burn down the rivals and those who seek to harm us.
O Agni, with your radiance, shine upon the earthly things—that is, those existing on the earth—and [overcome] the *jyāṃsi*, which are actions whose function is movement.

You have spread out and covered the places to be traversed along with the great, bold, and impelling ray of light. As such, drive away all that is terrifying. Thus, with your conquering powers—your forces or splendors capable of overcoming—strike down those who challenge you, harming those who seek to harm.
"śatrūn iti | ni jūrva nijahi | the root jūrvi means 'to kill'."
In the *ukhāsaṃbharaṇīya* sacrifice, the verse beginning with “sa citra” is the *yājyā* for Agni Kṣatravat.
It is also stated in the Sūtra: “‘sa citra citraṃ citayanta asme abhīraśe bṛhataḥ kṣatriyasya’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.1).
O Citra, making us perceive that wondrous thing— O you of wondrous dominion, bestower of most wondrous vital strength—
bestow upon the singer, with your radiant rays, splendid wealth that is vast, full of heroes, and resplendent.

He—wondrous, most wondrous, making us conscious, O Lord of wondrous dominion, the most wonderful bestower of vital strength, the bright, vast wealth consisting of many heroes—bestow upon the singer that bright wealth with your bright rays. 7.

O *citra*, wondrous one; O *citrakṣatra*, you of marvelous power or wondrous wealth; O *candra*, gladdening one—such as you are, bestow upon the singer who praises you with gladdening hymns. (There is an irregularity in the verbal form. For those who praise us, O *rathi*, separate out and grant us wealth.
What kind of wealth?
"Wonderful" (citra), meaning worthy of being admired (cāyanīya) and making known (citayanta);
for by means of wealth, a person is made manifest.

The meaning is: "Grant us such wealth as is most wonderful (*citratama*), exceedingly marvelous; a bestower of vitality (*vayodhām*), that is, a giver of food; radiant (*candram*), which brings delight; possessed of many heroes (*puruvīram*), joined with numerous heroic sons, grandsons, and so forth; and great (*bṛhantam*)."
The seventh hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with “mūrdhānam,” is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Bharadvāja; its deity is Vaiśvānara.
The sixth and seventh verses are Jagatī meters, while the remaining five are Triṣṭubh meters.
Thus it has been cataloged: “mūrdhānam [is] dedicated to Vaiśvānara, ending with two Jagatīs.”
The application of the hymns (*sūkta-viniyoga*) has been concluded.
At the Viṣuvat day, the first triplet of the *Ābhimāruta* hymn is optionally the *stotriya*.
Accordingly, it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘The head of heaven, the messenger of earth,’ or ‘The head of heaven, the navel of earth, Agni’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.6).
The gods generated Vaiśvānara Agni— the head of heaven, the steward of earth,
the sage, the sovereign, and the guest of men— as a vessel placed within their mouths.
The head of heaven, the messenger of earth, Vaiśvānara born through the *ṛta*, Agni the seer, the sovereign king, the guest of men—the gods have generated him as a vessel for their mouths. 1.

The gods—the worshippers or the deities themselves—have generated (produced) Vaiśvānara, who is endowed with such qualities, by means of the sacrifice, bringing him forth from the two kindling woods (*araṇī*). He is the *mūrdhānam* (head), having become the head; of what? Of *divaḥ* (heaven), the celestial world, and of *pṛthivyāḥ* (earth), the celebrated ground. He is the *aratim* (attainer), the one who goes toward them. Or rather, he is the one to be attained, the Lord (*svāmin*), Vaiśvānara, who belongs to all men (*viśveṣāṃ narāṇām*). [He is] *ṛte*: *ṛta* is a name for truth or for sacrifice; this [word] is used here as an instrumental of cause. For the sake of *ṛta*, he was born (*ā-jātam*) facing toward us, produced at the beginning of creation. He is the *kavim* (seer), one of far-reaching vision; the *samrājam* (universal ruler), shining perfectly; the *atithim* (guest) of *janānām* (people), the sacrificers, constantly going to carry the oblations—or rather, one worthy of being honored as a guest. He is *āsani* (in the mouth)—the locative case used in the sense of the accusative—meaning "become the mouth. For the gods consume the oblations through the mouth characterized by Agni. He is the *pātram* (protector), the drinker, the guardian; or rather, the sustainer by means of his mouth. Thus distinguished by these qualities, the gods have generated Vaiśvānara. They brought him forth by facing toward the sacrifice, producing him from the two kindling woods.
The gods have brought together Vaiśvānara, the navel of sacrifices, the seat of riches, the great receptacle; they have generated him, the charioteer of the rites, the banner of the sacrifice.
The navel of sacrifices, the seat of riches, a great vessel for libations—the gods have brought together Vaiśvānara, the charioteer of rites, and have generated him as the banner of sacrifice. 2.
The navel—the binding center—of sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and other rituals; likewise, the seat, the single abode of riches (wealth); the great one;
and the *āhāva* (the place where oblations are summoned). Such [is he].
Alternatively:
1. In the manuscripts kha, gha, jha, bha, ya, ra, the phrase "yadvā... pūjyam" is absent.
2. [The root] *jan* takes the prefix *ā*.
This pouring forth of streams of water is like a watering place;
thus the singers praise him from all sides, they praise him perfectly.
Likewise, they praise Vaiśvānara, who belongs to all men (viśveṣāṃ narāṇām), the lord of the rites (adhvarāṇām), the charioteer (rathyam) of sacrifices.

Just as a charioteer leads his own chariot, so too do the gods—the singers or the officiating priests, or indeed the gods themselves—generate, that is, produce by friction, such a one as this: the one who makes known, the one who causes others to understand, the one who makes the sacrifice known, and the banner of wisdom.
From you, O Agni, is born the vigorous steed; from you come the heroes who overcome the enemy.
O Vaiśvānara, O King, bestow upon us desirable riches.
From you, O Agni, is born the inspired singer, the vigorous one; from you come the heroes who overcome the enemy. O Vaiśvānara, O King, bestow upon us desirable riches. 3.
From you, O Vājī—the one possessing the sacrificial oblation (*havis*)—the wise man (*vipra*) is born;
through the offering of oblations to you, one becomes wise.
Likewise, from you are born heroic men (*vīrāsaḥ*), conquerors of adversaries (*abhimātiṣāhaḥ*), who overcome their enemies.
Since this is so, therefore, O Vaiśvānara, O shining Agni, bestow—that is, place within us—those desirable riches among us who offer proper hymns of praise.
O Immortal One, all the gods sing together in praise of you as you are born, like unto an infant;
through your cosmic seasons, O Vaiśvānara, you have attained immortality when you shone forth from your two parents.

O Immortal Vaiśvānara, as you were being born, all the gods celebrated you together like a newborn infant; through your seasonal rites they attained immortality when you shone forth from your two parents. 4.

O Agni, you who are immortal and free from the nature of death, all the gods— the singers— celebrate you as you are being born, emerging from the two kindling woods, just as they would their own young son;
or rather, the "gods" (devāḥ) are the rays, so called because they shine.

All these beings sing out toward you as you are being born; they gather around you just as fathers approach their son. Moreover, O Vaiśvānara Agni, when you shine forth—that is, when you blaze in the midst of the two parents, heaven and earth—then by means of your most delightful seasons (ṛtubhiḥ), that is, by your sacrificial acts such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and others, the sacrificers attain immortality or the state of divinity.
O Vaiśvānara Agni, no one has ever dared to violate those great ordinances of yours,
when, being born in the lap of your parents, you found the banner of light in the sacred ways.
O Vaiśvānara Agni, those great ordinances of yours—no one has ever dared to violate them—when, being born in the lap of your parents, you discovered the banner of light in the appointed places. 5.
1. The connection of *gha*, *jña*, *ta*, *na*, *śa*, and *yajña*.
2. The one who has abandoned *jña* and *ta*.
3. O Fire, free from *ya* and death (*maraṇa*).

4. They do not cling [to others]; they cling to thee and praise thee. O Vaiśvānara, Agni who art related to all men (viśveṣāṃ narāṇām), no one else dares to oppose or obstruct those well-known, great deeds (vrata) of thine. When, being born in the lap of thy parents, Heaven and Earth, or in the intermediate space (upastha), upon the paths to be traversed by Vāyu, thou didst find—the indicator (ketu) of days, the Sun—which had been obscured by Svarbhānu.
The meaning is: "restraining by your own splendor the demon whose form is darkness, establish him.
In that case, the connection with the preceding words is "those vows."

By the vision of Vaiśvānara and by the signal of the immortal, the summits of heaven have been measured out. Upon his head, indeed, all beings have grown like branches; seven streams have sprouted forth.

By the eye of Vaiśvānara, by the signal of immortality, the ridges of heaven have been measured out. Upon his very head, indeed, all beings have grown like branches; seven spreading shoots have risen upward.
The eighth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "vaiśvānarasya viśvāpṛkṣasya," is the seer Bharadvāja's composition; its deity is Vaiśvānara.
Of these, the first six are Jagatī meters and the seventh is Triṣṭubh.
And thus it has been listed in the Anukramaṇī: "The last [verse] of the hymn beginning with *pṛkṣasya* is a Triṣṭubh.
On the twenty-fourth day, during the Ābhimāruta litany, this hymn serves as the insertion for Vaiśvānara.
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "*pṛkṣasya vṛṣṇo vṛṣṇe śardhāya*" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.4).
In the *ābhiplavika* [rite], on the fifth day of both the *pṛṣṭhya* and *ābhiplava* six-day periods, this very hymn serves as the *vaiśvānara-nivid-dhāna*.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "The *ābhimāruta* [laud] is 'pṛkṣasya vṛṣṇo', 'vṛṣṇe śardhāya', and 'n citsahojāḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.7).
At the *viṣuvat*, the first two triplets of the *ābhimāruta* are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Stotriya and Anurūpa [verses] are 'pṛkṣasya vṛṣṇo aruṣasya nū sahaḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.6).

Now indeed shall I proclaim the power of the nourishing, virile, ruddy one; the sacrificial assemblies of Jātavedas. For Vaiśvānara, a newer, pure hymn flows forth like Soma—beautiful for Agni. Of the nourishing, virile, ruddy one; now; his power; forth; now; I shall proclaim; the sacrificial assemblies; of Jātavedas; for Vaiśvānara; a thought; newer; pure; like Soma; it flows; beautiful; for Agni.
Of the *vpṛkṣa*, that which is thoroughly mixed (*saṃvṛkta*) and pervasive (*vyāpta*);
or alternatively,
*pukṣa* refers to food characterized by the oblation (*havis*).

I shall quickly proclaim—that is, I praise with excellence—the power (*sahas*) of that *Vṛṣan* (the showerer), who rains down desires; of *Varuṇa*, who is ascending; of *Jātavedas*, the knower of all that is born; and of *Vaiśvānara*. I proclaim it at the *vidatha*, that is, at the sacrifice. (Note: The term *taddhataḥ* is interpreted as *tam hataḥ* [of him, the smiter], though the provided text suggests *taddhataḥ* may be a corruption or specific reading for *tasya hataḥ* [of his smiting] or *tasya dhātaḥ* [of its bestower]. Here, the translation follows the sense of the deity's attributes as described in the subsequent nouns.)
The single word *anu* is a filler (*pūraka*). A newer, more recent, pure, and stainless— or rather,
a purifier of the worshippers— beautiful and excellent *mati*, that is, a hymn worthy of reflection, flows toward this Vaiśvānara, the foremost one.
It flows from my manifestation;
the meaning is that it issues forth by itself.
It is indeed like Soma.
Just as Soma flows from the ten-strand filter, so it is in that case.

Being born in the highest heaven, Agni, the guardian of vows, protected the sacred ordinances. With his excellent wisdom, Vaiśvānara measured out the mid-air; in his greatness, he touched the firmament. He, being born in the highest heaven, Agni, the guardian of vows, protected the sacred ordinances. He, of excellent wisdom, measured out the mid-air; Vaiśvānara, in his greatness, touched the firmament.

Vaiśvānara, indeed, is Agni, the protector of vows (*vrata-pā*), the guardian of sacred observances. Being born in the supreme, most excellent sky—the expanse of the atmosphere—in the form of the Sun, he protects the vows, that is, both worldly and Vedic actions. And he measured out the intermediate space; by this it is implied that he created the worlds characterized by that space.

Likewise, Agni Vaiśvānara, of beautiful rites and excellent action, touched—the word *spṛśat* meaning he indeed touched—*nākam*, the heavenly world, by his own greatness, that is, by his majesty and splendor.

1. *Ta-ādyāḥ* (The hymns beginning with "ta"): He, the wondrous Mitra, propped apart the two worlds; he brought light within and dispelled the darkness. Like two skins, he spread out the two bowls of heaven and earth; Vaiśvānara assumed all manly vigor. *vi astambhāt rodasī mitraḥ adbhutaḥ antaḥ āvat akṛṇot jyotiṣā tamaḥ vi carmaṇīva dhiṣaṇe avartayat vaiśvānaraḥ viśvam adhatta vṛṣṇyam* || 3 || He, the wondrous Mitra, propped apart the two worlds; he brought light within and dispelled the darkness. Like two skins, he spread out the two bowls of heaven and earth; Vaiśvānara assumed all manly vigor.
The friend, who has become a friend to all, the wonderful and great Vaiśvānara fire, specially propped up the two worlds, heaven and earth—
meaning he established them in their respective places so that they would not fall.
Likewise, by means of his light and splendor, he made the darkness hidden and concealed within.
*vāvaditi* is a form of the root *vāti*, meaning "to go," from which the suffix has been elided.

Furthermore, *dhiṣaṇe* refers to the two supporters, heaven and earth; just as a butcher spreads out two skins for the purpose of drying after slaughtering an animal, so did he *vy avartayat*—he made them open and wide apart.
What more need be said? This *Vaiśvānara* Agni *adhatta*—that is, he placed, or maintains—*viśvam vṛṣṇyam*, all heroic power.

In the lap of the waters, the mighty ones seized him; the subjects approached the King who was worthy of being approached. As a messenger, Mātariśvan brought Agni Vaiśvānara from the far distance for the sake of the threefold light. apām upasthe mahiṣā agṛbhṇata | the mighty ones seized him in the lap of the waters. viśo rājānam upa tasthur gamiyam | the subjects approached the King who was worthy of being approached. ā dūto agnim abharat trisvataḥ | as a messenger, [Mātariśvan] brought Agni from the threefold light. vaiśvānaram mātariśvā parāvataḥ | Mātariśvan [brought] Vaiśvānara from the far distance.
"Āpas" is a name for the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). "In the lap," that is, in the place of rest, in the midst of the waters—that is, of the intermediate space—"the buffaloes":
this is a term for the great ones.
The great Maruts seized him;
they grasped this Vaiśvānara who exists as the soul of all people, for the purpose of establishing him.
And having seized him, the subjects—the progeny—stood near their king, their master, and praised him as one worthy of worship.

Moreover, the swift messenger—the messenger of the gods, or Mātariśvan, the wind—brought this Vaiśvānara Agni from afar, from the distant region of Vivasvat, the Āditya; he brought him back to this world.

In age after age, O Agni, bestow upon those who praise you a wealth that is worthy of the assembly, glorious, and ever-new. Like a king with his foot, O imperishable one, strike down the reviler; crush him low with your brilliance, as if with a sharp tool. 5. In age after age. Worthy of the assembly. To those who praise. O Agni. Wealth. Glorious. Bestow. Ever-new. Like a foot. O King. The reviler. O imperishable one. Low. Down. Crush. With a sharp tool. As if with brilliance. 5.

O Agni, at every age, at every time, bestow—grant and provide—wealth and a glorious son upon us, who are the reciters of praise, as a newer, more recent hymn directed toward you, for we are worthy of the sacrifice (*vidatha*). *Note:* *Vidatha* refers to the sacrificial assembly or rite; *guṇadbhyaḥ* means "to those who utter" or "reciters"; *rayim* is wealth; and *yaśasam* qualifies the son as one who possesses glory.
