1. That which is to be worshipped by Kha, Jha, Ta, Na, Bha, and Ra—furthermore, O King, O shining one, O Agni free from decay, like a lord with his own thunderbolt, strike down the enemy who proclaims evil—that is, who proclaims misfortune—as one would a tree, so that he may be cast low, humbled, and brought to the ground.
O Agni Vaiśvānara, maintain for us among our patrons an unaging sovereignty and great heroic power. May we, through your protections, O Agni, win booty in hundreds and thousands.

O Agni, maintain for us among the liberal patrons uncrushable dominion, undecaying, and full of heroic vigor. May we win booty consisting of hundreds and thousands, O Vaiśvānara Agni, through your protections. 6.
O Agni, [for] us—
here the genitive case is used in the sense of the locative—
among us who are wealthy, that is, endowed with wealth in the form of oblations, maintain and establish *kṣatra*, meaning wealth.

Of what nature is it? It is unbending (*anāmi*), that which cannot be bent down; unassailable (*anavahārya*); undecaying (*ajara*), meaning free from old age and imperishable; and endowed with excellent vigor (*suvīrya*).

Furthermore, O Vaiśvānara Agni, through your protections (*utibhiḥ*)—that is, by means of the guardianships belonging to you—may we win and obtain food (*vāja*) consisting of a hundredfold, whether numbering one hundred or accompanied by a hundred men, or likewise a thousandfold.
O you who abide in the threefold station, protect us, your worshippers, with invincible guardians;
O Agni Vaiśvānara, guard our host of singers and, being praised, cause them to cross over to prosperity.

With your unassailable guardians, O Desired One, protect our patrons who stand upon the three worlds; guard us, O Agni Vaiśvānara, and lengthen the lives of those who offer oblations while you are being praised. 7.

O Agni, who art worthy of being sought at the sacrifice (*iṣṭe yajñasya eṣaṇīya*), who art established in the three stations (*tripadastha*)—dwelling together with [the gods] in the three worlds, or rather, abiding with the gods through sacrifices in the three sacrificial hearths such as the Āhavanīya—protect (*pāhi*) our patrons (*sūrīn*), our own singers of praise, with your unassailable (*adabdhebhiḥ*), by no one harmed, guardian-protectors (*gopābhiḥ*), your own guardians, and with your splendors. O Vaiśvānara Agni, protect (*rakṣa*) the strength (*śardhaḥ*) and power of us who have given oblations;
being praised (*stavānaḥ*), do thou further increase (*pra ca tārīḥ*) us.
The ninth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with "Ahaśca," is the seer Bharadvāja’s composition and has Vaiśvānara Agni as its deity. It is cataloged thus: "Ahaśca.
In the ten-night *vyūḍha* sacrifice, on the sixth day, this is the insertion (*nividdāna*) for the Vaiśvānara hymn in the *āprī* litany.
For it is stated [in the scripture]: "And the day is black; 'macca' is your name" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.8).
Day and night, the dark and the bright, these two worlds revolve through the spheres of knowledge;
Vaiśvānara, like a king being born, surpasses all lights and overcomes the darkness.
The day—thus—the black day and the white one roll apart by means of the sacred knowledges. Vaiśvānara Agni, being born like a king, overcomes the darknesses with his light. 1.
1. *Śa* means "to cut completely. A *vāha* is that in which a person brings forth actions (*karmāṇi*). *Vakṛṣṇam* means black-colored (*kṛṣṇavarṇam*).

Due to this grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the word "day" (*ahar*) refers to the night. The night is dark-colored because of its darkness; the day is white-colored because of the solar light.
Both the day and the night should be known through their own activities—which are to be understood as favorable—by which they delight the entire world with their respective splendors.
It moves variously and revolves;
or rather,
it refers to the two worlds, heaven and earth, which belong to the realm of space (rajas).
This is an elliptical indication;
[the meaning is that] he returns to the three worlds.
And this refers to the consecration of Vaiśvānara Agni—this is the remainder of the sense.
For he is to be understood here as a deity.

And he, indeed, as Vaiśvānara—being born as Agni, appearing as a king, and shining forth like a sovereign with his light and splendor—overcomes the darkness; "avātirat" is a verb meaning "to overcome," and "avati" means "he destroys."
I do not know the warp nor the woof, nor that which they weave while striving together in the contest.
Who here, as a son, shall speak the words before his father who is behind him?
I do not know the warp, nor do I know the woof, nor that which they weave while striving together in the contest. Whose son stands here to speak words before his father who is behind him? 2.

The proponents of the sacrifice (*yajñavādinaḥ*) maintain that this [verse] describes the creation of Vaiśvānara’s great form as having the nature of a sacrifice; by characterizing it as such, they demonstrate its difficulty to comprehend through this [verse].
"Warp" (*vataṃtum*):
warps are the threads stretched lengthwise in a cloth.
And those meters, such as the Gāyatrī and others, which constitute the chest of the sacrifice, as well as the Stomas and Śastras—
I know them all; likewise, I am able to recite them.
There are sūtras known as the *Avataṃsaka* and others; these, along with the various branches such as the *Vaipulya*, and the ritual actions (*karma*),
I know them all thoroughly.

Moreover, we do not know that cloth characterized by sacrifice which is to be accomplished by both [the sacrificer and the priests]. However, in this world, at the place of sacrifice (*devayajana*)—the meeting point (*saṃgamana*) where we dwell—the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), constantly exerting themselves, weave it;
they extend thread after thread and produce it in the form of a garment. This is the meaning. Indeed, in this world, there is the wealth of the weaver.
The word *svid* expresses a conjecture.

Who indeed, as a son of Manu, could speak these things that ought to be spoken—that is, these very words—while being situated in this world below, unless he were instructed by that Sun who exists in yonder world beyond, acting as his father?
No one at all would be able to speak them; such is the meaning.
And this has been stated by those who know the tradition: "He who stands as if beyond is the son of Vaiśvānara;

the meters are the chest of the sacrifice, the *stotra*s and *śastra*s are the threads, and the *yajus* verses are the ritual acts. That which is heard from the *Śruti* is the *varuṇa*, and that which is to be blown forth is the *adhvara*."
"The sun stands as the highest, fire is considered the father, and the earth is the mother"— thus,

the knowers of the Self (ātmavidas) consider that this [verse] establishes the nature of the world's creation as being knowledge through the figure of metaphor (rūpaka). "I do not know the thread, nor the threads"— even the ether and other elements, which stand in the place of the warp-threads, I do not understand.

Nor do I perceive that effect, which stands in the place of a cloth—that manifold world (*prapañca*) which transmigrating beings, constantly striving and exerting themselves in the weaving together of the threads and the weft, weave or produce.
It is only by way of metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) that God is called the "agent," as if He were creating it for their enjoyment.

In this matter, regarding these things that exist beyond the reach of the intellect (*buddhi*), what son indeed would speak them out, even when instructed by his own father—a recent being who appeared after the creation? These things are to be spoken of only by one who stands beyond the highest, outside the scope of the intellect.
One should say this: the meaning is that no one who is ignorant of the events prior to their own birth would speak [in such a manner].
1. [In the variants] kha, jha, ta, na, bha, and ra, the phrase ‘svapravṛttibhiḥ’ is absent; in śa, it is ‘svavṛttibhiḥ’.
2. Gha: of this. 3. Kha, Jha, Na, Bha: [the oblation] of King Vaiśvānara; Ra: [the oblation] of Vaiśvānara; Śa: Vaiśvānara [is] of the king.
He knows this thread, he knows the warp; he shall speak the words in due season.
He who perceives this, the guardian of immortality, moving downward yet looking ahead with his other [eye].

He knows this thread from here; he knows how to weave the warp. He shall speak the words of wisdom according to the seasons—he who, as the guardian of immortality, has perceived this, moving here while beholding with one eye what is beyond.
Although these things are difficult to know in the manner described, nevertheless Vaiśvānara, the Fire, knows them; he speaks and establishes them through his consciousness.

He alone—Vaiśvānara, the Fire—discerns the *tantu*, that is, the meters such as the *gāyatrī* and others which stand in the place of a warp, as well as the hymns and recitations (*stotra-śastra*). Likewise, he alone discerns the *otu*, that is, the *yajus* formulas and the rituals of the Adhvaryu priest which stand in the place of the woof.
At the proper times (*ṛtuthā*), at each occasion for their performance, he shall speak those things which are to be spoken.

This Vaiśvānara, who is the guardian of immortality—the protector and preserver of the waters—who moves below, wandering upon the earth in a terrestrial form, and who looks on from beyond in the heavens through another self as the Sun, illuminating the entire world; he alone "takes note of" (ciketat)—that is, he knows—all these visible beings. This is the connection with what precedes.
Or alternatively:
he alone, and no other, "discerns the thread"—that is, the subtle elements which stand in the place of a thread.
In the same way, he alone discerns the gross elements which correspond to the seasons.

He alone speaks these things that are to be spoken and are about to be uttered at the proper times—at whatever time whenever the tradition of knowledge is interrupted—he would speak them. Who is it that would discern this? To this he says: "He who knows thus."

He who is Vaiśvānara, the protector (*gopā*) of Viśvānara—the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the immortal (*amṛta*)—who guards the liberation (*vimokṣaṇa*) from death; who, moving below in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), endowed with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and wandering in the form of the individual soul (*jīvātman*); who, being beyond—that is, existing above ignorance (*avidyā*)—perceives by means of another form distinct from what was described, which is free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*) and characterized by Being-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*); and who, illuminating the entire universe, knows (*ciketat*) these things.
And likewise, with reference to the Supreme Self, it is heard in scripture: "Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.14).
This is the first Hotṛ; behold him! This immortal light among mortals—this one has been born, firmly seated, immortal, increasing in body.
This one is the Hotṛ; let him, as the first, behold this immortal light among mortals. He has been born, firmly seated, the immortal one, increasing in his body. 4.
This Vaiśvānara Agni is the first, the primordial Hotṛ;
for the human Hotṛ is second.
O man, behold him—meaning, partake of him.
The meaning is that among mortals—embodied beings whose very nature is death—this light called Vaiśvānara exists in the form of the digestive fire (*jāṭhara*), being immortal, i.e., free from death.

Moreover, this Agni is *dhruva*, immovable; he is *samantān niṣattaḥ*, seated or established everywhere, and thus all-pervading. For this very reason, although he is *amartya*, free from death, he is said to "be born" (*jajñe*) because of his connection with a body (*tanvā*); and he is figuratively described as "growing."
1. By the manner described by Śa; 2. endowed with the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) denoted by Śa; 3. in bodies whose nature is death (maraṇa), denoted by Śa; 4. "Sva" is said [to mean] one's own.

A fixed light has been established for the sake of vision; the mind, the swiftest among those that fly, is within. All the gods, of one mind and one intention, move rightly toward a single purpose. Fixed. Light. Established. For the sake of seeing. Whom? The mind. Swiftest. Among those that fly. Within. All. Gods. Of one mind. Of one intention. One. Purpose. Toward. They move. Rightly. 5.
The mind is indeed firm and immovable; yet the light of Vaiśvānara is even swifter than that mind, possessing exceeding velocity.
It is placed—established by Prajāpati—in the midst of moving, walking creatures.
For what purpose?
To behold whom?
For the purpose of seeing him.

Furthermore, all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*), being of one mind (*samanasaḥ*) and of one intention (*saketaḥ*), approach, reach, and serve in various ways that one principal mover (*ekam... gantāram*), the performer of deeds (*kratum*), in a proper and correct manner (*sādhu abhi vi*). This is the meaning.
Or alternatively:

while living beings are moving—that is, going—within, in the midst of them, in the heart, that which is swifter than thought, possessing a velocity even exceeding that of the mind, is fixed, immovable, and free from conceptual construction.
Thus says the Vājasaneyaka: "The One is unmoving, yet swifter than thought" (Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā 40.4).
The Brahman of light is consciousness, which is self-abiding;
it has not been established by anyone.
For it is heard in scripture: "He who knows it as hidden in the secret cave, in the highest heaven" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 8.1).
For what purpose?
For the sake of seeing, that is, for the purpose of vision;
for by means of knowledge they know everything.
Moreover:
the gods are so called because they "shine" (dīvyanti), that is, the senses.

All the gods—meaning all the senses, beginning with the eye—together with the mind (samanasaḥ), existing with the mind and possessing brilliance (saketāḥ), move forth properly and correctly toward the one, non-dual Supreme Self (paramātmānaṃ), who is the performer of the acts of creation and so forth, the essence of the universe, and who is their goal. They proceed in various ways toward Him.
The gods themselves indeed approach this; they approach it in various ways from the front. The meaning is that they wait upon it.
And thus it is heard in scripture: "That indeed is the light of lights, the life of life, the immortal" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.16).

My two ears fly apart; my sight flies apart—this light which is placed within the heart. My mind, its thoughts directed afar, wanders away. What indeed shall I speak? And what, now, shall I contemplate? 6. My two ears fly apart; my sight flies apart—this light which is placed within the heart. My mind, its thoughts directed afar, wanders away. What indeed shall I speak? And what, now, shall I contemplate? 6.

The two ears of mine, who desire to hear Vaiśvānara, fly apart—that is, they move in various directions—because of the multiplicity of his qualities that ought to be heard. Likewise, the eye-faculty of mine, who desires to see Vaiśvānara, flies apart; it moves in various directions.
Because of the multiplicity of his forms that are to be seen;

likewise, the light—that which illuminates—is placed or established in the heart, namely in the lotus of the heart (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*). This reality called *buddhi* also "flies about" (*vipatayati*), meaning it moves in various ways, in order to know the Vaiśvānara Self.
Moreover, its thoughts are directed toward the distant.
My mind wanders far away, toward a distant object; it is distracted by intense longing. Here, there is a Vedic change of gender. My mind also moves about in various ways.
Thus, when all the sense-faculties are active in a state of competitive striving (*ahamahamikā*), what indeed does [the self] know?
(Note: *gacchatsu* is not present in manuscript *kha*;
*jānāti* is present in manuscripts *kha*, *śa*, and *jā*).
3. Consisting of space, breath, and the universal fire (vaiśvānara)—this, I shall declare, is the form of Vaiśvānara.
What indeed, what on earth, shall I now conceive with my mind or perceive?
The meaning is that because the qualities of Vaiśvānara are infinite, they cannot be known by me, who am of dull intellect.
All the gods, bowing in awe, paid homage to you, O Agni, as you stood within the darkness.
May Vaiśvānara protect us for our welfare; may the Immortal protect us for our welfare.
All the gods, trembling with fear, paid homage to you, O Agni, as you stood in the darkness. May Vaiśvānara protect us for our aid; may the Immortal protect us for our aid. 7.
All the gods pay homage to you, O Vaiśvānara, who have taken your stand in the darkness and gloom;
for what reason?
Because they are terrified by that darkness.
May such an immortal (*amartya*), deathless Vaiśvānara Agni, protect (*avatu*) us for our well-being (*ūtaye*) through his saving power (*ūtyā*).
The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.

The tenth hymn, consisting of seven verses beginning with “puro vaḥ,” is the seerly composition of Bharadvāja and is addressed to Agni. The seventh verse is a *dvipadā virāṭ* of five syllables; the remaining verses are *triṣṭubh*s.
Thus it has been enumerated: “puro vo, ending in a *dvipadā*.”
In the *prātaranuvāka*, during the *āprī* litany, in the *ṛtu* section, and in the *triṣṭubh* metre, there are these four hymns beginning with *idam*.
It is stated in the Sūtra: “*puro vo mandram*—these four; *taṃ supratīkam*—these six” (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 4.13).

*puro vo mandraṃ divyaṃ suvṛktiṃ prayati yajñe agrimadhvare dadhidhvam* | Place before you the pleasant, divine Agni, worthy of beautiful praise, at the commencement of the sacrifice, at the head of the ritual.
Place him before you with hymns—he who is radiant for us, Jātavedas, who shall make our sacrifices well-performed.

Place before you at the advancing sacrifice and the ritual, the delightful, divine, and well-fashioned one; place him before you with hymns, for he, Jātavedas, the performer of good rites, shall make us possessors of threefold light.

O you priests and sacrificers (*ṛtvig-yajamānāḥ*), place Agni— who is delightful (*mandram*), worthy of praise, celestial (*divyam*) as existing in heaven, well-fashioned (*suvṛktim*), and free from blemishes or difficult to avoid— before you in this sacrifice (*adhvare*) which is proceeding (*prayati*) and is free from harm or transgression caused by demons and the like; that is, maintain him in front in the form of the *āhavanīya* fire,
or rather, make him your presiding priest (*purodhasam*).

And having been praised with hymns, place him in front—Agni, who is *vibhāvā*, shining forth preeminently; *jātavedas*, the knower of all that is born; for since he makes us *svadhvarā*, performers of beautiful sacrifices, therefore place him in front.
O Hotṛ of many aspects, Agni, kindled by mortals, [is] the burner of light.

O Agni, you who possess many faces, O Hotṛ, being kindled by the fires of mortals, you have made this hymn swell for him like refreshing strength; like ghee, it flows pure for the one who is worthy of praise.

O Agni, you who possess many faces, O Hotṛ, being kindled by the fires of mortals, you have made this hymn swell for him like refreshing strength; like ghee, it flows pure for the one who is worthy of praise. 2.

1. O Agni Vaiśvānara, who possesses the sounds *kha*, *gha*, *bha*, and *vaiśvānara*; 2. O Knower, O Wealthy One! O Radiant One, O You of many flames (*purvaṇīka*), O Hotṛ, the invoker of the gods, O Agni—being kindled (*idhāna*) together with the other fires that have become your limbs, shining brightly, you hear this very hymn (*stoma*) of the human being, the worshipper; [this is] the ellipsis.
The particle *u* serves to fill out the meter.

To this Agni, the *matayaḥ*—the thinkers, the chanters, the praisers—[offer] that hymn of praise (*stoma*), which is a song (*stotra*) that brings happiness (*śūpa*), purified like clarified butter (*ghṛta*) by the two strainers (*pavitra*), and pure (*śuci*) like clarified butter; [they offer it] as if with *mamatā*.
*Mamatā* was the name of the mother of Dīrghatamas, who was a teacher of sacred knowledge (*brahmavādinī*).
The meaning is that they purify, cleanse, and refine it, pronouncing it free from defects;
"that hymn" is the syntactical connection.

He has flourished with glory among mortals, the inspired singer who has offered worship to Agni with hymns; him, the mother of the bright-shining one, bestows upon the possessor of cattle through her wondrous aids. He has flourished with glory among mortals, that sage who has given gifts to Agni with hymns; him, the mother of the bright-shining one, provides with wondrous protections, she who possesses a stall full of cattle.
That wise patron among mortal men prospers and increases through fame—that is, through food—who, as a sage, offers oblations along with hymns of praise.

To that patron, Agni of wondrous luster bestows, through marvelous protections, the acquisition of a cattle-filled stall at the time of its winning. He maintains him in the possession of wealth consisting of kine.

He who, being born, filled the two wide worlds; he whose path is black, visible from afar by his light; the purifier, with his flame, has made himself manifest across the many-minded, surging ocean. 4. He who, being born, filled the two wide worlds; he whose path is black, visible from afar by his light; the purifier, with his flame, has made himself manifest across the many-minded, surging ocean. 4.

That Agni, whose path is black and whose track is black, as he is being born—manifesting himself—fills with his far-reaching light the two wide expanses of heaven and earth that are visible from afar;
that purifier, Agni, immediately thereafter, casting aside even the very thick darkness associated with night by means of his radiance, is seen.

Now, O Agni, bestow upon us a wondrous wealth with many strengths and through your protection, both for us and for our liberal patrons—those who, by their bounty and their fame, surpass other people with their heroic deeds. 5. Now. Us. Wondrous. With many strengths. Through protection. O Agni. Wealth. And for the liberal patrons. Those who. By bounty. And by fame. Beyond others. And with heroic powers. Surpass. People. 5.
1. This is the letter śa.
2. Between jha and na; [the letter śa is] among jha, tara, ra, and manuṣya.
3. There is no [occurrence of the letter śa] with the letters kha, jha, ta, na, bha, ya, ra, and śa, nor with the words ūti and rakṣā.
O Agni, O Maghavan—possessor of wealth characterized by the oblation—bestow upon us, together with manifold protections (*ūtī*), wonderful and praiseworthy riches (*rayi*) quickly;
indeed, the word *nu* has the sense of conjunction with what follows.

Grant us such sons who, through their wealth (*rādhas*), fame (*śravas*), and splendor (*agni*), and through excellent heroic powers (*suvīryebhiḥ*), surpass and overcome other people. This is the meaning.
Place this sacrifice within yourself; desiring it, the sacrificer seated before you offers the oblation with his mouth.
Among the Bharadvājas, you have accepted the well-fashioned hymn for the winning of booty that brings the prize of victory.

Bestow this sacrifice upon us, O Agni, you who desire it, which the offerer of oblations presents to you while seated; among the Bharadvājas you have accepted the well-fashioned hymn for the winning of booty that brings the prize. 6.
O Agni, you who desire it, place this sacrifice—the means of worship—before you; bestow wealth characterized by the oblation upon yourself;
and that cake (puroḍāśa) and so forth which the sacrificer, seated and possessing the oblation, offers for your sake—that [you should accept]. This is the syntactical connection.
Moreover, among the Bharadvāja seers, maintain—hold fast to—a *suvṛkti*, a hymn of praise that is perfectly free from defects.
[This is for] Gadhya;
the root *gadh* has the sense of "mixing."
And protect those woolly sheep for the sake of obtaining and partaking in the mixed *vāja*, that is, food.
Cast away hatred; may we increase our prosperity, enjoying exhilaration for a hundred winters with noble heroes.
Drive away the enemies; increase our prosperity; may we go forth for a hundred winters with brave sons. || 7 ||
O Agni, drive away our haters, our enemies; scatter them in all directions.
Increase our own nourishment and food.
And may we, endowed with excellent heroes—sons, grandsons, and the like—rejoice for a hundred winters, for a hundred autumns, being satisfied and full of joy.
"Yajasva hotaḥ" (1.26) is a hymn of eleven verses, consisting of six ṛks; it is the seer Bharadvāja’s composition, composed in the Triṣṭubh metre, and addressed to Agni.
It is catalogued thus: "Yajasva, [consisting of] six.
Its application is prescribed for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina Śastra.
Sacrifice, O Agni, as one more skilled in sacrifice, impelled by the Hotṛ-priest; do not neglect the incitement of the Maruts.
May Mitra and Varuṇa, the Nāsatyas, Heaven and Earth, turn toward our oblation for the sake of the Hotṛ.
Sacrifice, O Hotṛ, impelled, most skilled in sacrifice, O Agni! Like the incitement of the Maruts, bring hither Mitra and Varuṇa, the Nāsatyas, Heaven and Earth, to our invocation as priests. 1.

O Agni, you who are the most excellent sacrificer (*yajīyān*), the invoker (*hotṛ*) of the gods, being impelled (*iṣitaḥ*)—that is, sent forth or entreated by us—now, while this sacrifice is being performed (*prayukti*), enter as the subduer (*bādhaḥ*) of the Maruts, the gods, that is, the oppressor of enemies. (Note: *naḥ* is used here in the sense of *saṃprati*, meaning "now"; *prayukti* refers to the performance or application of the rite.)
2. O Śa, sacrifice to this troop of seers and descendants of Anu and Vatsa; [O Gaṇa], worship them.
Regarding these two sentences:
"O Hotṛ, sacrifice those gods for him"—this is one sentence.
*Prayukti* means application; it is the power of application (*prayuktibala*).
"Like the impulse of the Maruts, the strength of the great"—from this [verse], "drive away the enemies, drive them away! is the second sentence.
Moreover, *mitrāvaruṇā*:
Mitra is the deity presiding over the day, and Varuṇa is the deity presiding over the night.

And those two Nāsatyas—leaders of truth, or rather, whose very nature is truth, or perhaps born from the nose (nāsikā)—the Aśvins, [bring] both Heaven and Earth, and these gods, for our sacrifice (hotrā), that is, for the purpose of our rite; "ā vavṛtyāḥ" means having turned them hither, bring them here.
You, the most delightful invoker for us, a god among mortals, have milked the sacred rites within;
as the bearer with your purifying tongue and mouth, perform the sacrifice for your own self.

You, the most delightful Hotṛ, have been milked within us—you, the god among mortals, at the assemblies. As the bearer with the purifying tongue and mouth, O Agni, perform the sacrifice for yourself, for your own body. 2.

O Agni, you, dwelling among mortals—among human beings—become the Hotṛ, the invoker of the gods, at the *vidatha*, that is, at the sacrifice. Of what nature are you? You are the most pleasant (*mandratamaḥ*), the most worthy of praise; and for us, you are the non-deceitful (*adruhaḥ*), free from malice toward us.
The meaning is that he is always a friend. He is a *deva*, endowed with qualities such as generosity.
Furthermore, O *agne*, by means of the *juhū*:
the *juhū* is the flame, for oblations (*āhutis*) are offered (*hūyante*) within it.
Having purified with that purifying [tongue], which is the mouth of the gods, you, the bearer of oblations, should worship that body of yours known as Sviṣṭakṛt, which is your own inherent nature.
For even the fruitful prayer longs for you, so that the singer may worship the gods at the sacrifice;
when the most eloquent among the Aṅgirases, the inspired Madhucchandas, the Reba, utters his song at the rite.

For even the fruitful prayer yearns for you, so that the singer may worship the gods and proclaim their lineage. When the most inspired sage of the Aṅgirases, the bard, utters the sweet melody at the sacrifice. 3.
O Agni, the blessed *dhiṣaṇā*—meaning praise—which desires wealth and is the cause of wealth, longs for you (*tve*) through you;
the particle *cit* is used here merely to fill the meter.
For what purpose?

In order to sacrifice pre-eminently to the gods to be worshipped, Indra and the others, for the sake of the sacrificer who praises—that is, for the purpose of the sacrificer who extols—your birth, your manifestation;

when indeed, among the Aṅgirases, the most inspired sage, the most impelling of praise, the wise singer Rebha Bharadvāja, utters at the sacrifice a hymn of praise that is like honey, a source of exhilaration, then Dhiṣaṇā desires it. This is the syntactical connection.

1. When [the letters] kha, jha, ta, na, bha, and ra are present; 2. the meaning is "kha, jha, na, bha, and ya" [is not there]; 3. [she is] one who has obtained wealth that serves as a cause for further wealth, or one who has acquired a multitude of riches.

He has shone forth beautifully, O Agni, the protector from afar, the radiant one. Sacrifice to the two wide-spreading worlds, Heaven and Earth. Like Āyu, whom the people—bestowing oblations with reverence—anoint with their offerings, he is well-pleasing to behold like a beast. He has shone forth beautifully; he shines intensely. Of what nature is he? *Apākaḥ*—*pāka* means one whose wisdom is to be matured, a fool; *apākaḥ* is one characterized by that [absence of such foolishness]. He is *vibhāvā*, full of splendor. The rest is evident. O Agni, you—[addressing him directly]—[sacrifice to] the two *rodasī*, Heaven and Earth, which are *urūcī*, wide-reaching and expansive.
Grant [it].

O Agni, son of strength (*vṛṣasah), O son of power (*vṛṣaṇa), we who clothe you with the oblation (*havis*)—may we overcome, as one overcomes a hostile army, the enemy, that is, evil (*enas*); we would pass beyond it.
The meaning is "we would transcend it."
The hymn beginning with "madhye hotā" consists of six verses; it is the twelfth hymn, composed by Bharadvāja, in the Triṣṭubh meter, addressed to Agni.
It is introduced with the word "madhye."
The application of the Prātaranuvāka and the Abhilaṣṭa-śastra has been stated.
In the middle [of the ritual], the Hotṛ [recites]: "In the dwelling, the king of the sacrificial grass, he who is praised—may he worship these two worlds.
He, the son of strength, the observer of Truth, has shone from afar like the sun with his brilliance."

In the midst of his dwelling, Agni, the Hotṛ, has come to the sacred grass; he shall worship the two worlds for the impeller. This is that son of strength, the observer of Truth, who from afar spreads his brilliance like the sun.

He who is the invoker of the gods, the master of the sacrificial grass, the king of the sacrifice, Agni—whose impetuous power is most brilliant, like a ruler in the forest, like a goad on the path, he has shone forth as he grows strong. Like a guileless runner, he perceives himself; the immortal one, unobstructed, dwells among the plants. Most brilliant is his power, a ruler in the forest; like a goad upon the road, he has shone forth as he increases. Guileless like a swift courser, he takes notice by himself; the immortal one, unhindered, is present within the plants.

Having spread out, the flame of Agni— the one who moves, the most brilliant, exceedingly radiant— is the sovereign of the forest, shining in the wilderness in the form of a conflagration. Increasing, that Agni shines and illuminates his own path in the atmosphere like the *todas*, the impeller of all, the Sun.
Moreover, he is free from guile and the destroyer of guile;
or rather, like Vāyu, who is non-deceptive toward all by virtue of his nature as the vital breath (prāṇa), such is that immortal Agni, free from death, [present] among the plants.
Because burning and ripening are deposited within them, they are called *oṣadhayaḥ* (herbs/plants), as are the forests.

Within them, Vṛtra—being swift-moving and irresistible by anyone—by his own self (*ātmanā*), that is, by his own luminosity alone, perceives and makes the entire world conscious; he causes all creation to know.

Agni Jātavedas, the consumer of wood, is praised like a swift steed with our beautiful hymns in this firm dwelling; winning through his wisdom like a racer, he is to be magnified by sacrifices like a father cherishing his offspring. 4. With our [hymns], like a swift steed with [its] beauties, Agni Jātavedas is praised in the house; winning [booty] with his power, like a courser, like a father [cherishing] his offspring, he is to be magnified by sacrifices. 4.

That Agni, who is *vijātavedas*—meaning one whose wealth is born, or whose wisdom is born—is praised with our own hymns of praise (*stotra*). When a person approaches him as a supplicant, he is praised face-to-face in our sacrificial hall (*yajñagṛha*) with auspicious, joy-bestowing hymns that are truly conducive to happiness.
Moreover, he is the fulfiller of desires.

"Durvṛñaḥ": he is so called because he is difficult to restrain. For this very reason, "vanvan" means desiring; "vanāni" means the woods; "ṛtunā" means by his own ritual action (*karman*); and "varvā" means one who goes. Thus, he becomes a goer by means of his own rite.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like a bull to its calves. A father is a protector, the progenitor of calves, or like a draft-ox, a bull.
Just as he goes quickly for the sake of sexual union,
so too is he praised by those who perform sacrifices, by the learned, and by the sacrificers; this is a form derived from the root *jṛ*, which has the meaning of "to praise."

Now they admire his splendors as he hews freely, following after the broad earth. He who is swift, impetuous, and most vigorous, like a debt-collector or a thief, the king traverses the desert wastes. Now they admire his splendors as he hews freely, following after the broad earth. He who is swift, impetuous, and most vigorous, like a debt-collector or a thief, the king traverses the desert wastes. (5)
1. In the versions *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *dā*, the form is *rūpe*.

2. In version *kha*, "cetayati" is absent; in *tara* and *ra*, it is "citayati"; in *na*, it is "cintayati". 3. In *kha*, it is "etarī tadupari"; in *jha*, "etarī na upagantari"; in *jha*, *ta*, *la*, and *bha*, "etarī tadupagantari"; in *tara* and *ra*, "etarī nadupagantara"; in *na*, "etarī tadupagantari".
4. In the case of *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*, [the suffix] *ātmiya* does not exist.
5. In the case of those [consonants] excluding *gha*, *ca* does not exist. 6. In the case of *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *ya*, this form [is used].
Now, in this world—
"sma" is a filler particle—
the singers praise, that is, they extol, the splendors, the rays, of this Agni.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: when that fire, cutting through the forests with ease and without exertion—that is, carving them out—truly burns and pursues the earth, its vast and delightful terrain, then people praise him.
That fire which is swift, moving, released, and free from obstruction, for that very reason becomes immediately and rapidly the swiftest of movers. Like what? [Like a horse.]
*ṛṇo* means "not stealing.
The root *ṛṇoti* has the sense of "going.
*Tāyuḥ* is a name for a thief.
Just as a thief becomes one who travels swiftly, even so this Agni, having traversed the *dhanvan*, the desert land, shines as a king (*rāṭ*).
Or alternatively,
*dhanvan* refers to the atmosphere (*antarikṣa*), because from it the waters flow.
Having ascended exceedingly into the intermediate space, he shines.
As such, O steed, being kindled by all the fires, come to us; you bestow wealth and you drive away misfortune. May we rejoice for a hundred winters, blessed with heroic sons.
As such, O courser Agni, being kindled with all fires, protect us from reproach; bestow upon us riches, drive away misfortunes, and may we rejoice for a hundred winters, blessed with heroic sons. 6.
O Agni, come hither; such as you are, protect us from reproach—from contemptible offspring or indeed from censure—this is the ellipsis. Being of what nature?
Kindled, that is, being ignited, by all the fires that constitute your own abode.
"Veri" means "gamaya," which is to say, cause us to reach or attain riches and wealth;
or alternatively,
"veri" means you desire riches characterized by sacrificial offerings.
You drive away and scatter in various directions the enemy armies that cause misery and bring suffering;
and we, being possessed of excellent heroes—meaning fine sons and grandsons—may we rejoice and delight for a hundred winters, for a hundred years.
The thirteenth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “tvadviśvā,” is the seerly composition of Bharadvāja; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is addressed to Agni.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī entry “tvadviśvā.
Its application (viniyoga) has been stated for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina Śastra.
O fortunate Agni, from you all blessings issue forth like branches from a tree;
through your readiness to hear, there comes wealth, strength, victory over Vṛtra, rain from heaven, and the flow of waters.

From you, O blessed Agni, all fortunes go forth like the branches of a tree laden with fruit. Through your prompt obedience come wealth, strength, and victory over the foe; from heaven comes the praiseworthy rain and the flow of waters. 1.
O fortunate Agni, all—meaning every single—*saubhagāni*, that is, riches, issue forth diversely from you.
Since gold is the root of all wealth, and gold was produced from Agni, as the Śruti declares:
"His seed became gold" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.1.3.8).
The illustration for the departure is:
"the trees, not the branches.
Just as various branches issue forth from a tree, so it is here.
Likewise, wealth (*rayi*) and the herd of cattle depart quickly from your presence in obedience (*śruṣṭī*).
Regarding this, the *Taittirīyaka* states: "Wealth is indeed cattle; verily, by means of cattle he wins them" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 1.5.7.2).
1. *Śa*: having surpassed. 2. *Kha₁-bha-sa*: *idhānaḥ*; *ja-jha-ṇa-ta-na-ra-sa*: *idhānaḥ*; *kha-jha-jha-ta-na-bha-ra-śa*: *idhyamānaḥ*. 3. *Na*: for a hundred years. 4. *Na*: beautiful riches.
1. In the battle that destroys enemies—that is, in the conflict which slays foes—strength (*vāja*) issues forth from you to conquer the enemies. 2. And power (*bala*) also proceeds from you. 3.
That rain which comes from heaven and from the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), 4. even that proceeds only from you. [As it is said:
“An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun.”
For it is recorded in the Smṛti: "From the sun rain is born; from rain comes food; from that, living beings" (Manu 3.76).
Therefore, you, being worthy of praise and laudable by all, become the *rītiḥ*—the one who causes the flow or the bringer—of *apām*, that is, of the waters.
O Agni, you are indeed our lord for the sake of wealth; like a traveler, you dwell among us with unforgetting luster. O God, like Mitra, you are the steward of the great *ṛta* and of abundant beauty.

You are Bhaga; for you indeed bestow wealth upon us for our nourishment. Like one who traverses all, you dwell with a splendor difficult to forget. O Agni, like Mitra, you are the guardian of the vast *ṛta*; O God, you are the dispenser of abundant beauty.

O Agni, you are Bhaga, the one worthy of being shared; [grant] us our own delightful wealth, O Son of Strength (Sahasas Sūno). O Agni, that mortal, that human sacrificer, who—by means of songs (*gīrbhiḥ*), praises (*ukthaiḥ*), ritual recitations (*śastraiḥ*), and sacrifices (*yajñaiḥ*) which are the instruments of worship—having become a wise ordainer (*vedhāḥ*), brings your sharpened sharpness to bear upon the sacrificial ground (*vedhām ānaṭ*), that mortal, O radiant God Agni, [attains] everything (*viśvam*) in its entirety (*aram*).
[The word *aram* is used here in the sense of *vāśat*, i.e., "sufficiently" or "fully"].
He bestows and maintains grain;
and he is joined with and possesses riches through the Vasus.
O Agni, Son of Strength, may you bestow upon men those glorious and heroic riches that prosper them;
for with your power you provide abundant food for cattle even against the ravenous wolf.

O Agni, son of strength, may you bestow upon men glorious renown and heroic sons; for by your power you provide abundant nourishment for cattle, even against the ravenous wolf and the hungry enemy. 5.

O Agni, son of strength, O you who are born of strength, having brought from the men—that is, from the enemy host—those various glorious deeds accompanied by noble sons and excellent renown, bestow them upon us.
For what purpose?
For our nourishment.
Or rather:
O you who are to be led by the praises of men, bestow upon us—that is, grant to us—[that which you possess].

Endowed with *śavas*, or strength, you create for the wolf, for the non-giver, for the destroyer, and for the enemy, that abundant (*bhūri*) food (*vayas*) consisting of curds and the like belonging to cattle (*paśvaḥ*); the meaning is: take that away from them and give it to us.
O Agni, son of strength, you who are most expansive, grant us offspring and descendants who are victorious;
through all these songs of praise, may we, possessing excellent heroes, rejoice for a hundred winters in the fulfillment of our desires.

O Agni, son of strength, most expansive one, grant us offspring and descendants, O powerful one! Through all our songs of praise, may we attain abundance; may we rejoice for a hundred winters, blessed with heroic sons. 6.
O Agni, son of strength,
you who are far-reaching, this greatness of mine is great; as such, be for us a loud speaker and a teacher of what is beneficial.
Moreover, grant us—give to us—*toka*, a son, and *tanaya*, his son, as well as *vājin*, food joined with strength.
I, the praiser, through all *gīrbhiḥ*, songs directed toward you, may I attain *pūrtim*, the fulfillment of desires. This is another prayer.
The fourteenth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “agnā yaḥ,” is the seer’s work of Bharadvāja; it is dedicated to Agni.
The sixth verse is a Śakvarī, while the remaining five are Anuṣṭubhs.
Thus it has been declared in the Anukramaṇī: “‘agnā yaḥ’: an Anuṣṭubh hymn ending in a Śakvarī.”
In the *prātaranuvāka* (morning recitation) dedicated to Agni, when the *āśvina-śastra* has been performed, this hymn is used.
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: “*agnā yo hotājaniṣṭa*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.12).
Furthermore, in the third day of the four-night *ahīna* sacrifice called the *caturviṃśa*, this hymn serves as the *ājya-śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The verse beginning with 'agnā yo martyo duva' [is used] at the third [pressing]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 10.2).
1. For the sake of nourishing [the body];
2. The meaning is: "Give [this] to us";
3. By means of praises directed toward you.

The mortal who with his thoughts has delighted in the service and the prayer for Agni—may he now consume [the enemy]; may he, the ancient one, grant us food for our protection. 1. The mortal who has taken pleasure in the worship and the prayer for Agni through his meditations—he shall indeed consume [the foe]; may he, the ancient one, grant us nourishment for our well-being.

That mortal man who, in every fire-altar, with his thoughts (*dhībhiḥ*) and hymns (*dhītībhiḥ*), enjoys, serves, and practices worship (*duvaḥ*), attendance (*paricaraṇaṃ*), devotion (*dhiyaṃ*), and ritual action (*karman*) characterized by sacrifice and the like—he, that mortal being the foremost of the ancients (*pūrvyaḥ*), shall indeed quickly shine forth;
he shall become possessed of supreme radiance.
For the sake of protection (*avase*)—for the preservation of his sons and others—he shall choose (*burīta*), seek, and enjoy nourishment (*iṣam*) and food.
The meaning is that one may obtain [it] from the presence of an enemy.

Agni is indeed the wise one; Agni is the most skillful seer. At the sacrifices, the human clans invoke Agni as the Hotṛ-priest. agnir it hi pracetā agnir vedhastama ṛṣiḥ | agniṃ hotāram īḷate yajñeṣu manuṣo viśaḥ || 2 || Agni alone is truly the wise one; Agni is the most skillful seer. At the sacrifices, the human clans invoke Agni as the Hotṛ-priest.
Agni alone is the wise one (*pracetāḥ*), possessed of preeminent knowledge, and no other whatsoever.
For because it is so, he is the most skillful ordainer (*vedhastamaḥ*), the supreme performer of rites such as the carrying of oblations, the seer, and the beholder of all.
Men—the human sacrificers—along with their subjects, characterized as officiating priests, praise and extol such an Agni as the invoker of the gods in sacrifices and rituals.
For in various ways, O Agni, the riches of the noble foe vie with one another for your favor; the Āyus, overcoming the Dasyu, strive by their sacred observances to overcome the lawless.

O Agni, the wealth and riches of the noble enemy—the foe—belong to you for the protection of those who offer good praise. Separated from various enemies, they vie with one another, competing by saying, "I alone shall protect them! I alone shall protect them!

And the living men, those very singers, overcoming and harming the Dasyu, the destructive enemy, through their vows and hymns devoted to you, desire to withstand and overcome the man who is without vows and who opposes the sacred law.
1. Kha, jha, ta, na, bha, ya, ra—there is no other; there is none besides.
2. Kha, ga, gha, ṅa, jha, ta, na, bha, ya, ra, śa—the one who opposes the vow, who opposes the sacrifice.
Agni bestows a hero, a conqueror of waters, a subduer of enemies, a lord of the good.
At whose sight the enemies tremble in fear because of his might.
Agni bestows a hero, a lord of the people, who overcomes the waters and withstands the onset of enemies; at the mere sight of whose power the foes tremble with fear. 4.

This Agni bestows—that is, grants to his worshippers—a heroic son. What kind of son? One who is an *apsā*, a winner (*sanitā*) of ritual actions (*ap*) through their performance; an *ṛtīṣah*, an overcomer and subduer of *ṛti*s, that is, of enemies; and a *satpati*, a protector of the good, that is, of ritual acts.
The syntactical connection is as follows: that hero at whose sight (*sañcakṣi*) the enemies (*śatravaḥ*) tremble (*trasanti*) out of fear (*bhīyā*) due to his power (*śavasaḥ*).
For Agni, the wise god, protects the mortal from reproach;
he is the victorious one whose wealth is encompassed in the battles.
For Agni, the wise god, protects the mortal from reproach; he who possesses abundant wealth that is won in battles. 5.
The one who possesses *sahas*—

*sahas* meaning strength— the god *Agni*, endowed with qualities such as generosity and being possessed of knowledge (*vidvān*), protects (*uruṣyati*) that esteemed (*matam*) man, the sacrificer, from the reviler (*nidaḥ*).
The word *vi* is a filler (*pūraka*).

The syntactical connection is as follows: for that mortal whose wealth—wealth characterized by the oblation (*havis*)—is *avṛtaḥ*, meaning unobstructed by Rākṣasas and the like, and which is *avṛtaḥ* in sacrifices, meaning not shared by other sacrificers; [Indra] protects that sacrificer who possesses such an oblation.
O great god Mitra, speak clearly for us first among the gods; proclaim the goodwill of Heaven and Earth.
Grant us well-being and a secure dwelling from heaven. May we cross over hostilities, the days of trouble, and all difficulties; may we cross them by your protection.

O Agni, god of great bounty like Mitra, speak for us a favorable word to the gods; [speak] from both heaven and earth. Grant us well-being and a secure dwelling from heaven. May we overcome our enemies, the days, and evil paths; may we cross over them, may we cross over by your protection. 6.
This has been explained.

As for the words: *anūkūdīse*—addressed to one endowed with qualities such as generosity, speak forth (*vocaḥ*) our excellent praise (*sustutim*) directed toward the gods who pervade the sacrifice, concerning the sovereignty attained by Heaven and Earth.
"O Great One, by this praise, lead us to a great dwelling that is secure and indestructible.
And we—[this is] not shared by him alone, nor common to him alone; [it is] not unshared, nor not common."
The complete commentary on this mantra (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 6.2.11) exists in the Kha and Gha manuscripts:
"By your grace, may we transcend hatreds, their evil fruits, and the difficult paths;
may we transcend those [obstacles] that are remote and those committed in other births."
"By means of your own protection, may we transgress [all obstacles] completely."

The hymn beginning with "imam ṣu vaḥ" consists of nineteen verses; it is the fifteenth hymn, composed by Vītahavya Bharadvāja, the son of Aṅgiras, addressed to Agni in the Vṛṣan meter. Of these, the first nine are Jagatī verses; the third and sixth, however, are Śakvarī and Atiśakvarī respectively; the fifteenth is a Śakvarī; the seventeenth is an Anuṣṭubh; the eighteenth is a Bṛhatī; and the tenth, eleventh, twelfth, sixteenth, and nineteenth—these seven—are Triṣṭubhs. Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Imam ṣu vaḥ: nineteen verses; Vītahavya Bharadvāja [composed] a Jāgata [hymn]; before the tenth verse, the third and fifteenth are Śakvarīs; the sixth is an Atiśakvarī; the penultimate [verses] are Anuṣṭubh and Bṛhatī."
In the *prātaranuvāka* dedicated to Agni, and in the *āśvina-śastra*, the first nine verses are recited.
As it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Imam ṣu vo atithim uṣarbudham’—these nine" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 4.13).
On the fifth day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), the first nine verses constitute the *ājya-śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The nine verses beginning with 'This guest of yours, kindled at dawn' constitute the Ājya [laud]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.12).
With my song, I honor this guest of yours who awakens at dawn, the lord of all peoples;
he who from birth belongs to heaven, the pure one, who by his very nature knows every secret and consumes that which is unshakable as the embryo within the womb.

This one—*ūm*—I strive toward with my song for you, this guest who awakens at dawn, the lord of all the tribes. He comes from heaven by his very birth; whatever is pure, even though long established, he, the embryo, eats as soon as it is unshakable. 1.
O Rishi Vītahavya, or you, Bharadvāja, [grant] protection;
there is an inversion of case and number.
"With this very song"—that is, with praise—"well direct" (su-ṛñjase) this very Agni.
Yāska states that "the root ṛñjati has the sense of 'to direct' (prasādhana).
Of what kind [is he]?
"One who constantly goes to a guest," or alternatively,
"one who is worthy of worship like a guest."
"He who awakens at dawn, who is awakened at the break of day, the protector and lord of all people (viśām) and subjects (prajānām);
who by birth (januṣā)—that is, by his very nature—is pure (śuciḥ), stainless, or bright; does he ever (kaccit), at any time, on some occasion of sacrifice, come from heaven (divaḥ)?
At that time, one should propitiate him—this is the syntactical connection."
Thus consecrated, Agni— remaining like an embryo within the two kindling woods (*araṇī*),

or rather, being the embryo of heaven and earth— consumes for a long time (*jyok cit*) that oblation (*havis*) which is "unswerving" (*acyuta*), meaning free from deviation, consisting of milk and other substances used as the means for the *agnihotra* and other rites.
Him whom the Bhr̥gus have established like a well-placed friend, the one to be praised, with upward-flaming radiance—
he, O wondrous one, being well-pleased, you are magnified day by day with hymns of praise by Vītahavya.

Not [that fire] which the Bhr̥gus established well in the wood, the adorable one with upward-flaming brilliance; but you, O wonderful one, being well-pleased at the offering of the oblation, are magnified day by day with praises. 2.

The Bhrigus—the great seers—placed you, O Agni, like a friend (mitra), as one who has become a companion, within the forest tree; you who are well-established, beautifully deposited, worthy of praise, and possessed of lofty radiance. They established you in their home. (Note:
1. kha-gha-bha read *januṣā* instead of *it*).
O Vītahavya, known by that name, may you be well-pleased and truly delighted with this ṛṣi;
for day after day, you are magnified—that is, worshipped—with praises consisting of these very hymns.
If the ṛṣi Bharadvāja is intended here, the connection should be made as "Bharadvāja [being] one to whom the oblation has been offered (dattahaviṣke) by Vītahavya."

As such, you are the one who bestows skill, the increaser of many, the conqueror of the enemy and of the stranger. O Son of Strength, grant protection among mortals to Vītahavya; grant wide-reaching shelter to Bharadvāja—wide-reaching shelter!

You have become the harmless strengthener of Dakṣa; the overcomer of the enemy, whether distant or near. O Son of Strength, bestow a wide dwelling among mortals upon him who offers the oblation, and a wide dwelling upon Bharadvāja. 3.
O Agni, you who are such, being *avṛka*—free from harm—you are the *vṛdha*, the increaser, of *dakṣa*, the one capable of performing [sacrificial] rites.
Likewise, you are the *taruṣa*, the overcomer, of the *para*, the distant *arya*, the enemy, as well as the *antara*, the nearer, more proximate enemy.

For this reason, O son of strength (*sahasas sūno*), you who are all-pervading (*saprathas*) and wide-reaching in every direction, bestow (*ā yaccha*) wealth (*rāyas*) and a dwelling (*chardis*)—that is, a house—upon Bharadvāja among mortals; that is, upon him for whom the oblation (*havis*) has been brought (*vīta*) as his sacrificial offering, or rather, it should be construed as "to Bharadvāja" himself. Grant us riches and a home.
The repetition of the word *saprathas* is for the sake of emphasis.

With well-fashioned hymns, I honor you— the guest who dwells in heaven, Agni, the invoker for mankind, the performer of the perfect sacrifice, like a sage with celestial luster, the divine one who brings delight.

I strive toward you with well-fashioned hymns—the guest who dwells in heaven, Agni, the invoker of men, the priest of the perfect sacrifice, like a sage of celestial luster, the divine messenger who conveys the oblation. ||4||

O Vītahavya, with beautiful hymns of praise (*suvṛktibhiḥ*), you should propitiate Agni, the god who carries the oblations (*havyavāham*). Of what nature is he? He is the shining (*ghṛtam*) guest (*atithim*) of you all, worthy of worship like a guest; the leader to heaven (*svarvaram*); the invoker of the gods (*hotāram*) in the sacrifice of Manu Prajāpati; the performer of the excellent rite (*svadhvaram*); and like a wise sage (*vipram na*), he possesses celestial luster (*dyukṣavarcasam*).
*Dyukṣam* means dwelling in the light;
*aryam* means the master who possesses such speech as a protector.

1. *Kha-jha-na-bha-ya-ra-sapratha*: this repetition is for the sake of emphasis (*ādarārtha*). [The phrase] "there is no one like you" (*evaṃvidhas tvaṃ nāsti*) is implied. *Rāyaḥ* means wealth (*dhanāni*); *chardiḥ* means a house (*gṛham*); *āyaccha* means bestow (*prayaccha*). *Ta-sapratha*: this repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
With a purifying (*pāvakayā*), observant (*citayantyā*) grace (*kṛpā*), you have shone forth upon the earth (*kṣām*), as with the radiance of the dawn (*uṣasaḥ na bhānunā*).

You who are swift (*turvan*), who are to be praised by both sides (*ubhayataśasya*), who are now a source of joy (*raṇaḥ*), and who, like the sun (*ghṛṇe na*), do not grow old (*ajareḥ*) while consuming (*tattuṣāṇaḥ*).

He who, with his purifying and observant grace, has shone upon the earth like the radiance of the dawn; he who, like Turvaṇ, in the joy of Etaśa’s course, has rushed forward like one burning in the heat of the ageless [flame].
Agni has shone upon the earth with his purifying, discerning, enlightening, and wise light,
as if with the radiance of the dawn; that is, he shines just as the dawns shine with their splendor.

Moreover, in every journey and in battle, Agni—who overcomes enemies and destroys them like a man [acting] at the wound of the seer named Etaśa—was kindled for assistance in the conflict with Sūrya; he was quickly (vnu) or indeed (vā) ignited in the heat (vghṛṇe).
"Etaśa, dwelling in the sun... (Ṛgveda 10.73.9).

I praise with song and fuel Agni who has been kindled—the pure, purifying, and steadfast one placed at the front of the sacrifice. We implore Jātavedas, the wise sage, the priest, the bringer of many boons, the guileless, with our prayers for his favor. samiddham | agnim | samidhā | girā | gṛṇe | śucim | pāvakam | puraḥ | adhvare | dhruvam | vipram | hotāram | puruvāram | adruham | kavim | sumnaiḥ | īmahe | jātavedasam || 7 ||
I praise— that is, I laud— with song, which serves as the means of kindling, the fire that has been kindled, meaning it has been properly ignited;
or rather, [kindled] by the *samidh* (fuel), meaning it has been properly ignited by those things worthy of being kindled.

Moreover, the remainder [of the verse] is: "I place that Agni at the forefront in the *adhvara*—the sacrifice—who is pure, self-purified, purifying for all, constant, and immovable. Likewise, we approach (*īmahe*) with hymns that produce bliss—that is, we honor—with Agni, who is wise (*vipra*), the invoker (*hotṛ*) of the gods, possessed of many boons (*puruvāra*), free from malice (*adruha*), a seer (*kavi*) of far-reaching vision, the knower of all beings (*jātavedas*). Or alternatively: [The verse continues: "We approach with hymns that produce bliss—the wise one, the invoker of the gods, the possessor of many boons, the non-malicious, the seer, the knower of all beings. Or else: [the interpretation follows].
The instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative;
we implore, that is, we beg for, *sumnāni*, meaning riches.

Thee, O Agni, the immortal messenger, the bearer of oblations, the protector to be praised, they have established in every age; both gods and mortals have seated thee, the watchful, the all-pervading lord of the people, with reverence. 8. Thee, O Agni, the immortal messenger, the bearer of oblations, the protector to be praised, they have established in every age; both gods and mortals have seated thee, the watchful, the all-pervading lord of the people, with reverence. 8.
O Agni, the gods and mortals—both deities and human beings—have established you as their messenger; they have appointed and made you so.

Of what sort are you? You are immortal, never subject to death; at every age, at every time, on the occasion of performing those respective sacrifices, you are the bearer of oblations (*havyavāha*), the protector (*pāyu*), and the one worthy of praise (*īḍya*).

Moreover, both these [classes of beings] have approached—that is, they have drawn near with reverence (namas) or with oblations characterized by food—to that Agni, who is ever-watchful (jāgṛvi), pervasive (vibhu), expansive (vyāsa), and the lord of the people (viśapati), the protector of all creatures.

Adorning both worlds according to the sacred laws, you, the messenger of the gods, traverse the two realms. Since we choose your devotion and your favor, therefore, O Agni, be auspicious to us, providing a triple protection. 9. Adorning both, according to the sacred laws, as the messenger of the gods, you traverse the two realms. Since we choose your devotion and your favor, therefore, be auspicious to us, providing a triple protection. 9.

O Agni, adorning—specifically beautifying and embellishing—both kinds, both the gods and humans, you, acting as the messenger of the gods, traverse and move between the two realms, heaven and earth (*rajasī*), in accordance with the sacred laws (*vratā*) during the rites and sacrifices;
you go to the world of the gods to bring them hither, and to this world to carry the oblations.
Furthermore, because [this praise] is for you, for your sake...

We choose—that is, we embrace—the protection from fear, the deed, the good-will, and the beautiful praise; for this reason, may you, who possess a triple refuge and abide in three places, be auspicious—that is, a bringer of happiness—to us. The particle *sma* is used here as a verse-filler (*pādapūraṇa*).
In the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, during the Prātaranuvāka recitation, within the Triṣṭubh metre, there are six verses beginning with "taṃ supratīkam.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "Six [verses] beginning with 'taṃ supratīkam'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
May we, the ignorant, serve him who is beautiful of face, fair to behold, and possessed of noble steeds—he who is the wiser among the wise.
May he, knowing all ways, sacrifice; may he announce our offering and our song among the immortals.

Him, the one of fair countenance, fair to behold, with noble horses—the one more wise than we who are ignorant—let us serve. May he, knowing all the ways, perform the sacrifice; may Agni announce our offering among the immortals. 10.
May we, who are ignorant—devoid of wisdom and small-minded—serve and attend upon that Agni, the most wise, the most learned, the omniscient.
Of what nature is he? He is *supratīka*, one with beautiful limbs; *sudṛśa*, a beautiful beholder; and *svaśva*, one who moves with excellent horses. Furthermore, may that Agni worship the gods.
"Viśvā" means all; "vayunāni" means this knowledge. But here, it refers to that which is to be known.
The wise one, knowing the various objects to be known, may Agni proclaim our oblation among the immortal gods who are free from death;
let him declare: "The oblation has been prepared for you; therefore, come for its sake."
Shall I drink of it first, or dost thou satisfy him who has brought a hymn to thee, O hero, as a sage?
Whether it be the sharpening of the sacrifice or its fulfillment, him indeed thou satisfyest with wealth born of thy power.

O Agni, you protect that man and you deliver him who has brought to you, O Hero, a hymn for the Sage, or the sharpening of the sacrifice, or its impulse; him indeed you satisfy with strength and with wealth. 11.
You protect— that is, you guard— the man who is far away; and furthermore, you satisfy— that is, you fulfill with desires— that man, O Hero,
who has offered to you, the Seer, a pleasing hymn of praise or a ritual act.
Alternatively,
since the object is treated as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) according to the rule "the mention of 'action' (*kriyā*) must be made," the dative case is used.
[The word *dhītaye* means] it brings you, the poet, to the state of being inspired (*dhīti*).

The grammatical connection is "he saw him. Furthermore, it refers to the sharpening (*niśiti*)— that is, the refinement (*saṃskāra*)— of the sacrifice, or of the sacrificial act, or of the oblation (*havis*) which serves as its means.
Or rather, you cause that rising or ascending to reach its goal; with that very power (*śavas*), you fill it full, and furthermore, you fill it with wealth (*rāya*).
O Agni, protect us from the one who seeks to harm us; O possessor of power, guard us from the striker.
May the path leading to you, which is accompanied by smoke, come to us; may wealth that is desirable and thousandfold come to us.
O Agni, protect us from the one who seeks to harm us; O possessor of power, guard us from evil. May the smoke-enveloped path reach you, and may thousandfold wealth, which all desire, come to us. 12.
1. One who sees that which is beautiful through the knowledge of the self (jña-ta-ya).
2. Also, by means of *gha* and *śa*. 3. You fill [it] with *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *ta1*, *na*, *bha*, *ya*, and *ra*; [or, according to another reading: you fill [it] with *gha* and *ta1*.
O Agni, protect us thoroughly from the attacking, injurious enemy.
O powerful, mighty Agni, guard us alone from reproach and evil.
May the food characterized by oblations, which we have offered to you—you who possess the power to destroy and whose defects are destroyed—fully reach and come to you.
"May the desirable wealth, sought after by those who long for it, consisting of a thousandfold [treasures], reach you perfectly—the riches bestowed by you."
In the *vyūḍha-daśarātra* sacrifice, on the fifth day, during the *āgnimāruta* śastra, the verses beginning with "Agni is the Hotṛ" (*agnirhotā*) are to be recited as the *jātavedas-nivid-dhānīya*.
Furthermore, it is stated in the *Sattriṃta*: "The three verses beginning with 'Agni is the Hotṛ, the Lord of the House, the King' (*agnirhotā gṛhapatiḥ sa rājā*).
These are the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) for the *gṛhapati* in the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*Agnihotā gṛhapatir sa rājā havyavāḍ bharaḥ pitā naḥ*—these are the *patnīsaṃyāja* verses” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.10). This is indeed the opening verse (*pratipad*) of the *ādhina* recitation. And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*Agnihotā gṛhapatir sa rājā* is the opening verse; it is to be recited in single-footed order, foot by foot” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.5).
He is the invoker of the fire, the lord of the household, the king; Jātavedas knows all births.
He who is the best sacrificer among both gods and mortals—may he, the observer of eternal law, perform the sacrifice.

Agni is the Hotṛ, the lord of the house; he is the king. Jātavedas knows all generations—both those of the gods and those of mortals. May he, the most excellent sacrificer and the upholder of cosmic order (Ṛtá), perform the sacrifice. 13.
Agni, the Hotṛ who is the king of the gods and the shining one, is the Gṛhapati, the lord and sovereign of the household.
Likewise, as Jātavedas—whose wisdom is born—he knows and perceives all births, that is, all living beings.
That Agni is the most excellent sacrificer (*yajiṣṭha*) among both the gods, such as Indra and others, and among mortals, human beings; he is the observer of Truth (*ṛtāvā*).
*Ṛta* is truth or sacrifice;
that Agni, possessing it, shall "sacrifice forth," that is, worship the gods preeminently.
"O Agni, whatever today... is the *yājyā* for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering in the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the verse 'O Agni, whatever today... O Hotṛ of the sacrifice,' he performs the offering without pausing" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 1.6).
O Agni, Hotṛ of the sacrifice, purifier with your radiant flame, come today to the people; for you are the sacrificer.
Worship the Truths with your greatness, as you distribute the oblations; O youngest one, bring here today those offerings which are yours.

O Agni, O Purifier, O Radiant One, you who today attend to the people of the sacrifice as the Hotṛ-priest—for you are the sacrificer; you shall worship according to the Truth with your greatness, since you have spread abroad. O Most Youthful One, carry the oblations that are yours today. 14.

O Hotṛ of the *adhvara*, O accomplisher of the sacrifice, O Agni of purifying luster—O you who are thus characterized, at this time, desire (*vei*) that which is to be done for the people (*viśaḥ*), that is, for the human sacrificer.
For since you are a sacrificer (*yajvā*), one who offers to the gods, therefore, in accordance with *ṛta* (the cosmic order), sacrifice to the gods.

Moreover, since you, O most youthful Agni, by your greatness—that is, by your own majesty—are pervasive and extend everywhere, for that reason, O youngest one, carry today these oblations which we offer for your sake;
carry these offerings to your own form known as Sviṣṭakṛt.

For the offerings are well-prepared; indeed, O praiser, may one establish you here to worship Heaven and Earth. O Maghavan Agni, come to us in the winning of booty! May we cross over all difficulties; may we cross them, may we cross them by your protection. abhi prayāṃsi sudhitāni hi ravyo ni tvā dadhīta rodasī yajadhyai | arvā no maghavan vājasātāvame viśvāni duritā tarema tā tarema tavāvasā tarema ||15|| For the offerings are well-prepared; indeed, O praiser, may one establish you here to worship Heaven and Earth. O Maghavan Agni, come to us in the winning of booty! May we cross over all difficulties; may we cross them, may we cross them by your protection.

O Agni, you behold the well-placed, well-deposited oblations—those foods characterized as sacrificial offerings (*havis*) set down by the wise ordainers (*vedhas*). For you are the fulfiller. Such as you are, Heaven and Earth (*rodasī*)—by which all the gods are implied—shall establish you for the purpose of sacrifice, that they may worship you.
This sacrificer has offered [the oblation].
O bountiful Agni, protect us in the contest for booty—that is, in battle—or in the acquisition of food.
And may we cross over and transcend all difficulties and sorrows.
15. Regarding another ritual: at the carrying forward of the fire (agnipraṇayana), this verse "O Agni, with all [the gods]" (agne viśvebhiḥ) should be recited.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Agni, with all the gods, O fair-faced one"—one should begin from this lower half-verse (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.17).

"O Agni, with all the gods, O fair-faced one, sit first upon the wool-lined womb. Lead the sacrifice, which is nest-like and rich in ghee, straight to Savitṛ for the sake of the sacrificer. O Agni! With all! O fair-faced one! With the gods! Wool-lined! First! Sit! Upon the womb! Nest-like! Rich in ghee! To Savitṛ! The sacrifice! Lead! For the sacrificer! Straight! 16.

O Agni of beautiful host and swift flame, together with all the gods, without exception, do thou, as the foremost among all the gods, sit down—that is, take your place—upon the woolly womb characterized by the high altar (*uttaravedi*). Of what kind is that womb? It is *kulāyinam*, possessing a nest-like interior.
*Kulāya* means a nest.
This [fire-altar] is endowed with a mass of various substances such as *guggulu* resin and so forth.

And thus it is heard in scripture: "For this which is constructed at the sacrifice is like a nest; namely, these noble enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*), the *guggulu* stalks, and the fragrant ointments" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 1.24).
It is provided with clarified butter and prepared through the sprinkling and other rites.
Thus, you, having been completed upon the *uttaravedi*, [are offered] to Savitṛ, the impeller, for the sake of the sacrificer;
the dative case is used here in the sense of the genitive.

Lead the sacrifice of such a patron rightly and with integrity; cause him to reach the gods. The wise ones churn this very Agni, as Atharvan did, whom they brought forth from the dark night, unerring, as he was being guided by the hook. 17. 1. The letters *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, *ya*, and *śa* are well-placed (*sudhita*).
2. The foods characterized by *ta*, *ya*, *ha*, and *vi*.
3. *Kha-bha-tvā*: you who are such; *jha-tvā*: you who are such; *na-ra-tvā*: you who are such; *śa-tvādeśa*: you who are the substitute for *śa*.
4. "kha-jha-na-bha-śa"—this is the subsequent formula (anuvākyā).
According to Ṛgveda 3.6, the *vedhasaḥ* are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the ordainers of rituals.
They churn— that is, they rub— this very one who is being seen and possesses the qualities previously mentioned;
they produce him from the two kindling woods, just as in ancient times the seer of the Atharva mantra churned [the fire] for Atharvan.
[He drove] the unerring one— *aṅku* being that which goes toward contemptible ignorance—
and [he drove] that Agni, who, desiring that for himself, had gone forth from the gods and was fleeing hither and thither, [from] the *śyāvī* cows; [he drove him] the unconfused, the undeluded.
*Śyāvī* is a name for night;
those masses of darkness occurring therein are *śyāvyāḥ*. The connection [of the verse] is: "churning him while bringing [him] from their presence, i.e., while causing him to come."
Be born for the enjoyment of the gods, for complete well-being and prosperity;
bring hither the immortal gods who increase the cosmic order, and cause our sacrifice to reach the gods.
Be born for the enjoyment of the gods, for total success, and for well-being. Bring hither the immortal gods who increase the cosmic order; let them touch the sacrifice among the gods. 18.

O Agni, at this sacrifice being performed with full completion, as you are being churned, be born— that is, manifest yourself— for what purpose? For the enjoyment of the gods, that is, for the sake of the sacrificer who desires the gods.
The dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
For the well-being—that is, for the non-destruction—of such a sacrificer;
and having generated the immortal gods, those who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*) and promote the sacrifice, bring them hither.
Immediately thereafter, among those gods, cause our sacrifice to touch them; that is to say, cause it to reach them.
O Agni, Lord of the House among men, we have kindled for you a great hymn of praise;
may our household duties not be neglected, and sharpen them with your keen splendor.

We [invoke] you, O Agni, Lord of the House of men, with the syllable *ūm*. With kindled fuel, we offer a great hymn of praise. May our household duties not be solitary; sharpen us with your keen splendor. 19.

O Gṛhapati Agni, protector of sacrifices, among the people—that is, among living beings—we alone have made you great with fuel, that is, we have kindled you as a vast light. For this reason, our *gārhapatyāni*—our states of householdership—are *asthūri*. A cart drawn by a single animal is called *sthūri*; its opposite, a cart equipped with many animals, is *asthūri*.
And by that, fullness is indicated:
may [our homes] not be empty, but be filled with sons, cattle, wealth, and so forth. Moreover, sharpen us thoroughly with a sharp, keen splendor; polish us completely and make us truly sharp.
The meaning is "one should join together."
In the second Anuvāka, there are eight hymns (*sūktas*).
Among them, the first hymn, "O Agni, yours among sacrifices" (*svam agne yajñānām*), consists of forty-eight verses; it is the *ṛṣi*-seer Bharadvāja’s composition, addressed to Agni.
The first and the sixth verses are *vardhamāna-gāyatrīs*, because they possess the characteristics stated as: "That [gāyatrī] which has six and seven syllables [respectively] is *vardhamānā*."
The twenty-seventh is an *anuṣṭubh*.
The two verses beginning with "ā te agne" and "agnirdevāḥ" are *anuṣṭubhs*.
Of these two, the former is a *triṣṭubh* [as seen in the variant reading] "vītī yo devam."
The remaining forty-two verses are in the *gāyatrī* meter; thus it is stated in the *Anukramaṇī*: "In 'tvam agne,' there are forty-eight [verses]; [the first] twenty-four are *vardhamāna*s.
(Note: The manuscript variants *kha*, *ja*, *jña*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *aṅku* refer to specific recensional readings.)

2. The grammatical connection is "they churn" (*manthanti*). 3. Regarding the variants *kha*, *na*, and *bha*: "In that way he has compassion" (*tathānukampate*); *śa*: "and in that way it was compassionately regarded" (*tathā cānukāntam*).
Furthermore, there is the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) [in the reading] *mānādhā*. All these are *anuṣṭubh* verses, while the others preceding them are *triṣṭubh*.

The hymn beginning with "tvam agne yajñānām" is called the *gāyatra-sūkta* because it is to be recited first by means of the *prātaranuvāka* and other rites, and it is composed in the *gāyatrī* meter.
In this context, three other verses must be omitted.
For it is stated: "One should omit the last three [verses] of 'tvam agne yajñānām'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, if the Bṛhat-sāman were to be the Abhiplava-stomasāman, then the five stotriyas and anurūpas would be as follows.
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘tvam agne yajñānām’ are the stotriya and anurūpa" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.7).

O Agni, you have been appointed as the Hotṛ-priest of all sacrifices by the gods among the human races. 1. O Agni, you have been appointed as the Hotṛ-priest of all sacrifices by the gods among the human races. 1.
O Agni, you are the *hotṛ*— the performer of the oblation— for all (*viśveṣām*) sacrifices (*yajñānām*) in the form of their completion;
or rather,
you are the invoker of the gods associated with the sacrifices.

Why is this so? To this he says: because you have been placed—that is, appointed as the Hotṛ priest—by the gods among the human race, that is, among the people of Manu who are performing sacrifice; such is the meaning.

With your delightful tongues, do you, O Great One, sacrifice for us at the ritual; bring hither the gods and worship them. 2. He—for us—with delightful tongues, at the ritual, sacrifice to the great ones; bring the gods hither and worship them. 2.
O Agni, as such, at our sacrifice (*adhvara*), with your gladdening, intoxicating, or praiseworthy tongues—meaning your flames—worship the great gods with oblations; satisfy them. How so? It is said:
bring hither, conduct here, the gods who are to be worshipped, Indra and the others.
Therefore, sacrifice and perform the ritual;
the meaning is: "Offer oblations to them."
The invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the *pāthikṛt* fire-offering is "vetthā"; this is the verse beginning with "vetthā.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "vetthā hi vedho adhvana ā devānām panthām aganma" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.10).

For you, O Ordainer, know straightway the ways and the paths of the gods, O Agni, at the sacrifices of the well-doers. 3. You; for; Ordainer; ways; paths; and; O god; straightway; O Agni; at the sacrifices; of the well-doers. 3.

O Vedaḥ, O Vidhātaḥ, O Śukṛt, O performer of auspicious deeds, O Deva endowed with qualities such as generosity, O Agni, you know directly and straightforwardly the *adhvan*—the great paths—and the *pathaḥ*—the minor paths—in the sacrifices, namely the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other rites.
Indeed, because this is so, for that reason, please cause the sacrificer who has strayed from the path of sacrifice to reach that path once again; this is the meaning.

I praise you, and furthermore, Bharata has twice praised you for prosperity with his swift steeds; he has sacrificed to you, the one worthy of sacrifice, in the rites. 4. You. I praise. And. Twice. Bharata. With swift steeds. For prosperity. He sacrificed. In sacrifices. To the one worthy of sacrifice. 4.
1. Kha-bha read *hotā yajñānām*; jha-ya read *devaḥ yajñānām*; jha-ta-na-2 read *devayajñānām*.
2. Gha-śa read *madakārībhiḥ*.
O Agni, you [were served] by Bharata, the son of Duṣyanta, a king known by this name, with [horses] possessing speed.
Vāja is food characterized by the oblation;

together with the officiating priests who possess that [food], I have praised you—twofold (*dvitā*), meaning divided into two ways in the form of attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired—with a view toward *śunaṃ*, happiness.
And having praised you, the one worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiya*), in the sacrifices...
The locative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
"With sacrifices" (yajñaiḥ) means he performed sacrifices (īje). The meaning is that you granted him both kinds of happiness.
Do thou bring these riches to Divodāsa, who presses the Soma,
and to Bharadvāja, the donor.
You, O Vāyu, brought these [cows] to Puru Divodāsa, who presses the Soma, and to Bharadvāja, the donor. 5.
