O Agni, you [bestow] these—these many, numerous, desirable, and worthy objects of choice—to Divodāsa who presses the soma;
this is comparable to the pressing of soma.
Just as you gave [wealth] to the king named Divodāsa who performs the soma-pressing, so too, give it to the seer Bharadvāja, who has offered oblations (*dāśuṣe*); this is the sense of the remainder.
As an immortal messenger, bring hither the divine folk,
listening to the well-spoken hymn of the sage.
You are the messenger; you are immortal. Bring hither the divine host, listening to the excellent praise of the sage. 6.
O immortal one, you whose nature is deathless, having become our messenger, bring hither—the divine folk associated with the gods—to our sacrifice.
What while doing so?
Listening to the beautiful hymn of praise from the wise Bharadvāja.
O Agni, you who are worthy of praise, mortals invoke the god at the sacrifices for the banquet of the gods.
O Agni, mortals with pious thoughts invoke you, the god, at the sacrifices for the enjoyment of the gods. 7.
O Agni, mortals—human beings of excellent meditation—praise, laud, or entreat you, the radiant god, at the sacrifices for the sake of satisfying the gods.
I worship your appearance and your will, O bounteous ones;
may all who desire it find pleasure in them.
I worship you for your appearance; may all the bounteous ones, desiring [you], take pleasure in your wisdom. 8.
O Agni, I offer with reverence— that is, I worship most excellently— the sight of you, which is beautiful to behold, or rather, the one who perceives correctly, the light that illuminates all;
and furthermore, I honor the will, the action, or the wisdom of you, the bountiful giver of excellent gifts.
Not only I, but all others—every single sacrificer who possesses desires—having been endowed with those various longings through your grace, they rejoice;
they serve your vision and your ritual wisdom.
1. Kha, gha, bha, and ca signify "then" (adha atha). 2. Ga, gha₁, ubhayavidha-sukha; jha, jha, ta, and na₂ signify "both kinds of happiness" (ubhaya-sukha).
3. Kha, gha, etc., [signify] "for Divodāsa"; śa signifies "for the one named Divodāsa."

4. One who is free from the nature of decay and death. 5. Those with beautiful meditations (dhyāna) characterized by the letters *kha*, *gha*, and *śa*; those with beautiful meditation (*adhyena*) characterized by *jha* and *ra*; those with beautiful study (*adhyayana*) characterized by *jha*, *ta*, *na*, and *ya*.

O Agni, you are the invoker (*hotṛ*), established by Manu, the bearer of oblations (*vahnī*), most wise with your mouth; worship the clans of heaven. || 9 || You are the invoker, established by Manu, the bearer of oblations, most wise with your mouth; O Agni, worship the clans of heaven. || 9 ||
O Agni, you are the Hotṛ; by virtue of being the Hotṛ, you have been established by Manu, placed here by Manu.
As the bearer (vahni) with your mouth—that is, with your flame which has become your mouth—you are the most wise (viduṣṭara), the one who knows best.
For this reason, perform the sacrifice for the divine subjects (viśaḥ), the celestial people belonging to the world of heaven (divaḥ).
In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, there are three *sāmidhenī* verses beginning with "O Agni, come hither" (*agna ā yāhi*).
This is stated in the Sūtra: "‘O Agni, come for the feast, being praised; the other [priests] are to be honored’" (*ādha. śrau. 1.2*).
When there is mutual contact between the *gārhapatya* and *āhavanīya* fires, an eight-potherd *puroḍāśa* cake is offered to Agni Vīti.
For this [offering], "O Agni, come hither" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘O Agni, come for the feast,’ and ‘He who [established] Agni for the feast of the gods’" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.13).

O Agni, come for the feast, being praised for the giving of the oblation; sit down as the Hotṛ-priest upon the sacred grass. 10. O Agni! Come! For the feast! Being praised! For the giving of the oblation! Sit down! As the Hotṛ! Upon the sacred grass! 10.
O Agni, come, do thou arrive;
for what purpose?
For the *vīti*, that is, for the sake of consuming the oblations.
Furthermore, for the purpose of giving the *havyas*— that is, the sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*)—
to the gods, being praised (*gṛṇānaḥ*), you, as the *hotṛ*, sit down (*ni satsi*), that is, take your seat upon the *barhis*, the spread-out *darbha* grass.

We strengthen you with fuel-sticks and with clarified butter, O Aṅgiras; blaze forth mightily, O youngest one! 11. Him | thee | with fuel-sticks | O Aṅgiras | with clarified butter | we strengthen | mightily | blaze | O youngest one || 11 ||

O Agni, son of Aṅgiras—endowed with qualities such as beauty and so forth, or whose form is like glowing coals—we cause you, who possess the aforementioned qualities, to increase by means of fuel-sticks which serve as the causes of kindling, and by means of clarified butter (ājya). Therefore, O most youthful Agni, shine forth intensely with great brilliance.
O God Agni, do thou win for us broad, glorious, and great heroic power. 12. He, O God Agni, wins for us broad, glorious, and great heroic power. 12.

O radiant Agni, you who possess the qualities previously mentioned, bring—that is, cause us to attain—toward us wealth that is broad, extensive, praiseworthy, glorious, great, and endowed with excellent heroic power.
Regarding this, the Vājasaneyaka states: “‘O God, bring [it] toward us’—by this he says, ‘O carpenter, make it go. (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.4.1.27).
1. For this reason: during the churning of the fire, the three *ṛc*s beginning with "tvāmagne puṣkarādhi" are to be recited.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'tvāmagne puṣkarādhi'—of these three [verses], one should leave off at the half-verse" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.16).
From the lotus, O Agni, Atharvan churned you forth from the head of the universe, you the worshiper.
O Agni, Atharvan churned you forth from the lotus, from the head of the entire universe, for the sake of the one who offers worship. 13.
O Agni, the seer named Atharvan churned you forth from the lotus—from the lotus leaf;
that is, he generated you from the two kindling woods.
From what kind of lotus?
"From the head"—that is, from the head that supports (*vāghataḥ*, *vāhaka*) "the entire world," the whole universe.
For, according to the Vedic scripture: "Upon that lotus-leaf, Prajāpati spread out the earth; he spread it upon that lotus-leaf" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.1.3.6).
Since the earth is the foundational support of the entire world, the lotus-leaf possesses the quality of supporting the whole world.
In this context, the word *puṣkara* denotes the lotus leaf (*puṣkaraparṇa*).
This is clearly stated in the *Taittirīyaka*: "O Agni, Atharvan found you upon the lotus leaf, having discovered you resting there" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 5.1.4.4).
The seer Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan, kindled you,
the slayer of Vṛtra, the shatterer of forts.
Thee, O slayer of Vṛtra, breaker of forts, Dadhyañc, the seer and son of Atharvan, kindled with the syllable "Ūm. 14.
O Agni, you who possess the aforementioned qualities—that very same You, the son of Atharvan, the Ṛṣi named Dadhyañc, kindled.
Of what sort?
A slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of obstructing enemies; a shatterer of forts, the breaker of the cities of the Asuras.
The bull Pādhya kindled you, the greatest slayer of Dasyus,
the winner of wealth in every battle.
Thee, O Pādhya, the bull has kindled with the sound "ūm"—thee, the greatest slayer of Dasyus, the winner of wealth in every battle. 15.
"O Agni, a certain pious friend named Avṛṣan kindled you—yes, you yourself—he inflamed you, he made you blaze.
Of what sort?
The greatest slayer of Dasyus—the most extreme destroyer of enemies who cause harm—and a winner of wealth in every battle, in every conflict."
In the Ukthya sacrifice, at the third pressing, for the Maitrāvaruṇa, the two triplets beginning with "eṣū ṣu" are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.1).
However, in the case of the Ukthyas belonging to the *ābhiplavika* [six-day] period, these two are optional as the *stotriya* and *anurūpa*.
Regarding the Ukthyas of the *ābhiplavika* period, it is stated in the Sūtra: "eṣū ṣu... bhavāni... ta ābhir agāmi bhārataḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8).
In the *paunarādheyikī* sacrifice, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the second *ājyabhāga* offering is "eṣo u.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two *ājyabhāgas* are 'eṣo u' and 'bhavāni te'. (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.8).
1. *Kha-jha-bha-yaṃ-ra-puṣkare* means "in the lotus, in the leaf of the lotus.

2. Regarding *kha-bha-pādhya*: *pādhyo vṛṣā* (vṛṣo-kha) refers to a certain seer named Pādhyo Vṛṣā; *gha-śa-pādhyo vṛṣā* (vṛṣo-gha) states that a certain seer, Pādhyo Vṛṣā, praises [you]. 3. Regarding *kha-jha-ta-na-bha-ya-ra-evaṃguṇa* (guṇaḥ-ta-ra): "O Agni, he who possesses such qualities (*evamguṇa*), even he, that Atharvan, has kindled you, indeed, you yourself, O Agni"; *gha-śa-he agne tamu tameva tvā tvāṃ he agne samīdhe*; *jha-so'pi he agne tamu tameva tvā tvāṃ samīdhe*. (In all these cases, it means: "O Agni, he too has kindled you, indeed, you yourself.")

4. *kha-jha-bha-ra-samaindhata*; *gha-śa-sādhu*; *na-rāmaidhata*. "Come here, O Agni, I will speak these other songs to you; may you grow strong by these drops. (16) *Ā*, *ihi*, *ūm*, *su*, *bravāṇi*, *te*, *agne*, *iti*, *ā*, *itarāḥ*, *giraḥ*, *ebhiḥ*, *vardhāse*, *indubhiḥ*. (16) "Come! Hither! Yes! Well! I shall speak to you, O Agni! These other songs—by these drops may you increase! (16)
"O Agni, come! Approach!
For you—for your own sake—I shall thus, in this manner, well proclaim these songs of praise," so it is prayed;
those praises are for the purpose of hearing.

7. This [verse] is a supplement. The remainder, "the other praises composed by the Asuras," is to be supplied with the word *śṛṇvati* ("hears"). And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "O Agni, these other songs"—"for the other songs are indeed asuric" (AiB 3.49).
Moreover, you shall be strengthened—grow strong—by these, by these drops of soma that have arrived.
Wherever you set your mind and your superior skill, there you shall establish your seat. 17. Wherever—wherever—your mind and your superior skill you employ, there you shall establish your seat. 17.

O Agni, wherever—be it in any place or with any sacrificer—your mind, which is of the nature of grace, dwells within the internal organ, there, upon that sacrificer, you bestow and maintain an exalted, most excellent, and strengthening power or food;
likewise, you prepare a dwelling-place for him;
you establish it for that sacrificer.

For you, O Vasu, have never failed to bestow the fulfillment of those who offer oblations; therefore, you shall win over the two worlds. 18. For you, O Vasu, have never failed to bestow the fulfillment of those who offer oblations; therefore, you shall win over the two worlds. 18.
O Agni, let that filling brilliance of yours—which protects the eyes and destroys [disease]—never fail us;
may it always grant us the power of sight.
O Vasu of these [people].
The word *nema* signifies "few.
It refers to the dwelling place of only a few among men who are sacrificers.
Therefore, for this reason, accept with favor (*vanavase*) the service (*duvaḥ*) performed by us, the sacrificers.

Agni has come, the descendant of Bharata, the slayer of Vṛtra, the one of many insights, the true lord of Divodāsa. 19. Agni has come; the descendant of Bharata, the slayer of Vṛtra, the one of many insights, the true lord of Divodāsa. 19.
This Agni has come;
he has been approached by us with our hymns of praise.
Of what nature is he?
Bhārata: the sustainer of oblations; Divodāsa’s: belonging to the king known by this name; Vṛtrahā: the slayer of Vṛtras, that is, enemies; Purucetana:
the perceiver or knower of many, meaning omniscient; Satpati: the protector of the good, namely the sacrificers.

For he, by his greatness, shall bestow all earthly wealth; winning it, he is unassailable and unconquered. 20. He—indeed; all; beyond; earthly; wealth; shall give; with his majesty; winning; unhurt; unconquered. 20.
1. I shall proclaim, I shall declare.
2. With praises; with our praises.
For he indeed—that Agni—transcending all earthly beings existing upon the earth by his greatness and his own majesty, shall grant us wealth as a prize; let him give it to us.
Or alternatively:
may he give—that is, bestow in abundance—the entire (*viśvam*), all-encompassing (*sarvam*) wealth (*rathim*) existing on earth (*pārthivam*).
Of what nature is Agni?

By his greatness—that is, by his majesty and splendor—he strikes down the obstacles or destroys the enemies; he is unassailed, being unopposed by other foes, and unhurt, being uninjured by anyone whatsoever.
O Agni, being ancient yet renewed by your newest [form], you have spread far with your gathered brilliance and your light.
O Agni, like the ancients, with your newest [flame], joined with you all, you have spread forth greatly with your light. 21.

O Agni, you who are distinguished by the qualities previously mentioned—you, being such, like the ancient one, with your most new, youthful, radiant, and well-restrained light that moves perfectly toward the goal, have spread out, that is, you extend, the vast intermediate space.
O friends, boldly offer a hymn and a sacrifice to Agni; sing and chant for the Ordainer.
O friends, for you, with bold resolve, offer a hymn and a sacrifice to Agni; sing and chant for the Ordainer. ||22||
O friends—meaning you officiating priests who share a common station—sing a hymn of praise to Agni, the ordainer and creator, for his boldness against enemies;
likewise, offer up the sacrifice and the oblation that accomplishes the rite.
For he, the Hotṛ of sage-like wisdom, who sat among the human generations,
is the messenger and the bearer of oblations.
For he is the one who, as the Hotṛ, has sat down through the human ages; is he not the seasonal messenger and the bearer of oblations? 23.
He is indeed that Agni: let him sit down, let him take his seat upon the *barhis* grass at our sacrifice.

He who is Agni, the invoker (*hotṛ*) of the gods, possessed of the wisdom of a seer (*kavikratu*), [who attends] the human ages—the human ages, those specific times connected with mankind in which sacrifices are performed.
The second case ending is used to express continuous connection (atyantasaṃyoga).
For all this time he has been the messenger of the gods;
he is the bearer of oblations, the carrier of your sacrificial offerings.
O Vasu, worship here those two kings, the Ādityas of pure vows, the host of Maruts, and the two worlds, Rodasī.
O King, O you of pure vows, worship here the Ādityas, the host of Maruts, and the two worlds, O Vasu. 24.

O Vasu, O Agni, the dweller, worship here at this sacrifice these deities: Mitra and Varuna, those two well-known kings who shine and whose vows are pure; the Adityas, the sons of Aditi, beginning with Dhātṛ; the host of Maruts, the assembly of the Maruts; and Rodasī, Heaven and Earth. Perform the sacrifice to them.

1. *kha*, *jña*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra* are the substitutes for *dha*. 2. *jha*, *ta*, *bha*, *ya*, *ra* are the substitutes for *yajamāna-sādhana*. 3. *śa*, *yāgādayaḥ* (the group beginning with *yāga*). 4. *sa* becomes *bha*; *gha* becomes *śa*; *jha* becomes *san*. 5. *gha* becomes *bhavasi*. "O Agni, thy sight is auspicious, desired by mortals, O Son of Strength, of the Immortal. (RV 6.16.34) *vastvīm* | *te* | *agne* | *saṃdṛṣṭiḥ* | *iṣyate* | *martyāya* | *ūrjaḥ* | *napāt* | *amṛtasya* || 25 || "Auspicious," "thy," "O Agni," "sight," "is desired," "by mortals," "O Son of Strength," "of the Immortal. || 25 ||

O Agni, Son of Strength, Son of Power, the splendor—that is, the radiant light—of you, the immortal one who is free from death, is excellent; it is "vasvī," meaning it provides dwelling or clothing. This is for the sake of praise. It is sent forth, or desired, for the mortal, the human sacrificer. That is to say, it bestows [blessings]. 2 || 25 ||

Through his wisdom, may he be the most excellent giver today; winning you, the one with beautiful wealth, the mortal has attained the well-fashioned hymn. 26. Through his wisdom, let him be the best giver today; winning you, the one with beautiful wealth, the mortal has attained the well-fashioned hymn. 26.

O Agni, may the sacrificer who today, at this very moment, wins you over by means of his *kratu*—that is, by his ritual action consisting of service—and who offers the oblations (*havīṃṣi*), be the most excellent, the most highly praised;
may he also possess beautiful wealth (*surekaṇāḥ*).
Likewise, may that mortal man attain a well-fashioned hymn of praise directed toward you.
May this Agni, with his sharp and piercing flame—that is, his splendor—strike down and slay every devouring demon, such as the Rākṣasas and others.
Furthermore, may Agni bestow wealth and riches upon us.

Bring hither wealth with brave sons, O Jātavedas, for the sake of the hero; slay the demons, O you of noble power! 29. Bring hither wealth with brave sons, O Jātavedas, for the sake of the hero; slay the demons, O you of noble power! 29.

O Jātavedas—possessor of innate wisdom or possessor of innate wealth—O Virṣaṇi, the special seer, bring hither (ā bhara) wealth (rayi) consisting of excellent heroes (suvīra), that is, accompanied by sons, grandsons, and the like.
Likewise, O Sukratu, knower of good deeds, slay (jahi) and destroy the Rākṣasas.

Do you, O Jātavedas, protect us from distress and from the one who intends evil; guard us, O Sage, as the protector of sacred prayer. 30. Do you; us; protect; from distress; O Jātavedas; from the one intending evil; guard; us; O Sage; as the protector of sacred prayer. 30.
O Jātavedas, do you protect us from distress— that is, guard us against sin.
Likewise, O Brahmaṇaspati, O Sage of the mantra consisting of praise, O Agni who causes sounds to be uttered—
for it is Agni who produces sound.
And so it is recorded in the Smṛti: "The mind strikes the bodily fire; that [fire] impels the wind;
the wind, moving within the chest, produces the deep tone.
Protect us from such an enemy who, being malevolent (*aghāyataḥ*), desires harm (*agham*) for us.

O Agni, whatever mortal man, acting with evil intent, offers us up for slaughter—protect us from that sin. (31) O Agni, whatever mortal man, acting with evil intent, offers us up for slaughter—protect us from that distress. (31)
O Agni, that mortal man of evil intent who delivers us over to his own weapon— to slay us— meaning,
who strikes us with his armament;
from that man and from calamity, protect us, O Agni.

O God, with your tongue, drive away from us that evildoer, the mortal who seeks to kill us. 32. You; him; O God; with the tongue; away; drive away; the evildoer; the mortal; who; us; seeks to kill. 32.
O radiant God Agni, do thou with thy tongue—thy flame—drive away and destroy on all sides that evildoer, the man who performs evil deeds;
[destroy] that mortal, the human being, who seeks to strike us down.

O Agni, most victorious one, grant wide-spreading protection to Bharadvāja; grant him desirable wealth. 33. To Bharadvāja; O wide-spreading one; protection; grant; O victorious one; O Agni; desirable; wealth. 33. To Bharadvāja; he; wide-spreading; protection; grant; O victorious one; O Agni; desirable; wealth.
1. Possessing wisdom born of *kha*, *gha*, and *ṅa*. 2. There is no *kha*, *na*, *bha*, or *ya*.
O Agni, conqueror of enemies, grant and bestow upon me, the seer Bharadvāja, a wide and expansive *śarma*—a protection, happiness, or dwelling that is broad on all sides.
Likewise, grant us that which is most excellent (*vareṇya*) and desirable wealth (*vasu*).
On the full moon day, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the butter-portion (*ājyabhāga*) dedicated to Agni is this: "Agni [who] struck down the Vṛtras.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'Agnir vṛtrāṇi jaghnan' is the invitatory verse for the first butter-portion" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.5).

In the *iṣṭi*, *paśu*, and *soma* sacrifices, wherever no specific injunction is seen—such as those involving the *vṛdhanvatī* or *puṣṭimant* verses—this very [verse] is everywhere the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the first *ājyabhāga*.
This is the invitatory verse for the *Āgneya* offering at the *upasad*, but it is the offering verse (*yājyā*) specifically for the evening [offering].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Agnir vṛtrāṇi jaghnathe’ and ‘ugra hava śaryehe’—there is a reversal of the offering and invitatory verses" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.8).
Desiring wealth, he has overcome all obstacles with his various powers—kindled, bright, and invoked with offerings. 34.
Agni, seeking wealth, has slain the Vṛtras with his inspired praise; kindled by the sacrificial food, he is bright and invoked with oblations. ||34||

Being praised with eloquent hymns, Agni—desiring wealth, that is, desiring riches for the praisers, or rather, desiring for himself the wealth characterized by the oblation—shall strike down, or slay utterly, the *vṛtras*, which are the obstructing forces such as the Rākṣasas or the darknesses. What kind of Agni? One who is well-kindled, and therefore bright and white-colored, and one who has been invoked with oblations.
The father of the father, shining within the womb of the mother in the imperishable, has settled in the seat of Truth. 35.
Within the womb; of the mother; of the father; the father; shining with triple light; sitting in the imperishable; the seat of the Eternal Order (Ṛta). //35//

In this context, by the words "mother" and "father," the earth and the sky are intended, according to the Vedic scripture: "The sky is indeed the father, the earth is the mother" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.191.6).

Within the womb—the interior place—of the mother, that is, the earth; specifically, within the imperishable (akṣara), i.e., the unchanging, station known as the altar (vedi); he who is "vididyutānaḥ," shining forth intensely, is the "father of the father," the protector of the celestial world (dyuloka) through the offering of oblations.

Agni, being thus situated, sat down—that is, he took his seat—upon the *uttaravedi*, the sacrificial hearth known as the *dhiṣṇya* (the accusative case here serving the sense of the locative). The syntactical connection is: "while sitting upon the *uttaravedi*, he struck down the Vṛtras."
35 | O Jātavedas, you who are far-seeing, bring us Brahman that is accompanied by progeny, O Agni, which may shine forth through the two worlds. 36 |
O Brahman, bring hither that which brings offspring, O Jātavedas, thou who art far-seeing; O Agni, that which shines in heaven. ||36||

O Jātavedas, knower of all that is born, O far-seeing Agni, bring hither—that is, procure—for us the *brahma*, which is food accompanied by progeny, sons, and grandsons. Bring that food which shines in the heavenly world (*divi*) among the gods, and that which is most excellent and resplendent; this is the meaning.
O Agni, son of strength, we have sent forth our songs toward you, who are beautiful to behold. 37. O Agni, son of strength, we have sent forth our songs toward you, who are beautiful to behold.
O Agni, you of great deeds, we have sent forth our songs of praise toward you, who are lovely to behold. 37.
1. [The letters] *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *'ca'* do not exist.
2. [The letters] *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *r-thauḥ* [do not exist].

O *sahasrakṛta*, you who are produced by force (*sahasā*) and power (*balena*), O *agne*, we, possessing *prayas*—that is, possessing oblations characterized by sacrificial food (*havir-lakṣaṇa*)—offer up our *giraḥ*, our hymns of praise, toward you, who possess a delightful appearance (*raṇada-saṃdarśam*), that is, one whose sight is beautiful or whose sight is worthy of praise; we release them, meaning we utter them.
Like the shade of a cloud from the heat, we have come to your protection,
O Agni, you who are like gold in appearance.
Like [one seeking] shade from the heat, we have come for refuge to you, O Agni, who are like gold in appearance. 38.
O Agni, of you who are like gold—whose splendor is most delightful, or rather whose splendor shines like gold—of you, the glowing one, we have approached your protection, your refuge, your shelter;
therein is the illustration:
as if [approaching] shade.
Just as those afflicted by heat, being tormented, approach the shade, so it is in that case.
In the Upasad rite, for the offering to Agni at the morning time, "ya ugraḥ" is the *yājyā*, and for the evening time, "sve daivyāya" is the *anuvākyā*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "agnim trāṇi jajñānaḥ, ya ugraḥ śarya-hā" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.8).
O Agni, like a fierce bull with sharpened horns, you have shattered the fortresses as the slayer of Śarī.
Like a fierce archer, like a sharp-horned bull, O Agni, you have shattered the fortresses. 39.

O Agni, you who are fierce, possessing uprooting strength, like an archer who slays with arrows—slaying enemies with his shafts; like a bull with sharp horns, one whose movement is desirable—you, O Agni, shattered the three Asuric fortresses in front of you; you are the destroyer. For according to the Śruti, "This Agni is indeed Rudra" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.1.3.1), the burning of the triple city performed by Rudra is also attributed to Agni, and thus he is praised.
Or alternatively:
Because fire exists as an army within the arrow that serves as the means for burning Tripura, it is said that "fire wanders through the cities.
This should be understood in accordance with the Brāhmaṇa passage beginning: "The gods and the Asuras contended for these worlds" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 1.23).
When the fire is being produced by friction, "ā yaṃ haste" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "One should begin with the half-verse, 'ā yaṃ haste na khādinam'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.16).
They bear him in their hands like a ring, like a newborn infant—
the Agni who performs the sacrifice well for the people.
Him whom they bear with their hands like a child at birth who does not yet gnaw [at wood], Agni, the one who makes the sacrifice successful for the people. 40.
The Adhvaryu priests hold in their hands—that fire produced by churning—as if holding a newborn son in their arms; they bear it facing them in their hands.
The first "na" (like) is used in the sense of comparison even when placed before the object. It is like a "khādin," that is, like a devourer such as a tiger or similar beast.
The meaning is that the men who carry him are as if they have become absorbed in that very act.
Alternatively, in the sense of "now" (*saṃprati*), [he is] now (*saṃprati*) a sword-bearer (*khādinaṃ*).

1. Kha, Jha, Na, Bha, Ra, Ra: *raṇasaṃdarśaṃ* (the sight of battle); *raṇavam* (the sound of battle). 2. Ta, Śa: *°māśrayaṇaṃ sukhaṃ vā* (or the refuge/comfort thereof). 3. Kha, Jha, Ta, Na, Bha, Ra, Śa: *°śaryaiḥ* (with arrows). 4. Kha, Bha: *vyāghrādikamiva*; Gha: *vyāghramiva* (like a tiger, etc.; like a tiger).
O Agni, come toward us; approach us.
Likewise, having focused upon the oblations characterized as *ayās*, bring the gods here.
For what purpose?
Bring those gods here for the sake of their consuming the oblations— that is, for eating them— and likewise for the sake of drinking the Soma— that is, for the drinking of the Soma.
O Agni, descendant of Bharata, shine forth with brilliant, straight-tipped flame;
endowed with a ladle, blaze up, O ageless one.
O Agni, descendant of Bharata, shine forth with splendor; endowed with a straight path and a ladle, blaze and radiate, O ageless one! 45.
O Bhārata, O Agni, lord of oblations, blaze forth, shine most intensely!
He explains that very point:
O ageless one, free from decay, shining brightly, you, being radiant, [shine] with radiance—that is, with luminous splendor.
The third case ending is elided by the rule "supāṃ suluk".
7. Shine forth with undecaying and uninterrupted splendor; manifest yourself preeminently.
Alternatively,
the root *bhā* contains an implied causative sense (*ṇyartha*).
It should be construed as follows: "First, you yourself shine forth; afterwards, illuminate the entire world with your own splendor."
The man who, with an oblation, honors the god in his thought, and at the sacrifice praises him with an offering—
let him, with uplifted hands and reverence, seek to win the Hotṛ priest, the true sacrificer of heaven and earth.

The one who, with an offering, would serve the god Agni in his thought, and being possessed of oblations, should praise him at the sacrifice—the Hotṛ priest whose sacrifices are true—should seek to win him over with outstretched hands and with reverence from both worlds. 46.

Whatever mortal man, being possessed of oblations (*havirmān*), as a sacrificer (*yajamāna*), should serve (*duvasyet*) any deity whatsoever with a desirable food characterized by oblations (*vītyā vītyā*), he should praise (*īḷīta*) Agni at that sacrifice (*adhvare*).
The meaning is that Agni is honored in all sacrifices.
Of what nature is Agni?

The invoker (hotṛ) of the gods dwelling in the two worlds of heaven and earth (rodasī), the offerer of true sacrifice (satyayaj)— that is, one who sacrifices with an offering that is real and not false—
this sacrificer, with hands uplifted and palms joined in reverence (añjali), should seek to win over or serve such an Agni with homage (namas) or with an oblation.
We bring to you first with a verse this oblation fashioned by the heart;
may these be for you: bulls, oxen, and even barren cows.
To you, O Agni, we bring with a verse an oblation fashioned by the heart; may these be for you: bulls, oxen, and even barren cows. 47.

Āśvalāyana considers that the study of other [Vedic texts] is also praiseworthy (ĀśGṛ 1.1.5). O Agni, for you—with a heart, that is, with a mind fashioned and prepared by means of the *ṛc*, which exists in the form of the *ṛc*—we bring forth the oblation; having made the *ṛc* itself the oblation, we offer it.
By the word "for you" (*te*), the aforementioned oblation is referred back.
With reference to those being pointed out, there is the masculine plural form:
"May your forms (rūpāṇi) be bulls (ukṣaṇaḥ)—that is, oxen (ukṣāṇaḥ) capable of sprinkling—bulls (ṛṣabhāsaḥ)—that is, bulls (ṛṣabhāḥ)—and also (uta) cows (vaśāḥ).
The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: "Having been transformed into the form of bulls and cows, may they exist for your protection."
1. *Kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *ya* are for the purpose of eating; *ta*, *ra*, and *sa* are for the purpose of sitting. 2. [The word] "manyate" is not used.

It has been stated that these belong to the *Vaitānika* [section]. Having begun with the words, "In this section there is indeed joy through knowledge alone," it was formulated in the Sūtra: "We bring to you first the oblation fashioned by the heart with a verse; may they become for you swift steeds, bulls, and cows. And thus, for one who studies this private recitation (*svādhyāya*), these very [syllables] become oxen, bulls, and cows.

The gods kindle Agni, the foremost, the best slayer of Vṛtra, by whom wealth is brought hither, who is a destroyer of demons, and full of vigor. 48. Agni. The gods. The foremost. They kindle. The best slayer of Vṛtra. By whom. Wealth. Is brought hither. A destroyer. Of demons. Full of vigor. 48.
The gods kindle this Agni, the foremost, the greatest slayer of Vṛtra—the one who most exceedingly destroys Vṛtra.

By means of this Agni, the riches (vasūni)—the wealth characterized by oblations or sacrificial offerings that had been seized by the Asuras—were brought back from the presence of the Asuras or recovered from Yama.
And by means of that powerful (vājina) Agni, the Rākṣasas, the obstructors of sacrifice, were crushed (tuḷahā) and destroyed (hiṃsitāni). Such is the syntactical connection: "they kindle that Agni."
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of ignorance,
may Vidyātīrthamaheśvara bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the fourth book of the Commentary on the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the glorious King of Kings, Supreme Lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
The sixth chapter of the fourth Aṣṭaka begins.
In the second Anuvāka of the sixth Maṇḍala, the first hymn has been explained.
Therein, the second hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "Drink the Soma," is the Ṛṣi Bharadvāja’s composition and is in the Triṣṭubh metre.
The last [verse] is a two-footed *triṣṭubh*.
Thus it is stated in the index: "The hymn beginning with 'piba' consists of five fewer [verses], is addressed to Indra, is in the *triṣṭubh* meter, and ends with a two-footed [verse].
This is the insertion (*nirviva*) for the *marutvatīya* śastra at the Abhijit sacrifice.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘Piba somam, tam u duhi’—this is for the midday [pressing] (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.5).
This Sūtra occurs in the Marutvatīya Śastra on the eighth day of the Daśarātra sacrifice.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘Piba somam abhi tam asya dyāvāpṛthivī’ (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.7).
On the *ekāha* day, at the *marutvatīya* [śastra], this hymn is introduced with the *nivid*.
For it is prescribed: "O Sūryastuta, desiring glory, drink the Soma" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 9.8).
This hymn is also used at the *marutvatīya* of the *mahāvrata*.
Likewise, it is stated in the *Pañcamāraṇyaka*: “Drink the Soma, O fierce one, for whom you have been the slayer; with what splendor do those of equal age dwell in the same abode? (Ai. Ā. 5.1.1).
At the midday libation (*mādhyandina-savana*), these first three verses serve as the *prasthitayājyās* for the Hotṛ, Maitrāvaruṇa, and Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priests.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘Drink the Soma, O fierce one, for whom you have been the slayer’—these three [verses]; ‘Come hither, they call thee, O lover of Soma, Svāhā! (Āśva. Śrau. 5.5).

Drink the Soma, O fierce Indra, whom you have sought; being praised, open wide the great stall of cattle. O bold one, wielder of the thunderbolt, may you, increasing all things, strike down Vṛtra and all hostile forces with your arrows. 1. Drink the Soma! Toward that which you, O fierce one, have sought—the vast stall of cattle—being greatly praised, O Indra! You who, O bold one, wielder of the thunderbolt, have increased [all things], [strike] Vṛtra and all hostile powers with your arrows. 1.

1. [The variants] *kha*, *jha*, *na*, and *bha* read *dīpayante*. 2. [The variants] *kha*, *jha*, *bha*, and *sāyaṇāmāsyena*; [the variant] *ra* reads *sāyaṇāyaṇa*. 3. [The variant] *ta1* reads *mahasvati*. 4. [The variants] *jha*, *ta*, *bha*, and *ya* read *mādhyandinasavane*.
O *ugra*, O Indra of fierce power, being praised (*guṇānaḥ*) by the Aṅgirases, you—[having] *abhi-iśya* (aimed at) that Soma, meaning, for the purpose of drinking it.
You have revealed that great, vast, and extensive mass of cattle that had been seized by the Paṇis;
for the root *gṛdh* here signifies the act of revealing.
Drink that Soma; perform the drinking.
O bold one, subduer of enemies, O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt in your hand—you who, accompanied by your powers and strengths, [overcame] all Vṛtra, the obstructer, and all unfriendly enemies.
From the word *amitra*, there is the substitution of *iy* for the singular accusative case ending.
"You have struck him down, you have struck him apart; therefore, O Soma, drink"—this is the connection [of the words].

Drink this, O Indra—you who are the possessor of the *ṛjīṣa*, the overcomer, the one with beautiful jaws, the bull among hymns, the breaker of the cow-stalls, the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the one who stands upon the bay horses; pierce through to wondrous spoils of war!

Drink this, O Indra—you who are the possessor of the *ṛjīṣa*, the deliverer, the one with beautiful jaws, the bull, the one who is the master of hymns, the breaker of the cow-pens, the wielder of the thunderbolt, and the one who stands upon his two bay horses—O Indra, pierce through to the wondrous spoils of war! 2.

O Indra, you who possess the *ṛjīṣa*—by the word *ṛjīṣa*, the Soma whose essence has been extracted is meant—you who are the *tarutra*, the deliverer of enemies; you who are *śipravat*, possessed of beautiful jaws; you who [are the master] of *matīnām*, the hymns of praise.
The suffix *ktic* is applied to the root *man*, which has the sense of praising, to form the agentive noun.
O Bull, you are the showerer of desires; as such, drink this Soma.

O Indra, you who are the wielder of the thunderbolt, you who are the breaker of the enclosures—whether of mountains or clouds—and you who are the rider upon the two bay horses, O Indra, pierce open for us the various and wondrous prizes; reveal them to us.
Thus protect us as in the ancient days; let [the soma] exhilarate you. Hear our prayer and grow strong through our songs.
Make the sun manifest, cause the nourishments to swell, slay the enemies, and pierce open the cattle-pens, O Indra.

Thus! Protect us! As in the ancient way, may [the Soma] exhilarate you! Hear our prayer! Be strengthened by our songs! Make the sun manifest! Cause the nourishments to swell! Slay the enemies! O Indra, break open the enclosures for the cattle! 3.
O Indra, just as you drank the ancient Soma-sacrifices in the manner of the ancients of old, even so, drink this our Soma.
And may that Soma, once drunk by you, exhilarate you.
Listen to the *brahman*, the hymn of praise composed by us.
Moreover, increase—grow stronger—through the *gobhiḥ*, that is, through the songs consisting of praise.
Furthermore, O Sūrya, the impeller of all, make him manifest; reveal him.
The meaning is: act in such a way that we may behold Sūrya.
Cause our food and our wisdom to swell; make them overflow for us. Slay the enemies who revile us, so that they may perish.
O Indra, disclose and bring forth the cattle that were carried away by the Paṇis.

1. You have illuminated the light of the knower (*jña-prākāśaya*); illuminate that which is beyond fear (*ta-bha-ya-prakāśaya*). 2. Possessing the essence of *gha-śa*, you do not abandon the moon (*soma*) even when its substance has departed.
3. You, who are [composed of] *kha-jha-ta-na-bha-ra*, do not exist.
4. jña—make him intoxicated; gha—make him endowed with joy.
5. kha-bha—cause him to drink; śa—cause him to swell.

O Indra, possessor of self-power (*svadhāvan*), may these exhilarating draughts, once drunk, sprinkle you—the radiant one—copiously with greatness. O Indra, may these intoxicating soma juices cause you, the great, the perfect, the powerful, the all-pervading, and the subduer of enemies, to rejoice intensely. *te tvā madā bṛhadindra svadhāva ime pītā ukṣayanta ghumantam | mahāmanūnaṃ tavasaṃ virbhūti matsarāso jahṛṣanta prasāham || 4 ||* O *svadhāvan* (possessor of food/energy), O Indra, these exhilarating draughts, when drunk, shall sprinkle you—the luminous one—with vast abundance. Furthermore, O Indra, let these intoxicating soma juices cause you—who are great, complete, powerful, all-encompassing, and the overcomer of foes—to exult greatly. 1. "Sprinkle" (*ukṣayanta*) means they shall drench you exceedingly. 2. "Great" (*mahān*) means abundant; "perfect" (*anūnam*) means devoid of deficiency in any quality, i.e., endowed with full attributes. "Powerful" (*tavasam*) means increased in strength; "all-pervading" (*virbhūtim*) means possessing pervasive power; "subduer" (*prasāham*) means the conqueror of enemies.

With which [Soma juices], being exhilarated, you caused the Sun and the Dawn to shine forth, rending asunder the firm enclosures; with which, O Indra, you pushed aside the great mountain that encompassed the cows, [the mountain] which was immovable from its place and unshakable from its seat. O Indra, with those [juices], being exhilarated—that is, rejoicing—you caused the Sun, the impeller of all, and the goddess Dawn to shine in their own places. Or rather, you acted so that the Sun and Dawn dispelled the darkness. Doing what? Rending asunder the firm and difficult-to-pierce darkness. Furthermore, O Indra, you pushed aside—the word *nutthāḥ* means you drove away—the great mountain (*adrim*) which surrounded the cows stolen by the Paṇis. Of what nature was it? It was situated within its own dwelling (*sadasaḥ*), immovable (*acyutam*), and unshakable (*pari khāt*), meaning it was stable and indestructible. 3.

By your wisdom, by your impetuous deeds, and by your power, you have placed the ripe milk within the raw cows; you have opened the doors for the ruddy ones. You, like the Aṅgirases, have released the cattle from the enclosure and have cleansed them from the obstructing bonds. O Indra, by your wisdom (*kratvā*), that is, by your own inspired insight; by your impetuous deeds (*taṃhasanābhiḥ*), that is, by your own actions; and by your power (*śacyā*), you have firmly established (*ni dīdhaḥ*) that well-known mature milk within the raw cows, which were not yet ripened. Furthermore, O Indra, for the sake of the ruddy cows (*usriyābhyaḥ*)—that is, in order to let the cattle out—you have opened the firm doors (*duraḥ*) with your strength, breaking through the obstacles such as stones. And indeed, like the Aṅgirases, you have released the cows from the enclosure and purified them from their fetters.

1. May Kha, Jña, Ta, Na, Bha, Ya, and Ra be pleased; may Jha be pleased; may Śa rejoice. 2. The meaning is that [the lineage] is complete with Kha, Jña, Ta, Na, Bha, Ya, and Ra. 3. There is no "moved" (ācālita) for Kha, Jña, Ta, Na, Bha, Ya, and Ra. 4. The meaning is that it is established in Jña and Ta. 5. By nature, Gha and Śa. 6. From Śa and Go; the dative case is used in the sense of purpose (tādarthye). Of the Aṅgirases. 7. The meaning is that it is restrained by Śa. (Verses 3–5)

The meaning is "they were made. You have opened wide the doors; you, endowed with the Aṅgirases, [have released] the cows from the vast enclosure—that is, from the cow-pen. You have caused them to emerge.

You have reached the earth, O you of great wondrous power; you have filled the wide expanse and the sky, O Indra. You have propped up the vast [atmosphere] and held firm the two worlds, whose sons are the gods—the ancient, mighty Mothers of the Eternal Order (Ṛta).

You have reached the earth; great is your wondrous deed! O Seer, you have propped up the wide heaven on high. O Indra, you have supported the two worlds, the parents of the gods, the ancient and mighty mothers of the Eternal Order (Ṛta). 7.
O Indra, you, by means of a great and wondrous deed, have spread out—the wide and expansive earth—and have especially filled it.
(The root *prā* means "to fill.
O lofty Indra, you, being great, have propped up the vast heaven above.
The meaning is that Indra acts so that she remains unsupported, like the sky which does not fall;
moreover, you have sustained and indeed do sustain the two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*), with nourishments. Of what nature are they?
"O Devaputras!
Those two whose sons are the gods.
The two ancient, primordial Mothers, the fashioners of the *ṛta*—whether that be water or the sacrifice—the two great sacrifices."
Or alternatively:
the two mothers of the universe, the great and holy ones of the *ṛta* (cosmic order) and the *brahman*;
"yat" is a name for the Lord.
All the gods, O Indra, placed you alone—the one powerful one—in the forefront for the sake of battle;
when the godless one assailed the gods, they chose Indra here in the struggle for the light of heaven.

All the gods, O Indra, placed you alone—the one powerful one—in the forefront for the sake of battle. When the godless one defied the gods, they chose Indra there at the winning of the light of heaven. 8.

Now, at this time, O Indra, all the Viśve Devās—the Vahnis and others—have placed you, the one preeminent, powerful, and mighty one, in front for the sake of battle; they have set you at their head. When the godless Asura Vṛtra marched against the gods for the purpose of combat—*āṃhati* being a verb meaning "to go."
Furthermore, at this time, during a lack of rain or even during a drought, they chose Indra—that is, the Maruts—during the battle; they shared in his favor.
For it is said that when the other gods had fled, the Maruts alone remained with and supported Indra.
Now, regarding the city: the connection is "they took.
Then indeed the heaven itself, through its own fury, was struck down by the thunderbolt and trembled with fear.
When Indra, with his full vital power, struck down the serpent who was plotting against him so that he might lie dead,

then even the heaven itself bowed away from your thunderbolt out of fear of its own wrath— when Indra, with all his life-force, struck down the serpent who was plotting against him so that he might lie dead.
1. *jha*—all the gods; *ta*—all the gods, all.
2. *kha-jha-jha-ta-na-bha-ya-ra-devāḥ*—the remainder is that these are the Maruts.
Excluding Indra, they used to share [the offerings] together.

Even the well-known *dyauḥ*, the celestial world, which serves as the support for the gods—O Indra, at this very time, out of fear (*bhiyasā*) of your two-fold (*dvitā*) thunderbolt (*vajrāt*) and of your own wrath (*manyoh*), it bowed down (*apāmanat*).
The particle *nu* is a filler.
When the all-knowing (*viśvayuḥ*) Indra [struck] the serpent Vṛtra, who was approaching him, upon his bed (*śayathe*), that is, for the purpose of his lying down.
The meaning is "for the sake of death.
*nyavadhīt* means "he struck down" or "he killed. *cit* is an expletive used for metrical completion.
When he slew Vṛtra at that time, then the sky was called by that name—this is the connection [of the verse].

Then Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned for you, O mighty one, the fierce thunderbolt with a thousand spikes and a hundred edges, well-fashioned and free from blemish, with which, O consumer of the soma-residue, you crushed the serpent Nahus here. Then Tvaṣṭṛ, for you, O mighty one, fashioned the fierce thunderbolt with a thousand spikes and a hundred edges, well-fashioned and free from blemish, with which, O consumer of the soma-residue, you crushed the serpent Nahus here.
Now, O Ugra, Lord of the host of the Udganas, Tvaṣṭṛ, the divine artisan, fashioned for you—that great one—your thunderbolt; he turned it back, having brought it to completion.
Of what sort was it?
It had a thousand points, a thousand edges, a hundred facets, and a hundred joints.
O Indra, possessor of the *ṛjīṣa*, like Soma whose essence has been consumed; with that thunderbolt by which [you act] according to your desire—he whose desire is restrained;
[he who is] not delighting.

You crushed—that is, you ground to powder—the serpent Vṛtra, the Asura, who possessed a mind intent on attacking his enemies and who was roaring like a horse; the meaning is that you fashioned that thunderbolt [to destroy him].

May all the Maruts, acting in harmony, increase him; O Indra, cook a hundred greatnesses for you. May Pūṣan and Viṣṇu pour forth three lakes—the exhilarating, intoxicating soma-portion—for this slayer of Vṛtra. 11. May they increase him; whom; all; the Maruts; acting in harmony; cook; a hundred; greatnesses; O Indra; for you; Pūṣan; Viṣṇu; three; lakes; poured forth; the Vṛtra-slayer; the exhilarating; the portion; for him. 11.

O Indra, may all the Maruts— the gods who take delight together— those who magnify you with hymns, for your sake, may Pūṣan, the god of that name, and Viṣṇu, the god of that name, cook a hundred great sacrificial animals.
Moreover, for you, the three vessels— the Droṇakalaśa, the Patabhra, and the Ādavanīya— have come to the Soma shoots, meaning the Soma fills the vessels.
What kind of Soma? "Madi" means intoxicating; "vṛtrahan" means the slayer of Vṛtras, that is, enemies.
Here, by the term "vṛtrahan," the Soma is designated.
For it is only when there is a vessel that Indra becomes capable of slaying the Vṛtras; such is the meaning.

He released the great, obstructed flood of the rivers, the swelling wave of the waters that lay encompassed. Along their downward flow, O Indra, you cleared the path; you sent the waters rushing down toward the ocean. (12) He released the great, obstructed flood of the rivers, the swelling wave of the waters that lay encompassed. Along their downward flow, O Indra, you cleared the path; you sent the waters rushing down toward the ocean. (12)

1. In the manuscripts kha, gha, ma, and śa, the phrase "dvitā...dvipakārān" does not exist. 2. In the manuscripts kha, gha, ma, and śa, [the reading is] "by means of wood that is doubled (dvitā) and of two kinds (dvipakāreṇa)," and by mind (manasā) at the time of *bha*. 3. Regarding the word *nū cid*. 4. In manuscript śa, [the reading is] "he struck (*jaghāna*) in that. 5. In manuscripts jha, ta, na, and bha, [the reading is] "unmindful" (*aramanasam*). 6. In manuscripts kha and ma, [the reading is] "having drunk" (*āpīte*).

O Indra, you released (*āsṛjaḥ*), poured forth on all sides, the great (*mahi*) flood (*kṣodaḥ*)—the water belonging to the rivers and streams—which was encompassed (*vṛtam*), surrounded, covered, and situated on all sides (*pariṣṭhitam*) by Vṛtra.
By which [power] the rivers flow full; this is the meaning.
You have created a mass (*ūrmi*) of waters (*apām*), that is, of water.
The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.

O Indra, you have made the paths—meaning the roads and routes—of those rivers flow downwards, that is, along their slopes; this is the sense of the verb "anvakārṣīḥ" (you have made following). The verb is supplied through the connection with the prefix "anu. Furthermore, [you have made them] "nīcīḥ," meaning directed toward the downward slope.
The meaning is "endowed with speed.
*Apamaḥ* means "waters" (*apaḥ*, *udakāni*). The form *apasaḥ* functions in the sense of "waters" itself.
You reached the ocean, the vast reservoir; you brought it forward.
Your activity consists of providing food and the movement of people.

May this new prayer turn toward you, O Indra, who have performed all these deeds— the great, fierce, and undecaying bestower of victory, possessed of excellent heroes, well-armed, and wielder of the thunderbolt— for our protection.

May this new prayer turn you hither for our protection—you, Indra, who have performed all these deeds, the great, the fierce, the undecaying, the giver of victory, the possessor of noble heroes, well-armed, and wielder of the excellent thunderbolt.
O Indra, may this new, fresh hymn composed by us—this prayer without a prior precedent—turn you toward us for our protection.
Of what sort are you?

Thus, in the manner described, [we praise] that very Indra—the Lord—who has performed all those celebrated deeds; who is great, mighty, fierce, powerful, and undecaying; the giver of strength, the bestower of force; possessed of excellent heroes, whose warriors are beautiful; well-armed with splendid weapons, and bearing a magnificent thunderbolt—him, this one.
O Indra, bestow upon us inspired singers strength for battle, glory, nourishment, and splendid wealth;
O Hero, among the Bharadvājas, be mindful of our patrons and stand by us on the decisive day.

Bestow upon us, O Indra, inspired singers who possess cattle for the sake of strength, renown, nourishment, and wealth; O Indra, hero in the battle for booty, protect our patrons, and be with us on both sides, O Indra, as our protector in the decisive hour. 14.
O Indra, as such, bestow upon us—upon us who are wise and inspired—splendor, strength, fame, glory, nourishment, food, and wealth; maintain and sustain them.
Furthermore, O Indra, grant these to me, the descendant of Bharadvāja, who am accompanied by men—that is to say, provided with attendants.
"Make our wise ones (*sūri*)—your praisers—possess sons and grandsons; this is the ellipsis.
O Indra, on the decisive day, on the future second or third day, be with us (*edhi sma naḥ*).
The meaning is: indeed, become our protector."
On the sixth day, during the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), in the *Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin* section, the third verse of the *anurūpa* is "ayā vājam.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The *stotriya* and *anurūpa* are 'ayā vājaṃ devahitaṃ sanema'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.3).
By this [prayer], may we win god-ordained strength; may we rejoice for a hundred winters, blessed with heroic sons.
Through this [prayer], may we win god-sent booty; may we rejoice for a hundred winters, blessed with brave sons. 15.
1. That which was previously performed by *gha*, *jha*, and *ra*; that which was previously performed by *ta* and *ra*.
2. By means of the method released from *gha*.
3. [The fruits of] sons, grandsons, and so forth, belonging to *kha* and *bha*.
4. Indeed, [the day] is protected by *bha*. 5.

On the day following the *kha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ta*, *bha*, or *ra* *pṛṣṭha*; on the day following the *ṇa* *pakṣya*; on the sixth day following the *na* *pṛṣṭha*; or on the day following the *ya* *pṛṣṭha*.

You indeed, alone, have devoured those Dasyus; you have protected the people for the sake of the Ārya. Is that heroic power yours, O Indra? Or is it not yours? Declare that truly according to the facts. You indeed, alone, have devoured those Dasyus; you have protected the people for the sake of the Ārya. Is that heroic power yours, O Indra? Or is it not yours? Declare that truly according to the facts. (3)
"O Indra, that [which is] yours, that indeed art thou.
"That" (*tyad*) is a synonym for the word "that" (*tat*);
here there is a change of gender.
O subduer of the teeth, you have swiftly subdued the *dasyus*, those people devoid of ritual action;
the particle *ha* here signifies completion.
Furthermore, as the sole preeminent one, you bestowed your own subjects—sons, slaves, and so forth—upon the noble person who performs ritual labor.
Even while praising him in this way, when he did not see Indra, he then spoke the latter half-verse, doubting whether his heroic power actually existed:
"O *indra*, does that *vīrya*—that capacity (*sāmarthya*) previously mentioned by you—indeed exist?
What indeed is it?"
The word *svinnu* expresses doubt.
Alternatively, there is no such thing as *svin*.
Therefore, you should speak forth—that strength—distinctly and specifically at the proper times, from time to time.

Truly, I acknowledge your conquering power, O you who are born of many; may you, the most victorious, overcome the swift victor. Of the fierce one, you have become fiercer; of the powerful, more powerful; of the non-bestowing, the bestower of wealth. Indeed, I acknowledge your conquering power, O you who are born of many; may you, the most victorious, overcome the swift victor. Of the fierce one, you have become fiercer; of the powerful, more powerful; of the non-bestowing, the bestower of wealth.
Having raised doubt regarding the presence or absence of Indra's power in the preceding mantra, he says this [verse] to determine that he indeed possesses power;
for the word *hi* signifies "because."

For indeed, O most powerful Indra, I consider your strength (*sahas*)—which exists as it is—to belong to you, who are born for many sacrifices, who are swift, and who are the destroyer of those who harm us or the destroyer of enemies through your majesty.
Of the fierce, the powerful, the mighty, the fully grown, the unassailable by enemies—*radhas* here has the sense of being brought under control. *Radhatuḥ*:
your strength, which destroys those enemies who ought to be subdued, truly exists (*babhūva*).

Of what kind? "Fierce" (*ugram*) means most powerful (*tavīyaḥ*), that is, more greatly increased. Since you slay enemies such as Vṛtra, it follows that your strength indeed exists; this is the meaning.

May that ancient sun be for you; thus, with the Angirases who increase [the light], O shaker of the unshakable, strike Vala. May he, bestowing protection upon us, open wide all his doors. 5. May that ancient sun be for you; thus, with the Angirases who increase [the light], O shaker of the unshakable, strike Vala. May he, bestowing protection upon us, open wide all his doors. 5.
"Pratnam" means ancient; that is, it has continued for a long time.
"Tat," meaning well-known; "naḥ," our; "sakhyam," friendship—characterized by praise and hymns—O Indra, let that friendship "yuṣme" be with you.
The plural number is used for the sake of honorific worship.

O *acyutacyut*, you who cause even the immovable (*acyuta*) to tremble; O *dasma*, wonderful Indra, you [drive away] *vala*—the Asura of that name—who was *iṣayantam*, brandishing his weapons, and who [seized] *itthā* (in this manner) their sons, wives, and so forth.
2. [The syllables] jha, ta, na, bha, ra, and tva constitute the *īryāpatha* (proper conduct).
3. [The syllables] kha, jha, ta, na, bha, ra, and va constitute the *vaśīkaraṇa* (subjugation) mantras.
4. kha-bha-ahiṃsi; jha-ya-ahiṃsaḥ; na-ahiṃsī; śa-hiṃsi.
5. *kha*: the meaning is that it persists for a long time.
6. *kha*: the characteristic of a hymn (*stotra*); *jha-jha-ta-na-bha-ya-ra*: the characteristic of a hymn.
Together with the *Aṅgirases*, who were praising you by speaking only the truth, you struck (*han*)—that is, you slew.
Moreover, you opened wide the fortresses, that is, the cities, of this Vala;
the meaning is that you separated them from their functions.
You also opened all the gates, the doors of the cities.

For he, the fierce one who acts as a sovereign, is to be invoked with prayers in the great battle against Vṛtra; he, the wielder of the thunderbolt, has become the victor in the contests for offspring and progeny amidst the battles. He, indeed, is to be invoked with prayers, the fierce one who acts as a sovereign, in the great battle against Vṛtra; he, the wielder of the thunderbolt, has become the one who wins the prize in the contests for offspring and progeny amidst the battles.
Fierce and powerful,
he is the "maker of lords" (*īśānakṛt*), so called because he makes his worshippers lords— that is, capable.
That Indra [acts] in the great, extensive battle for the conquest of Vṛtra.
"Vṛtratūrye" is a name for battle. "Dhībhiḥ" means by the worshippers, or by hymns of praise; "havyaḥ" means he who is to be invoked by those seeking victory; "asti" means he exists.
The word "hi" is a filler for the meter.
On account of the acquisition of offspring—that is, for the sake of obtaining a son—and on account of his progeny—that is, for the sake of his son—Indra is to be invoked.
That Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrī*), becomes—or rather, is—the one to be extensively celebrated through hymns (*vitantasātyaḥ*) in battles;
or alternatively, *vitantasātyaḥ* means the destroyer of enemies.
The verbal root *taṃsa* has the meaning of "to injure";
this form is its nominative singular.

With his mind, he has transcended the birth of mortals through his immortal nature; he has not been surpassed here. He, together with you, with power, and with wealth—he, the most heroic, is the one who dwells in harmony. He, with his mind, [transcends] the birth of men, by means of his immortality; he has not extended beyond this. He, with you, with strength, and also with wealth—He, the most manly, is the one whose dwelling is common [to all].
That Indra, by means of his immortal name— that is, his power which causes enemies to bow—
and by his strength (for *manman* is a name for strength),
[overcomes] the progeny, the birth, of humans.
The meaning is "to the Saṃgha. He has gone far beyond; that Indra becomes one who shares the same dwelling place with you through your glory.
Furthermore, that Indra becomes one who dwells together with power and strength;
moreover, that Indra, the most excellent leader, becomes one who dwells together with wealth, riches, and heroic prowess.

He who has not been deluded, nor has he become a false person; he whose name is well-remembered—Indra, for the shattering and the destruction of the cities, has indeed shattered Curbhu, Dhurṇi, Pipru, Śambara, and Śuṣṇa. 8. He, who, not being deluded, nor becoming a false person—he whose name is well-remembered—Indra, for the shattering and the destruction of the cities, has indeed shattered Curbhu, Dhurṇi, Pipru, Śambara, and Śuṣṇa. 8.
He who is Indra never faints (*muh*) in battle at any time;
and he who is not a false (*mithu*), deceptive, or vain person (*jana*), but rather one named *Sumantu*— that is, one whose name signifies wisdom (*prajñāna*),
meaning one of renowned fame.
That Indra— [whose name is] known [as such] by the enemies of the hundred fortresses (or, according to the *jha* recension, "known among his subjects")—

performs this deed quickly (*ncit*), for the purpose of piercing (*vyaudhanāya*), shattering (*vyadhanāya*), and destroying (*nādhanāya*) the related fortresses, and for the death of the enemies. This is the sense of the ellipsis.
Likewise, he struck down—that is, he harmed—the two Asuras named Cumuri and Dhuni;
his deed was the harming of Vṛtra. Moreover, he harmed the three Asuras named Vipū, Śambara, and Śuṣṇa.
With your victorious and praiseworthy power, O Indra, mount your chariot for the slaying of Vṛtra.
Take the thunderbolt in your right hand; O giver of many gifts, crush the magical illusions of the enemy.

Moreover, O Indra, mount your chariot with your swift and most praiseworthy power for the slaying of Vṛtra; take the thunderbolt in your right hand and, O bounteous giver, overwhelm the magical illusions.
O Indra, with your saving power, rising up— descending as you move—
and endowed with a most praiseworthy strength that pierces enemies, mount your own chariot for the slaying of Vṛtra, for the destruction of the foe.
Likewise, O bounteous Indra, take up, place upon your right hand—that is, your right paw—the thunderbolt, which is your own weapon.
Immediately thereafter, O you of many gifts, having encountered the demonic illusions (*māyāḥ*), strike them down and utterly destroy them;
for here the root *mandati* signifies the act of killing.
Like Agni with his bolt, O Indra, burn down the Rakṣas like dry forest;
with your deep and lofty [thunderbolt], you who have shattered the paths, strike them down according to the cosmic order.

Like fire upon a dry forest, O Indra, let your weapon consume the *rakṣas* like a terrifying thunderbolt; he who with his deep and lofty [power] has shattered [the obstacles], has caused the distresses to resound, and has struck them into fear. 10.
"Agnir-na" means "like fire. The word "na" is used for the purpose of comparison.
Just as fire burns a dry, sapless forest—a collection of trees—so too, O Indra, does your weapon, the thunderbolt (*vajra*), destroy the enemies.
He says that very thing:
"Like a terrifying thunderbolt.
Just as a thunderbolt is terrifying, so you, the bringer of fear, shall utterly consume the *rakṣas*, the demon; burn him completely with your thunderbolt.
Indra, who with his deep, unassailable, lofty, and great weapon (*hetī*)—
*ṛṣva* being a name for "great"—
smote and shattered the enemies.

He roared in battle, making a sound characterized by thundering; likewise, he struck down and shattered the misfortunes of the wicked. He, such as you are, shall utterly consume the Rakṣas—this is the syntactical connection with what precedes.
O Indra of manifold splendor, come hither with wealth consisting of a thousandfold lands and abundant strengths, O Son of Strength!
For you, O Much-invoked One, even the godless man is subject to your protection.

O Indra of many glories, come hither with a thousandfold wealth and abundant strength, O Son of Strength! For no godless man, however much he may strive, can master the light of you who are invoked by many. 11.
"O thou of abundant splendor, O possessor of much wealth, O Son of Strength, O Son of Power, Indra!
I consider him to have been born indeed from vigor"—by this other scriptural citation (*nigama*), his status as the son of strength (*bala*) is established.
"Endowed with wealth, you [grant] a thousand..."
1. By means of the interval between *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *stu*.
2. *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra* in the right hand; *śa* with the right hand. 3. *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ya*, *ra*, *gamaya* (*ta-gamaya* is not present).
In this context, the root *bha* signifies the action of moving slowly (*mandagati*). It is well-known through its association with the letter *ya*. This is by way of their coexistence.
The meaning is "by many. By "tuvivājebhiḥ" is meant "by those possessing great strength. Regarding "pathibhiḥ": they fall upon or go by means of these, thus "paths" refers to the draft animals.
Come hither toward me with them;
come, O Puruhūta, Indra invoked by many! No godless asura whatsoever has power over you, whose splendor through its strength and other qualities is beyond compare.
Here, the particle *n cit* functions in the sense of negation.
The greatness of the steadfast one of abundant splendor has resounded through heaven and earth with his bold [powers].
There is no enemy for him, no counterpart, and no standing ground for him of many wiles, who acts instantly.

The greatness of the one of abundant splendor, the steadfast one, has spread boldly across heaven and earth. Of him, who possesses manifold wisdom, there is no enemy, no counterpart, and no firm foundation—none that can stand against him in an instant. 12.

The greatness (*mahimā*)—the vastness—of this Indra, who possesses abundant splendor, great fame, or immense wealth; who is ancient and fully grown; and who is bold against those who crush his enemies, has surpassed both heaven (*divaḥ*) and earth (*pṛthivyāḥ*).
Since *virapśin* is listed among the names for "greatness" and names are generally derived from verbal roots, the root *rapś* here signifies "excess.
Of this Indra, who possesses manifold wisdom (*purumāya*) and who instantly overcomes his enemies, there is no adversary (*śatruḥ*) who can strike him down.
There is no counterpart or substitute for him;
there is no foundation or support for him;
he alone is the meaning of the foundation for everything.
Today let your performed deed be known, that you, O Atithigva, for the sake of this long-lived Kutsa, subdued many thousands upon the earth; with boldness, you brought down the rushing one.
That deed of yours was accomplished today: that you subdued Kutsa, Āyu, and Atithigva for him; you struck down many thousands upon the earth, and you boldly carried Turvīya away.
Even now, O Indra, that deed performed by you—your act—is preeminent; it prevails and shines forth. What is that? It is said:

that you protected Kutsa from Śuṣṇa, the Rākṣasa of that name; Āyu, the descendant of Puru, from his enemies; Atithigva, the one who goes to guests, namely Divodāsa; and Śambara from Uraṇa—that very deed prevails. This is the connection with what precedes.
The second *śruti* (Vedic word), "he protected" (*rarakṣa*), implies the supply of an appropriate verb.
Furthermore, for this very guest from the adjacent body, you bestowed—*ni śiṃśāḥ*, i.e., gave down—many, indeed thousands upon thousands of Śambara’s riches.
The meaning is that Indra, having slain Śambara, gave his riches to Divodāsa.

Likewise, O Indra, having slain Śambara with your bold, crushing thunderbolt, you brought forth Divodāsa—him who moves swiftly (turvyāṇa) upon the earth (kṣām), directed toward the earth—from out of heaven (divaḥ). You raised him up for his rescue.
On the Ekāha day, during the Marutvatīya Śastra, the hymn beginning with “anu tvāhinvan” is the introductory verse.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “anu tvāhinvan adha deva devā anu te dāyi maha indrāya” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.5).
1. Not [the work] of one lacking great power. 2. Because it is known to have arisen from the element (*dhātu*).

But after thee, O slayer of the serpent, O God, all the gods rejoiced, thee, the most wise among the sages. Wherein thou didst create wide space for the oppressed heaven and for the people, being praised for thy own body. 14. O Agni! Thee, O slayer of the serpent, O God, all the gods rejoiced, thee, the most wise among the sages. Wherein, being praised for thy own body, thou didst create wide space for the oppressed heaven and for the people. 14.
O radiant Indra, at this very time, all the gods— your praisers— rejoice in you, following you, for the slaying of the serpent (ahi),
that is to say, for the bestowing of rain.
They exult and sing hymns of praise after you.
Of what sort are you? Among poets—that is, among the wise—you are the most poetic (*kavitama*), the supreme seer.

At which time, being praised by singers (*gṛṇānaḥ*), you bestowed—indeed, you did bestow—wealth (*varivaḥ*) upon the singer who was oppressed by poverty and other such misfortunes, and for the sake of the singer’s offspring (*tanvai*).
Alternatively, O Lord of the Gods, at this time all the gods— the Suras— are said to be "slayers of the serpent" (Ahighnas).
They rejoice after you, the most eminent among poets, for the sake of slaying him.

In which hymn—when that praise exists—for the sake of heaven, for the people dwelling in the celestial realm who were oppressed and afflicted by the Asuras, and for the sake of your own splendor through the slaying of Vṛtra, you have created wide space for beauty.

Heaven and Earth yield to that power of yours; O immortal Indra, the gods submit. O Accomplisher, perform what remains undone for you; generate a newer hymn through the sacrifices. 15. Heaven and Earth. That. Your. Power. Immortal. They yield. O Indra. Gods. Perform. O Accomplisher. What. Is. Not-done. Which. Is. Yours. Hymn. Newer. Generate. Through. Sacrifices. 15.
O Indra, heaven and earth bow down before that well-known power and strength of yours;
the immortal gods, possessing the nature of immortals, bow down before—that is, they follow—your strength.
O Kṛtnu, performer of many deeds, perform that unaccomplished task which is yours to do.
Thereafter, through sacrifices, produce among the sacrifices a newer, more recent hymn of praise.
The fourth hymn, consisting of thirteen verses beginning with “mahā~ indraḥ,” is the ṛṣi Bharadvāja’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is dedicated to Indra.
It is introduced as follows: “mahāntasonā.
It is recited at the midday pressing (mādhyandina-savana) when there is an abundance of Soma.
In this regard, there is this well-spoken verse;
and it is set forth in the Sūtra: "Great indeed is Indra, who has now driven away the enemies" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.7).
This hymn is recited at the second Chandoma day, in the Mahattvatīya Śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Marutvatīya [offering] is 'Great is Indra, he who drives away... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.7).

Great indeed is Indra, the filler of the peoples, doubly mighty and undiminished in his powers. He has grown toward us for heroic valor; vast and wide, he has been made well-fashioned by the makers. Great is Indra, truly so; he who fills the peoples, and who is doubly powerful, undiminishing in his mights. Toward us he has grown for heroic strength; broad and wide, he has become well-fashioned by the fashioners.
1. *kha-jha-na-bha-ya-ahighne* refers to the [hymn] of that Vṛtra.

2. *kha-gha-jha-bha-anujihate* means they follow or go after; *jha-ta-na-anujihate*. 3. *kha-jha-bha-somātirekaṃ śastraṃ*; *jha-ta-na-ra-somātireke ekaṃ* (variant *jha-eka*) *śastraṃ*; *śa-somātirekaśastraṃ*.

Just as a king who leads like a man fulfills the desires of those such as the Ṛtis, so may the great Indra, the fulfiller of the desires of the "rain-giving" (varṣaṇī) worshippers, come hither. From the presence of the prefix *ā*, the verb "may he come" (*gacchatu*) is supplied. Furthermore, Indra—who is doubly exalted (*dvirbarhāḥ*), being sovereign over the two worlds; who is unassailable (*aminaḥ*) by the powers of his enemies (*mahaḥ*); and who is directed toward us (*asmadryak*)—has grown (*vavṛdhe*) for the sake of heroic deeds (*vīryāya*).

He is "wide" (uruḥ), being extensive in body; "broad" (pṛthuḥ), being renowned for his qualities; and he is "well-made" (sukṛtaḥ) by the performers—the sacrificers—meaning he becomes one who is well-served.
The prayer has established Indra alone for the winning of booty— the vast, lofty, ageless, and youthful one,
who is heard from afar with his swift power, and who grows even instantly in his might.

May the *dhiṣaṇā* (the creative impulse) establish Indra himself for our protection—the great, lofty, undecaying, and youthful one, who is heard of even from afar through his power, and who has grown strong enough to overcome even those who obstruct us. 2.
Our *dhiṣaṇā*, our hymn of praise, impels Indra alone toward giving; it sustains him.
Of what sort?
The vast, the sublime, the far-reaching, the ageless—free from decay—the eternal youth, who has grown great through his irresistible power and strength, being heard [by all].
This is a form derived from the root *śri*.
That Indra, even immediately upon being born, grew—meaning he increased—so as to become exceedingly great.
Having made your two hands broad and many, bestow upon us glories;
like a herdsman driving his cattle to the fold, O Indra, turn us toward the prize.
Making thy two arms broad and many-sided, bestow upon us glories directed toward us. O Indra, as a herdsman drives his cattle home, turn us toward thee in the fray.

O Indra, you—being the performer of deeds—should extend your two broad and vast arms, which bestow much, so as to mete out glories—that is, food—to us, directed toward us. (Supply "in order to give" as the ellipsis. You should fashion them for our sake.
Furthermore, O Indra, you who are *damūnāḥ*—one whose mind is self-controlled—turn toward us (*abhi ā vavṛtsva*) in battle (*ājau*), that is, come to our aid.
Therein lies the illustration:
just as a herdsman (*paśupāḥ*), the protector of cattle, turns back the herds (*yūtheva*) of animals (*paśvaḥ*), so do you.
We, seeking strength, shall now invoke that Indra here with his powers—he who overcomes.
Just as the singers of old were, O blameless ones, so may we be unharmed and prospering through our offerings.
We, seeking strength, shall now invoke here that Indra of yours, the deliverer, by means of his powers—just as the singers of old were unharmed, blameless, and uninjured. 4.

1. *Gha* and *śa*: *aṃhisitaḥ* (who was struck down); *yaḥ*. 2. *Kha*, *bha*: *avadhayat* (he struck down); *ja*: *avardhata* (he grew); *a*, *ta*, *na*, *ya*, *ra*: *avadhayata* (he caused to strike down); *śa*: *vardhate* (it grows). 3. *Kha*, *gha*, *bha*: *karatvā*, *kartvā*; *śa*: *karatvā*.

4. [The syllables] *jha-ta-ya-ra* are unobstructed (*anāvṛta*). Truly, today at this sacrifice, we, the praisers, seeking strength and desiring the enemy, have not been able [to overcome] you—the destroyer of enemies—accompanied by those Maruts who are your capable and powerful helpers. The meaning is that we were unable [to prevail].
O Indra, we invoke and praise you, the Supreme Lord, who are well-known to us.

Just as the ancient singers of old—the praisers who were wise, blameless, irreproachable, free from sin, and unharmed—attained their prosperity, so may we also become likewise through your grace, O Indra. This is the meaning.
Firm in his vows, giver of wealth, increased by Soma, he indeed possesses much food and beautiful riches.
All paths have come together unto him for wealth; they flow toward him like rivers joining the ocean.

Firm in his vows, giver of wealth, increased by Soma—O Indra, for you indeed are the possessor of many cattle and desirable riches. May the earthly wealth converge upon him, like rivers flowing together into the ocean.
O Indra, bring to us that exhilarating joy which overcomes enemy armies, which is unassailable, and which you grant to one who listens and inquires. Bring that joy to us!

Protected by you, we have been victorious; when there was the occasion for the acquisition of the wealth of the son of Tura, the grandson of that [son], with what joy we might praise you—that [joy] he brings here—this is the connection with the preceding [verse].
O Indra, bring to us manly vigor, victorious, renowned, and most effective,
by which we may overcome our enemies in battles— whether they be kin or strangers— with your protections.

O Indra, bring to us manly vigor that wins the prize, which is renowned and most skillful—by means of which we may overcome our enemies in battles, through your protections, both those who are kin and those who are strangers. 8.
O Indra, bring—bring to us—that bull-like, raining strength characterized by an army;
what kind? A protector of wealth, one who hears [our call], one who has increased, and one who is most skillful with excellent power.
O Indra, through your aids—your own protections—in battles, in the midst of conflicts.
"Pṛtanā" is a name for battle.
"By which strength we may strike down (*vaṃsāma*) the enemies"—
here, the word "ut" is displaced from its proper position.
"By which auspicious power we may overcome our kinsmen, as well as our non-kinsmen and enemies—bring that vigor (śuṣma)! This connects with what precedes.
O Bull, let your impetuous strength come from behind, from above, from below, and from the front;
let it gather from every side toward us, O Indra, as splendor belonging to all the gods.
Let your bull-like vigor come from behind, from above, from below, and from the front; let it come toward me from every side. O Indra, bestow upon us glory from all quarters. 9.
O Indra, that bull, the showerer of benefits—may your own vigor and strength come hither toward us from behind, from the western part;
may it come from above, from the northern part;
and may it come from below, from the southern part.
May he come from the front, from the eastern part;
may he approach us fully from every direction, toward us.
O Indra, bestow upon us wealth that is well-apportioned everywhere.
Now, O Indra, may we win through your most manly aids and through our glorious deeds;
for you, O King, rule over both kinds of wealth—bestow upon us that which is firm, vast, and great.

Now, O Indra, most heroic one, may we win through your most manly aids a dwelling place with glorious deeds; for you, O King, behold the wealth of both worlds; bestow upon us great, firm, and lofty treasure. 10.
O Indra, may we, through your most heroic protections (*ūtī*), obtain from you that desirable wealth which is accompanied by men as attendants and joined with glorious fame worthy of being heard;
for, O radiant King, you are the master of both kinds of riches—
those of the earth and those of heaven.
Because you behold and rule [all], for that reason, bestow—that is, grant—the great, massive, vast, and extensive treasure, which is magnificent in its qualities and delightful.
Here, the word *ratna* is masculine. Grant it!
We invoke here for our newest protection that Indra, the bull accompanied by the Maruts, who has grown mighty, the celestial ruler of the waters, the all-conquering, the fierce, the giver of victory.

The bull, accompanied by the Maruts, who has grown great, the foe-subduing, celestial ruler, Indra, the all-conquering, the fierce one, the giver of greatness—him we invoke here for new protection. 11.
In this sacrifice, for the sake of new protection— that is, for fresh preservation— we shall invoke, praise, or call upon that renowned Indra. Of what nature is he?
