[We invoke] the one possessed of greatness, joined with the Maruts, the bull who rains down desires, the increasing, the fully grown, the one whose enemies are not contemptible, the divine, the shining, the ruler, the subduer of all the world, the fierce, the powerful, the giver of strength, the bestower of power.
O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, subject those men to me—who think themselves great—among whom I am;
for we call upon you on earth in the struggle for heroes, for offspring, for cattle, and for waters.

O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, subject even the great man who considers himself such to these heroes, among whom I am; for it is for them that we invoke you upon the earth in the struggle for heroes, for progeny, for cattle, and for waters. 12.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, O Indra, among whichever men I am present as one, subject those people who consider themselves great— meaning those who think highly of themselves—
to me; bring them under my control.
The word *citra* is for the purpose of filling the meter.

Now, when a battle for heroes has commenced upon the earth—the ground—and with a son as the cause, and with cattle, livestock, and waters as the causes, O Indra, we call upon you who abide in the heavenly world.
Through these many-invoked friendships of yours, may we prevail over every enemy.
O Hero, slaying both kinds of Vṛtras, protected by you, we are filled with great wealth and exhilaration.

O you who are invoked by many, through these friendships may we be superior to every enemy; O Hero, slaying both kinds of obstacles, may we, protected by you, be filled with great wealth and exhilaration. 13.

O *Puruhūta*, invoked by many, O Indra, with these well-known forms of friendship characterized by hymns—that is, through these acts of friendship—with you, may we, while striking down (*ghnantaḥ*) both kinds of kin and non-kin enemies (*jāmirūpāṇi ajāmirūpāṇi vṛtrāṇi*), be superior to every enemy;
indeed, may we be preeminent. O heroic and valiant Indra, protected by you, may we rejoice in great wealth and exhilaration.
The fifth hymn, consisting of thirteen verses beginning with "dyaune ya indra," belongs to Bharadvāja; it is addressed to Indra and is composed in the Ṛṣabha meter.
The seventh verse, "vi piproḥ," consists of four pādas each containing ten syllables, thus forming a Virāj.
It is also enumerated in the Anukramaṇī: "dyaune vi piprorvirāṭ."
1. *pṛṣṭhya-śa-viśvāsāham* (trustworthy in the back);
2. *jha-ra-hṛṣyāsma* (we rejoiced in the sound *jha-ra*).
3. [The hymns] consisting of four sets of ten verses beginning with *kha-bha-da*; [and] four sets of ten verses beginning with *jha-a-ta-na-ra*.

If on the sixth day of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), the Ukthya-stotras were to be chanted upon *dvipadā* verses, or if the sacrifice should conclude with the Agniṣṭoma, then at that time, during the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), the Acchāvāka priest should recite this hymn after the *ārambhaṇīyā* verses in his own *śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Acchāvāka [recites] *dyaur na ya indra...* (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.4)."
This very hymn, "dyaur na ya indra" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.7), is the *nikṣepya* *nivid*-hymn for the *akrānti-nāman* one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) dedicated to Indra and Viṣṇu.

Like heaven, O Indra, he who is the master has surpassed all others; wealth stands firm through his power over the people in battles. Grant us that wealth which brings a thousandfold gain, which wins fertile fields, and which overcomes the Vritras, O Son of Strength. Like heaven, O Indra, he who is the master has surpassed all others; wealth stands firm through his power over the people in battles. Grant us that wealth which brings a thousandfold gain, which wins fertile fields, and which overcomes the Vritras, O Son of Strength.
The swelling wealth, in the form of sons, by means of his power (*śarvasā*) and strength, has overcome the noble enemies, the hostile people, in the battles; he has stepped over them.
Therein is an illustration:
like heaven.
Just as the rising sun traverses the earth and all beings,
even so, O Indra, son of strength (sahasaḥ sūno), grant us that son— of what kind?— to us. Of what nature is he?

The bearer of a thousandfold wealth, the supporter of thousands, the sustainer of fertile fields—that is, of crops and the like—and the winner, the distributor, the overcomer of Vṛtras—that is, of enemies—or the one who swiftly transcends them.

For you, O Indra, all divine power was established from heaven, entirely together with the gods, when you, O impetuous one, joined by Viṣṇu, slew the dragon Vṛtra who had enclosed the waters. divaḥ | na | tubhyam | arnu | indra | satrā | asuryam | devebhiḥ | dhāyi | viśvam | ahim | yat | vṛtram | apaḥ | vavrivāṃsam | han | ṛjīṣin | viṣṇunā | sacānaḥ ||2||
Like the sun from heaven day after day, O Indra, for you alone all the true power of the Asuras has been pervasively established; it has been bestowed and performed by the gods, the worshippers.
The meaning is that when a deity is praised with hymns, it becomes powerful.

O *ṛjīṣin*, O Indra who has drunk the juiceless [soma], you, acting in concert with Viṣṇu—[the form *sacānaḥ* is from the root *ṣac* meaning "to accompany"]—you, having come upon the serpent Ahi who had obstructed the waters, slew Vṛtra, the Asura; that power was shattered. This is the connection with what precedes.

More powerful, more vigorous, Indra—by whom prayer was made, whose greatness has increased—became the king of the sweet Soma, when he overturned the fortress of all the evil-doing cities. 3. More powerful; more vigorous; by whom prayer was made; Indra; whose greatness has increased; king; became; of the sweet; of the Soma; of all; when; of the cities; the evil-doing; he overturned. 3.
Whenever Indra took up the thunderbolt, the shatterer of Danu, to break through all the ancient fortresses, at that time he became the king—the sovereign—of the sweet-flavored Soma-juice;
what kind of king?
One who is swift.
1. Kha-na-bha shall step upon; jña shall be stepped upon. 2.
Kha-jña-ta-na-ra steps upon; gha transcends. 3. Jña-ta [is the name] of the cities of the Asuras.
4. [He is] sweeter than the sweetness of *kha*, *jña*, *na*, and *bha*; he whose sweetness is even more excellent than that of *jña*.

Being a slayer of those who do harm, he is *ojīyān*—more exceedingly powerful—and *tavasaḥ*—of strength—he is *tavīyān*, more forceful. He for whom a *brahma*—a hymn of praise—has been performed by the singers is *kṛtabrahmā*.
Or rather, he is the one by whom food has been prepared as a gift for his worshippers;
he is the one of increased greatness, whose splendor has grown.
Such is Indra who became the king.

By the hundreds, the pious ones have perished here at the hand of Indra, for the sake of the ten-fingered sage in the winning of light. Through his strengthening deeds, he did not leave even a trace behind of the magic powers of the swift-moving Śuṣṇa; he has surpassed them utterly, as if consuming food. śateḥ | apadran | puṇaryaḥ | indra | atra | daśoṇaye | kavaye | arkasātau | vṛdhaiḥ | śuṣṇasya | āśuṣasya | māyāḥ | pitvaḥ | na | arirecīta | kim | cana | pra || 4 ||
In this *arkasāti*, where the *arka* (the sun or light) is attained; that is, in battle (*sāti*), which is so called because it is reached quickly— therein,
for the wise poet (*kavi*) who possesses much sacrificial food (*havikā*).
The dative case is used in the sense of the ablative.
O Indra, the *vaṇayas*—demons of that name—fearing Kutsa with you as his ally, fled together with their forces numbering in the hundreds; they ran away.
They retreated.

Moreover, Indra did not leave the illusions— the deceptions— of Śuṣṇa, that enemy of Kutsa, who was "aśuṣa," meaning one whose strength was unwithered or full, deficient by means of weapons intended for slaughter. He did not allow them to remain superior or excessive.
"Having drunk of the *akṣa*— *akṣa* being a name for dice— he did not leave behind even *kiṃ cana*, that is, not even anything at all."
He consumed all of his food as well.

The great, life-sustaining [weapon] was hurled; at the falling of the thunderbolt, Śuṣṇa was struck down. Indra made wide room for his charioteer, for Kutsa, in the winning of the sun. Great, life-sustaining [was it]; it was hurled. At the falling of the thunderbolt, Śuṣṇa was struck down. Wide space he made for his charioteer; Indra did so for Kutsa in the winning of the sun.
When that Asura Śuṣṇa fell under the protection of the wielder of the thunderbolt— that is, when he came [under his power]—
then the long-reaching [missile] of the great Druhu reached all-pervading Śuṣṇa.
"Strength" is the word understood [from the context].
"It was laid aside" (apadhāyi) means it was placed away;
that is to say, it was set aside.

Indra made for Kutsa—who had become his charioteer—a broad, wide chariot, so that they might share the same vehicle on the occasion of winning the sun; thus it is said: "Desiring to slay the Asura Śuṣṇa, Indra, making Kutsa his own charioteer, struck down his enemy Śuṣṇa with a great blow."
"It is stated by this [verse] that he provided abundant protection for Kutsa."

Like a falcon, the exhilarating Soma, churning the head of the Dāsa Namuci for him, protected Nami Sādhyasvant. He filled him with wealth, with food, and with well-being. Like a falcon, the exhilarating Soma, churning the head of the Dāsa Namuci for him, protected Nami Sādhyasvant. He filled him with wealth, with food, and with well-being.

1. *kha-jha-na-bha-ya* read *pravṛddhatejāḥ*. 2. *śa-daśonaye*: [the form] *avataḥ* is derived from the root *av* in the sense of "satisfying" (*tarpaṇa*), with the suffix *ṇi* used according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). 3. *gva-jha-bha* read *haviṣmataḥ*; *na* read *haviṣyatat*. 4. *kha-jha-na-bha-ra* read *apadravan*; *jña-ta* read *apādravan*, which does not exist [in these versions]. 5. *kha-jha-jha-ta-na-bha-ya-ra* read *kutsasya*, which does not exist [in these versions]. 6. *jña-ta* read *saḥ*, which does not exist [in these versions]. 7. *kha-jha-na-bha-ra* read *mapakāri*. *Śyenaḥ* and *suparṇaśca*:
the word *na* here functions as a particle of conjunction (*samuccaye*).
For this Indra, he brought the exhilarating, intoxicating draught of Soma;
the word *pra* here functions in the sense of *ā*. He brought it.
A verb is called a verb because it is seen to be preceded by a prefix (*upasarga*).

Furthermore, this Indra, while "churning" (*mathāyan*)—that is, performing the act of churning—the "head" (*śiraḥ*, *śīrṣam*) of the demon named Namuci, who was "of the Dāsa," meaning one who oppresses living beings; he protected (*prāvat*) the seer named Namī, who was "sleeping" (*sasantaṃ*, *svapantaṃ*) and the son of Sāpya. He fully endowed (*saṃ pṛṇak*) that seer with well-being (*svasti*), that is, with non-destruction, with "wealth" (*rāyā*) such as cattle and the like, and with "food" (*iṣā*).
O wielder of the thunderbolt, you shattered the strongholds of Pipru, the son of Mayu, which were difficult to overcome, like a bull tearing through reeds;
O bounteous one, you gave to the worshipper Ṛjiśvan an imperishable gift of wealth that was beyond measure.

O wielder of the thunderbolt, you shattered the strong fortresses of the one with serpent-like guile, like reeds. O bounteous giver, you bestowed that imperishable wealth as a gift upon the worshipper R̥jiśvan.

O Vajrin, O wielder of the thunderbolt, you shattered with your might (*śavasā*) the strong, impregnable fortresses—the walls and other defensive works—belonging to that Asura named Ahi-māya, whose magic (*māyā*) was to be destroyed.

The word *na* is used here as a filler (*pādapūraṇa*). This is seen from the [Vedic] texts: "They call you the shatterer of the fortresses" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.51.5) and "Protect us with a hundred iron fortresses" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 7.3.7).

Moreover, O Sudāman—O Indra of beautiful gifts—you gave that irrepressible wealth, which cannot be obstructed by anyone, as his own property (*rekṇas*) to Ṛjiśvan, a king of that name who had offered the oblation (*dāśuṣe*). You have indeed bestowed it.
Indra, who possesses his own excellent aid and favor, brought forth Vetasu for the sight of Darśoṇi, the swift one;
he sent forth Tugra, the ever-impetuous, for the sake of illumination, so that he might come near as if to his mother.

Ma: | Vetusu | Darśamāyam | Darśoṇim | Turtujim | Indra | svabhiṣṭisumnaḥ | ā | Tugram | śaśvat | ibham | ghotanāya | mātuḥ | na | sīm | upa | sṛja | iyadhyai ||8|| Ma: O Indra, you whose favor is sought for our aid, release for the sake of striking down the eternal, impetuous Tugra—him who is like a calf—to come hither, as one would let loose a mother's [calf]. Vetusu! Darśamāya! Darśoṇi! Turtuji! Release him so that he may hasten toward us.

Indra, whose blessings and favors (*sumna*) are most desirable and worthy of being approached—that is, by whom happiness is to be bestowed—released for the sake of King Ghotana these [demons]: Daśamāya, the deceiver; Vetusu, the Asura named Vetusu; Daśoṇi, so named; Turtuji, named Turtuji; furthermore, Tugra, the Asura named Tugra, as well as Ibha, the Asura so named—he released them all to be captured. He brought them under his control. In this regard, there is an illustration: *svabhiṣṭisumnaḥ*: "He whose blessings and favors are most desirable and worthy of being approached. *suṣṭhu abhyeṣaṇīyānyabhigamyāni sumnāni sukhāni yena deyāni saḥ*: "He by whom excellent, approachable, and accessible blessings and happinesses are to be given. *indro daśamāyaṃ bahuvañcanaṃ vetusuṃ vetusunāmānamasuraṃ daśaoṇim etannāmakaṃ ca turtujiṃ turtujināmakaṃ ca ā api ca tugraṃ tugranāmakamasuraṃ tathā ibham etannāmakamasuraṃ ca iyadhyai etuṃ ghotanāya etatsaṃjñāya rājñe śaśvat upa sṛja upāsṛjat*: "Indra... released Daśamāya, the great deceiver; Vetusu, the Asura named Vetusu; and Daśoṇi, so named; and Turtuji, named Turtuji; and also Tugra, the Asura named Tugra; likewise Ibha, the Asura so named—all these he released to be captured for Ghotana, the king known by that name. *vaśīcakāra*: "He brought them under his control. *Tatra dṛṣṭāntaḥ*: "In this regard, there is an illustration:"
"Like a son [is obedient] to his mother, that is, to his own mother;
just as a son becomes submissive to his mother, so he brought [her] under control—this is the meaning.
*Sīm* is for the purpose of completing the meter."
He, unopposed, overcomes his adversaries, bearing in his hand the Vṛtra-slaying thunderbolt.
Standing firm like a tall tree upon its base, he mounts the chariot; may the two steeds yoked by our word bring Indra hither.

He, irresistible, wins the prize; bearing in his hand the Vṛtra-slaying thunderbolt, he stands upon his two bay steeds. Like a charioteer on his seat, they carry Indra, the seer, yoked by the word. 9.

1. *bha-naśabda*: here the word is *nañ*. 2. *jña-yasya tasya*: of whomsoever. 3. *kha-gha-ta-na-śa-°vacanam*: [the reading] ending in *-vacanam*. 4. *te- putrā vaśībhavanti*: those sons become submissive. Ṛgveda 3.30:

Holding in his hand (*gabhastau*) the *vajra*—his own weapon—which is the slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of enemies (*vṛtrāṇām*), that Indra, being unassailed (*apratītaḥ*) by his foes, strikes down (*vanate*) these contending rivals (*spṛdhaḥ*), namely Vṛtra and others. He mounts (*adhi tiṣṭhat*) his two bay horses (*harī*).
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"As one who throws [the spear] stands upon the chariot, so too is the hero. Just as a thrower stands upon a chariot, so it is.
Likewise, "yoked by speech" means being joined by mere words;
or rather,
those two bay steeds (*harī*), being joined by the hymns of the praisers, carry the lofty, great Indra.
O Indra, hero among men, the ancient ones have praised you with these sacrifices, thinking,
"May he destroy the seven autumnal fortresses, the Dāsa strongholds, for the sake of the many. 10.

I think of you, O Indra, as one who is bountiful and heroic. Through these sacrifices, the ancients praise you, since you granted them seven autumnal fortresses as a refuge. O Indra, shaker of enemies, you sent forth the waters—those "shaking" ones (dhunimatīḥ) in which the demon Dhuni was present as an obstructer—like flowing rivers; you caused them to flow.
The meaning is that by slaying Dhuni, you set free the waters that had been blocked by him.

O Hero, O Lord of Heroes, when you have crossed over and are advancing across the ocean, having reached the further shore, then bring Turvaśa and Yadu, who stand on the far side of the sea, safely across; carry them over in safety;
ferry them across the ocean.
All this, O Indra, you indeed [conquered] in battle—Sudās, Dhuni, and Cumuri, whom you struck down with your might.
Then, being pressed with Soma juices, you shone forth for yourself, O fearless one, through the offerings of Pakthya and the Bhṛtis.

Truly, O Indra, all that was yours in the battle; you struck down Dhuni and Cumuri. Dabhīti, pressing the Soma for you with hymns, kindling the fuel, offered the cooked oblation with his songs of praise. 13.
O Indra, O Vāja, in battle, yours alone is that power by which the entire universe is pervaded; such is the deed that occurs.
As to what kind it is, that is now stated:
[the slaying] of Dhuni and Cumuri.
Dhuni and Cumuri— these two Asuras were fashioned by Tvaṣṭṛ;
you, O Indra, laid them both to sleep, those two Asuras who were victorious in battle—
that is to say, they died.
The suffix *laṭ* is used for the past tense (*bhūta*) by way of grammatical anomaly;
the second occurrence of the word *ha* is for the purpose of completing the meter.

Immediately after that, O Indra, for your sake—*tvubhyam* meaning for you—the one pressing the Soma juices, *sunvan*, namely the royal seer named *Dabhīti*, who possesses cooked offerings (*pakthī*), the bearer or bringer of fuel (*idhmabhṛtiḥ*), has indeed shone forth with Soma libations and with oblations characterized by sacrificial food.
This is because we see it stated: "You [O Indra] struck down the Dasyu Cumuri and Dhuni" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 7.19.4). The meaning is that they slew Dhuni and Cumuri for his sake.
The hymn beginning with "imā u tvā" consists of twelve verses and five stanzas; it is the seer Bharadvāja’s composition, in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is dedicated to Indra.
The ninth and eleventh verses, however, are addressed to the Viśvedevas.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Imā u [tvā] consists of twelve verses; the ninth and eleventh are addressed to the Viśvedevas."
In the one-day sacrifice named Upahavya, this hymn serves as the locus for the Marutvatīya Nivid.

It is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Imā u tvā,’ ‘ya eka id’—these are for the midday [pressing]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.7). Furthermore, in the one-day sacrifice of the Indrāviṣṇu Hāyana, this same hymn serves as the locus for the Marutvatīya Nivid.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘imā u tvā dyaur na ya indra’ [is the Marutvatīya hymn] at midday" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.7).
This same hymn is also used for the Marutvatīya at the third Chandoma;
and it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘pra mandine’ and ‘imā u tvā’ are the Marutvatīya" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.7).

O Hero, these invocations of the most frequent singer call upon you, the one to be invoked; the newest prayers, rich in wealth, flow toward you, the ageless one who stands upon the chariot, with eloquent speech.

These [prayers]: "Oṃ!"—thus [they call] you, the most abundant one, the agent of action. O Hero, the invokers call upon you as the object of invocation; the prayers call upon you who stand upon the chariot, the ageless one, the newest. Through eloquence, the manifestation of wealth is impelled. 1.
O Hero, O Lord of the Gods, for him who desires the manifold abundance of the most ancient one—
the root *kāṅkṣ* meaning "to desire"— the offerings (*havyā*),
which are worthy of praise and laudable, the hymns (*imā dhiyaḥ*) and recollections of the worshipper Bhadvāja, call upon you; they invoke you, the one to be invoked.

Of what kind? Standing in the chariot (*vrathesthām*), situated in the chariot; "unaging" (*avajaram*), free from old age; "newer" (*navīyaḥ*), more recent or newer. 1. [Variant readings: *kha-jha-ta-bha-ra* read *nirodhayitāny udakāni*.]
2. Ma—The Viśvedevas are the deities; Ja, Jha, Na, Ra, Na, Bha, Ya, Ra—the Viśvedevas (with Jha as Va) are the deities; Ta1—the Viśvedevas are the deities.
3. Kha, Jha, Ta, Na, Bha, Ra, U—tvā.
4. Kha1—havyaṃ hātavyam; Ja, Ṇa—havyaṃ hotavyam; Bha, Ya—havyaṃ hātavyam.
5. *Kha*, *jha*, *bha*, and *ra* are new [consonants].
*Ḍa* is for the sake of filling the meter.

Furthermore, by means of your speech—that is, through praise—the most excellent glory, which is the cause of the world's prosperity, and *rayi*—wealth characterized by the oblation—approaches you, coming to its rightful master.
Praise that Indra, who is known as the one borne by songs, who increases the sacrifice through hymns;
whose greatness, consisting of many wondrous powers, surpasses both heaven and the great earth.

I praise him with "Ūm!"—Indra, who is well-known, who is borne by songs, who is strengthened by hymns at the sacrifice, whose greatness surpasses both heaven and earth, he who possesses manifold powers. || 2 ||

I praise that very Indra—the wise one, who knows all, or who is made known as omniscient; him who is to be carried by songs (*gīrvāhasam*), who increases through sacrifices (*yajñavṛdham*); I praise that Indra alone.
The greatness (*mahitvam*) of that Indra, who possesses manifold wisdom (*purumāyasya*) or manifold power (*bahuvajñasya*), [surpasses] heaven (*divaḥ*), from the celestial world (*divaḥ*).
(The second case ending is used in the sense of the fifth.)
He who has surpassed, or excels, the earth—that is, the world of beings—by his great majesty; praise him.

O Indra, O hero, sustainer of the poets, listen now to the prayer of this contemporary worshipper! For you have been from of old the friend of our fathers, ever ready to be invoked in the sacrifice. O Indra, O hero, sustainer of the poets (kārudhāyaḥ), you who are well-known—listen quickly (śṛdhi) to the hymn of me, the present-day worshipper (brahmaṇyataḥ) who desires to perform the sacred prayer (brahma). For, O Indra, when there is a desire for sacrifice (eṣṭau) or a longing for worship, you, being easy to invoke (suhavaḥ), have from of old (pradivi) been the constant friend (āpiḥ) of the fathers (pitṝṇām), that is, of the Aṅgirases; therefore, listen to my hymn. This is the connection.

Bring Varuṇa, Mitra, Indra, and the Maruts forward for our protection today; bring Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, Agni, Purandhi, Savitṛ, the plants, and the mountains forward. (9) In this verse, all the gods are praised. O Bharadvāja, now at this moment, bring Varuṇa—the presiding deity of sovereignty—and Mitra—the presiding deity of the day—and Indra, who is well known, and the Maruts—the hosts of Maruts—forward for our *ūtaye* (satisfaction) and *avase* (protection). Furthermore, bring Pūṣan by name, Viṣṇu the all-pervading god, Purandhi (the one of many thoughts or many deeds), Agni, Savitṛ the impeller of all, the plants—the deities presiding over the herbs—and the mountains; bring these gods forward with devotion for our satisfaction and protection.

O you of many powers, O most worshipful one, these singers praise you with hymns. Listen to the call of the one who invokes you; being invoked, O Immortal One, there is no other like you besides you. O you of many powers (*puruśāka*), O most worshipful one (*prayajya*), these singers (*jaritāraḥ*) praise (*abhyarcanti*) you with hymns (*arkaiḥ*). O Immortal One (*amṛta*), being invoked (*huvānaḥ*), listen (*śṛdhi*) to the call (*havam*) of me who invokes (*ā huvataḥ*). Furthermore, there is no other god (*devaḥ*) like you (*tvāvān*) besides you (*tvat*).
1. Kha, jha, ta, na, bha: *puraṃdhiyam*; gha, śa: *purudhiyaṃ* does not exist.
2. Kha, jha, ta, na, bha: the gods who are the ordainers (*vidhān*).
3. Kha, jha, bha, ya: for protection (*ūtaye*) and for satisfaction (*tarpaṇāya*).

Now, O Son of Strength, come to my speech as one who knows, together with all your worshipful ones; those who were drinkers of the Truth (*ṛtasāpa*) with Agni as their tongue, who were divine, and who made Manu the later [beneficiary] for the sake of the Dasa. Now, O Son of Strength, come to my speech as one who knows, together with all your worshipful ones; those who were drinkers of the Truth (*ṛtasāpa*) with Agni as their tongue, who were divine, and who made Manu the later [beneficiary] for the sake of the Dasa.
And this is the Vaiśvadevī hymn.

O Indra, son of strength (sahasaḥ sūno), you who are all-knowing (vidvān), come quickly (nu) with all the gods (viśvebhir devaiḥ) worthy of sacrifice (yajatraiḥ) toward my words (me vācaḥ)—that is, toward my praises in the form of speech. Thus he prays to Indra, because the hymn belongs to Indra.

Those gods whose tongue is Agni—meaning those for whom Agni stands in the place of a tongue—and who are *ṛtasāpaḥ*, those who touch (*spṛśanti*) and abide in the *ṛta* (the sacrifice)—and those gods who [are led by] Indra:

since Indra alone is the one to be invoked (*havyaḥ*) among the *varṣaṇīḥ* (procreative) beings, namely the waters, I praise and extol that Indra with these songs (*gīrbhiḥ*), that is, with words in the form of hymns;
Indra, who approaches and comes to his worshippers.
Or rather:
he who pervades (padyate) and rules over the worlds;
of what nature is he?

*Vṛṣabha*: the showerer of desires; *vṛṣṇyāvān*: possessing virile strength; *balavān*: powerful; *satyaḥ*: truthful, non-deceptive; *sakhā*: a friend, or one who destroys enemies and bestows desires.
*Saṃdevān* is a form derived from the root *san* (to give).
*Purumāyaḥ*: possessed of manifold wisdom; *sahasvān*: victorious or overcoming. The connection is: "I praise that Indra."
Him our ancient fathers, the Navagvas, the seven sages, sought with their hymns as they strove for strength—
him who shines like a star, who speeds across the mountains, whose speech is guileless, and who is most powerful in his thoughts.

Him, our ancient fathers, the Navagvas, the seven sages, seeking strength, [invoked] with their prayers—the one who shines like a star, the swift one, who stands upon the mountain, whose speech is guileless, and who is most powerful. 2.

The previous questions: The *navagvas* performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*) for nine months; the seven wise ones (*viprāsaḥ*), meaning the seven intelligent ones, were striving for strength (*vājaryantaḥ*), that is, providing food in the form of oblations (*vāja*) for Indra, or making Indra strong and powerful.
The suffix *ṇic* is used in the sense of "one who performs that [action]."
Our ancestors, the Aṅgirases, being such as they were, praised— that is, they extolled with hymns and praises— that very Indra alone.
Of what sort was he?
Resplendent as the stars,
performing the movement and action of the stars,
the subduer and destroyer of approaching enemies, the one who overcomes, the one who dwells upon the mountains, he whose speech is free from guile.

We implore that most powerful Indra, whose speech is free from guile and cannot be transgressed, which is like a sharp arrow; we implore him for this wealth consisting of many heroes, abounding in men and rich in food.
O Lord of the bay horses, bring hither the celestial draught that is ageless and undecaying, so that you may rejoice.

We implore that Indra for this wealth which possesses many heroes, O leader of men, and much food—wealth that is unfailing, undecaying, and self-luminous. O Lord of the bay steeds, bring that hither so that we may rejoice.
Of him who possesses many heroes, who is endowed with many sons and grandsons, who has a retinue of attendants, who possesses much food—or much fame—this is his wealth;
the genitive case is used here in the sense of the accusative.
We implore that Indra; we beg for him.

O Lord of Bay Horses (Harivaḥ), O Indra, accompanied by your own horses, bring hither—that wealth which is undecaying, uninterrupted, free from old age and decay, and endowed with heavenly bliss—in order to gladden us. Tell us this, O Indra, if you have indeed remembered us as your singers from of old. What is your portion? What is your food? O Much-invoked One, O Lord of Abundant Wealth, O Slayer of Asuras, satisfy our desires.

Do not speak thus: "If even in former times you have favored the singer, O Indra, what is your portion? What is your food?"—O much-invoked, O possessor of many riches, slayer of Asuras, you who are difficult to deceive! 4.

1. [The syllables] kha, jha, ma, ya [represent] enemies. 2. Ta [represents] the one who has deceived. 3. Gha, jha, bha, śa [represent] the form of the sacrifice of speech. 4. Kha, gha, ma, śa [represent] being free from old age; jha, ta [represent] being accompanied by the destruction of old age. O Indra, if in former times your singers—that is, those who praise you—attained happiness (*sujñam*), then declare that same happiness to us; grant it to us.

O *Durdhara*, difficult to restrain; O *Khiddha*, tormentor of enemies; O *Puruhūta*, much-invoked; O *Puruvaso*, possessor of many riches; O *Indra*, slayer of the *Asuras*—in your sacrifices, what portion is there for you? Where is it? What food characterized by oblations (*vayas*) is there? Or where is it? The meaning is this: having reflected that "if even some ancients obtained happiness from you in former times, then I too shall obtain that happiness," one should think that any delay in attaining such happiness is intolerable to me.
Seeking him, the thunderbolt-wielder Indra who stands upon his chariot— to him whose song is trembling and eloquent,
the one of mighty grasp, many deeds, and giver of bounty— she, desiring the path for her nourishment,
approaches the powerful one. 5.

Seeking him, the thunderbolt-wielder standing in his chariot—Indra—to whom the trembling, eloquent song belongs, who is the great-grasper, the great-actuator, the giver of strength; [she] approaches Tugra for the sake of finding a path to nourishment. 5.
Indra granted desires to the seer who had previously reproached him; then that seer, his desires fulfilled, spoke.

[The hymn] addresses Indra—*vajrahastaṃ* (thunderbolt-handed), *vajrapāṇim* (holding the thunderbolt in his hand), *ratheṣṭhām* (standing on the chariot)—that one stationed upon the chariot, while questioning and praising him.
The root *pracchati* (to question) has the sense of "praising."
*Vepī*: *vepa* is action characterized by sacrifice and so forth;
*vakkarī* means possessing that [action], [namely] the speaker of virtues; *gīḥ* means such praise as this; [the word refers to] the sacrificer for whom such praise exists.
What kind of Indra are you asking about?
One who is *tuvigrābham*—the seizer of many (*tuvīnām*); *tuvikūrmiṃ*—one of many deeds; *rabhodām*—the giver of impetuous strength (*rabhasaḥ*);
and *nu* is a filler particle.
That sacrificer goes to *gātu*, i.e., happiness, for the sake of nourishment (*iṣe*). Furthermore, he approaches (*accha*) and reaches (*nakṣate*) the powerful (*tugram*) enemy who causes withering.

With this very power, O self-strong one, you shattered by means of the mountain—swift as thought—that one who had grown great through illusion; with your own vigor, O exuberant one, you boldly broke down even the unshakable, the firm, and the solid.

With this very power of illusion, O self-strong one, you shattered with your mind-swift mountain even those things that were unshakable and firmly fixed—those solid fortresses, O most powerful and overflowing hero, by means of your boldness.
O Indra, whose power is inherent (*asvatavas*), by means of this mountain-like, many-jointed thunderbolt (*vajra*)— your own weapon that moves as swiftly as thought (*manojuvā*),

as seen in the mantra "with the hundred-jointed thunderbolt" (*vajreṇa śataparvaṇā*, Ṛgveda 1.80.6)— you shattered, you utterly destroyed, *tyam* that well-known *vṛtra*, who was growing great (*vavṛdhānam*) through this *māyā*.

Thus, O *svoja*—O you of splendid luster—O *virapśin*, O mighty Indra, you shattered with your bold (*dhṛṣatā*) thunderbolt even those *acyutā*—indestructible, unshakable, firm (*vīḷitā*), and solid (*duḷhā*) fortresses.
1. kha-gha-bha—O *puruhūta*, invoked by many.
2. gha—O *puruvaso*, possessor of abundant wealth.
3. One should be reproached by those beginning with *kha*, *jha*, *bha*, and *ya*; or one has been reproached by those beginning with *ta* and *ra*. 4.
[He is] one who causes to fade by means of *kha*, *gha*, *jha*, and *bha*; one who causes to reach by means of *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *ya*, and *ra*; one who causes to blow forth by means of *ta*. 5.
By means of *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *ya*, and *ra*, [he is] without a vehicle.
6. In *jha-jha-ta-na-ya-ra*, there is no *ayā* or *anayā*.
7. In *kha-bha*, there is *ciddha*.

Him, the ancient one, for you I would cause to dwell around us with a new prayer, O most powerful one, as of old. May that Indra, the measureless and well-guiding, carry us across all difficulties. tam vaḥ dhiyā navyasā śaviṣṭha pratnam pratnavat paritasyadhyai | sa naḥ vakṣat animānaḥ suvaha indraḥ viśvāni ati duḥhaṇāni || 7 ||

With a new, most recent prayer of praise, O Indra, may I proceed to extend you— O most powerful one, ancient and of old— as the ancient seers did of yore. May that Indra, immeasurable and easy to invoke, carry us across all difficulties and obstacles.

For the person who harms us, O burner, illuminate the earthly, celestial, and intermediate realms. O scorching bull, with your flame from every side, consume those who hate sacred prayer, as well as the earth and the waters.
O Indra, you [are the one] for the person who harms virtuous people—that is, for a person such as a *rākṣasa* who bears malice toward others;
here the dative case is used in the sense of the ablative.

O *vṛṣan* (rainer), O Indra, you who shower down desires, heat—that is, burn with your own radiant glow—those *rakṣasas* and others existing on all sides. Heat them thoroughly from every direction. Furthermore, [heat] the hater of Brahman—the *rakṣasa* and others who hate the Brāhmaṇas. [And heat] the terrestrial places, those existing on the earth; the celestial places, those existing in heaven; and the intermediate places, those existing in the atmosphere. Illuminate them completely, heating them all around. O *vṛṣan*, O Indra, you who shower down desires, heat—that is, burn with your own radiant glow—those *rakṣasas* and others existing on all sides. Furthermore, [heat] the hater of Brahman—the *rakṣasa* and others who hate the Brāhmaṇas.
The meaning is: "in order to burn the hater of Brahman.
Heat the earth (*kṣām*) and the waters (*apaḥ*), that is, the intermediate space (*antarikṣam*); illuminate them.
"Waters" is a name for the intermediate space.

Grasp the thunderbolt in your right hand; O undecaying one, you destroy all magical illusions. bhuvaḥ | janasya | divyasya | rājā | pārthivasya | jagataḥ | tveṣa-saṃdṛk | dhiṣva | vajram | dakṣiṇe | indra | haste | viśvāḥ | ajūrya | dayase | vi | māyāḥ || 9 ||

Place the thunderbolt in your right hand.
And by that thunderbolt which has been hurled, you shatter—that is, you utterly destroy—all the magical powers (*māyā*) of the Asuras.
The verbal root *day* is used in the senses of giving, harming, going, and protecting. O Indra, O undecaying one—Indra who cannot be worn down—you [perform this].

O much-invoked one, O wise ordainer, O most worshipful Indra, come to us with your teams of horses that bring all desirable things. O you whom neither the godless nor the god can restrain, come swiftly toward us, directed toward our exhilaration. O much-invoked one, O wise ordainer, O most worshipful Indra, come to us with your teams of horses that bring all desirable things. Neither the godless asura nor the god can restrain those teams of horses; with them, come quickly, directed toward our exhilaration. (The reduplication of *ā* at the beginning of the verse is a Vedic archaism.)
The eighth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “*suta iha*,” is the seerly composition of Bharadvāja; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and is dedicated to Indra.
It is introduced by the words “*suta iha*.
This hymn is recited at the *viṣuvat* day during the *nikevalya* śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Suta ityevaṃpūrvaḥ’" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.6).
In the Mahāvrata as well, these three hymns beginning with this one are used in the Niṣkevalya [Śastra].
Likewise, it is stated in the Pañcama Āraṇyaka: "‘Suta itvaṃ nemiśla indra soma iti trīṇi’" (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 5.2.2).

O Indra, when the Soma is pressed, when the great prayer is offered, when the hymn is being chanted and the litany recited—whether, O Maghavan, you come with your two harnessed bay steeds, O Indra, bearing the thunderbolt in your arms. When the Soma is pressed—that is, when it has been extracted—and while the great prayer is being uttered, when the hymn is being chanted and the litany recited, O Indra, you, being closely joined [with your steeds], yoking your two bay horses, O Maghavan... *Note: The provided text contains a partial repetition of the verse. The translation reflects the full meaning of the verse as it appears in the Ṛgveda.*
1. O Indra, you who possess the letters *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *ya*.
2. By means of the excellence (*prakarṣeṇa*) of the letters *gha* and *śa*.
3. The letter *ma* is not present in the word *mahati*; [the letter] *śa* [is used for] *mahata*.

O Indra, you who are wealthy, bearing your own weapon, the thunderbolt (*vajra*), in your two arms—that is, in your hands—you go, or rather, you come, by means of the two well-yoked bay horses (*hari*) harnessed to your chariot; this is to be connected with the phrase "when the soma has been pressed."

Or when you, O Indra, protected the powerful one in the decisive battle against Vṛtra for the sake of winning heroes; or when, being yourself fearless, you brought the Dasyus under control, O Indra, while they were threatening the trembling Dakṣa.

Whether it was on the decisive day in heaven when you, O Indra, protected the mighty one in the slaying of Vṛtra and in the winning of heroes; or whether, being yourself fearless, you brought the defiant Dasyus under control for the sake of the terrified Dakṣa—O Indra. || 2 ||

O Indra, when the battle for Vṛtra—where heroes, that is, warriors, must exert themselves—is to be won in the celestial realm, you protect the vigorous sacrificer who presses the soma, or else you guard him;
"ca" (and) serves as a conjunction.

O Indra, you—being fearless (*abibhyat*)—subdued (*arandhayaḥ*), or rather brought under your control (*vaśīkarosi*), the *dasyus*, those plundering enemies who were bold (*śardhataḥ*) and exerting themselves in battle against the people who were capable (*dakṣasya*) in sacrifices and the like yet trembling with fear (*bibhyuṣaḥ*) of their foes; all this is connected with the preceding phrase, "when the Soma has been pressed."

And so it has been said: "O slayer of Vṛtra, whether you go with your two bay horses while wielding the thunderbolt in the forepart [of the day], or whether you protect men in battle as they press the Soma."
And whatever enemies belong to the sacrificer who is skillful in his rites, you bring them under control; thus, though they are terrified, you remain free from fear.
"When these two have been pressed and the Stotra and Śastra have commenced," thus [it is said]; "this is one meaning of the Ṛc, and 'the Soma has been pressed' and 'you'—these two [are the other]."
May Indra drink the pressed Soma; may he, the fierce one, lead the singer forward with his aid.
He creates a wide space for the hero and bestows wealth even upon the praising singer.

May Indra be the protector; may he, the fierce one who leads forward, be the drinker of Soma for his singer with his aid. He is the creator of space for the hero who seeks prosperity, and the giver of wealth even to the praising singer. 3.
May Indra drink the pressed-out, freshly extracted soma; may he become one whose nature is to drink.
Now, by the rule "na lokāvyayaniṣṭhā," there is a prohibition of the sixth case (genitive).
Of what kind?

By means of *ūtī* (aid) and *ūrjayā* (strength), as a path, he is the *praṇenīḥ*—the one who leads excellently—the *jaritāram*, the singer or praiser. He is the *ugraḥ*, the exalted one, who for the sake of the *vīrāya*, the hero capable in sacrificial and other rites, and for the *sūraye*, the patron performing the pressing of Soma, shall *kartā lokam*, create a place;
that is to say, he shall bestow it.
*ū* is a filler for the verse (*pādapūraṇa*). *Stuvate* means "to one who praises," that is, to one who performs a hymn of praise (*stotra*). *Kīraye* means "to one who sings.
*Cit* is used in the sense of *ca* ("and").
And in the mantra:
"Kīri" is a name for those who offer praise;
may he be the giver of "vasu," which means wealth.
He goes forth with his two bay horses; he wields the thunderbolt, he has drunk the Soma, and he has bestowed cattle.
He makes the hero who is manly and possessed of all heroes; he hears the call of the singer, for he is borne by the hymns of praise.

The goer; these many; all names; with the two Haris; with the seven; the thunderbolt; you have drunk; the Soma; you have given; the cows; the doer; the hero; manly; possessing all heroes; the hearer; the call of the singer; you who carry the hymn of praise. 4.
May Indra, who is accustomed to going, come by means of his two bay horses (*haribhyām*) to the three *savana*s—the libations situated within the heart.
Of what nature is he?
He is the bearer (*babhriḥ*), the holder of his own weapon, the thunderbolt (*vajram*); he is the drinker (*papiḥ*), the one who drinks the pressed soma; [and] the cows (*gāḥ*).

1. *Kha-jha-ta-na-bha-ra-arandhaya*—thus [it is said]. *Dadiḥ* means the giver; *naryam* means beneficial to men; *sarvavīram* means endowed with many sons; *vīram putram* means a heroic son; *kartā* means the one who bestows such a son upon the sacrificer (*yajamāna*); *gṛṇataḥ* means of the one who praises; *havam* means the invocation or hymn of the singer; *śrotā* means the listener or hearer; and *stomavāhāḥ* means one who is to be carried or honored by hymns (*stoma*).

To him we offer that which he possesses—Indra, who from of old has been our protector. When the Soma is pressed, we praise him with hymns and recitations, so that our prayer may be a source of strengthening for Indra.

To him—him indeed we serve—that Indra who from of old has made for us our waters. When the Soma is pressed, we praise him; reciting hymns, we offer strengthening prayer to Indra, so that it may be effective. 5.

Indra, who from of old is ancient, performs for us—on our behalf—the work of nourishing and so forth; whatever hymn of praise and the like this Indra desires (*vavāna*), that we strive to attain (*viviṣmaḥ*) for this Indra—we perform it, such is the meaning. When the *soma* has been pressed, we offer praise.
We perform hymns for Indra;
reciting the *ukthas*, that is, the *śastras*—
the elision of the nominative plural ending [is applied].
The meaning is: "We shall act so that the food characterized by the oblation (*havis*) may become a source of increase (*vardhana*) for Indra—that is, something which brings about his growth."

For we have fashioned strengthening hymns for you who made the *brahmans*; thus, O Indra, with our prayers we serve you. When the Soma is pressed, O drinker of the pressed juice, let us perform through sacrifices the most auspicious and delightful deeds that bring you joy.

For you who have performed the sacred hymns, O Indra, we offer these strengthening songs with our prayers. When the Soma is pressed, O drinker of the pressed juice, let us perform for you the most auspicious and delightful acts through sacrifices.

O Indra, because you yourself have performed (*cakṛṣe*) the *brahmāṇi*—that is, the hymns of praise that are *vardhanāni*, which bring about your own increase—for that reason, we, with our *matibhiḥ* (thoughts or intellects), pervade (*viviṣmaḥ*) such hymns as those for you. The meaning is: "You have fashioned such hymns of praise as will become my means of increase."

Moreover, O Soma-drinker, when the pressed soma is being offered for you, and when the meat has been prepared, let us perform most blissful, most delightful, and pleasing hymns—hymns joined with oblations and sacrificial offerings—that shall carry [you] hither.
Be mindful of us, graciously accepting the *puroḷāśa* cake; drink the Soma, O Indra, which wins the cattle.
Sit upon this sacred grass (*barhis*) of the sacrificer; make wide room for us who are devoted to you.
Be mindful of us, graciously accepting the sacrificial cake; drink the Soma that wins the cattle, O Indra. Sit here upon this sacred grass of the sacrificer; grant wide space for us who seek you.
O Indra, being gracious and rejoicing, do thou take notice of our *puroḷāśa*—this sacrificial offering characterized by such qualities—and be aware of it.
Furthermore, drink quickly the pressed *soma* prepared with products of the cow, such as curds and the like;
for that purpose, sit upon this *barhis* (sacrificial grass) belonging to the sacrificer.
Immediately after that, for the sake of the sacrificer who desires his own master, make (*kṛdhi*) his world—his place—broad (*uruṃ*), extensive;
*u* is a filler particle.
1. gha-ca: *sute some*; 2. gha-śa: *govikāraṃ dadhyādibhiḥ*;
3. kha-jha-jha-ta-na-bha-ra: the phrase *'uṃ vistīrṇaṃ'* is absent.

Rejoice indeed according to your pleasure, O fierce one! Let these seekers of sacrifice speed toward you; let these oblations go forth to you, who are invoked by many. Toward you, O Indra, may this prayer go for our protection, reaching you with its two wings. 8. Rejoice indeed according to your pleasure, O fierce one! Let these seekers of sacrifice speed toward you; let these oblations go forth to you, who are invoked by many. Toward you, O Indra, may this prayer go for our protection, reaching you with its two wings. 8.
O you whose power is uplifted, O Indra, rejoice and exult according to your pleasure, in accordance with your desires, as it may be.
The word *hi* is for the purpose of completing the meter;
because it is joined with *hi*, the verb *mandasva* becomes entirely unaccented due to a grammatical displacement (*vyatyaya*).
"May these sacrifices, these offerings, and these Soma-libations reach you;
O Indra, invoked by many, may these our invocations— our hymns of praise— reach you."
"May this prayer—this hymn of praise—be extended toward you for our protection; may they draw you near and restrain you [for our aid]."

O friends, fill him up with pressed Soma juices, even as you do, so that he may satisfy Indra, the liberal giver. Will it not be for our support? For will not Indra, the mighty one, neglect us in his desire to help? O friends, just as you do, fill him up with pressed Soma juices—him, Indra, the generous one. Will it not be for our support? Will not Indra, the powerful one, fail us in his desire to protect?

O friends, you who are his praisers, when the Soma juices have been pressed—that is, poured out—fill him full, satisfy that very Indra with Soma-juices according to your desire. Is this not much for him? For *kuvid* is a word signifying "much."
"Let there be [this] even when it does not exist.
For what purpose?
'Not for us,' that is, for our support, maintenance, or nourishment."
Indra does not neglect—that is, he does not obstruct—the vigorous sacrificer who is inclined toward overcoming [enemies], for the sake of his protection and satisfaction.

Thus has Indra been praised when the Soma was pressed among the Bharadvājas; may he, the lord of the wealthy, dwell among us. So that he may be present for the singer, may Indra, the patron, be the giver of wealth containing all desirable things. 10. Thus indeed has Indra been praised when the Soma was pressed among the Bharadvājas; may he, the lord of the wealthy, dwell among us. So that he may be present for the singer, may Indra, the patron, be the giver of wealth containing all desirable things. 10.

"Indra, the inexhaustible lord, has been thus praised (*astāvi*) among the Bharadvājas—that is, by me, Bharadvāja—when the oblation-offering of the wealthy Maghavan, the sacrificer possessing the *havis*, was performed upon the pressed Soma.
May Indra become a patron (*sūri*) who impels the singer (*jaritre*) onto the path of truth, so that it may come to pass;
and furthermore, he has been praised so that he may become the giver of wealth (*rāyaḥ*) that is desirable by all. This is the connection of the meaning.
The two syllables "i-d" serve as a filler.
1. *Gha-puruhūtam*: Indra, who is invoked by many.

2. *Kha-jña-na-bha-āyamyāḥ*: Let them come (*kha-jña-ācchatu*); let them restrain themselves; *jña-tara-āyamyāḥ*: let them come; *ta1-ra-āyamyāḥ*: let him come. 3. *Kha-jña-jha-na-bha-ra-āgacchatu*; *ta2-ācchatu*; *ya-āgacchatu* (let him come) and *niyacchatu* (let him restrain himself).
4. Kha, jña, jha, ta, na, bha, ya, ra, e, na.
There are twenty hymns in the third Anuvāka.
Among them, the first hymn, "vṛṣā madaḥ," consisting of ten verses, is the seer's work of Bharadvāja; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and is addressed to Indra.
"Vṛṣā" is the heading [of the section].
This hymn is recited as the Niṣkevalya at the Viṣuvat day.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘vṛṣā madaḥ pra maṃdidhāya’" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.6).

The bull-like exhilaration, the hymn of praise, and the recitations are with Indra; he is the drinker of the pressed Soma, the consumer of the dregs, the worshipful Maghavan for men through their hymns, the King who milks the songs, and whose protection endures.

The bull, the exhilaration, the fame, and the hymns are with Indra. Among the pressed Soma juices, he is the drinker of the residue, the impetuous, the one worthy of praise, the bounteous lord for men through their hymns—the King of songs, whose protection is inexhaustible. 1.
In those sacrifices where Soma is present, the exhilaration (*mada*) produced by Indra’s drinking of Soma becomes "virile" (*vṛṣā*), that is, a showerer of the sacrificer's desires;
or alternatively,
it becomes the performer of the act of raining for the one who gladdens all people.
O heroic and valorous Indra, your great majesty, vast as the two worlds—heaven and earth—shines forth preeminently;
it surpasses even heaven and earth. This is the meaning.
Herein lies an illustration:
Like the axle of two wheels— that is,
just as the axle connected to a chariot extends beyond the two wheels—
O Indra, invoked by many (puruhūta), your many daughter-like protections (putrīḥ) indeed grow forth (vihahuḥ), that is, they spread out specifically.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"of the tree, indeed.
Just as the branches of a tree grow forth, so it is here.

O Indra, possessor of power, you who have many abilities, your aids are like the easily led herds of cattle that move together; they are like the continuous lines of calves, O bountiful one, which, though bound by cords, remain unbound.

They belong to the possessor of Śacī; O you of many powers, they are your powers. Like the well-crossable paths of cattle, easy for calves to traverse, so are they for you, O Indra—bound by ties, yet unbound, O giver of good gifts.
O *puruśāka*, you of many deeds, O *indra*, the *śākāḥ*—the powers or actions—belonging to you, the *śacīvataḥ*, the wise one, move everywhere; this is the implied sense.
Therein lies the illustration:
just as the *sutayaḥ*, the paths of cows—that is, of milch-cows—are *saṃcaraṇīḥ*, moving everywhere, so it is with those [powers].
Moreover, they are like "the cords for calves.
A *tantrī* (cord) is a long, stretched rope upon which many calves are bound by fixed, branching ties.

Just as cords are the binders of many calves, O Indra, O *sudāman* (giver of good gifts), so too your *śākās* (powers) are *dāmanvantaḥ*—possessing bonds—that is, they are the binders of many enemies; yet they are *adāmānaḥ*, themselves unbonded by others.
One thing Indra does today, another thing tomorrow; he repeatedly makes what is non-existent become existent.
Here, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Pūṣan are our friends, who go about according to the will of the noble one.

One thing today, another tomorrow; one thing this very day, and another the next. Indra has repeatedly brought these into being. Here, Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Pūṣan are our protectors; they are the masters who bring under their control the will of the enemy. || 5 ||
This Indra today, on this very day, performs another deed; for "karvara" is a name for action—
he performs an act.
Furthermore, he performs another action characterized by upward movement on the following day;
this very point is explained as follows:
both the non-existent, which is inauspicious such as the falling of thunderbolts, and the existent, which is auspicious such as praise and the like.
Alternatively:

Indra repeatedly becomes the performer (*ācakriḥ*) of both evil deeds, such as the slaying of Viśvarūpa Triśiras, and virtuous deeds, such as the slaying of Vṛtra and other Asuras who cause affliction to the world. Thus, by means of his own majesty, he repeatedly performs actions that are mutually distinct; the meaning is that every day he performs a different deed, one that is not shared with others.
May such an Indra be our "paryaitā," one who brings to fulfillment, at this sacrifice, our "vaśasya"—the desirable fruit such as heaven and the like.
(The form *astai* is the third person singular present indicative.

May Mitra, the deity presiding over the day; Varuṇa, the deity presiding over the night; Pūṣan, the nourishing deity; and Aryaman, the impelling Savitṛ—these also, being directed by Indra, be the fulfillers of our desire.
Alternatively, Mitra and the others are also mentioned here in their own primary capacity:
may Mitra and the others, as well as Indra, each individually fulfill our desire.
And so it is stated in the Bṛhaddevatā: "The two verses beginning with 'protaye' and 'anyat' are traditionally remembered as being addressed to the Viśvedevas."
1. Kha-bha-mahan. 2. Kha-bha is surpassed and exceeded; it is surpassed by jha-ta-na; it is surpassed by ra. 3. Kha-na-bha-ya-śa-tatra. 4. Kha-gha-bha-śa-bahuśaktimindra.
Like waters from the back of a mountain, O Indra of many powers, they have brought you hither with hymns and sacrifices.
Seeking booty, those who praise you well have come to you with these fine songs of praise, like horses carrying their master to the race.

From you, O Indra, as the waters from the back of a mountain, they have led you forth with hymns and sacrifices. Seeking booty, they have come to you with these fair praises, like horses bearing songs to the race-course.

O Indra, from you—from your very presence—the singers, through hymns (*uktha*), recitations (*śastra*), sacrifices, and oblations, have led forth their own desires; they bring them to fulfillment in various ways.
Therein lies the illustration:
just as waters flow from the back, the upper part, of a mountain or a rock, so it is.
Moreover, O Girvāhas— O Indra, who art to be carried by songs consisting of words of praise—

the Bharadvājas, the singers, seeking strength (or desiring food, *vāja*), have approached and attained you, the renowned one, with these aforementioned beautiful hymns (*sustuti*) while making you powerful.
The illustration for swift movement is as follows:
just as horses, the draft-animals, quickly reach the race-course—that is, the battle—so too [is it here].
Neither autumns nor months, nor days, cause Indra to grow old;
even though he is ancient, his body is made to flourish when it is praised with hymns and recited verses.
No autumns grow old upon him, nor months, nor the days wear Indra down. Though he is already grown, let his body continue to increase, being extolled with hymns and recited praises. 7.
The autumns and the years do not age him, nor do they cause Indra to grow old, nor do they cause him to waste away;

likewise, the months do not cause him to waste away. Furthermore, the days do not draw him down nor diminish him. Even though he is already aged and fully grown, may the body of this Indra increase—becoming further augmented—as it is being praised and extolled by our hymns (*stoma*) and sacrificial recitations (*uktha*).
He does not bend before the stubborn, nor before the steadfast, nor before the defiant one incited by the Dasyus;
for Indra, even the lofty mountains are but a trifle, and even in the deep he finds a firm footing.

Not for the one who is weary, not for the one who sports, not for the steadfast, nor for the one incited by the Dasyus—having praised him, the ignorant ones [are surpassed]; even the lofty mountains of Indra become a ford for him, even in the deep. 8.
Even when praised by us, Indra does not bow down to the sacrificer who is *vīḷu*—that is, one with firm limbs; he does not become subject to his will.
Nor does he bow down to one who is *sthira*—one who is unshakable in battle.
He does not become subject to the will of a sacrificer who is *śardhat*—one who is arrogant, incited by Dasyus, and driven by those devoid of ritual action.
The meaning is that although Indra possesses many virtues, he does not come under the sway of those who possess them along with the *dasyus*.

Furthermore, even the lofty, great mountains (*giryas*) quickly go toward Indra—just as they reach him—by means of his beautiful hymns (*ṛṣvāḥ* = *mahāntaḥ*). [Thus] they attain him. (Rigveda 3.7) 1. *jha-ta*: by means of beautiful hymns. 2. *kha-na-bha-ya*: they went quickly. 3. *kha-na-bha-ya*: they reach him, just like that. 4. *kha-gha-ma-jñā-na*: for the sake of the steadfast one. 5. *kha-utsāyanāya*; *jha-na-ma-utsāhanāya*: for the sake of inciting/exalting. (Rigveda 3.7)
The fires become easy to traverse and are cast forth;
even in a place that is deep and bottomless, for this Indra, a ford—that is, such a standing place—is found.
O Atri, with your deep and far-reaching inspiration, bestow strengths upon us, O drinker of the pressed juice.
Stand upright for our aid, you who are unassailable, at the dawning of the day when the night has passed away.

With your deep and wide [flow], O wielder of the stone, bestow nourishment upon us, O drinker of the pressed juice; stand upright with your aid, unharmed at the dawning of the night when the time has come.

O you who possess a vessel— *amatram* meaning strength— O Indra, drinker of the pressed Soma, with a deep mind that is difficult to fathom and a vast, expansive mind, bestow upon us *iṣaḥ*, that is, foods, and *vājān*, that is, strengths. Grant them to us!

Furthermore: at the dawning of the day, at the breaking of the night, during the day, and during the encompassing night—O Indra, for our protection! O Indra, O powerful one, O Indra, that protection which is yours, which is most excellent—that protection which is lowest, and that which is highest.
With those aids which are intermediate, protect us—us who are like Vṛtra-slayers—in battle; protect us exceedingly well.
Furthermore, O fierce and woolly Indra, unite us with these great spoils of enjoyment and with foods; this is the ellipsis.
With these [songs], O Indra, may you, seeking no harm, unsettle the fury of the adversary who contends in battle;
with these, you have cast down all the attacking Dāsa tribes in every direction for the sake of the Ārya.

With these [songs], O Indra, while remaining unharmed, cause the fury of the enemy to falter as you contend with rival hosts. With these, you have scattered all assailants in every direction and brought the Dāsa tribes under the power of the Ārya.
O Indra, with these our praises, do thou— unharmed and not injuring our own armies which are warring against and destroying the enemy hosts—
agitate and destroy the wrath of the adversary, the anger existing in battles and the like.

Moreover, by means of these very praises, destroy—drive away—the attacking assailants, the all-pervading Dāsīs who exhaust all labors, and all the tribes (viśaḥ), for the sake of the Ārya, the sacrificer who performs sacrifices and other rites.
Indra has yoked those who are kin and those who are not kin, these seekers of boons, turning them hitherward.
Strike down their wavering strengths; destroy their manly powers and drive them away.
O Indra, those who are kin and those who are not kin, who have turned their horses toward us—thou hast harnessed them; weaken their powers, strike down their manly strengths, and drive them away. 3.

O Indra, those enemies who are *jāmayaḥ*—kinsmen in form and closely related—and moreover those who are *ajāmayaḥ*, standing at a distance; those enemies who, being *arvācīnāsaḥ* (turned toward us) and *vanuṣaḥ* (assailing), have become *yuyujaḥ* (ready for battle)—of both these kinds of enemies, make their *śavāṃsi* (powers and strengths) *vithurā* (unsteady and diminished); indeed, leave nothing remaining. Likewise, strike down (*jahi*) and destroy their *vṛṣṇyāni* (heroic powers).
Furthermore, make both kinds of enemies turn away—render them *parāñc*, facing away from you.
The hero seeks the hero with his bodies when they both display their brilliance through their forms;
or when they roar aloud over offspring, cattle, progeny, or waters, they call out to one another across the wide fields.

The hero wins the hero with his bodies, when they both act with radiant forms in the heat; when two armies cry out against each other for offspring, for cattle, for progeny, or for waters, O wide one, they speak thus in the midst of the fields. || 4 ||
O Indra, that hero, aided by you, slays even a brave warrior or a hero with his own limbs and body;
the word *vanate* here functions in the sense of "he kills.
Or alternatively: [the text continues].
By means of this expression of conceptual construction (*vikalpābhidhāyaka*), the *asura*—being favored by you—wins over the hero.

1. [In the variants] kha, jha, na, bha, ra, it is read as *vithurā vithurāṇi*; in kha, jha, na, bha, it is read as *jñātavitthurā vithurāṇi*; in śa, as *vithurāṇi*. 2. In kha, jha, na, bha, it is read as *ya-asuro'bhidhīyate śaro vāśaro*; in ra, it is read as *aśuro'bhidhīyate*.

The two heroes. When do they strike? To this he says: when, with their bodies (*tanvā*) shining, those two who are mutually opposed engage in battle (*vyat*), that is, when they wage war (*saṃgrāmaṃ kṛṇvate*).

And when, on account of offspring (*vtoke*), or for the sake of sons (*putranimitte*), or with cattle (*goṣu*) as the cause, or with descendants (*tanaye*)—that is, grandsons—as the cause, or with waters (*apsu*) as the cause, or with all kinds of water-bearing lands (*urvarāsu*) as the cause, two wailing and crying parties (*krandasī*) engage in dispute (*vivrate*).
O Indra, the victory consisting in the acquisition of sons and so forth belongs to you who have been chosen by us; such is the meaning.
Neither the hero, nor the swift one, nor the bold, nor any warrior thinking himself such has ever fought against you. O Indra, no one stands as your equal; you surpass all these created beings.

No, O Indra; neither the brave, nor the swift, nor the bold has ever fought against you, nor one who considers himself a warrior. There is no one among these who can stand against you; you surpass all created beings. 5.
O Indra, with you as his ally, the hero—the man of valor—does not fight; he does not engage in battle (1).
Likewise, the swift one—the destroyer of other enemies—does not fight with you;
the bold one—the assailant—does not fight.
Thinking thus, the warrior, enraged in battle, did not fight with you;
O Indra, among those such as the heroes, there is no one at all who can be a substitute for you. You overcome all those beings that have come into existence, including the heroes and the rest.
He beholds the manly power of both; the impetuous one, the ordainer, is invoked in the assembly.
Whether against Vṛtra or in a great dwelling full of men, he shines forth when the two radiant ones extend the thread.

He rules over the manly power of both [worlds], when he, the ordainer, is kindled; they offer oblations whether against Vṛtra, or in a great dwelling rich in men, as he and his radiant counterpart extend the thread of sacrifice.
Between these two, that person possesses—that is, rules over—*nṛmṇa*, which means wealth.
He states both of these: between which two, and who rules?
[He says: "if" (*yadi*), referring to that person.
The particle *yat* functions in the sense of *yasya* (of whom).

In the *samitha*—that is, in the sacrifice (*yajña*)—the *vedhasaḥ*, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) who are the ordainers (*vidhātṛ*) through their ritual action (*karman*), "invoke" (*hvarente*) Indra; they praise him. This is the connection with the word *iṣṭa* ("sacrificed to").

Whether it be in the case of a great (*mahaḥ*) and abundant (*prabhūte*) obstruction (*vṛtra*), or on account of confinement (*nirodha*), or in a place (*kṣaye*) provided with human attendants (*nṛvat*), or on account of a dwelling (*gṛha*), [Indra is praised] by two people (*janau*) who possess wide space (*vyacasvantī*). 4. *yadi*. 5. *yau*.
The word *yadi* functions in the sense of possibility (*yāviṣya*).
The connection is: "it is stretched out" (*vitantasate*) and "it is separated" (*viyujyate*) between those two.
The root *tasi*, meaning "to perish," preceded by the prefix *vi-* becomes *vitantasaite*.
Alternatively, the root *tantasa* is listed among the *kaṇvādi* group; from that, this form is derived.
1. Kha-putrādi; the attainment of sons and so forth through Bha; for the attainment of sons and so forth through Śa. 2. One should fight with Kha, Jña, Na, Ta, Na, Bha, Ya, and Ra.
