In the Sākamedha rites, during the Mahendra sacrifice, there is a *yājyā* verse for Indra Vṛtrahan.
It is stated in the Sūtra: “*anu te dāyi maha indriyāya viśvakarman haviṣā vāvṛdhānaḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.18).
This is after reciting the *sūktamukha* of the Niṣkevalya [Śastra] in the one-day (*ekāha*) rite named Anukī.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Anu te dāyi maha indriyāya... katho nu te paricarāṇi vidvān’—these two [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.5).

For the sake of your great power, O Indra, everything was granted to you; truly, all was granted for the slaying of Vṛtra. Sovereignty was granted to you, and conquering might was granted to you, O Indra, worthy of sacrifice; together with the gods, all was granted to you for the subduing of men. O Indra, for the sake of your great majesty (*mahe*), for the sake of your sovereign power (*indriyāya*), it was granted to you (*anu dāyi*). Truly (*satrā*), for the purpose of the slaying of Vṛtra (*vṛtrahatye*), everything (*viśvam*) was granted to you. By what? And what was granted? To that he says both: that by which one sustains the universe—that *kṣatram*, or ruling power—was granted to you. That which overcomes enemies, distinguished by such qualities—that *sahaḥ*, or conquering might—was granted to you. O Indra, worthy of worship (*yajatra*), for you (*te*), in the battle for men (*nṛpaha*), all this was granted by all the gods (*devebhiḥ*).

Thus, O Indra, drive our rivals together in battles; subdue the hostile, godless armies. May the Bharadvājas, praising you with their protection at the break of day, find a dwelling place, O Indra, even now. Thus, O Indra, being thus praised, drive our rivals—the enemy hosts—into the *samats*, the battles, for the sake of slaying the foe. Furthermore, subdue the warring, godless, demonic armies; bring them under our control. May the Bharadvājas, singing your praises with your aid at the dawning of the day, obtain a secure abode, O Indra, even now.

1. [The syllables] *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *śa* do not exist [in this context]. 2. *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *bha*: "O slayer of Vṛtra" (*vṛtraghnaḥ*); *ta*, *ra*: "O slayer of Vṛtra" (*vṛtrahaṇe*); *śa*: "O slayer of Vṛtra" (*vṛtrahaṇa*). 3. *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*: [the word] *viśiṣṭakam*. 4. *jha*, *ta*: [the word] *nṛsahye*. 5. *kha*, *bha*, *śa*: "O Indra, you... (*indra tvam*). 6. *jha*: "the contending armies" (*spṛdhāmānāḥ senāḥ*).
Furthermore, O Indra, we Bharadvājas, praising you—that is, extolling you—with food (*avasā*) for the sake of dwelling (*vastoḥ*), meaning for the purpose of a habitation (*nivāsa*).
Now we shall surely obtain our portion.
The third hymn, consisting of the ṛc beginning with “śrudhī na indra,” is the seer Bharadvāja’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and addressed to Indra.
Thus it is enumerated: “śrudhī no [beginning with] eight [verses].
Its application is indicated by its internal characteristics (liṅga).

Hear us, O Indra; we invoke you for the winning of great booty, we who are full of vigor. When the people come together in the struggle for heroes, grant us fierce protection on the decisive day. Hear us, O Indra! We invoke you for the winning of great booty, we who are full of vigor. When the people come together in the struggle for heroes, grant us fierce protection on the decisive day.
O Indra, we, the chanters who pour out the Soma-pressings, call upon you for the sake of obtaining great, mighty booty—food—for its acquisition.
O Indra, hear that call of ours!
When the people, the clans, come together in the battle for the prize of heroes, then on that final day, grant us fierce and victorious protection.

The prize-winning steed, the son of a prize-winner, invokes you for the winning of great booty to be seized. O Indra, the boxer, fighting for cattle, looks to you as the true lord and deliverer in the midst of enemies. tvām | vājī | havate | vājineyaḥ | mahaḥ | vājasya | gadhyasya | sātau | tvām | vṛtreṣu | indra | sat'patim | tarutram | tvām | caṣṭe | muṣṭi'hā | goṣu | yudhyan ||2||

The *vājī*, one possessing the characteristic of sacrificial food (*havis*), the son of *Vājinī* named Bharadvāja—O Indra, he praises you for the sake of obtaining (*sātau*), that is, as the cause for gaining, great (*mahaḥ*) food (*vājasya*) which is accessible to all (*gadhyasya*). Furthermore, O Indra, Bharadvāja invokes you—the lord of the virtuous (*satpatim*), the protector of people, and the deliverer (*tarutram*) from the wicked—on account of the obstacles (*vṛtreṣu*) or calamities.
*Muṣṭihā*, the slayer of enemies by the strength of his fist, *bharadvājaḥ*, fighting with the enemies when cows have become the occasion for battle, *caṣṭe*—he beholds you;
he protects you.

You incited the sage in the winning of the sun; you struck down Śuṣṇa for the worshiping Kutsa. You struck off the head of the one who was vulnerable at no vital spot, performing a deed worthy of praise for Atithigva. You incited the sage in the winning of the sun; you struck down Śuṣṇa for the worshiping Kutsa. You struck off the head of the one who was vulnerable at no vital spot, performing a deed worthy of praise for Atithigva. 3. You incited the sage in the winning of the sun; you struck down Śuṣṇa for the worshiping Kutsa. You struck off the head of the one who was vulnerable at no vital spot, performing a deed worthy of praise for Atithigva. 3.

O Indra, you impelled—that is, you urged on—the seer Kavi Bhārgava for the sake of obtaining food; that is, you sent him forth. Furthermore, O Indra, you struck down—that is, you cut to pieces—the Asura Śuṣṇa for Kutsa, who had offered the oblation.
Regarding *varka*:
1. In the versions kha, jha, jha, ta, na, ma, ya, ra, and te, it is from you (*tvattaḥ*).
2. In the versions kha, jha, jha, ta, na, bha, ra, and śūrasātā, it is in the battle of heroes (*śūrasātau*).
The form *vṛṇakti* is the *luṅ* (aorist) form of the root meaning "to break" or "to cut."

Likewise, for Divodāsa, who approached you as a guest, you—desiring to bring him well-being worthy of praise and hymn—struck down the head of Śambara, who considered himself invulnerable and devoid of any vital point. You slew him.
You brought forward the chariot for the warrior; you helped the fighting bull so that he might be seen.
You, O Indra, together with Vetasu, struck down Tugra and strengthened Turjina as he sang your praises.

You brought forward the chariot; you protected the lofty warrior, the bull, the visible one, as he fought. You slew Tugra together with Vetasu; O Indra, you struck down Turjī as he was singing praises. ||4||

O Indra, you brought forth—that is, you delivered—to King Vṛṣabha, who was known by that name, a lofty and great chariot as a warrior-weapon for battle. Moreover, you protected King Vṛṣabha, so named, from the fight, when ten days had passed while he was fighting and contending with his enemies. Furthermore, acting as a companion to King Vetasu, who bore that same name, you slew the Asura Tugra.
There was a certain asura named Vetasu;
here, someone other than him is being referred to.
Or else:
The word *vetasave* is a dative used in the sense of the instrumental (*tṛtīyārthe*).
You slew Tugra together with the Asura Vetasu.
Thus it is heard in another Manvantara: "Like a father, for the sake of aid, I have delivered Vetasū, Tugra, and Smadibha unto Kutsa" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.49.4).
O Indra, you slew Turjī, the king known by that name, who was chanting and praising you.
O Indra, you made that hymn of praise swell; O Hero, you struck out thousands as they were being presented.
You cast down the Dāsa Śambara and protected Divodāsa with your wondrous aids.

O Indra, you have made that hymn of praise swell; for you, O Hero, have shattered hundreds and thousands, and you struck down Śambara the Dāsa from the mountain. You protected Divodāsa with wondrous aids.
O Indra, you who are powerful by nature, the destroyer of enemies—by what greatness did you perform that praiseworthy deed?
What was that deed? It is said:
O heroic Indra, you shattered and tore asunder hundreds upon hundreds and thousands upon thousands of Śambara’s followers and warriors.
And likewise in another Nigama: "O Adhvaryus, he who [slew] a hundred [fortresses] of Śambara" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.14.6).
Similarly: "You struck down—that is, you slew—the Dāsa Śambara, the destroyer of sacrifices and other rites, who was within the mountain.
For it is also heard: "He who [slew] Śambara dwelling in the mountains" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 2.12.11).
Furthermore, with various and manifold aids—that is, with diverse forms of protection—you indeed protected King Divodāsa, guarding him preeminently.
O Indra, being exhilarated by our acts of faith, you struck down Cumuri with the *Ṛbhīti* weapon for the sake of Ṛbhu;
you, bestowing favor upon Piṭhīnas, struck down Pṛṣṭi along with his thousands of followers through your power.
Gladdened by acts of faith, O Indra, you struck down Cumuri for the sake of Dabhīti; you, bestowing favor upon Piṭhīnas, slew Raji along with his thousand followers through your power. 6.

1. [The syllables] *kha*, *jña*, *ta*, *na*, *ma*, and *ra* signify the act of cutting. 2. *Kha-jña-na-ma-ra-śa-yudhyanto*; *ta-yuddhanto*. 3. *Kha-na-bha* and likewise. 4. *Gha-śa-vicitrābhir indra tvamābhiḥ*.
O Indra, by these various [actions] performed with faith (*śraddhā*)—that is, preceded by faith and executed with great reverence—being exhilarated (*mandasānaḥ*), that is, rejoicing;
for whatever action is joined with faith, it becomes substantial.
And thus it is heard in scripture: "Whatever one performs with knowledge, with faith, and with the secret doctrine (upaniṣad), that alone becomes more powerful" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.1.10).
And while exhilarated by the Soma juices, you caused Cumuri—the Asura of this name—to sleep for Dabhīti, the royal seer of this name;
that is, you slew him.
Furthermore, O Indra, you, bestowing—granting with faith and wisdom—the maiden named Raji or the kingdom to him called Pithīnas, slew at once, simultaneously, sixty thousand warriors.
And may I too, O noble Indra, attain that favor and strength of yours,
when heroes with you as their threefold protection, O most powerful one, overcome the Nahuṣas through your heroic deeds.

May I also, through the patrons, attain that glorious favor of yours, O Indra—your strength-bestowing benevolence—by which, O most powerful one, the heroes among men, protected by you with your triple-layered defense, are praised as true sons of Nahuṣa.

O most excellent Indra, accompanied by the heroes, may the heroic singers praise with their triple-layered protection— that which has three layers as its coverings, the worlds— those blessings, the happiness, and the strength bestowed by you, O subduer of enemies, which they celebrate. O Indra, may I too, Bharadvāja, together with my patrons and singers, attain that supreme and most praiseworthy blessing and strength granted by you.
O Indra, may we be your dearest friends in this invocation for glory;
may he who is free from distress, the glory of sovereignty, be the most excellent in the winning of Vṛtras and the acquisition of riches.

O Indra, in this invocation for glory, may we be your friends; O Mighty One, may we be your most beloved. May he who wards off distress be the foremost glory of our dominion, the best for the winning of Vṛtras and the acquisition of riches. 8.

O Indra, worthy of worship, we who are your friends and your praisers shall be most beloved— exceedingly dear— to you at this invocation for glory, at this hymn for the sake of wealth. May Pratardana— the king named Pratardana—
and his son, the king named Kṣatraśrī, my patron, be the best, may he be the most excellent among all.
For what purpose?
The connection is as follows: "May he be the most excellent for the slaying of *vṛtra*s—enemies—and for the winning (*sanaya*), that is, the acquisition, of riches (*dhana*) and treasures (*vasu*)."

The fourth hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "kim asya made," is the seerly composition (*ārṣam*) of Bharadvāja. It is cataloged thus: "The last verse is a praise of the gift by Āyamāna Abhyāvartin. The seer (*ṛṣi*) is Bharadvāja.
The metre is Triṣṭubh.
Since it consists of a praise of giving, according to the principle that "that by which [an act] is expressed is its deity," the deity is indeed the act of giving itself.
The application (viniyoga) is established through indicative marks (laiṅgika).

What did Indra do in his exhilaration from this [Soma], what upon drinking it, and what in its friendship? What battles did he perform in its presence, or what did he achieve in the past, and what indeed in the present?

What [did he do] in his exhilaration? What [did he do] at its drinking? Indra, what did he do in its friendship or in its joy? What was his seat? What have those of old known of it? And what do the present ones know? ||1||
1. By the obstructor *kha-jha-na-bha-ya*.
2. In this [text], *kha-1-jha-na-bha-* does not exist. 3. *Kha-jha-bha-ra-* has the nature of *arūpa*.
The sage Bharadvāja, being patient with the delay of the fruit, censured Indra by means of this [verse].
In the exhilaration of this Soma, what has Indra done?
What indeed has he done upon drinking this Soma?
And what has he done in friendship with this Soma?
The meaning is that before drinking, Indra dwells together with Saṃman.
Regarding this Soma, in its dwelling place (*niṣad*), those who are the singers (*raṇā*) or the praisers—O Indra, what did those praisers obtain from you (*te*) in former times (*purā*)?
And what indeed have these new (*nūtanāsaḥ*) praisers of the present time obtained?
In the exhilaration of the Soma, in its drinking, and in its manifestation, Indra has performed his deeds;
those ancient battles which were won by him when he was seated in the assembly, and those new ones as well, have been celebrated.

Truly, in his exhilaration; truly, at his drinking, Indra performed great deeds; truly, in his presence, he wrought battles, or those which occurred when he was seated. Truly, these ancient ones have found him; truly, so too have the modern ones. ||2||
Thus challenged, Indra bestowed upon that seer the wealth he desired.
Immediately thereafter, having had his wishes fulfilled by Indra, the seer now refutes those words he previously spoke as reproaches.
In the exhilaration of this soma, Indra performed a glorious deed.
Upon the drinking of this Soma, he performed auspicious deeds; in his friendship, he performed auspicious deeds;
and those who are warriors or singers, they [performed them] in the dwelling of the sacrifice.
The meaning is "in the sacrificial hall.
In former times (*purā*), indeed, O Indra, they obtained (*vividre*) auspicious deeds from you (*te*);
even now, the contemporary worshippers (*nūtanāsaḥ*) have likewise obtained only auspicious deeds.

O Maghavan, no one has ever measured your greatness; O Sage, no one has seen the limit of your bounties, nor, O Indra, the full extent of your new-found power. No one has beheld the majesty of your might.

Not indeed, O Maghavan, has anyone ever beheld such power as yours; neither in your greatness, nor in your totality, nor in your generosity, O Sage, nor even in your newest bounty—no one, O Indra, has seen such an Indra-power as yours.
O bountiful and wealthy Indra, we, the sages, do not know the full extent of your greatness—the majesty of your entire majesty.
The word *nu* is used as a filler.
Likewise, we do not know the full extent of your wealthiness—your status as a possessor of riches.
We do not know all your wealth, even of your newest and most praiseworthy bounty (*rādhas*).
In every instance, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
O Indra, your power (*indriya*)—your capacity—is not seen by anyone; it has never been perceived.
This very thing, O Indra, you perceived with your senses, by which the remainder of Varaśikha was destroyed;
for when the thunderbolt was hurled, from its fury and its roar, O Indra, you shattered him utterly, O most bounteous one.

This—that very power of yours—was perceived, by which you slew the offspring of Varaśikha with your thunderbolt; for when you were struck down, O Indra, even from the sound of your own breath, the highest [enemy] was shattered.
O Indra, with that heroic power by which [you slew] Varaśikha— Varaśikha being the name of a certain asura—
[you struck down] his offspring, the Śeṣas.
"Śeṣa" is a name for offspring. "Avadhīḥ" means you killed; "te etat" means this of yours; "etat indriyam" means this vigor;
"aceti" means it was perceived by us.

O Indra, by that very roar of your own thunderbolt as it was hurled—when it was struck down and impelled—a certain son, the most excellent among your sons due to his superior strength, was torn asunder from the force of that sound alone, which possessed the highest and most excellent crest.
Indra slew the offspring of Varaśikha, bestowing aid upon Abhyāvartin Cāyamāna;
when he struck down Vṛcīvanta at Hariyūpīyā, the other fled in fear to the eastern region.

Indra slew the sons of Varaśikha for Abhyāvartin Cāyamāna, bestowing upon him what he desired. When he struck down the sons of Vṛcīvān—who was born of the lineage of Varaśikha—in the eastern half at Hariyūpīyā, then the other, the eldest son of Varaśikha, was shattered by fear. This verse explains the same meaning previously stated: this Indra, bestowing desired objects upon Abhyāvartin—the king named Abhyāvartin, who was the son of King Cāyamāna—slew, that is, killed, the sons of the Asura Varaśikha. He destroyed them. O Indra, invoked by many, three thousand armored men together harnessed their steeds out of a desire for glory upon the Yuniyāvatī river.
The Vṛcīvants, fleeing from the arrow, broke their vessels and went down to the depths.

Three hundred and thirty armored men, O Indra—desiring glory (*śravasyā*), O much-invoked one (*puruhūta*)—in the battle at the *Yadhyāvatī* river, the sons of Vṛcīvat, fleeing from the arrow (*śaru*), shattered their vessels and went to their destruction. Now [the poet] explains the very meaning just stated: O much-invoked Indra, desiring glory—where "glory" (*śravaḥ*) means food or fame—wishing that by conquering you in battle they might obtain it or attain fame; rushing toward you for the sake of slaughter—that is, to strike you down—the sons of Vṛcīvat, three hundred and thirty in number, wearing armor, simultaneously at the aforementioned *Yadhyāvatī*, the Hariyūpīyā, shattered their vessels (the implements of sacrifice) and went to their aimless end; that is to say, they met with destruction.
He whose two bay steeds, seeking good pasture, move freely within the enclosure, licking their lips— He,
desiring to help Devavāta, gave Turvaśa to Sujñāya, the son of R̥cīka.

He whose two ruddy steeds, well-nourished with good pasture, move gracefully within the sacred enclosure, licking [the sacrificial butter]—he, for the sake of Sujñaya, delivered Turvaśa from Vṛcīvat, bestowing him upon Daivavāta as a gift. 7.

1. By the predominance of *jha*, *ta*, and *ba*. 2. The remainder of *jha*, *ta*, and *ra*. 3. By the will of *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *ya*. 4. Coming by means of *kha*, *gha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *ya*; *śa* signifies "going. *Aruṣā* (feminine dual) means the two shining red ones; *suyavasyū* means desiring beautiful grass; *rerihāṇā* means licking repeatedly, tasting the fodder again and again. Or else:
They perform a specific movement;
the two *gāvaḥ* (steeds) belonging to that *indra*, moving within the space between heaven and earth—that is, in the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*)—go forth.
The two particles *u* and *su* are merely expletives.
That Indra gave Turvaśa, the king, over to the king named Sṛjaya;
what was he doing?
Subduing—that is, bringing under control—the Vṛcīvatas and the Vāraśikhas for King Abhyāvartin, who was born of the lineage of Devavāta.
Or, it means "giving them wealth."
At the forefront, the liberal sovereign Maghavan, the great overlord, bestows two chariot-warriors, twenty oxen, and a stallion;
and this Āyamāna, who is difficult to overcome, gives as his sacrificial fee these cattle of the Pārthavas.

Two at the head, twenty chariot-warriors, and twenty oxen—Maghavan, the sovereign Samrāj Abhyāvartin Cāyamāna, gives these to me. This sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) of the Pārthavas is difficult to attain. 8.
Now Bharadvāja first mentions the mass of wealth given by his sister’s son, Abhyāvartin.

O Agni, this wealthy (maghavan) or liberal giver, the sovereign (samrāj) Cāyamāna—the son of Cayamāna—namely King Abhyāvartin, gives and has bestowed upon me twenty (twenty in number) cattle, both types (dvayān), meaning pairs consisting of males and females, along with chariots (rathinaḥ) and accompanied by women (vadhūmataḥ). These belong to Abhyāvartin, the king of the Pārthavas, born of the lineage of Pṛthu.
The plural number is used for the sake of honor.
This sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is "hard to destroy" (*durnaśā*), meaning it cannot be destroyed by anyone.

“Ā gāvaḥ” is the fifth hymn. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “Ā gāvo; the second [verse] is addressed to Gavya, or else it is addressed to Indra; another foot is in the Anuṣṭubh meter, while the others are in the Jagatī; the second verse and those following are Trishtubh. The seer (ṛṣi) is Bharadvāja.
The verse beginning with “Indro yajvane” is in the Jāgata metre;
“Upedam” is another Anuṣṭubh, and the remaining verses are Triṣṭubhs.
The deity for the entire hymn is Gauḥ (the Cow), while for the second verse and the *sūktānyapāda* (the supplementary foot of the hymn), Indra is optionally the deity.
This hymn is for the worship of cows.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Some [recite] the Āgāvīya" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.10.7).
The cows have come; they have brought auspiciousness. Let them settle in the cow-pen and rejoice among us.
May they be here, prolific and many-formed, yielding their milk for Indra throughout the many dawns.

The cows have come; they have brought auspiciousness. Let them sit in the cow-pen and find delight among us. May they be here, prolific and many-formed, yielding their milk for Indra through many dawns. 1.
The cows have come;
may they come to our house.
And moreover, may they perform what is auspicious, worthy of worship, and beautiful.
Likewise, let them sit—that is, let them settle—in our cow-pen, the place for cattle. Immediately thereafter, let them take delight—that is, let them rejoice—in us.

Moreover, in this cow-pen, may there be many cows of various forms and colors, possessing offspring—that is, accompanied by progeny—who, yielding milk toward the dawns, may be for Indra's sake during the times of dawn.
1. *gha*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *śa*, and *sūyavasyu*.

The *Ṛgveda* [Book 4, Chapter 6, Section 25]:
Indra bestows gifts upon the sacrificer who gives offerings; he grants them and does not steal what is his own.
Increasing his wealth more and more, he places the seeker of the gods in the open expanse.

Indra bestows gifts upon the sacrificer and the giver; he gives even more, he does not steal away what is his own. Increasing his wealth ever further and further, he places the god-seeking man upon the high ground and the stony ridge.

Indra bestows the desired wealth upon the sacrificer who is habitually performing sacrifices, and upon the singer who gratifies him with hymns of praise. He does not give only once, but rather, he says, "He gives evermore," for having approached, he always gives indeed. Furthermore, he never steals away the wealth that belongs to the sacrificer and the singer; he never takes it from them.

Moreover, increasing again and again—repeatedly—the wealth (rayi) consisting of cattle given by himself to this [sacrificer] of both kinds, and thus bringing about its growth, [the sacrificer says]: "O cows, you who seek the gods (devayu), may you be rich in offspring for yourselves; remain joined with your own calves. [And further:
"May you be those who roam through excellent pasture (suyavasa), grazing—that is, consuming—for the sake of food."
Drink the pure, stainless waters from the reservoir that is easy to drink;
and let no thief or robber have power over you—
may he not prevail.
Nevertheless, let the malevolent enemy—the tiger and the like—have no power over you. Moreover, may the weapon (*heti*) of Rudra, the Supreme Lord who is Time itself, avoid you; may it spare you.
May it turn away from you.
Mix this with that; let it be mixed with these cows.
Mix it with the seed of the bull, O Indra, within your own vigor.
"upa | idam | upāpṛcainam | āsu | goṣu | upa | pṛcyatām. [Maṇḍala 6, Anuvāka 3, Sūkta 29] The meaning is: "they are performing [the act of] mixing."
Likewise, "for the sake of good-will" (*sumataye*): *sumatiḥ* is his intellect, whose nature is beautiful favor;
"desiring" (*cakānāḥ*) means longing for that.
The term "action" (kriyā) must be supplied; thus, the object (karman) receives the designation of recipient (saṃpradāna). The form *cakānā* is a Vedic form of the root *kāmayate*.
Or alternatively:
performing great deeds—that is, carrying out magnificent actions—and desiring a good mind—that is, uttering beautiful praise—[we approach].
The form [‘ke gai śabde’] is derived from the root *gai* with the suffix *kānac* following the optative marker (*liṅ*).
Since Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt (vajrahasta), is the giver of great wealth, therefore worship him with oblations for protection—him who is delightful and truly great among the great.
In whose hand men have placed their strength, who stands upon the golden chariot; in whose two firm hands the reins are held, and the stallions, the draft-horses, are yoked for the journey.
In whose hand the heroic ones have mingled; who has mounted the golden chariot; in whose two hands the reins are held; and whose stallions, the virile steeds, are yoked for the journey. 2.
"In that Indra, manly riches beneficial to men have been poured forth (*mimikṣuḥ*); they are being poured out or filled.
[The suffix] *kartṛ* is used in the sense of the object due to a grammatical anomaly (*vyatyaya*). If one asks, 'In which Indra?'"
"In his hand" means on his arm;
or rather,
it is an epithet of Indra that is in grammatical apposition with this [word].
The meaning is that Indra is "in the hand" (*haste*) of the one who strikes;
as Yāska has stated: “*hasta* is from the root *han*; *prāśu* is from *han*” (Nirukta 1.7).
Or else:
In such an Indra as this, the personified riches existing abide, seeking to pour themselves out; they resound and fill the worshippers.
And that Indra, being the one who stands upon the chariot (*ratheṣṭhāḥ*), possessing that very nature, mounts the golden (*hiraṇyaye*) chariot.
Or rather:
Standing on the chariot, stationed upon the chariot— he who, standing on the golden chariot, Indra shall bestow and rain down riches and treasures.
And he whose two arms are thick, that is, broad and extended—
[of these] this is a name for the arms.
The reins are the rays; they are poured forth, that is, they are stretched out.
And his horses—steeds that are virile, capable of impregnating, and youthful—are being yoked to the chariot; on every path, along the way, they drip, that is, they neigh and fill [the air].
The meaning is that they come.
"We praise that Indra"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
For the sake of glory, your feet have been anointed with homage; bold wielder of the thunderbolt, you are rich in power and gifts.
Clothed in the fragrant hymn for all to see, O dancer, you have become radiant like the sun, full of vital energy.

For the sake of glory, your feet have been anointed with offerings; bold wielder of the thunderbolt, endowed with power and the right hand, you have clothed yourself in the fragrant hymn to be seen, O dancer, and like the sun, you have become the voice of the people. 3.

O Indra, for the sake of glory—that is, for the sake of sovereignty—let the services (duvas), that is, the acts of attendance, be poured out (ā mimikṣuḥ) upon your two feet; they offer them up, they present them.
Bharadvāja offers them. The plural number is used by way of grammatical substitution (vyatyaya).
Or rather:
they perform service—that is, they attend upon—your two feet for the sake of prosperity (*śriye*).
You, who by your might (*śavasā*) are bold (*dhṛṣṇuḥ*), the subduer of enemies, wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrī*), and possessor of skill (*dakṣiṇāvān*).
The *dakṣiṇā* is the wealth that must be given to the singers.

O *nṛto*, leader, you who possess that, you, Indra, clothing yourself (*vasānaḥ*) in your own form—the *surabhi*, the praiseworthy, the *arka*, which is by nature constantly moving—for the sake of being seen (*dṛśe*) by all, have become, or are, like the sun (*svar*), one who is to be approached or desired (*igiraḥ*).
The word *kam* is a filler.

1. *Kha*, *jña*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ya*: those who go, those who are going. 2. *Śa* and it is said (*ukta*). 3. *Kha*, *bha*: *āmimikṣuḥ*; they are poured out, they come. *Gha*: *ārmimikṣuḥ*. *Jha*: *āsicyante ādhrīyante*. *Śa*: *āmimikṣuḥ āsiñyante ādhrīyante*.
4. Continuous with *kha*, *jña*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*—that Soma has become most thoroughly mixed when pressed, in which the cooked offering is cooked and roasted grains are present;
while men, praising Indra, performing sacred formulations (*brahman*), and reciting hymns (*uktha*), are most beloved by the gods.

That Soma, most thoroughly mixed, has been pressed—the one in which the cooked offering is prepared. There are parched grains; the men, praising Indra, performing sacred formulations, and reciting hymns, are most beloved by the gods. 4.
That Soma which is about to be spoken of— this Soma, having been pressed (*suta*) and being thoroughly mixed (*āmiśratama*), meaning most completely blended—
is joined with Indra for the sake of being worthy of him (*āyya*).
When that *soma* has been pressed, the *pūkti*— the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and other such items to be cooked— is cooked;
the roasted barley grains (*dhānā*) are polished,
and these become prepared for the purpose of the oblation.

When that Soma has been pressed, the men—the leaders, the performers of sacred hymns (*brahmakārāḥ*), the officiating priests who prepare the oblation (*havis*) characterized by the *brahma*—praising Indra with hymns (*stotra*) and reciting and uttering the *ukthas*, they become most highly favored by the gods (*devavātatamāḥ*). The syntactical connection is that this Soma became mixed with Indra.
There is no limit to the power of that Śarva; he has indeed forced apart the two worlds with his greatness.
The patron, hastening forward, satisfies those [desires] with his aid, like one driving cattle into the waters with a well-aimed spear.

No; they are within the reach of Śarva’s arrow. But he has forced apart the two worlds, heaven and earth, by his greatness. The patron, striving with haste, satisfies them both with his aid, like one driving herds into the waters while seeking the prize. || 5 ||
O Indra, no limit has been set for this exalted power and strength of yours; it has not been contained.
(In this context, although the root *dhā* alone is used, its meaning should be understood as preceded by the prefix *ava*, i.e., "to contain" or "to confine.
It has not been confined.
The meaning is: "It is known by us.

That power (*bala*) by which he swiftly forced apart the two worlds, heaven and earth (*rodasī*), with its greatness—that is, by which power he split heaven and earth apart—the wise patron (*sūri*), the praiser, being impetuous and striving, honoring that power with strengthening oblations and sacrificing correctly, fills it completely.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"Like herds of cows in the waters"—just as a cowherd, while causing the cattle to drink, satisfies them with water, so it is here.
Thus is Indra, the great one, easy to invoke; with his golden jaws, the hero comes to our aid. For thus, when born, he of unequalled strength slays many Vṛtras and strikes down the Dasyus.

Thus indeed, let Indra be easy to invoke, sublime, with his aid—whether in his favor or in his wrath, he who is the hero with golden jaws; for even as soon as he was born, he possessed peerless strength, and he slays many Vṛtras and strikes down the Dasyus.
In this very manner as described, may the lofty and great Indra be easy to invoke—that is, he who is easily summoned.
The word "iti" is a filler.
He is the one with golden jaws (*hiriśipra*).

Whether his nostrils are wide or narrow, Indra— possessing such [features] as greenish color— is a *satvan*, a bringer of wealth, by means of his aid (*ūtī*), that is, through his coming, or by his non-aid (*anūtī*), that is, through his not coming; he is one who brings wealth whether he has come of his own accord or has not come at all.

1. The letters *kha*, *jha*, *bha*, and *ya* are mixed with *tama*; *gha*, *śa*, and *m* are abundant with *vata*. 2. The *śa*-sounds are the agents (*kartāraḥ*). 3. *Kha*, *gha*, and *bha* are not to be approached (*nopagantāraḥ*). 4. By means of *ya* it is to be abandoned;
the meaning is that he bestows wealth upon those who praise him.

Indeed, having been thus born or manifested, this Indra—possessing incomparable, peerless, and most excellent vigor (*ojas*)—shall slay many, indeed many, Vṛtras, that is, the obstructors such as the Rākṣasas.
Likewise, may he strike down the *dasyus*, the destroyers, and the enemies.
The seventh hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "bhūya it," is the seerly composition of Bharadvāja; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to Indra.
It is cataloged as "bhūyaḥ pañca.
This hymn is to be recited by the Acchāvāka at the midday pressing during the Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Of him who has risen, more is left over" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.16).
This hymn is also [recited] at the Niṣkevalya of the Mahāvrata.
Likewise, it is stated in the Pañcamāraṇyaka: "O Indra, for further increase of heroic power, thee among men... (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 5.1.6).
Furthermore, for the sake of increasing his heroic power, Indra alone, undecaying, bestows riches;
Indra has surpassed heaven and earth, for both worlds are but half of him.
Furthermore, for the sake of increasing his heroic power, he alone, undecaying, bestows riches. Indra has surpassed heaven and earth; indeed, both worlds are but equal to one half of him.
This Indra has grown even more— indeed, he has increased exceedingly—
for the sake of heroic deeds, such as the slaying of Vṛtra and others.
He alone is the preeminent one, undecaying—that is, incapable of being worn out—and that Indra bestows treasures, giving wealth to his worshippers.
Likewise, this Indra surpasses both heaven and earth;
moreover, both the worlds, heaven and earth, are but half of him.
The meaning is that this half-portion of Indra serves as a representative of both Heaven and Earth.
I consider half [of him] to be vast and sunless—that which no one can diminish;
day by day the sun has become visible, and he of good wisdom has established everything far and wide.
I consider it vast; that which he has established is beyond the sun. No one violates it. Day by day the sun has become visible. The one of excellent wisdom has spread all things far and wide. 2.
Now, indeed, I praise—that is, I extol—the great, vast, and sunless (asūrya) strength of this Indra, which is skilled in slaying the Asuras;
for the root *man* signifies the act of praising.
And whatever deeds that Indra maintains (*dādhāra*), no one at all (*nakiḥ*) diminishes them—no one whatsoever harms them.
What, then, are they? It is said:
day after day (*divedive*), every single day, the sun (*sūryaḥ*), though obstructed by Vṛtra, becomes (*bhūt*) visible (*darśataḥ*), that is, worthy of being seen (*darśanīyaḥ*).

One deed was that by the slaying of the obstructing Asura, Indra caused the sun to shine. Furthermore, that Indra, possessing beautiful rites—that is, of excellent action—established all worlds far and wide; he made them vast and extensive.
This is another deed.
The meaning is that he performed many such deeds.
1. And [the syllables] *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ya*, *ra*, and *yā*. Ṛgveda 3.8.3:

Even today, indeed, that deed of the rivers remains, when you, O Indra, made a path for them. The mountains sat down as if exhausted; by you, O doer of good deeds (*sukrato*), the firm regions were made stable. Even now, indeed, that work of the rivers [remains], when you, O Indra, made a way for them. The mountains sat down as if they had grown weary; by you, O doer of good deeds, the firm regions were made stable.

O Indra, even now, even today, even until now, and even in the past, that deed of yours regarding the waters—that which pertains to the rivers—continues to exist. You have carved out a path, a way for these rivers to flow; the meaning is that this deed of yours remains ever-present and has not perished. Moreover, by your command, the mountains and hills have settled down and remained fixed.
Abandoning their flight, they sat down motionless in a certain spot;
they did not eat,
for today was the day of fasting.
For that purpose, they are like men who are sinking;
just as those [men] do nothing at all for the sake of food.
Generating—that is, manifesting and illuminating—simultaneously and at once this triad: the sun, the sky, and the celestial realm (dyuloka) shrouded in darkness.
‘Abhūrekaḥ’ is a hymn consisting of five verses; it is the ṛṣi-sequence of Bharadvāja Suhotra.
The penultimate verse is a Śakvarī, and the remaining four are Triṣṭubhs.
Indra is the deity.
And it is enumerated: “*abhūrekaḥ suhotra ratu caturthī śakkarī*.
These eight hymns beginning with this one are to be recited in the *nikevalya* of the Mahāvrata.
Likewise, the Pañcamāraṇyaka states: “*abhūreko rathipate rathīṇām*—these are eight hymns” (AiĀ 5.2.2).
On the sixth day of the *pṛṣṭha* [stotra], this hymn is the *nivid*-insertion for the *nikevalya* [śastra].
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "‘*endra yāhy apa naḥ*, ‘*pra ghā nvasyābhūḥ*, and ‘*eko ’si’ constitute the *nikevalya*’” (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 8.1).
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, at the midday *iḷā-vākya* recitation, this very hymn is to be chanted as a *sāman*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Sāman-hymns [beginning with] 'O Lord of charioteers, you alone were the charioteer of charioteers' are [to be used]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.7).
You alone, O Lord of Charioteers, were the charioteer among charioteers; you placed the peoples within your two hands, O Indra.
For the sake of offspring, waters, progeny, and the sun, the contending tribes have cried out in various voices.

You have become the sole lord of riches, the charioteer of chariots. O Indra, you have placed the peoples within your two hands. Among their offspring, their waters, their progeny, and their sunlight, the contending tribes have raised their voices in praise.
O Indra, Lord of Wealth, you alone are the principal one; you have become, or are, the master of riches (rayīṇām). Or rather, there is a connection between "rayīṇām" and "rayipate."
The single word *rayi* is a restatement (*anuvāda*), as in the verse: "O Indra, you alone are the lord of cattle" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 7.98.6).
In that context, it should be construed as: "At that time, you alone are the preeminent one.
Furthermore, O Indra, you have placed—indeed, you maintain—the *kṛṣṭīḥ*, the subjects, within your own two hands, that is, your two arms.
The meaning is that the entire world abides under your command.

Furthermore, when there are men (*carṣaṇīyaḥ*)—on account of their offspring (*toke*), their sons (*putre*), the waters (*apsu*), the sun (*sūre*) who impels enemies, and their grandsons (*tanaye*)—they have uttered, they speak forth, various praises (*vivācaḥ*).
O Indra, at your roar all the earthly realms and even the unshakable regions of space are shaken;
heaven and earth, the mountains, and the forests—all that is firm fears you at your onset.

Out of fear of you, O Indra, all the earthly realms—even those that are immovable—are shaken; the regions of space, heaven and earth, the mountains, and the forests—everything solid trembles at your onset. 2.

O Indra, out of fear of you—from you—out of dread, all the pervasive earthly realms (the word *pārthivāni* refers to the earth and the intermediate space), the waters existing therein, even those very waters that are immovable (*acyutā*) and impossible to cause to move, are set in motion; the clouds retreat. This is the meaning to be described.

Moreover, O Indra, at your coming (*ā-ajman*), both heaven and earth (*dyāvā-kṣāmā*), the mountains (*parvatāsaḥ*), the hills (*girayaḥ*), the forests (*vanāni*), and the trees (*vṛkṣāḥ*) are seized with fear. What need is there to say more? The entire universe (*viśvam*), all that is firm and stable (*dṛḷham sthiram*), and every living being (*prāṇijātam*) trembles with fear (*bhayate*).

1. This triad: *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, *ya*. 2. *gha*, *śa*, *dhanapālaka*. 3. Ending with the name *śa*. 4. *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *bha*, *ya*, *ra*—to cause to fall away. 5. *ta*, *na*, *ā*—there is not.
O Indra, you who are full of vigor, with contemptuous force, protect our vigor in the struggle for cattle;
at the first onset of the sun, you stole the wheel, and you have made the evils vanish.

O Indra, with Kutsa you fought against the impetuous and insatiable Śuṣṇa in the quest for cattle; at the onset of the tenth [day], you stole away the wheel of the sun, for you have uncovered all hidden evils.

O Indra, you fought against—that is, you engaged in battle with—the Asura named Śuṣṇa, who was difficult to dry up (aśuṣam), powerful, and a drier-up of all; that is to say, for the sake of assisting Kutsa, you waged war against that Asura. Likewise, in the quest for cattle (gaviṣṭau).
The cows are arrows; because they are sought (*iṣyanti*) or go (*gacchanti*), it is called *gaviṣṭi*, a battle.
In that [battle], you have bitten ten times at this *kuyava* and at the demon *saṃjama*. You have harmed them.
The form [amuṣāyaḥ] is derived from the root *daṃś* (to bite) in the Vedic imperative (*loṭ*).
Furthermore, in the *prapitva*, that is, in the onset of the battle, you stole—meaning you took away—the wheel, which is a constituent part of the chariot, of the Sun;
from that time onwards, the chariot of the Sun has been single-wheeled.
O you whose warriors are true! He whose soldiers (*satvānaḥ*) or combatants (*bhaṭāḥ*) are truthful is so described.
O you who are very great! (*tuvinman*)!
He who possesses abundant manly strength and wealth is thus described.
O such Indra, you—mount your own formidable, terrifying chariot for the sake of a great battle, for the purpose of combat.
O Prapathin, Indra of the excellent path, come toward me with protection (*avas*) and with that chariot; approach, facing me.
Likewise, O Śrutaviśvatendra, proclaim us aloud among the people;
that is to say, make us renowned among all creatures.
‘Apūrvyā’: this fifth hymn, the ninth [in the maṇḍala], is in the Triṣṭubh metre and is dedicated to Indra.
It is listed in the Anukramaṇī as beginning with ‘Apūrvyā’.
This hymn is used for the Niṣkevalya śastra on the second day of the Chandoma sacrifice.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Those most numerous, unprecedented [deeds]—that fame of yours" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.7).
Furthermore, its application to this hymn in the Niṣkevalya section of the Mahāvrata is also declared.

For him, the unprecedented, most abundant, and most excellent words—most auspicious for the sake of the wondrous, heroic, powerful, and swift one, who possesses radiant rays and wields the thunderbolt—for that ancient and steadfast one, I have fashioned them with my mouth. 1. *Apūrvyā purutamānyasmai muhe vīrāya tavase turāya virāśvine vajriṇe śaṃtamāni vacāṃsyāsā sthavirāya takṣam.* 1. I have fashioned with my mouth the most unprecedented, most numerous, and most auspicious words for this wondrous hero, the powerful and swift one, who possesses radiant rays and wields the thunderbolt—for that ancient and steadfast one. 1.

With my mouth, I have fashioned, I am fashioning—for this Indra—unprecedented words, unprecedented yet anciently created, ever-new, most numerous, most abundant, and most blissful, that is, speech in the form of hymns. To what kind of one? To him who is such.

To the great one, to the mighty hero who sends forth various [missiles] against his enemies, to the powerful one, to the possessor of power, to the strong, to the swift, to the one who utters a roar, to the one who possesses a multitude of heroes, to the one especially worthy of praise, to the wielder of the thunderbolt, to the one endowed with the thunderbolt, to the steadfast, to the fully grown.

He, being praised by the seers with well-intended hymns, caused his two parents to dwell together with the Sun; rending the mountain while chanting, he, bellowing, released the source of the waters that were held captive. 2. He; the two parents; with the Sun; of the seers; caused to dwell; he rent; the mountain; being praised; with well-intended; hymns; bellowing; upward; of the waters; he released; the source. 2.
That Indra, for the sake of the Aṅgirases—the seers of far-reaching vision—caused the two parents, heaven and earth, to shine forth by means of the sun.
What was he doing?
Breaking asunder with his might the mountain that had been placed there so that the cows would not be seen.
Alternatively, the genitive case in "kavīnām aṅgirasām" is used in the sense of the instrumental; thus, the connection is: "being praised by the Aṅgirases, the sages."

Moreover, being repeatedly desired by the Aṅgirases—the singers of hymns who possess beautiful meditations—he, being invoked, released and liberated the cause of bondage, the fetters of the cows that had been carried off by the Paṇis, the servants of Vala.
1. The *jña*-truths are uncontradicted.
2. *kha* has the *bha* and *ra*; *jha* has the *ya*, *ra*, and *bha* vowels; *ta* has the *na* and *bha* vowels. 3. *kha*, *jhā*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra* [occur] even in the *niṣkevalya*.

4. There is no [combination] of *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, or *'ka-v*. He, the bearer of oblations, exulting among the cattle with the *ṛc*-verses, has conquered through those of many deeds. The destroyer of forts, a friend to his friends, he shattered the strongholds with his companions, being himself a seer among seers. *saḥ* (he); *vahni'bhiḥ* (with bearers of oblations); *ṛk'bhiḥ* (with *ṛc*-verses); *goṣu* (among the cattle); *śardhat* (exulting); *mitajñu'bhiḥ* (with those of measured knees/limbs); *purukṛtvā* (through those of many deeds); *jigāya* (has conquered); *puraḥ* (forts); *purohā* (destroyer of forts); *sakhibhiḥ* (with friends); *sakhiyan* (acting as a friend); *dṛlhā* (the strongholds); *ruroja* (shattered); *kavi'bhiḥ* (with seers); *kaviḥ* (seer); *san* (being). || 3 ||

Puruhatvā, the performer of many deeds, that Indra, together with the *ṛks*—the chanters who carry the oblations (*haviṣām voḍhṛbhiḥ*)—and with the *jharas*, the singers who always (*śaśvat*) have their knees drawn together (*mitajñubhiḥ*), conquered the Asuras for the sake of the cattle. Having conquered them, that Indra, the destroyer of fortresses (*purohā*), being himself a seer (*kaviḥ*) and possessing expansive wisdom, together with his friends—the seers of equal chariots and the *jharas*—desiring friendship for his companions, shattered the firm and stable fortresses of the Asuras.

With girdles, with many strengths, and with great powers, O bull among the peoples, you who possess many heroes—O lover of songs, come hither toward the singer for our prosperity. 4. He [comes] with girdles, toward the singer; with many strengths and with great powers, O bull among the peoples, you who possess many heroes—O lover of songs, come hither for our prosperity. 4.

O bull (*vṛṣabha*), showerer of desires, O lover of song (*girvaṇas*)—O Indra, worthy of being honored by hymns—come toward us with great spoils (*vāja*), with great foods, and with great powers; come face-to-face among the peoples (*kṣitīnām*) to the singer, the praiser, with new, most recent, and abundant songs that bring forth many heroes. For what purpose?
For the sake of auspicious well-being (*suvitāya*).
The meaning is: for the sake of attaining happiness.

Impelled by his own impetus and power with his coursers, Indra, the subduer of the swift, [drives] the waters to the south. Thus released, they have opened the floodgate; day by day they have carried forth that which is unassailable for their purpose. He, by his impulse, by his might, urged on by his coursers—Indra, the conqueror of the swift, [drives] the waters to the south. Thus released, [the waters] have opened the floodgate; day after day they have carried forth that which is unassailable for their purpose.

Turāṣāṭ, the overcomer of the *turāṇ*, that is, the subduer of those who cause harm—he, Indra, having come together with *atyaiḥ*, swift-moving horses, or with *tejobhiḥ*, splendors, and with *sargeṇa*, ever-exerted power (*śavasā*), releases the waters (*apaḥ*) during the *dakṣiṇataḥ*, the southern course (the summer solstice); this is the sense of the verse.

Being thus created in this manner, those waters daily pervade the ocean—the goal to be reached, which is unshakeable by others and imperturbable—so that there may be no turning back, no returning again.
And thus, the form ending in the suffix *tva* denotes the meaning [of the base].
1. *jha* means he struck and shattered;
2. *jña*, *ta*, and *ya* do not have the meaning "he";
3. *kha*, *jña*, *jha*, *ta*, *bha*, *ra*, and *śa* mean "he emits."

4. Kha-1-jha-bha-na-ya: *punarāgamanaṃ* (return) is not *apāvartanam* (turning back); it is non-return, non-turning back, and non-return. Ja-ṇa: *punarāgamanaṃ* is *apāvartanam*; it is non-turning back and return. 5. Kha-1-ta-na-bha-ya: the word ‘na’ does not exist. “*ya ojiṣṭhaḥ*” is the fifth hymn of the tenth [maṇḍala]; it is the seer’s portion of Śunahotra, in the *triṣṭubh* meter, addressed to Indra.
And it is enumerated thus: “*ya ojiṣṭhaḥ*: [the seer] is Śunahotra.”
The application [of this verse] is stated even in the *Mahāvrata* during the *Niṣkevalya* chant:
"O Indra, grant us that most powerful exhilaration which is manly, most helpful, and full of strength—
that exhilaration which wins the prize of the sun, possesses good horses, and overcomes Vṛtras and enemies in battles."

O Indra, grant us that most powerful exhilaration which is excellent, O Bull, providing great assistance, bountiful, and which wins the prize of cattle; which, accompanied by fine horses, may conquer Vritras and subdue enemies in battles.
O Indra, you are the showerer of desires; you are the son who is most powerful, most mighty, and strongest. Your exhilaration is that which intoxicates you through hymns—that is, by means of praise.
You are well-seeking, having excellent aspirations, and a giver—meaning one who bestows the offering of oblations—and you possess that quality.
Such was the appearance of that son, distinguished by such qualities.
O Hero, you have slain both types: the noble ones (āryāḥ), who are excellent because they perform noble deeds, and the obstructors (vṛtrāṇi) such as Viśvarūpa and others.
Among men, O Indra, the most manly leader (nṛtama), you rend even other enemies in battles (pṛtsu) with your well-placed weapons (arkaiḥ).
Therein lies the illustration.
Like forests—
just as species of trees are split by axes and the like, so it is here.

As such, O Indra, with your aids like those of the sun, be our friend, the protector of all life, and our strengthener for our prosperity; for we call upon you, O Hero, when we fight in battles for the sake of winning the light of heaven.
O Indra, you—our friend, possessing all life, the protector and promoter for our growth—have become [our helper] with your hymn-accompanied aids in the winning of the light.

Many songs have come together unto you, O Indra, and from you they go forth again with various thoughts. Both of old and now, the praises of the seers, their hymns and songs of praise, have vied for your attention in Indra. sam ca tve jagmurgira indra pūrvīr vi ca tvad yanti vivvo manīṣāḥ | purā nūnaṃ ca stutaya ṛṣīṇāṃ paspṛdha indre adhyukthā'arkā || 1 ||
O Indra, in you many—numerous—songs and praises converge;
from you, manifold, pervasive, and expansive thoughts and the prayers of the worshippers go forth in various directions.
(The remainder of the verse is spoken in the third person.)

In former times, and indeed even today, the hymns and praises of the seers (*ṛṣis*)—such as Bharadvāja and others—who perceive objects beyond the senses, have vied intensely for Indra; that is to say, they became eager to praise Indra through a spirit of emulation, each thinking "I first, I first.
Likewise, the *ukthas* and *ṛks*.
The *uktha* is a recited hymn (*śastra*).
The non-actions of that nature and the hymns (*stotra*) which are the means of worship contended—that is, they vied—with one another.

He who is invoked by many, praised by many, the one who is celebrated by the Ṛṣis through sacrifices—he, Indra, like a chariot harnessed for great power, has become one to be celebrated in song by us. puruhūtaḥ (invoked by many), yaḥ (who), purugūrtaḥ (praised by many), ṛbhvā (the skillful one), ekaḥ (the one), purupraśastaḥ (highly extolled), asti (is) through yajñaiḥ (sacrifices). Like a rathaḥ (chariot) yujānaḥ (harnessed) for mahe (great) śavase (power), indraḥ (Indra) has become anu-mādyaḥ (to be celebrated) asmābhiḥ (by us). 2.

Indra—who is invoked by many (*puruhūtaḥ*), praised by many (*purugūrtaḥ*), and who alone is great (*ṛmbhā mahān*) and preeminent; he who, distinguished by such qualities, is highly extolled (*purupraśastaḥ*) by sacrifices, by worshippers, by men, or by hymns of praise—being thus praised and lauded in manifold ways, let that Indra, like a chariot (*ratho na rathaḥ*), yoke himself for the sake of great power (*mahe śavase balāya*), and being yoked by our praises, let him be ever worthy of our celebration (*anumādyaḥ*), always to be extolled by us.

Neither the inspired thoughts nor the songs harm him; reaching Indra, they indeed cause him to grow strong. Whether his singers praise the lover of song by the hundreds or by the thousands, may that be for his well-being. Neither do the inspired thoughts nor the songs harm him; reaching Indra, they indeed cause him to grow strong. Whether his singers praise the lover of song by the hundreds or by the thousands, may that be for his well-being.

Indra, whom his mental faculties (*dhītayaḥ*), his ritual acts (*karmāṇi*), and his services (*paricaraṇāni*) do not harm or obstruct; whom his voices (*vāṇīḥ*) and hymns of praise (*stutayaḥ*) do not obstruct—

the meaning is that while an ordinary man who is unable to give becomes greatly distressed by the services and praises performed for him by others, such services and hymns directed toward this Indra did not become causes of obstruction, because of his possession of abundant wealth and his capacity to bestow gifts.
To the question "What then?", he says: "Increasing him"—that is, making Indra grow—they "approach," meaning they go toward him.
Moreover, if a hundred—that is, those numbering one hundred—praisers "sing," that is, they offer hymns of praise to Indra, the "lover of songs" (*girvaṇas*), who is the enjoyer of hymns.
And if a thousand—that is, those numbering one thousand—praisers offer praise, all that hymn of praise becomes *śam*, a source of happiness, for this Indra.
1. Kha: By means of the sacrificer's instruments (yajamānasādhana).
2. Ja, Jha, Ṇa, Na, Bha, Ya: One is distressed (vyathate). 3. Kha, Bha: They indeed approach (abhigacchanti).
For him, the divine months have indeed been mixed; Soma has been poured into Indra.
As waters gather toward a person in the desert, so have the forests together increased through sacrifices.

To him—this [Soma] has been offered like a song of praise in heaven; the months have yearned for him. Soma has been poured down into Indra, as people [rush] toward a desert when the waters have gathered together and strengthened his invocations through sacrifices. 4.

On this very day, on this auspicious morning, by means of worship alone—that is, by means of praise consisting of the act of honoring—and joined with the measuring [of the Soma] accomplished through mantras such as "For Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra," the Soma has been measured; that is, it has been sprinkled for Indra by means of the *vasatīvarī* and *ekadhana* waters. "Soma" [is the subject];
there is a transposition of case endings:
it has been poured into this Indra. It has become measured for him.
Or rather, the ellipsis is: "I shall proclaim this hymn to this Indra. Like the sun (arka) in the sky, the celestial world, he is the month.
This is an elliptical simile (*luptopamā*). "Māsa" means that which measures or defines; thus, it refers to the moon.
Like that [moon], he is *mimikṣu*, the sprinkler of the waters of the sacrifice. That Indra who exists in this [sacrifice]—in this Indra, the Soma, being stirred, is poured out.

Furthermore, Indra was strengthened (*vāvṛdhuḥ*) by means of sacrifices (*yajñaiḥ*)—that is, by the oblations such as the *puroḍāśa* used as instruments of worship—along with the invocations (*havanāni*) and the hymns (*satrā*).
Therein lies the illustration:
just as the waters (*āpaḥ*), flowing together (*sam yat*) toward (*abhi*) a desert region (*dhanvan*), strengthen the living beings (*janam*) there.
Just as water found in a desert region nourishes a living being, so it is in this case.
For him, for this Indra, this great hymn has been uttered with inspired thoughts,
so that in the great battle against Vṛtra, Indra may be the protector and the strengthener of all life.

For him—this great, swelling hymn has been spoken with inspired thoughts for this Indra. May it be so that in the great battle against Vṛtra, Indra, the life-sustainer of all, may be our protector and our strengthener. 5.
For this Indra, this great and vast *āṅgūṣa* hymn has been uttered with prayers by the singers; it has become spoken for him, for Indra.
The repetition of "for him, for Indra" is for the sake of emphasis.

Viśvāyu, he who goes everywhere—that Indra—has been so addressed so that in the great and abundant battle against Vṛtra, he may be our protector (*avitā*) and our strengthener (*vṛdhaḥ*) in whatever manner he may be. This is the syntactical connection.
The twelfth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “kadā bhuvana,” is the seer Naras’s; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre and is dedicated to Indra.
Thus it has been enumerated: “kadā naras tu.
Its application (viniyoga) is stated for the third Chandoma and the Mahāvrata.

When, O Brahman, will you destroy the ruin of the world? When will you grant the thousandfold prosperity to the singer? When will you clothe this hymn with wealth? When will you make our prayers rich with the prize of booty?

When [will you grant] the world’s axle-pins for our chariot, O Brahman? When will you give the singer thousandfold nourishment? When will you clothe this [singer] with wealth for his hymn of praise? And when will you make our thoughts rich in prizes? 1.
1. *kha-jha-bha-taṃ* means "properly going"; *jña-ya-samyagyantyo* [is similar].
O Indra, when (*kadā*) will our *brahmāṇi*—our prayers (*stotrāṇi*)—be situated upon the chariot (*rathakṣyāṇi*), that is, upon the chariot-seats?
The meaning is: when will they reach you as you stand upon the chariot?
When, at what time, would you grant to me, who praises you, a thousandfold prosperity—a herd of cattle nourishing a thousand men—or a son?
And when would you cause the hymn of this my praiser to be clothed in wealth?
And when, O you who are delightful with spoils (*vāja-ratna*), would you perform the sacred rites, such as the *agnihotra* and others?
Thus, the praiser, unable to endure a delay in the fruit [of his praise], questioned Indra with this [verse].

Where indeed, O Indra, do you gather men with men, heroes with heroes? Conquer the battles! You win the threefold cattle; O Indra, bestow upon us glory and the light of heaven. Where indeed, O Indra, do you—by means of men, by heroes—gather men, by heroes, heroes? Conquer the contests! You win the threefold [troop] of cattle; O Indra, bestow upon us glory and the light of heaven.
Unable to endure any delay in the result, the seer asks Indra by means of this verse:
"O Indra, when indeed will that come to pass?
When you shall unite our men with the enemy men, and our heroes, our sons, with the enemy heroes? (That is, when you shall cause them to be joined together.)
The root *nīḷ* has the sense of the action of joining together.
This is the reflection: when will such a healing in battle occur?
Moreover, for our sake, when will you conquer the battles?
And when will you fully conquer the cows—the sustainers of the threefold [products], namely milk, curds, and ghee—found among the cattle-raiding enemies?
O Indra, when will you bestow upon us—that is, maintain for us—splendid, pervasive wealth consisting of light?

Where indeed, O Indra, are you when you perform the all-pervading sacred word for the singer, O most powerful one? When will you yoke your teams as if they were our prayers? When will you come to the invocations accompanied by gifts of cattle? Where indeed, O Indra, are you when you perform the all-pervading sacred word for the singer, O most powerful one? When will you yoke your teams as if they were our prayers? When will you come to the invocations accompanied by gifts of cattle?
By means of this [verse] as well, several questions are posed:
"O Indra, where indeed, and when will that come to pass?

O most powerful (*śaviṣṭha*), most mighty Indra, "when will it be that you shall provide (*kṛṇavaḥ*) for the singer (*jaritre*), the worshipper, *brahma*—that is, food (*anna*)—of many forms (*viśvapsu*)"—this is the reflection (*vitarka*).
And when [will] the mental activities [be such that] they are not [obstructed]? The word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction.
You should yoke and unite the *niyutas* of hymns within yourself.

And when will you go to—approach—the *gomaghāni*, those which bestow cattle (*gomaghā*), the praises (*harvanāni*) which are the means for the act of giving (*maṃhateḥ*), whose final member is a form of the root meaning "to give"? 5.

Bestow upon the singer gifts of cattle, horses resplendent as gold, and food renowned for its strength; swell the nourishments, O Indra, and let the well-milking cow shine forth with beautiful luster among the Bharadvājas. 4. He [bestows] gifts of cattle, O singer; [gifts] brilliant with horses, [gifts] famous for their vigor—bestow these nourishments! Cause the nourishments to swell; O Indra, let the well-yielding cow shine forth with beautiful luster among the Bharadvājas. 4.

1. *gha*—being unable to endure it; *śa*—being unable to endure it. 2. *gha*—you should withdraw. 3. *kha*, *na*, *ma*—the action of joining together. 4. *jha*, *ta*, *ya*—you should unite with yourself. 5. *kha*, *1*, *ja*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*—you should come. Likewise, O Indra, cause those foods and the cow that yields milk beautifully (*sudughām*) to swell (*pīpihi*).
Furthermore, you should cause those nourishments (*iṣaḥ*) and the cow to shine with beautiful luster (*surucaḥ*);
that is to say, let them be endowed with a splendid radiance.
O Śakra, surely you consider that host as darkness; for you, O powerful one, are praised as the one who opens the doors.
Do not let the milch-cow that yields the bright [milk] go astray; O inspired sage, quicken the Aṅgirases with sacred prayer.

Him indeed—though otherwise a stronghold—O Hero, O Śakra, you praise as one who opens the doors. Do not let the cow that milks out the bright [soma] go to waste; O Sage, quicken the Aṅgirases with your sacred prayer. 5.
O Indra, you must surely today subdue our adversary, the oppressor; "vanvathā" means "you shall conquer" in some other manner.
The meaning is: cause him to meet with that mode of existence which is contrary to how all beings live—namely, the state called death.
The vowel "ā" is a filler (pūraka).

O Śakra, O Indra who is capable in all undertakings, O hero endowed with valor, O breaker— specifically the one who shatters the enemies; or rather, since you (*vyat*) open (*vyat*) the gates (*duro*) belonging to the enemy because you are praised (*vṛṇīṣe*) by us, therefore, from the praise (*stotrāt*) of the cow of speech (*dhenoḥ vācaḥ*) belonging to the pure (*śukra-*) milker (*dogdhuḥ*) Indra, may I (*mā*) not go away (*niraram*).
Or rather:
may I not depart from the cow—the milch-cow of Śukra’s milk—which has been given by you.
The form *ara* is derived from the verbal root *ṛ*, meaning "to go."
The meaning is: "May she dwell among us at all times.
O wise one, O lord of the learned, gladden—that is, satisfy—with sacred food (brahmaṇā) us who are born of the lineage of Aṅgiras (vāṅgirasān).
The hymn beginning with “satrā madasaḥ,” consisting of fifteen verses, is the thirteenth hymn; it is composed by Nara, is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is dedicated to Indra.
It is indicated by the word “satrā. This hymn is to be recited at the Niṣkevalya litany on the fifth day of the Pṛṣṭha sacrifice.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Preḍaṃ brahma indro madāya satrā madasaḥ’—this is the Niṣkevalya [Śastra]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.12).
In the Viśvajit sacrifice, during the midday pressing, this Sāman-hymn is to be recited as the Praśasta Śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Satrā madaso yo jāta evābhūrekaḥ’—these are the Sāman-hymns" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.7).
The application [of this hymn] has also been stated in the *Niṣkevalya* section of the *Mahāvrata*.
Truly, you are the one who bestows exhilaration upon all people; truly, you are the master of riches that exist upon the earth.
Truly, you have become the distributor of spoils of war, since you maintained your divine power among the gods.

Evermore, O Madasā, yours are all those riches common to all people; evermore, indeed, are those that belong to the earth. Evermore you have been the distributor of spoils, since among the gods you have maintained your divine power.

O Indra, yours are these most sweet exhilarations—the intoxications produced by drinking Soma. Truly (satrā)—this is a word for truth—these [intoxications] are truly beneficial to all people (viśvajanyāḥ). Or rather, *satrā* is a name for "great"; thus it should be construed as "your exhilarations are great. Furthermore, those collections of wealth (*vrāyaḥ*) belonging to you which exist in the three worlds, as indicated by the term *pārthivāsaḥ*, they too [are yours].
(Note: 1. *kha-jha-tara-na-bha-ra* read *anūnam*; 2.
*kha-gha-jha-ta1-na-bha-ra-śa* do not have "śasyaṃ"; *jha-śa* read *śaṃstyam*.)

3. Regarding that great vow (*mahāvrata*): the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the gods] are truly (*satrā satyam*) beneficial to all people. Furthermore, you have been—and indeed are—the true distributor and giver of foods (*vājānām*).
Alternatively, it should be construed as "satrā mahatām vājānām" (truly [you are the master] of great spoils).
Since you, among the gods, maintain *asuryam*—that is, power (*balam*)—therefore, for that reason, you alone act; this is the meaning.

They have truly extended their strength after him; they have fully established their heroic power.
