The person— the sacrificer— continually and pre-eminently offers worship and honors the power and strength of this Indra.
Moreover,
[he worships] his wealth— that which is the abode of many names and brings great joy.
Moreover, you have become peerless and incomparable; you have become the sovereign lord (*pati*) of all people, of all living beings.
Likewise, you have become the sole, unique king and ruler (*īśvara*) of the entire world, of the whole multitude of creatures.
Listen, O Śruti, to him who, like the heaven over the earth, has bestowed the riches of the noble;
may he, being pleased with us through his power, manifest himself in age after age.

Hear us, O Lord, with your hearing! He who, desiring to do you service, has meditated upon riches like the sky, like the earth—may he, delighting in our strength, manifest himself age after age through his vital power. 5.

O Indra, listen—listen quickly—to these hymns worthy of being heard. You, who, desiring for yourself the worship offered by me, surpass like the sun in the sky the abundant riches belonging to the enemy; such as you are, listen! This is the connection of the words.

Moreover, endowed with your own power (*śavasā*) which is worthy of praise, being yourself praised (*cakānaḥ*), and being made manifest (*cekitānaḥ*) through food (*vayasā*) characterized by oblations at every age (*yuge-yuge*), may you be such as you are—that is, remain our unique and exclusive lord—in whatever manner (*yathā*) that may be.
The fourth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “arvāgratha,” is the seerly composition of Bharadvāja; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to Indra.
It concludes with the verse beginning “arvāgratha. Its application (viniyoga) has been stated for the Mahāvrata ritual in the Niṣkevalya Śastra.
O fierce Indra, let your harnessed bay horses bring your all-desirable chariot hither;
for even the lowly man, seeking the light, calls upon you—may we today prosper through your fellowship at the feast.

Hitherward, O fierce Indra, let your harnessed bay steeds carry the chariot that grants all boons; for even the poor man, possessing the light of heaven, calls upon you. May we today prosper through your shared feasts. 1.

O *ugra*, O Indra of exalted power, let your *yuktāsaḥ*—the harnessed *harayaḥ*, your bay horses—bring your *viśvavāram* chariot, which is desirable by all, *arvāk*, toward us. For indeed, since the *svarvān*—possessing the *svaḥ*, the excellently desirable collection of qualities—the *kīriśrit*, the praising seer Bharadvāja, invokes you, therefore let them bring your chariot toward us; this is the meaning.
And may we now, at this very moment, being exhilarated together with you in joint revelry, attain prosperity and be successful.
In the third round, for the Acchāvāka, the verse beginning with “pro droṇe” serves as the *ājya* for the *śastra*.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: “‘pro droṇe harayaḥ karma’ is the regular *ājya*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).
For Drona, the bay steeds, speeding forward, have performed their task;
may Indra, our ancient king, drink first of this exhilarating, Soma-rich draught.

To Droṇa, the tawny ones have gone for the sake of the ritual; being purified, they have become straight-flowing. May Indra, our ancient one, drink first of this; may the King, the milker of the Soma-draught, drink of the exhilarating juice. 2.
1. *jha-babhūtha* and *babhūvitha*. 2. *jha-babhūtha*.
The bay-colored (*harayaḥ*) Soma drops have come forth (*pro agman*)—they go forth and reach our rite (*naḥ karma*), our sacrifice.

And having reached the *droṇa*—the wooden vat—they become purified, flowing straight as they move toward the *droṇakalaśa*. Ancient, the source of milk, the abode of light or the place of the *dhū* (wind), such is Indra, the sovereign lord of the exhilarating Soma; may he drink this Soma of his.
May the swift horses on well-wheeled chariots draw Indra toward the nearby oblations;
may they bear him straight toward glory. Now let the immortal nectar of Vāyu be distributed as a wondrous sight.

The swift horses, with their well-wheeled chariot, shall carry Indra toward the glory of the Śavasānas; speeding straight toward renown, they shall now bring him hither. Indeed, the immortal nectar of Vāyu shall now be revealed as wondrous.

May the horses yoked to the chariot, moving swiftly on all sides along the paths and galloping straight forward, carry our glorious oblation—which is worthy of being heard—toward you, O Indra, as you stand upon the chariot with beautiful wheels, acting with might like a sovereign power.

Let not the immortal oblation, characterized by Soma and serving as the cause of immortality, ever perish or come to destruction for the sake of Vāyu. (Note: The particle *nṛ cin* here functions as a negation; *amṛtam* refers to the Soma-oblation which is the cause of non-death; *vāyoḥ* means "for the sake of Vāyu"; *nu cit* means "never at all"; and *vidasyet* means "it would perish" or "reach destruction.")
The meaning is that Soma, once taken into the vessel, becomes spoiled by the wind; therefore, the horses must be driven toward Indra even before that happens, for the purpose of its preservation.
The most excellent one directs his sacrificial fee; Indra is the most active among the wealthy patrons.
With that [fee] you go around like a lover; O bold one, you bestow gifts upon the wise lords.

The most excellent Indra sends forth the sacrificial fee for these wealthy patrons—he who is most active in great deeds—by which you, O Vanivan, encompass the days; and, O Bold One, you distribute wealth among the wise leaders.

The most excellent, the greatest, the most active in many deeds— Indra impels the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to be given at the sacrifice for this patron among the wealthy ones, those possessed of the riches characterized by oblations.
Or rather,
the word "among the wealthy ones" (*maghonām*) is in grammatical apposition with "he who hurls" (*asyan*).
A change in the grammatical number of the words.
"Of the liberal givers possessing oblations"—that is, of this sacrificer.
The remainder [of the verse] is addressed directly:

"O wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), like the thunderbolt itself, O Indra, by which sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) you bind away evil from this sacrifice and destroy it; O bold one (*dhṛṣṇo*), O subduer, by which sacrificial fee you distribute (*vi dayase*) riches (*maghāni*) and patrons (*sūrīn*)—that is, their sons—such a sacrificial fee do you impel. This is the meaning.
Indra is the giver of enduring booty; may Indra, whose greatness has increased, be magnified by our songs.
May Indra be the most effective slayer of Vṛtra; as a hero, he, the patron, bestows gifts with swift impetuosity.

Indra is the giver of enduring strength; may Indra, whose greatness has increased, be magnified by our songs. May Indra be the slayer of Vṛtra. Thinking thus, the wise patron, hastening forward, bestows those gifts upon him. 5.
May this Indra be the giver of *sthavira*—of food (*vāja*) or strength (*bala*).
And may that Indra, being great and of increased splendor, flourish through our songs of praise.
Having understood [this], he is the destroyer of enemies; *sthavira* means the most excellent.
May that Indra, the most excellent slayer, strike down Vṛtra, the obstructing enemy; may he become our protector.
Furthermore, may that Indra, the wise impeller, acting with haste, bestow those riches upon us.
The fifteenth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "apāditaḥ," is the Ṛṣi Bharadvāja’s composition; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and is dedicated to Indra.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī entry: "apāt.
Its application (viniyoga) has been stated for the Niṣkevalya Śastra at the Mahāvrata ceremony.

He has drunk from here; let the most wondrous one lift up for us the great, radiant invocation of Indra. He accepts the rain-bringing prayer at the journeying of the divine, the gift of the people, as he, the bounteous giver, bestows his favor. He has drunk from here; let the most wondrous one lift up for us the great, radiant invocation of Indra. He accepts the rain-bringing prayer at the journeying of the divine, the gift of the people, as he, the bounteous giver, bestows his favor.
Most wonderful, most worthy of praise, or most marvelous— that Indra— let him drink the Soma from this vessel or ladle of ours;
or rather,
let him protect us from this [danger], shielding us from our enemies.

The two words *vadu* and *it* are full [of meaning]. Likewise, *vmahīm* means great; *vdyumatīm* means radiant; *vindrahūtim* means the praise of Indra; *vbharṣat* means may that Indra bear or maintain it.

*Vdaivyasya janasya* means of the divine host; *vyāman* means in the course, namely in the sacrifice being performed; *vparyanyasīm* means most praiseworthy; *vdhītim* means an act in the form of service; *vrātim* means the sacrificial oblation to be given; and *vsudānuḥ*, the giver of beautiful gifts, Indra, *vvanate*—may he enjoy or partake of it.

Even from afar, his ears hear; the speaker makes Indra’s ear ring with the sound. May this invocation of the gods bring him hither; may this hymn being recited turn Indra toward us. Even from afar, his two ears hear; the speaker makes Indra’s ear ring with the sound. May this invocation of the gods bring him hither; may this hymn being recited turn Indra toward us.

The two ears of that Indra come even from afar, from a distant place, for the sake of hearing the praise of the one who dwells [there]. Because of the sound—the praiseworthy hymn—of Indra, the praising singer, extolling him, makes a sound.
Or else:
It spreads everywhere.

*Devahūti*: This praise, which consists of the invocation of the god Indra, being recited and itself impelled, may it turn *venam*—that is, Indra—toward us (*madyak*) or cause him to turn back toward us.
Again, the word *viyam* is complete.

With our highest devotion, we have celebrated with hymns that ancient, unborn Indra for you. Both sacred prayer and songs have been gathered together in him; may the great hymn of praise increase further within Indra. For you—with the highest wisdom—we have praised that ancient, unborn Indra with hymns. Both the sacred formulation and the songs have been concentrated in him; may the great hymn of praise flourish further within Indra.
O Indra, find such a protector; O Indra, find you [a protector] for us.
The plural number is used by way of transposition.
With a most supreme and excellent intellect (*buddhi*), together with hymns (*stuti*) and various means of worship (*arcana-sādhana*), I praise (*abhy-anūṣi*) [him].
Of what nature is he? He is born in ancient times (*purājām*), existing from long ago; he is ageless (*ajara*), free from decay, and eternal.
For this reason, in that Indra— who is eternally sovereign and possessed of lordly power (*indra*)—
the great oblations characterized by sacrificial offerings and the songs of praise are united, joined, and closely integrated;
and the vast, increased hymn of praise (*stoma*) grows further and further.

May the sacrifice and Soma strengthen Indra; may the sacred formulation (*brahman*), the songs, the hymns, and the prayer strengthen him. May the dawns at their departure strengthen him; may the months, the autumns, and the days strengthen Indra. 4. May [the sacrifice] strengthen him; may the sacrifice and Soma strengthen Indra; may the sacred formulation, the songs, the hymns, and the prayer strengthen him. May the dawns at their departure strengthen him; may the months, the autumns, and the days strengthen Indra. 4.
The sacrifice (*yajña*), that is, the act of worship (*yāga*), strengthens (*vardhāt*) that Indra;
and furthermore, Soma, which serves as the means for that [sacrifice], also strengthens that Indra.
Likewise, the sacred formulation (*brahma*), characterized by the oblation (*havis*) such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth, also strengthens that Indra.

The songs of praise (*giraḥ*), the hymns (*stotrāṇi*), the thoughts (*manma*)—that is, the things to be meditated upon—and the recitations (*ukthāni*), the ritual chants (*śastrāṇi*), all of which magnify him; these, as well as the dawns (*uṣasaḥ*) and the nights (*aktoḥ*) at every movement (*yāman yāmani*), that is, in every journey, magnify this Indra.
The months (*māsāḥ*), the autumns (*śaradaḥ*), the years (*saṃvatsarāḥ*), and the days (*dyāvaḥ*) likewise magnify this Indra.

Thus have we brought near for our protection, O Sage, him who was born for irresistible power, who has grown for abundant and renowned wealth—the great and fierce one—for aid in the battles against Vṛtra. Thus: born; for power; complete; having grown; for wealth; and; renowned; the great; the fierce; for aid; O Sage; now; we; bring near; in the battles against Vṛtra.

O wise sage, we now, as a learned man, shall honor, serve, and attend upon you—Indra himself—who, being thus born and manifesting for the sake of overcoming enemies, has grown and increased mightily and abundantly; who is great, formidable, and possessed of uplifted power—for the sake of renowned wealth, for the sake of riches, and for protection in the battles against Vṛtra.
The sixteenth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “*mandrasya kaveḥ*,” is the *ṛṣi*-seer Bharadvāja’s composition; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and is addressed to Indra.
It is listed [in the index] as “*mandrasya*.
Its ritual application (*viniyoga*) has been explained.

Of the delightful, wise, divine, and carrying priest—the inspired, mind-stirring speech, the honey—having drunk of that companionable draught, O God, bestow upon the singer gifts of cattle as the foremost portion. Of the delightful, wise, divine, and carrying priest—the inspired, mind-stirring speech, the honey—having drunk of that companionable draught, O God, bestow upon the singer gifts of cattle as the foremost portion.

Of the melodious, gladdening, intoxicating poet; of the valiant, divine one who exists in heaven; of the bearer, O sage, who carries forth our prayers—of him whose prayers are borne by sages, that is, by the wise ones who are his praisers;
of his speech, which is worthy of being spoken and is fit for praise.

1. kha¹-ma-vardhaya, they cause to increase; jha-jha-na-vardhā, they cause to increase; tara-vardhā, you cause to increase. 2. kha¹-gha-ja-ṇa-bha-vardhanti, they increase; aha (kha¹-bha-ahaḥ), the filler. 3. kha-gha-bha-asāmi, completely full.
4. gha—vavṛdhānam;
5. gha—vṛtratūryeṣu raṇeṣu; jha and śa—vṛtratūryeṣu saṃgrāmeṣu;

Of that *madhvaḥ*—that is, of the honey-like Soma—which is thus characterized as being "famous everywhere" (*sarvatra prasiddha*), "to be approached" (*sacana*), and "worthy of service" (*sevya*).

The genitive case is used in the sense of the dative because the Soma is the recipient of the action, according to the rule: "The mention of the 'action' (*kriyā*) must be understood [so as to include its object]."
O Indra, drink— consume— this our Soma which has become such;
moreover, O radiant Deva Indra,
for the one who praises you (the dative case used in the sense of the instrumental).
O Agni, being praised by me,
unite for us those nourishing foods (*iṣas*) which have cows at their head— that is, those for whom cows are foremost.
Desiring this, he has gone around the mountain with those whose thoughts are fixed on Truth, harnessing his chariot through Truth;
Indra shattered the unbroken ridges of Vala and, purifying himself with sacred words, fought against him.

Desiring it, he has gone around the mountain; the Dawn, yoked with those whose thoughts are fixed on Truth, being herself joined with Truth, has shattered the unbreakable ridge of Vala. With his splendors, Indra has overcome the Purus in battle.
This Indra, by the power of the mountain, shattered the stone enclosure for the sake of recovering the cattle;
this Indra, shining and radiant, blazing with the nature of the sun, illuminates—that is, makes manifest—all the worlds that were unlit, devoid of light, and soiled by darkness.
Likewise, this Indra, by means of *ṛta*—that is, by true reality or by the splendor characterized by omnipresence—causes the many ancient deeds to shine forth; he causes them to be perceived.
The meaning is that he dispels the darkness found there.

Likewise, with horses yoked by the seasons through the *ṛta* (the sacred order) of praise, with a chariot bound at the navel, finding the light (*svarvid*), and bringing forth desirable wealth (*sudhraṇīya*), this very Indra goes forth as one who satisfies the desires of the people (*carṣaṇīprāḥ*).

Now, O ancient King, being praised, swell forth abundant nourishments for the singer to bestow as wealth; you have fashioned waters, plants, poisons, forests, cattle, horses, and men. You have brought them low.

Now, O ancient King, being praised by the one who praises you, swell forth abundant nourishments for the sake of bestowing wealth. For the sake of the singer, you have fashioned for himself waters, plants, sheep, forests, cattle, horses, and men. 5.

O ancient, primordial King, O radiant Indra, being praised and extolled by us, you—do you quickly cause to swell, that is, bestow, abundant foods for the singer who praises you, for one such as he to whom riches are to be given by you.

Furthermore, O Śirīṣa, bestow upon the singer who praises you—upon the worshiper and the praiser—the waters characterized by livelihood, the plants such as rice and others, the *avipā* which are either free from injury or are protections, the forests consisting of species of trees such as mango and jackfruit, the cows, the swift horses, and the men who are laborers.
‘Indra piba’: this hymn, consisting of fifteen verses and containing seventeen stanzas, is the *ṛṣi*-seer Bharadvāja’s composition; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and is dedicated to Indra.
It is introduced by the words ‘Indra piba’.
The application (*viniyoga*) of the hymn has been explained.
In the first watch of the night, this is the first *śastra* of the *acchāvāka*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘O Indra, drink! [The juice] is pressed for you for intoxication’—this is the *yājyā* (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).”
O Indra, drink; the juice is pressed for your exhilaration. Unharness your two bay steeds, O friend.
And sing forth, sitting down in the ritual enclosure; then bestow vigor upon the one who praises you for the sake of the sacrifice.

O Indra, drink! For you the juice is pressed for exhilaration. Unharness these two bay steeds at the ford; O friend, sing forth and sit down upon the seat. Bestow vital strength upon the singer who strives for the sacrifice.
O Indra, drink that Soma which has been pressed for you, for exhilaration, for intoxication.
Because the Soma is to be drunk by a friend, for that reason, O friend—meaning those of equal renown or those who have become allies—unharness your two bay horses, *hari*;
immediately thereafter, unyoke them from the chariot.
Moreover, having sat down facing us in the assembly—that is, in the gathering of our praisers—sing forth; celebrate with verses the hymn composed by us.
Then, immediately thereafter, bestow and grant *vayas*, food, to the sacrificer who praises and sings for the sake of the sacrifice.
In the second watch of the night, for the *śastra* of the Acchāvāka, the *yājyā* is "asya piba.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *yājyā* is 'asya piba'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.4).
1. When *gha*, *śa*, or *suṣṭhu* precede *carṣaṇīyasya*.
2. In the case of *kṣa-bha-*, there is the *ājya* and *śastra-yājyā*; in the case of *ra-*, there is the *ājya* and *śastrāyājyā*; in the case of *śa-*, there is the *ājya-śastra-yājyā*.
3. In the sequence of *jha-jha-na-na-bha-ya-ra*.

4. "Drink, O Indra, of that [Soma] at whose birth you cried 'Indra!'—this is the *yājyā* verse. Drink of this, O Indra, at whose birth you drank for intoxication and for the sake of the sacred law (*ṛta*), O mighty one! The cows, the men, the waters, and the pressing-stone have all together struck out this *indu* (Soma) for you, for his drinking, and for him. asya | piba | yasya | jajñānaḥ | indra | madāya | ṛtve | arpibaḥ | virapśin | tam | u | te | gāvaḥ | naraḥ | āpaḥ | adriḥ | indum | sam | ahan | pītaye | sam | asmai ||2||
O Indra, drink this Soma!
O Virapśin, as soon as you were born—that is, at the very moment of your birth—you drank that Soma for which [you are now] drinking.
For what purpose?

For exhilaration—that is, for joy—and for the performance of action, namely the heroic deed characterized by the slaying of Vṛtra and so forth; for that very purpose, the cows—meaning the products of the cow such as milk which serve as the means of cooking—the leaders—the Adhvaryu priests—the waters known as the *vasatīvarī*s—the pressing-stone used for crushing, and all these together, have brought this very *indu*, the Soma, together for him, for your drinking, O Indra. (The form [samahan] belongs to the root *hi* in the sense of "to go" or "to bring together").
Furthermore, "sam" is a filler word.

The fire being kindled, O Indra, the Soma having been pressed, let your bay horses, the swiftest of all, carry you hither. With a mind directed toward you, I invoke you repeatedly; O Indra, come for our great prosperity and well-being. 3. In the kindled fire, O Indra, when the Soma has been pressed, let your bay steeds, the most excellent carriers, bring you hither. With a mind intent upon you, I call out to you repeatedly; O Indra, come for our great and auspicious welfare. 3.
When the fire is kindled and blazing, and when the Soma has been pressed out—O Indra, let your bay horses, the most excellent carriers, bring you hither;
let them carry you to this sacrifice.
And I, with a mind longing for you, call upon you again and again.
O Indra, come hither to us for our great and auspicious prosperity.

Come hither; with your ever-desiring [mind], O Indra, you have come with a great spirit for the drinking of Soma. Listen to these our prayers, and then may this sacrifice bestow vigor upon your body. 4. Come! Ever with longing you have come, O Indra, with a great mind to drink the Soma. Listen to these our sacred words (brahmāṇi), and then may the sacrifice provide nourishment for your body. 4.
O Indra, you have gone to the sacrifice many times before for the sake of drinking Soma. For that reason, come with a great and longing mind to our sacrifice, where Soma is drunk;
having arrived, listen closely to these our prayers, the hymns being offered now.
Then, immediately after that, the sacrifice—the sacrificer—shall bestow *vayas*, food consisting of Soma, for your body, for the purpose of nourishing your physical frame.
1. gha-jha-na-bha-śa—vigorous action;
2. jha-ta-na-kṣa-samiddhe—in the well-kindled, blazing fire;
3. gha-jha-ta-na-bha-ra-śa—in this.
He stood firm; the oblation did not reach the place of the high altar.
Moreover, O Indra, desiring for yourself the cattle belonging to the enemy, let your vajra strike together with the enemies—meaning, let it slay them.
This drop, the bull of all forms, the Soma, has been prepared for Indra, the bull.
Drink it, O Lord of Bay Horses, O fierce one who stands firm, you who have ruled over it from of old as your own flood.
This one—the drop, the bull, the omniform—is prepared for Indra, the bull. Drink this, O Lord of Bay Steeds, O Mighty One, over whom you have lordship from of old; he who is your wave. 3.

This Soma—dropping (drapsaḥ), characterized by flowing (dravaṇaśīlaḥ), a bull (vṛṣabhaḥ) that showers desires, possessing all forms (viśvarūpaḥ), endowed with many kinds of shapes—has been prepared (samakāri) for Indra, the showerer of desires (vṛṣṇe), for the purpose of Indra’s drinking; it has been consecrated by means of purifying filters and other rites. O Lord of the two bay horses (harivaḥ)! [The two bay horses...]
Rejoice—that is, be satisfied—in our Soma offerings;
[the root *mad* is used here in the sense of satisfaction].
Immediately thereafter, protect us preeminently in battles, that is, in conflicts.
Not only in battles, but indeed among all creatures, protect us from every side.
The hymn beginning with “pratyasmai” is the twenty-fourth [hymn] and the nineteenth [sūkta] of the Ṛgveda; it is the seer Bharadvāja’s composition addressed to Indra.
The fourth verse is a Bṛhatī, and the remaining verses are Anuṣṭubhs.
Thus it has been declared in the Anukramaṇī: “pratyasmai consists of four verses; it is in the Anuṣṭubh meter, ending with a Bṛhatī.”

This is the hymn to be recited by the Acchāvāka at the morning pressing. And it is stated in the ritual manual: "The verses beginning with 'pratyasmāi' are for the [verses] being recited" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.7).
Bring all things to this man who desires to drink, who knows everything,
who comes readily, who moves swiftly, and who is a hero on the path beyond the waters.
Bring all things to him who desires to drink, the one who knows all, who goes straight to his goal, who moves swiftly, the hero whose path is never behind. 1.
"O Adhvaryu, bring forth—that is, present—the Soma to this Indra; offer it to him.
To what kind of Indra?"

To him who desires to drink (*pipīṣate*), who wishes to drink; to the one who knows all things that are to be known (*viśvāni vedyāni viduṣe*); to the one who goes sufficiently (*aramgamāya*); to the one who moves about (*jagmaye*), whose nature it is to go to sacrifices;
to the one for whom the path is not obstructed by waters (*apaśvadhvane*)—the root *dhā* here meaning "to go"—to the one who does not fail to proceed for all; to the leader (*nare*) of sacrifices.

In the third *svarasāman*, the *niṣkevalya* [śastra] has the triplet "em enam" as its *stotriya*. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The triplet 'em enam', 'pratyetana', or indeed all [the verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.5).
With these Soma juices,
satisfy this Indra, the greatest drinker of Soma, who possesses the *ṛjīṣa*, with the pressed drops in the vessels.
Come hither to him with Soma-draughts—the drinker of Soma most excellent, the possessor of the *ṛjīṣa*—to Indra with the pressed drops in the vessels. 2.
O Adhvaryus, with *somaiḥ*—that is, with the *soma* juices acting as the means—approach *enam*, this Indra, who is the *somapārtamam*, the supreme drinker of *soma*.
The particle *īm* is expletive.
Of what sort is Indra?
With the *amatrabhiḥ*—the great vessels, the Soma-cups that bring offerings—he [approaches] the *ṛjīṣiṇam*:
one who possesses the *ṛjīṣa*, the force that drives away enemies.
He is the possessor of that [force].
Alternatively,

the word *ṛjīṣiṇam* should be connected with the preceding [verse]. [It refers to] *ṛjīṣiṇam*, [the one who possesses the dregs], by means of the *indubhiḥ*, i.e., the pressed *somaiḥ*, i.e., the soma juices.
The *soma* has lost its essence; it is the dregs (*ṛjīṣa*).
[He is] possessed of that.
Or rather, [he is] the possessor of the dregs through the *soma*s—measured by their vessels, immeasurable, and overflowing.
The word *ṛjīṣa* is derived from the root *ṛj*, meaning "to go," with the suffix *vaṣ* used instrumentally;
thereafter, the possessive suffix *ini* is added.
The meaning is "assembled.
The grammatical construction is: "Go toward such an Indra.
Another [teacher] says:
With these vessels, with the oblations, with the pressed Soma juices that have reached their destination, go toward this Indra, the possessor of the *ṛjīṣa*, the most powerful one.
1. *ta1-amatraiḥ*; *ta2-amatrairmātraiḥ* | 2.
*śa-anyastu* | "If you honor him with the pressed drops, with the Soma juices..."
The wise one seeks the boldness of the Veda, which is the intellect of the universe.
If you adorn yourselves with the pressed drops, the Soma juices—the wise one knows all; he indeed approaches the bold one. 3.
O Adhvaryus, if you honor Indra with the pressed-out drops—the Soma juices that are habitually gladdening—or if you go toward him in response.
This is the form of the root *bhū* in the sense of "attainment."
At that time, the *medhiraḥ*— the wise one, or the possessor of *medha*,
which is sacrifice—
that Indra *veda*, knows, understands *viśvasya*, your entire desire.
And having known [this], being bold as a subduer of enemies, he seeks—that is, he brings about—each and every desire.
To him, O Indu, bring forth the pressed [juice] from the sheep's wool;
for he protects the sharp-pressed exhilaration that is full of strength.
This is that Soma pressed for you, O Indra; drink!
O Indra, this Soma pressed for you—which guards against the fierce, the mild, the moderate, and the final [excess]—is now pressed; drink it! 2.
O Indra, you [are the one] for whom there is this soma, whose pressed portion is "tīvrasuta"— that is,
"tīkṣṇasuta" (sharply pressed);
it is the [soma] belonging to the morning pressing (prātaḥsavanika).

"Drink that exhilarating Soma juice—the 'middle' juice belonging to the midday pressing and the 'end' juice belonging to the third pressing—for you; this Soma has been pressed for your sake. Thus [he says].
O Indra, this is that Soma pressed for you, for whose sake you released the cows held fast within the rocks in your exhilaration; drink it!
For whom you released the cows that were hidden within the rock for your exhilaration—this is that Soma pressed for you, O Indra; drink! 3.

When that Soma—whose juice causes exhilaration—was drunk, you released the cows that were hidden within the mountain (vala), which had been placed there by the demon Vṛtra; those cows were firmly secured with strong bolts and carried away by the Paṇis. You released them from the bond of Vṛtra. "That Soma," and so forth, is as explained previously.
O Indra, that exhilarating draught of yours from which you have assumed the power of Maghavan—this is that Soma pressed for you; drink!
Of which exhilarating draught you have assumed the power of Maghavan—this is that Soma pressed for you, O Indra; drink it! 4.
O Indra, you, being exhilarated— delighted and gladdened— by the drinking of that food characterized as *soma*, maintain (*dadhiṣe*) the power of Maghavan, your own unique strength,
by which your status as Indra was produced;
this very *soma* has been pressed, so drink it.
In the fourth section (anuvāka), there are six hymns.
Among them, the first hymn, "yo rayivaḥ," consisting of twenty-four verses, is addressed to Indra; it is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Śaṃyu, the son of Bṛhaspati.
Of these, the first six verses are Anuṣṭubhs; the seventh, eighth, and ninth are Virājs (or alternatively, only one of them is a Virāj); and the remaining verses are Triṣṭubhs.

And thus it has been enumerated: "The hymn beginning with *yo rayivān* consists of twenty-four verses; it belongs to Śaṃyu Bārhaspatya; for at the beginning there are six Anuṣṭubhs, and thereafter Virājs, among which the middle one is indeed [the same] as those.
The application (*viniyoga*) of the hymn is concluded. 1. [In the versions] kha, jha, bha, it is [attributed] to Aja.

That which is most wealthy, most rich; that which is most resplendent through its glories—that pressed Soma, O Indra, Lord of the Self-sustaining Power (Svadhā), is your intoxicating draught. 1. [Word-for-word gloss: *yaḥ*: which; *reyivaḥ*: wealthy; *rayitamaḥ*: most rich; *yaḥ*: which; *ghumaiḥ*: through glories; *ghumvattamaḥ*: most resplendent; *somaḥ*: Soma; *sutaḥ*: pressed; *saḥ*: that; *indra*: O Indra; *te*: yours; *asti*: is; *svadhāpate*: O Lord of the Self-sustaining Power; *madaḥ*: intoxicating draught. 1.

O Indra, Lord of *svadhā*—that Soma which is rich in wealth, most abundant in riches, and most resplendent with brilliant glories; that Soma, being pressed, is your exhilarating drink, O Protector of the food characterized by *svadhā*.

That which is blissful, O you of abundant bliss, the giver of wealth and of hymns—that pressed Soma, O Indra, is your intoxicant, O Lord of the Svadhā offering. 2. That which is blissful, O you of abundant bliss, the giver of wealth and of hymns—that pressed Soma, O Indra, is your intoxicant, O Lord of the Svadhā offering. 2.
O you who are being officiated as priests (*ṛtvij*), I praise that very Indra for your sake;
or rather,
you yourselves should praise him.
There is a transposition of words. Of what sort is Indra?

He who is *aprahan*, the non-slayer, the benefactor of his devotees; the *pānta* (protector) of *śavas* (strength); the *viśvāsāham*, the overcomer of every enemy; the *naram*, the leader; the *maṃhiṣṭham*, the most generous giver; and the *viśvacarṣaṇim*, the beholder of all.
Him whom they cause to grow with these [hymns],
the lord of swift bounty—
him, the impetuous one, both worlds and the goddess Rodasī honor.
Him indeed they magnify, the lord of the mountain, the swift one, for his bounty; him indeed do the two divine worlds, heaven and earth, revere for his vital strength.

The hymns (*giraḥ*)—the praises—[addressed to him] who, being joined with the *ghardabha* horses or the *hari* bay steeds that cause trembling, has come for the sake of his friends—the worshippers—with the desire to protect (*uruṣyā*), and has become their protector (*pāyuḥ*), that is, their guardian.
Or alternatively: [the hymns... [as before].
"Sasavān" is a form derived from the root *san* with the suffix *kasu*; the connection is that he is "sasavān," meaning "one who is sharing" by means of the *staulābhiḥ dhautarībhiḥ*.

On the path of Cosmic Order, the Ordainer has been drunk; for the sake of glory, the gods have set their minds [upon him]. Assuming a great name through his words, the beloved one has revealed his form for all to see.

On the path of Truth, the Ordainer has drunk; for the sake of glory, the gods have set their minds upon him. Assuming his great name through our words, the one worthy of longing has revealed his wondrous form to be seen. 8.
On the path of *ṛta*, the sacrifice, Soma—the ordainer (*vedhāḥ*) and seer of all—has been drunk;
that is, he was consumed by Indra.
Or alternatively:
May the Creator, the Ordainer, and Indra drink; let him drink the Soma.
The affix *ciṇ* is applied after the root *vyath* when used in the agentive sense (*kartari*).

In that Soma, the gods—the praising priests—have performed their rites (*akran*) so that Indra’s minds may take refuge for the sake of glory (*śriye*). And that Indra, bearing his own great body (*maho vapuḥ*) which is the very name (*nāma*) of his enemies, being desirable (*venyaḥ*) and worthy of worship through our words of praise (*vacobhiḥ*), may he reveal (*vyāvaḥ*) himself for us to see (*dṛśaye*);
[the ellipsis implies: "may he manifest his favorable splendor."
Alternatively:
*venyaḥ* is a form of the root *ven*, meaning "to desire" or "to shine," and *vapuḥ* is a name for "form.
Being praised with words, may he—desirable (*venyaḥ*) and possessing a radiant form (*vapuḥ*)—reveal (*vyāvaḥ*) himself for the sake of being seen (*dṛśaye*).
Bestow upon us splendor and skill; grant us many dwellings among the people.
With your powers, make our vital strength more abundant, and aid us in the winning of wealth.
Bestow upon us most resplendent skill; ward off the many hostilities of men. With your powers, grant us more abundant vitality; take heed of us in the winning of wealth. 9.
O Indra, bestow upon us—that is, maintain within us—splendor that is most brilliant and power that is most skillful.
Repel, drive away, and ward off the many hostilities—that is, the numerous enemy armies—of the people, of us who are your worshippers.
Furthermore, by means of your own powers of wisdom, make our food more abundant and superior.
Likewise, in the acquisition— that is, the enjoyment— of wealth, know us [and] lead us;
or rather,
protect us for the sake of enjoying wealth.
O Indra, Maghavan, Lord of Bay Steeds, we are yours; do not turn away from us as the giver.
No kinsman is to be seen among mortals—how much less so you, who are called the impeller of the weak?

O Indra, O Maghavan, we have truly become yours; O Lord of the Bay Horses, do not turn away from us as a giver. No kinsman is to be seen among mortals. Why indeed do they call you the one who impels the weak? 10.
O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, we have become your very own remnants for you, the giver of desires; or rather,
we have become intent upon giving oblations to you, the giver, solely for your sake.
O Indra, possessor of bay horses (*harivaḥ*), for this reason, [bestow] 1. your own [wealth], and 2.
that of the people, the sacrificers (*janānāṃ yajamānānām*).
Fourth Aṣṭaka,
May you not be *venaḥ*— may you not be one whose desire has departed.
Love us always.
*Venati* means "to desire.
O Friend (*āpi*), among mortals—among human beings—no other kinsman (*bandhu*) than you has ever been seen (*dadṛśe*), nor is anyone such seen at all.
What is the use of this detailed explanation?
O Indra, the ancient ones say that you are the *radhacodana*—the impeller, the one who urges forth wealth that is effective, successful, and abundant.
O Bull, do not abandon us to the one who exhausts us; O Wealthy One, may we not suffer harm in your friendship.
Many are your settlements among the people, O Indra; you have laughed at the Uṣṇig-songs and cast down the arrogant.

Do not withhold from us, O Bull, for you are glorious; let us not suffer harm in your friendship, O Wealthy One. Many are your suppressions among men, O Indra; strike down those who offer no libations and root out those who give nothing.

O Indra, bull of desires, showerer [of benefits], do not fail us—do not abandon us—to the one who causes destruction, such as a Rākṣasa; for *jas* is a verb meaning "to destroy. To him who destroys, do not give us over.
O Revata, O Dhanavat, while we abide in your friendship—that is, in your state of being a friend—may we not suffer harm; may we not be destroyed.
O Indra, your many and numerous *niṣidhaḥ*—your prohibitions or warding-off powers—are established among the people, that is, against the enemies.
Or alternatively:
The *niṣedha* ropes are those intended for binding;
these you possess in great numbers among your enemies.
For that reason, slay—kill—those who do not swell [with strength] and do not cry out in distress.
"O Aparṇā, uproot—tear out by the roots—the one who does not offer oblations (*havīṃṣi*);
the verbal root is *pṛṇ*, meaning 'to give'."
Like waters flowing from the clouds, Indra, you have brought these gifts of cattle;
you have been the sustainer of poets from of old. Let not the foolish, the stingy ones, deceive you.
Like thundering clouds, Indra sends forth these gifts of cattle; you have been the sustainer of poets from of old. Let not the stingy, the deluded ones, deceive you. 12.

Just as Parjanya, thundering and roaring like clouds, causes the rain-clouds to rise up, so Indra raises up—drives forth—the two kinds of *rādhas*, riches consisting of herds of horses (*aśvasambandhīni*) and herds of cattle (*gavyāni*);
he raises them up to bestow them upon his worshippers.
The second half-verse is addressed in the direct mode (*pratyakṣakṛta*).
O Indra, you are ancient from of old; you are the sustainer of the poets—the singers of praise.
May the wealthy, the wretched, those who do not give, and those who do not offer oblations, not deceive or harm you.
Or rather: [the same].
A change of grammatical number:
the connection is "you, who are Maghavan, the possessor of wealth."
O hero Adhvaryu, bring the pressed juices for the great Indra;
he is the king of this [sacrifice], he who has grown strong through the ancient and the new hymns of the praising Ṛṣis.
O Adhvaryu, O hero, bring forth the pressed juices for the great Indra; for he is their king, who has been magnified by the ancient and the modern songs of the chanting seers. 13.

O Adhvaryu, being especially impelled by the oblations, bring forth—present before—the pressed Soma juices for this great Indra; "of the pressed" is used in the genitive case of the object. Bring them forward, offer them, and present them.
Indeed, Indra becomes the leader and master over the enemies who are being brought under his own power by means of this Soma.

Indra has grown strong—indeed, continues to grow—through both the ancient hymns composed in former times and the new songs being offered now, through the chants of the praising singers, by means of these two kinds of laudations.
Since he is the King of Soma, therefore Soma must be offered to him; this is the meaning.
In the first watch of the night, the *yājyā* for the recitation (*śastra*) of Maitrāvaruṇa is "asya made.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *yājyā* is 'asya made puru vapāṃsi vidvān' (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4)."
In his exhilaration, the wise Indra struck down the irresistible Vṛtras with many weapons;
offer him that honeyed Soma for this hero with the handsome jaws, so that he may drink it.
In his exhilaration, Indra, the knower, struck down many Vṛtras irresistibly. Offer to him that honeyed Soma, rich in sweetness, for this hero with the handsome jaws to drink. 14.

When Indra, the wise and omniscient, was exhilarated by the drinking of that Soma and filled with joy, he— himself unassailable by others— struck down many, numerous *vapās*, that is, the obstructing enemies (*vṛtrāṇi*).
Or alternatively, *vapa* is a name for form.

Indra, the wise one who knows, struck down with his bolt many forms created by the magic of the Asuras—those Vṛtras, the obstructors such as the Rākṣasas, which had never before been overcome by others. O Adhvaryu, offer up for him to drink—that very same Soma, full of sweetness—for that Hero, Indra, the subduer of enemies, whose jaws are beautiful. Offer it forth!
In the second watch of the night, for Maitrāvaruṇa himself, the *ājyā* verse for the *śastra* is "pātā sutam" (May he drink the pressed [Soma]).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *ājyā* is 'pātā sutam indro astu somam hantā vṛtram'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
May Indra be the protector of the pressed Soma; exhilarated by it, may he slay Vṛtra with his thunderbolt.
May he come to the sacrifice from afar, the guardian of the treasures of wealth and the sustainer of the poets.

May Indra be the drinker of the pressed Soma; exhilarated, may he slay Vṛtra with his thunderbolt. May he come to the sacrifice even from afar, the benefactor who protects the prayers of the poet who offers his devotion.
May this Indra drink the pressed-out Soma; may he be a good drinker, may he be a drinker.
The suffix *tṛn* occurs after the root *kṛ* when preceded by *sādhu*.
For this very reason, because the sixth case (genitive) is prohibited by the rule "na lokāvyaya... [Pāṇini 2.3.69], the second case (accusative) is used.
This should be understood to apply similarly in cases such as *hanta* and so forth.

And being exhilarated and rejoicing by that Soma, may he slay Vṛtra—the obstructing enemy—with his weapon, the thunderbolt. For the sake of both these purposes, may he come even from afar; may he come toward our sacrifice. The meaning is: even though he is situated in a distant land, may he arrive quickly and come for the drinking of the Soma.
What kind of Indra is he?

He is *vasu*, the dweller of all; the *vavitā*, the finder or protector of *dhī*—that is, of the thoughts, the meditators, the singers, or the ritual acts; and the *kārudhāyāḥ*, the sustainer of the *kārūn*, the doers or sacrificers.
In the third watch of the night, for the reciter of the *praśāstṛ*, "This is it" (*idaṃ stha*) is the *yajyā* for the *śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *yajyā* is 'This is the vessel, the drinking-vessel of Indra' (*idaṃ stha pātram indrapānam')" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.4).
1. For the singers [beginning with] the letters *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *ya*:

This very vessel, the drinking-vessel of Indra, the beloved nectar of Indra, has been drunk. May you exhilarate the god for his goodwill; may he drive away our hatred and dispel the darkness. 16. This. That. Vessel. The drinking-vessel of Indra. Of Indra. Beloved. Nectar. Has been drunk. May I be exhilarated. For the sake of goodwill. The god. Away. From us. Hatred. May he drive away. Away. Darkness. 16.
The vessel, fit to be set down, the drinking-vessel of Indra—worthy of Indra's drink, beloved and favorable to Indra—that very one, this our Soma, has been drunk as nectar.
Let Indra drink it.
[The suffix] *ciṇ* is used in the sense of the agent with the root *vyath*.
Or rather:
this nectar has been drunk;
let it be drunk by Indra.

In whatever manner the Soma has been drunk so that it may exhilarate—make Indra, the god, joyful through *saumanasa* (good-mindedness)—in that same manner let it be drunk; this is the meaning. May that Indra, having drunk the Soma, drive away (*vi-yuyavat*) our haters (*dveṣaḥ*, those who hate us) from us (*asmata*), and may he also drive away evil (*ahaḥ*) from us.
Rejoicing in this [soma], O Hero, slay our enemies—both kin and stranger. Let your bay steeds, the stallions, being harnessed, bring you hither;

let the coursers with powerful chariots and powerful reins, the vigorous steeds carrying the thunderbolt, well-yoked, bring you toward us for the sake of the vigorous exhilaration. Let your bay steeds, the stallions, being harnessed, bring you hither; let the coursers with powerful chariots and powerful reins, the vigorous steeds carrying the thunderbolt, well-yoked, bring you toward us for the sake of the vigorous exhilaration. (19)
"O Indra, let the bay horses bring you hither—to you, the bull—to the most excellent exhilarating draught, the Soma, in order that they may cause you to drink this Soma.
What kind of horses?
Bulls, showerers of desires; yoking themselves, being harnessed to the chariot by their own accord; possessors of the bull-chariot."
Those whose chariots have the bull as their showerer of desires are so described.
"Vṛṣaraśmayaḥ" means those whose reins— the rays that rain down— are such [showerers].
"The steeds are ever-moving; our horses are coming toward us, bulls that cross over easily, carrying the thunderbolt and other weapons, well-yoked with excellent harnessing."

To thee, O Bull, the bulls have gone to the vat, like waves surging with drops of ghee, rejoicing. O Indra, for thee, the bull, they bring the pressed soma with the bulls; to thee, the showerer, they bring the soma. 20. To thee, O Bull, the bulls have gone to the vat, like waves surging with drops of ghee, rejoicing. O Indra, for thee, with the bulls, they bring the pressed soma; to thee, the showerer, the bull, they bring the soma. 20.

O Indra, showerer (*vṛṣan*) of desires, your own youthful horses—mighty (*vṛṣaṇaḥ*) as sprinklers (*sektāraḥ*), "butter-backed" (*ghṛtapṛṣaḥ*) like waves (*ormayaḥ*), pouring out water (*ghṛta*) like oceanic billows—rejoicing, exulting, and being intoxicated, have mounted (*ā asthuḥ*), that is, they are ascending, your wooden chariot (*droṇa*). Therefore, the sense is: come here [to them]. Why? To this he says:

O Indra, for you—the bull, the youth, the eternally young, the showerer of desires—since the Adhvaryus bring forth, offer, and lead forward for the sake of the oblation the Soma, which is your very self, from among the pressed-out Somas by means of the "bull-like" cows that shower down desires; therefore, come! This is the meaning.

You are the bull of heaven, the bull of earth; you are the bull of the rivers, the bull of standing waters. For you, the bull, the drop has swelled; it is a sweet juice, a honeyed draught for your choice. 21. You are the bull. Of heaven. The bull. Of earth. The bull. Of the rivers. The bull. Of standing waters. For the bull. To you. The drop. O bull. Has swelled. Sweet. Juice. Honey-draught. For your choice. 21.
O Indra, you are the bull of heaven— that is, the showerer of the celestial world through oblations—
and the bull of the earth, the rainer of desires.
"You are the bull (*vṛṣā*), the fulfiller, of the *sindhus*— the flowing rivers—
and likewise the bull (*vṛṣabhaḥ*), the showerer of desires, of the moving and stationary beings who have come together in a multitude.
Or else:"
The waters have become a community;
you are their showerer.
O bull, showerer of desires, for you—the most excellent, the bestower, the sprinkler—for your sake.
1. *Kha-jha-na-bha-ya* means "let them bring" or "let them cause to come.
2. *Kha-pṛṣantaḥ siñcantaḥ*; *na-pṛṣautaḥ siñcantaḥ*; *bha-pṛṣataḥ siñcantaḥ* means "sprinkling drops from *kha*," "sprinkling drops from *na*," and "sprinkling drops from *bha*.
3. *Kha-jha-jha-ta-na-bha-ra-tasthuḥ* means "they stood firm upon *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*."
4. Those standing in *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ā*; those remaining in *gha*, *jña*, *śa*, and *ā*.
5. With cows raining [milk] from *kha* and *na*; 6. O Indra, rain down the desires of those in *gha*; O Indra, showerer upon the desires of those in *ra*.
Sweet, pleasant, savory, praiseworthy, full of flavor, or consisting of essence—like honey, it is to be drunk; Indu, the Soma, has swelled, it swells, it increases.
Therefore, the sense is: "Come to him yourself and drink that Soma."
This god, being born with sudden power, together with Indra as his ally, firmly established the world.
This Indu has stripped away the weapons of his own father and the magic powers of Śiva.
This god, being born with sudden force, with Indra as his ally, propped apart the firmament. This Indu stole away the weapons from his own father and the magic powers of the malevolent one. 22.

The shining god, this very *indu*, Soma, being born— that is, manifesting— along with Indra as his companion and friend, [overcame] the Paṇi, the merchant who was the seizer of the cows, namely the Asura called Vala; or rather,
he is called Paṇi because he is the master of the Paṇis.
He suddenly paralyzed the demon Tama by his power—

he restrained and obstructed him— and moreover, he stole away the weapons, such as the thunderbolt and others, of the inauspicious and unhappiness-inducing Bala, who was the protector of his father’s wealth in the form of cows; he also stole away his magical illusions.
"O Indra, Soma has performed all this through his own power; therefore, by whom can his greatness therein be described?"—thus is the praise of Indra.
He made the dawns have a good husband; he placed the light within the sun.
He found the threefold nectar hidden away in the three luminous realms of heaven.
He made the dawns have good husbands; he placed the light within the sun. He found the threefold nectar hidden in the third luminous realm of heaven. 23.
This Soma made the Dawns—those whose excellent husband and protector is the Sun—possess such a lord at the time of dawn;
he placed the light, the brilliance, within the orb of the Sun.

This Soma, in the form of a creeper, found—that is, discovered—Amṛta, the nectar that is the cause of immortality, which was hidden (nigūḷha), meaning existing in a state of extreme concealment through invisibility, within the threefold triple-world (tridhātu) consisting of the three libations (savanatraya), specifically among the Tritas—the gods who shine in the luminous realms (rocana) of heaven (divi) in the third station (tṛtīye sthāne) and are spread abroad among them.
"O Indra, it was only through your assistance that Soma did this"—thus is the praise of Indra to be understood.
Or else: [the verse continues as follows].
By this word "this" (idam), Indra himself is referred to.
This Indra made [the women] have beautiful husbands;
he alone established the womb within the sun.

Among the three classes of gods (tritaḥ) shining in the heavenly world (divi), who have attained the three stations, this very Indra obtained the immortal Soma—the cause of immortality—which was hidden in a threefold manner through the three libations (tridhātu), and which was concealed within the sacrificial vessels. He drank it.
He propped apart these two, heaven and earth; he yoked the three-spoked chariot. By his power, Soma placed the cooked milk within the cows, manifesting the well that holds the source.
He propped apart heaven and earth; he yoked the swift chariot. By his power, he placed the cooked food among the cows; through Soma, he sustained the fountain that reveals its mechanism.
1. jha-ca: This is Soma. 2. kha-gha-jha-na-bha-ya: Indra-stuti (Praise of Indra).
Ṛgveda 3.10.
This Soma has established apart both Heaven and Earth—Heaven and the earth.
Moreover, this Soma has yoked the chariot of the Sun, which is endowed with seven rays—that is, seven reins—or seven horses, or seven wheels.
Likewise, this Soma sustains within the cows the ripe, fully developed milk, which is of the nature of wisdom, meditation, and creative intention, and which flows forth like a spring.
"Ten instruments":
this is a qualifying phrase containing a reason for the "fountain" (*utsa*).
It means being endowed with ten instruments or means, namely the eyes, ears, and so forth, which serve as the causes for its flowing forth.
And this word is explained by Khelika through another mantra: "The eye, the ear, the mind, the speech, the out-breath and the in-breath, and the body—this is the physical frame.
*Draḥ* [is] two visible, forward-directed emissions; I consider this to be a fountain with ten mechanisms.
Or else:
This Indra caused heaven and earth to tremble;
he established them each in their own place.
He, indeed, yoked the seven-rayed chariot of the sun.
This very Indra, possessing cattle, holds the cooked milk by means of his own power, Śacī.
For the sake of such an Indra, Soma holds—that is, maintains—the *daśayantra*, the flowing juice endowed with ten qualities, namely the ten vessels beginning with the Aindravāyava and so forth.
At the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*), these ten cups, beginning with the Aindravāyava, are drawn.
And so says the Brāhmaṇa: "Nine Pragrahas are drawn; while nine are being offered during the recitation of the hymns, he draws the tenth when the Stoma has been chanted" (Ai.
Brā. 3.1). It is recorded elsewhere: "The Adhvaryu draws these ten Pragrahas at the morning libation" (Śā.
Brā. 14.2). With this intention, the specific qualification "the ten-fold machine" is used.
The second hymn, consisting of thirty-three verses beginning with "ya ānayan," is the seerical composition (*ārṣam*) of Śaṃyu, the son of Bṛhaspati.

The verse beginning with "purutamam" is an *epātinicṛt*, according to the definition stated as: "Three *masaka*s [of eight syllables] constitute a *pādanicṛt*; the middle one [of twelve syllables] is an *aṣṭakchadatinicṛt*.
Of these thirty-three verses, the last is an *anuṣṭubh*, while the remaining ones are *gāyatrīs*.
In the verse beginning with "adhi bruvaḥ paṇīnām," however, another named Chandonāmakṣa is praised;
therefore, he has three deities. The remaining thirty are divine.

And thus it is enumerated: "The hymn beginning with 'He who brought from the thirty-three [gods] the threefold [sacrifice], most abundant,' is an Anuṣṭubh in the Nicṛt meter; others say the Tṛca [verses] have Takṣan as their deity.
This hymn is also used in the Niṣkevalya of the Mahāvrata, with the exception of the other Tṛca.
Likewise, the Pañcamāraṇyaka states: "'He who brought from the far distance'—these three [verses]; he omits the last ones" (Ai. Ā. 7.2.5).

He who, by his skillful guidance, brought Turvaśa and Yadu from afar—Indra, that youthful friend of ours. 1. He who brought [them] forth from the distant region through excellent leadership—Turvaśa and Yadu—Indra, he is our youthful friend. 1.

Indra brought Turvaśa and Yadu—these two kings who had been cast by their enemies into a distant land—back from that far-off place through *sunīti*, that is, by means of excellent guidance and beautiful leading. May that youthful Indra be our friend.

Even with a non-speedy steed that is not at all sluggish, Indra is the winner of the prize set before him. 2. Even with a non-speedy steed that is not at all sluggish, Indra is the winner of the prize set before him. 2.
The wise one (*vipra*) is the singer (*stotṛ*). Even in a person who is different from that [wise one], Indra maintains (*dhārayati*) "vayas," which means food (*anna*), bestowing it upon him.
What need is there to say that he bestows wealth upon the one who praises him?
That Indra, even with a horse that is not swift and whose pace is slow, becomes a conqueror—one whose nature is victory—over the wealth placed and established among the enemies.
The suffix *tṛn* is used here with the sense of habit (*śīla*).
Consequently, by the rule "ana-lokāvyaya," there is a prohibition of the genitive case.
Great are his guidances, and many indeed are his praises; his aids never fail. 3. Great are his guidances, and many indeed are his praises; his aids never fail. 3.

1. *jha-ta-ra* contains the causal element (*hetugarbha*) as a specific feature. 2. *gha-jña-sa-tara-na-bhara-tendrārthe*. 3. *kha-jha-ta-na-bhara-soma*; *gha-śa* does not exist in the sense of "praise" (*stome*). 4. Because of the characteristic of *kha-jha-na-bha*. 5. *śa-metrādī*.
The *praṇītayaḥ*—the excellent guidances, the leadings, the bringings—of this Indra are *mahīḥ*, that is, great and magnificent.
Furthermore, the *praśastayaḥ*—the excellent praises being performed by the singers—are *pūrvīḥ*, that is, numerous.
Likewise, the protections (ūtayaḥ) of this Indra do not diminish nor decrease;
rather, they always increase.

O friends, honor and sing forth to him who is borne by the sacred prayer; for he is our great providence. 4. O friends! To him who is borne by the sacred prayer (*brahmavāhas*), pay homage and sing forth! For he is indeed our great protector. 4.
O friends, you who share the same station, praise with hymns and recite verses for Indra, who is to be carried by sacred prayers (*brahman*) and who is worthy of attainment;
sing forth songs of praise as well,
for he, indeed, is our great and most excellent providence.
The meaning is: "having bestowed such an intellect."
O slayer of Vṛtra, you are the protector of one, and you are the protector of two; even of such as we are. 5. You—of one—O slayer of Vṛtra—protector—of two—are—also—of such—as we are. 5.
O Vṛtrahan, O Indra, slayer of Vṛtras—that is, enemies—you are the *avitā*, the protector, of one praiser and even of two;

the meaning is that you become the guardian of all praisers. Moreover (*uta*), you are a protector even for such a person as we are—those who have been protected by you and have come to possess manifold sons and grandsons.
The meaning is that for such a person as this, you alone are the protector and no other.

You lead away the enemies; you make those who recite the hymns [your] followers. With [your] men, you are called "possessing good heroes. 6. You lead away; indeed, you drive off the enemies; you make those who recite the hymns [your] followers. With [your] men, you are called "possessing good heroes. 6.
O Indra, you alone lead us beyond our haters; you protect us and carry us across.
(The particle *u* is a filler.
Likewise, you make us—the singers of hymns who recite the *ukthas*, the liturgical chants—possessors of the Maruts.

Since you are called—that is, praised—by men who are leaders of hymns as one "possessed of excellent heroes," meaning endowed with fine heroic sons, grandsons, and so forth, who are to be granted through praise; therefore, [the ellipsis is] that you should grant those [heroes] to us as well.

With hymns, I call upon Brahmāṇaspati, the bearer of the sacred word, the friend worthy of praise, as one calls a cow for milking. 7. Brahmāṇaspati; the bearer of the sacred word; with hymns; the friend; the one worthy of praise; like a cow; for milking; I call. 7.
The exalted Brahmāṇaspati, who is to be carried by the *brahmavāhas*—that is, by the mantras consisting of hymns of praise—and who is our friend, the one worthy of being praised (*ṛgmiya*).
*Ṛgmā* means *ṛcaḥ*; that which is worthy of them.
The meaning is "worthy of praise.
Such an Indra, as one would [call] a cow for the sake of milking—so with hymns (*gīrbhiḥ*), that is, with praises, I invoke him to grant our desires.

In whose two hands all treasures are said to reside doubly, that hero who is the vanquisher of hostile armies. 8. In whose two hands; all; treasures; are said to reside; doubly; that hero; the vanquisher of armies. 8.
1. [The manuscripts] kha, jha, na, and bha read *vividha*.
2. [The manuscripts] kha, jha, and bha read *asmān atitārayāṃsi*; jha, na, and ya read *asmān atinyāsa tārayasi*; and gha reads *avārayāṃsi*. 3. [The manuscript] gha reads *stotṛpābhiḥ*.

Of the hero, the powerful one; *pṛtanāsaḥ* means armies, that is, enemy forces; he is the conqueror of them. In whose hands and arms all (*viśvāni*) things—meaning all treasures (*vasūni*) existing in a twofold (*dvitā*) manner as celestial and terrestrial forms—are found. "The seers have spoken of him" (*ni ūcuḥ*) means they speak of that Indra emphatically; this connects with the word *huva* ("call upon") from the preceding verse.
O wielder of the stone, O Lord of Might, you have indeed rent asunder the days of men; you have uprooted their wiles, O unbending one. 9.

O wielder of the stone, O lord of power, Indra, like one who possesses a chariot drawn by wild beasts, tear asunder and shatter the ancient, firm, and solid fortresses— or the powers— of the people, even those that are difficult to overcome.
The meaning is: "Uproot them in various ways.
O Unbowed One, O Unyielding One, O Most Exalted Indra, utterly destroy the māyās created by the enemies.

So we, desiring glory, have called upon you, O true one, drinker of Soma, Indra, Lord of spoils. 10. So we, desiring glory, have called upon you, O true one, drinker of Soma, Indra, Lord of spoils. 10.

O Indra, whose nature is truth and non-falsity, O drinker of Soma, O protector of the Soma, O Lord of strengths, O guardian of foods—O you who are such as this, we, desiring glory and seeking food for ourselves, invoke you; that is, we praise you, such as you are.

Whether you were such as you were in the past, or whether you are now to be invoked when the prize has been set—be one who is to be called upon; hear our invocation! 11. Whether you were such as you were in the past, or whether you are now to be invoked when the prize has been set—be one who is to be called upon; hear our invocation! 11.
"O Indra, we praise you—indeed, we praise you alone"; this is the remainder of the sense.
You who were formerly, in earlier times, worthy of invocation (*havya*) for the sake of obtaining wealth;

or rather, you who even now (*nūnam*) remain worthy of invocation when wealth has been placed among the enemies as the occasion arises—such as you are, hear (*śrudhi*), that is, listen to our invocation, our hymn of praise.

With our prayers, with swift steeds, O Indra, may we win the prizes that bring renown; through you, may we conquer the wealth that is set before us. 12. With our prayers; with swift steeds; of the swift steeds; the prizes; O Indra; bringing renown; through you; may we conquer; the wealth; that is set before us. 12.

O Indra, may we—graced by you who are pleased with our prayers and hymns directed toward you—conquer through our own swift horses, the enemies, and the bonds of the foe; may we win horses worthy of renown, glorious and praiseworthy food, and the wealth placed among the enemies; through your favor, may we be victorious.
O Hero, lover of songs, you have become great, O Indra; for when the prize is set and the battle is joined, you are the one to be relied upon. || 13 ||

O Hero, O lover of songs, O Indra worthy of praise with hymns, when the wealth of the enemies was placed at stake—that is, when it served as the objective—thou, the great and exalted one, becamest the victor over the enemies in battle, having severed their thread.
The root *taṃsa* has the sense of "conquering the elements" (*dhātujaya*).
It is recited among the *kaṇva*-type roots;
therefore, the *tavya* suffix is applied according to the *uṇādi* rules to form *taṃsavya*.
1. O you who are worthy of drinking the Soma from the vessel!

2. O you who are the sign! That aid of yours which, O slayer of enemies, is most swift in its onset—with that, impel our chariot forward. (14) That aid of yours, O slayer of enemies, which is most swift in its onset—by means of that, urge our chariot onward. (14)

O slayer of enemies, O Indra, destroyer of foes, that protection of yours which is most swift in speed—exceedingly rapid in its motion—exists; with each such [protection], impel our chariot, drive it swiftly for the sake of conquering the enemy.

As the best of chariot-warriors with your chariot, O conqueror, may you overcome our adversaries and win the wealth that has been set before us. 15. He; with his chariot; the best of chariot-warriors; with our [allies]; overcoming the adversaries; may you win; O conqueror; the wealth that has been set [for us]. 15.

O victorious one, O Indra of conquering nature, you who are the best of chariot-warriors, the supreme great-charioteer (*mahāratha*), may you, with our own chariot—yoked by us and capable of overcoming enemies—win back the wealth placed among the foes; conquer it for our sake!

Praise him alone who is the most eminent among the people, the far-seeing one; he was born as the Lord, possessed of manly power. 16. He who is the one—him alone, praise! He is the far-seeing lord of the peoples; he was born with the will of a bull. 16.

He who is the observer of all, seeing everything with distinction, whose will is powerful and whose deeds are rain-like—that Indra alone, and no other, was born as the lord and sovereign of the people; O singer, praise that very Indra!

You who have indeed been the kinsman, the protector, the auspicious friend of those who sing your praises—O Indra, as such, be gracious to us. 17. You who have indeed been the kinsman, the protector, the auspicious friend of those who sing your praises—O Indra, as such, be gracious to us. 17.

O Indra, you who—being auspicious and a bringer of happiness through your protection and aid, acting as our friend and well-wisher—have been our kinsman and relative, our very protector (*apiḥ*), for those of us who sing your praises; you who were thus in the past, as such, favor us now and grant us happiness.

Grasp the thunderbolt in your two hands for the slaying of the Rākṣasas, O wielder of the thunderbolt; may you utterly conquer our adversaries. 18. Grasp the thunderbolt in your two hands for the slaying of the Rākṣasas, O wielder of the thunderbolt; may you utterly conquer our adversaries. 18.
O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, take up—that is, hold—the vajra, the lightning bolt, in your two hands, your own arms. For what purpose?
For the slaying of the rakṣases, for the sake of killing the demons.
And having taken up [your weapons], may you utterly overcome the rival, contending, attacking Asura armies.

The ancient one, the companion of riches, the friend who impels the singer—I invoke him whose hand bears the sacred prayer. 19. The ancient one; of riches; the companion; in friendship; the impeller of the singer; him whose hand bears the sacred prayer; I invoke. 19.
1. *kha-jha-ta-na-ma-ra-ya* is one [syllable]. 2. *sva-jha-na-bha-ra-śa-‘abhi’* does not exist; *ta-na*.

I invoke—that is, I call upon—Indra who is such as this: the ancient (*pratnam*), the long-enduring (*ciraṃtanam*), the uniter (*yujam*) and bestower of all purposes (*arthe*) and riches (*rayīṇām*); the friend (*sakhāyam*) who has become a companion; the impeller of the praisers (*kīri-codanam*, i.e., the stimulator of those who offer hymns); and the greatest bringer of sacred prayer (*brahmāvahastamam*). I call upon Indra.
For he alone rules over all earthly treasures—he who is most fond of songs of praise, the irresistible one. 20. He; for; all; earthly; alone; riches; rules over; most fond of songs; irresistible. 20.
For he indeed is that Indra; he alone rules over (*parpate*), possesses sovereignty over, all (*viśvāni*)—that is, every—earthly (*pārthivā*) treasures (*vasūni*), and no one else at all.
The root *paryati* has the sense of "to rule" or "to possess.
Of what nature is Indra?
*Girvaṇastamaḥ*: most worthy of being honored with songs of praise; *adhri-guḥ*:
one who does not go to that [obstruction], meaning one whose movement is unimpeded.

O Lord of Cows, boldly fulfill our desire with your teams of horses, with strengths consisting of swift steeds, and with wealth of cattle. 21. He [fulfills] for us; with his teams; let him fill; the desire; with strengths; with horses; with cattle-wealth; O Lord of Cows; boldly. 21.

O Gopati, protector of the cows, you—do you boldly (*dhṛṣat*), that is, courageously, fulfill (*ā pṛṇa*) our desire (*kāma*) with your teams of mares (*niyudbhiḥ*), so as to be capable of destroying poverty.
Alternatively, *dhṛṣat* is an epithet of Indra;
the meaning is: "you who are the subduer (*dharṣaka*) of enemies."
Likewise, fulfill our desire with many cattle accompanied by oxen, or with many horses accompanied by mares.

Sing that for you when the Soma is pressed, for the one invoked by many, the warrior, which is as a blessing to the bull, as it were, for the powerful one. 22. Sing that for you when the Soma is pressed, for the one invoked by many, the warrior, which is a blessing, like [milk] for the bull, for the mighty one. 22.

O you praisers, when the soma has been pressed out, sing that hymn together, being united, to Indra—the one invoked by many sacrificers, the subduer of enemies, the bestower of wealth, and the one who grants [boons]—for his sake.
The hymn which is beneficial and brings happiness to Indra, who is powerful and possessed of strength, is like [happiness] for a cow;
that is to say, it is just as refreshing grass is a source of comfort to a cow.

Truly, he does not withhold the wealth, the gift of booty consisting of cattle, when he hears these songs addressed to him. 23. He does not indeed withhold the riches, the gift of booty accompanied by cattle, when he listens to these hymns. 23.

Indra is the *vasu*, the one who causes [us] to dwell; he does not indeed withhold, nor does he restrain, nor does he cause to cease the gift—the bestowing—of *vāja* (food, strength, or booty) consisting of many cattle.
Provided that he should hear these our songs, our praises.
The meaning is that when the hymn of praise is heard, [the deity] grants [blessings] at all times.
1. Fill up the cavities, the joints, the fissures, the hollows, the depressions, and the chasms!
2. Or rather, [fill] the cavities, the hollows, and the fissures; or rather, [fill] the chasms and the fissures!

May the slayer of the Dasyus go toward the cattle-filled stall of Kuvitsa; may he open it for us with his powers. (24) Kuvitsa’s—indeed—toward the stall full of cattle, may the slayer of the Dasyus go; with his powers, may he open it for us. (24)
Regarding *kuvitsasya*: *kuvit* means "many times"; he who scatters or destroys [them] is *kuvit*, the name of a certain person.
His own, namely the *vraja*—the cow-pen—rich in cattle (*vgomantaṃ*), joined with many cows, Indra, the slayer of *dasyus* (those who cause harm), goes forth (*vpragmata*) with great force.
Since this is so, therefore, by means of *śacībhiḥ*—that is, by our own actions or wisdoms—he uncovered those cows for us (*naḥ*), which were hidden away in the enclosure (*vara*). He opened them up.

O Śatakratu, these songs have cried out toward you, as mother-cows low toward their calf— toward Indra. O lover of hymns, when the soma has been pressed again and again for me, these our songs reach and pervade you,
just as milch-cows reach their calf.
Just as they quickly envelop a calf, so it is in that manner.

May he who is most abundant among the many, who is praised by those who offer hymns, be distinguished by his victories; may he, being rich in spoils, cause us to win booty with his strengths. 29. Most abundant; of the many; praised by those who offer hymns; distinguished; with strengths; may he cause us to win booty. 29.

O Indra, may our praise reach you—the most frequent subduer of many, the one who exhausts numerous enemies—by means of the praises of us many who, at this sacrifice where various words consisting of hymns and recitations are uttered, strive to make you possessed of strength (*vājavantam*) through strengths (*vājaiḥ*), that is, through foods characterized by vigor. ¹ *tamayitāram*: "one who causes to cease" or "one who suppresses. ² *glapayitāram*: "one who makes weary" or "one who causes exhaustion. ³ *vājebhiḥ*: "by means of strengths" or "by means of sacrificial foods. ⁴ *vājyantām*: "striving for strength" or "possessing strength. ⁵ *tvām*: "you. ⁶ *kurvatām*: "making [you so]. (The ellipsis implies: "may our praise reach you.")

O Indra, may our hymn of praise be most effective and closest to you; impel us toward great wealth. 30. O Indra, may our hymn of praise be most effective and closest to you; impel us toward great wealth. 30.
O Indra, may our hymn of praise be most effective in carrying you; may it be the nearest to you. And do you impel us toward great wealth.
He has stood upon the highest head of the Paṇis, like a wide, unassailable thicket. 31. adhi | bubuḥ | paṇīnām | varṣiṣṭhe | mūrdhni | asthāt | uruḥ | kakṣaḥ | na | gāñjyaḥ || 31 ||
Bubu was the name of a carpenter among the Paṇis;
having obtained wealth through his craftsmanship, Bharadvāja praised that gift of his with this [verse].
And this is recorded by Manu: "But Bharadvāja, afflicted by hunger along with his sons in the lonely forest..."
"The highly illustrious one accepted many cows at the moment of his birth" (Manu Smṛti 10.107).

The *paṇis*—whether they be merchants known by that name or *asuras*—among them was *Bubhu*, a carpenter (*takṣan*). He stood upon the highest head, that is, on a head-like elevated place; he was established there, born on the bank of the Gaṅgā (*gāñjyaḥ*), as vast as a thicket (*kakṣo na kakṣaḥ uruḥ*). The meaning is that although lowly by birth, one becomes the best in every respect through the quality of being a donor.

Whose auspicious gift, like the swift [wind], is thousandfold; who immediately bestows it for the sake of giving. 32. Whose—like the wind—swift, auspicious, thousandfold gift, immediately bestows for the sake of giving. 32.

The connection with the following verse is as follows: "Whose *bubhu*—swift-moving like the wind—is the auspicious, thousandfold gift; he bestows (*maṃhate*) the desired wealth immediately upon me, who at the very time of praise am desirous of giving and making a request."

1. In *abhipyute*, there is no *jña-ta*. 2. In *purutamam*, there is *jña-ta*. 3. In *ślathitāram*, there is *ya*. 4. In *vegavantam* and *balavantam*, there is *jña*. 5. In *vā*, there is no *kha-gha-jña-na-bha*. 6. In *tvām*, there is no *gha-jña-ra-śa*. 7. In *nirjane*, there is *kha-jña-jha-ta-na-bha-ya-ra*. 8. In *varṣiṣṭhe varṣake*, there is *na*.

Therefore, all the noble singers ever celebrate that [deed] of ours: Bṛbu, the giver of thousands, the patron who wins thousands. 33. Therefore, all the noble singers ever celebrate that [deed] of ours: Bṛbu, the giver of thousands, the patron who wins thousands. 33.
All our bards—the singers who yearn for hymns—constantly and most excellently praise that Bṛbu of yours.

Of what sort? He is the giver of thousands, the preeminent bestower of wealth numbering in the thousands; he is the wise one (sūrī), or rather, the impeller; and he is the winner of thousands, the one who shares out wealth or the fruit of a thousandfold hymn.
The third hymn, consisting of fourteen verses beginning with "tvām id dhi," is addressed to Indra; it is the seerical composition (ārṣa) of Śaṃyu, the son of Bṛhaspati.
The odd-numbered verses—the first, third, and so on—are Bṛhatīs, while the even-numbered verses—the second, fourth, and so on—are Satobṛhatīs.
Thus it has been stated in the Anukramaṇī: "tvām id dhi; [this is] a Pakti hymn."
The application of the hymn (*sūkta*) is based on its indicative mark (*laiṅgika*).
If the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice has the *bṛhat* as its *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, then the *pragātha* beginning with "tvāmiddhi havāmahe" is the *stotriya* for the *niṣkevalya*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "If indeed the *bṛhat* [is used], 'tvāmiddhi havāmahe'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.15).
This *pragātha* is also to be recited in the *niṣkevalya* section of the *mahāvrata*.
Accordingly, it is prescribed in the *Pañcamāraṇyaka*: "‘tvāmiddhi havāmahe’ and ‘tvaṃ hyehi ceravaḥ’ are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* verses for the *bṛhat* [sāman]" (AiĀ 5.2.2).

For we poets invoke you alone for the winning of booty; O Indra, men invoke you, the lord of the virtuous, in battles against the Vritras, and you in the races of the steeds. 1. For we poets indeed invoke you alone for the winning of booty; O Indra, men invoke you, the lord of the virtuous, in battles against the Vritras, and you in the races of the steeds. 1.
O Indra, we, the singers (*kāravaḥ*), when there is the winning (*sātā*) or the gaining of booty (*vājasya*) as the occasion for its distribution, call upon you alone with our hymns.
O Indra, other men (*naraḥ*) also invoke you—the protector of the good and the most excellent—when obstructors (*vṛtreṣu*) or enemies are present, for the sake of victory over them.
Moreover, in those "stages" (kāṣṭhāsu) belonging to the "steed" (arvataḥ)—those stages where the horse, having galloped, comes to rest—in battles, those desiring combat call out to you alone.
Therefore, the meaning is: we likewise call out to you alone.

As such, O wondrous one, wielder of the thunderbolt, being boldly praised by us, O lord of the great stone, scatter for us cattle, horses, and reddish-brown kine, O Indra—bestow them like wealth upon a victor. saḥ | tvam | naḥ | citra | vajra-hasta | dhṛṣṇu-yā | mahaḥ | stavānaḥ | adri-vas | gām | aśvam | rudhyam | indra | sam | kira | sūtrā | vājam | na | jigyuṣe || 2 ||
O *citra*, the wonderful one; O *vajrahasta*, whose hand holds the thunderbolt;
O *adrivas*, possessor of the thunderbolt—or rather, *adri* refers to the thunderbolt (*śani*) by way of its initial and final sounds.

In that same way, O Indra, being such as you are—bold (*dhṛṣṇuyā*), a subduer of enemies, great (*mahaḥ*)—you, being thus praised, [attain greatness]. (Note: *kha-ma-āhayante* refers to the variant reading *āharyante*).
Being praised by us, bestow— grant fully— the earth, the chariot, and the horse that draws the chariot;
grant them abundantly to the victorious Puṣan for his enjoyment, like *vāja*, that is, food, in great measure and plenty,
just as you grant much for the sake of enjoyment to one who has conquered his enemies.
In the *mahāvrata* and the *nikevalya*, the remainder of the hymn beginning with “*yaḥ satrāhā*” is to be recited.
For it is stated: “‘*yaḥ satrāhā vicarṣaṇiḥ*’—this remainder of yours, ‘*astu haryataḥ*’, [is to be used] in the hymn” (*AiA* 5.2.4).
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing, the *pragātha* beginning with “*yaḥ satrāhā*” serves as an optional *anurūpa*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "He who is ever-conquering, the far-seeing one, has tasted the flowing [Soma]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).
Him who is the slayer of enemies, the far-seeing one—Indra him we invoke. O thousand-testicled one, of many heroic deeds, lord of power, be our strengthener in battles!
Him who is the ever-conquering, the far-seeing—Indra, him we invoke. O thou of a thousand testicles, of many heroic deeds, lord of the dwelling, be with us for our increase in battles! 3.
