We invoke—that is, we call upon with words of praise—that Indra who is the conqueror of hosts, the slayer of great enemies, and the far-seeing one who perceives everything in particular; the latter half of the verse is addressed directly:
O thou of a thousand testicles (sahasramuṣka), O thou of a thousand phalli!
Whatever woman Indra approaches out of a lust for pleasure, he emits semen at every joint of his body; this is known from the Kauryātakins.
With this intention, this address is made:
O Turvinṛmṇa, O you of abundant wealth, O Lord of beings, O protector of the virtuous, O Indra, be for our increase in battles, that is, in conflicts.
You strike down men with fury like a bull, O impetuous one, bountiful giver, worthy of praise. Be our protector in the great contest for wealth, for our bodies, for the waters, and for the sun.
O Bounteous One, like a bull with fury, you prevail in the exhilarating contest, O Worthy of Praise. Be our protector in the great battle for cattle, for our bodies, for the waters, and for the sun.

O *ṛcīṣama*, equal to the *ṛc* through the *ṛc*, you who manifest such a form; O Indra, in that *ghṛṣu*—the one who crushes and oppresses enemies—in the *mīḷha*, the battle, with a *manyu* (wrath) like that of a powerful bull (*vṛṣabha*), you oppress our enemies; oppress them!
Likewise, in the great battle where vast wealth is at stake, be our *avitā* (protector); be aware!
Know yourself as our protector.
"Be a protector," he said.
"For what purpose?
For the sake of obtaining those things—namely, for one's own body, for one's offspring, for waters, and for sunbeams that have been gained."
The acquisition of the sun is its manifestation;
the meaning is "for that purpose."
On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdinasavana*), the *pragātha* beginning with “*indra jyeṣṭhaṃ na ā bhara*” serves as the optional *anurūpa* for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin priest.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: “*indra jyeṣṭhaṃ na ā bharā svā sahasramā śatam*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).
1. Not in the *acchāvāka*’s *śastra* at the third pressing (*na-savane*).
2. Any *ra*-sound. 3. *gha*: possessing various kinds of wealth; *śa*: like one possessing various kinds of wealth.

4. Kha-bha-2: Acquisition of the Sun and its manifestation for that purpose; Jña-na: Acquisition of the Sun and its manifestation for that purpose; Śa: Acquisition of the Sun for the sake of manifestation.

O Indra, bring to us the most excellent, the most powerful, and fulfilling glory, by which, O wondrous one with the thunderbolt in hand, you have filled both these worlds, O fair-cheeked one. Indra! Bring to us the most excellent, the most powerful, fulfilling glory, by which, O wondrous one with the thunderbolt in hand, you have filled both these two worlds, O fair-cheeked one.
O Indra, bring, fetch, and bestow upon us that most excellent, most praised, most powerful, and exceedingly strengthening food which fills [the world];

O wonderful one, worthy of admiration, wielder of the thunderbolt, with beautiful jaws—O Indra, bring that food by which you fill these two visible worlds, heaven and earth. This is the syntactical connection.

We invoke you, O King, the fierce one who subdues the peoples, among the gods for our protection. O Vasu, make all our adversities easy to overcome; make our enemies easy to conquer. tvām | ugram | arvase | carṣaṇīsaham | rājan | deveṣu | hūmahe | viśvā | su | naḥ | vidhurā | pibdanā | vaso iti | amitrān | susahān | kṛdhi || 6 ||

O King, O shining Indra among the gods, we invoke you for protection—to guard us—among the gods, you who are fierce with formidable strength, the subduer of *carṣaṇīs*, that is, the conqueror of the subjects who have become our enemies. You [overcome] all *pibdanās*; *pibdanās* are those which cry out while hidden and unmanifest.
[The word] *pṛtanādiḥ* [means] those who incite armies. Make them well, very thoroughly, disordered, distressed, and oppressed.
O *vaso*, O Indra who provides dwelling, [subdue] our enemies, our adversaries, easily, with ease.
Make them capable of being overcome; do so.

O Indra, bestow upon the Nāhuṣas strength and manly valor; or whatever splendor belongs to the five peoples, bring all those heroic powers hither to us. 7. O Indra, bestow upon the Nāhuṣas strength and manly valor; or whatever splendor belongs to the five peoples, bring all those heroic powers hither to us. 7.
O Indra, among the Nāhuṣas— *nahuṣa* being a name for humans—
among their offspring, the *kṛdhis*;
the particle *ā* is used in a conjunctive sense.
Whatever vigor, strength, manliness, and wealth exists,
or whatever belongs to the five peoples—
the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth are the five peoples— [all that is yours].
Bring, fetch, and bestow upon us all that which is their own inherent splendor, their shining food;
likewise, bring to us all the great and universal manly powers.
1. We invoke those called Kha, Jha, Na, Bha, and Ra.
2. Through Śa and Pauṣya, [we attain] the powers of Pauṣya.
3. Kha, Jha, Na, Bha, and Mābhara.

Or whatever power, O Maghavan, exists among the people of Tukṣu, or among the Druhyus, or whatever virility exists among the Pauras—that, bestow fully upon us. For the sake of conquering enemies in battles, [bestow it] when men must endure the struggle. Or whatever power, O Maghavan, exists among the people of Tukṣu, or among the Druhyus, or whatever virility exists among the Pauras—that, bestow fully upon us, O conqueror of men, for the sake of overcoming enemies in battles. O Maghavan, Indra, whatever strength exists among the people known as the Tukṣus, or whatever strength exists among the people known as the Druhyus, and whatever virility exists among the king known as the Paura—all that, grant completely to us, your worshippers. When? When a battle has commenced that must be endured by men, the warriors. For what purpose? To overcome—that is, to strike down—the enemies in the *pṛt* (battles). On the twenty-fourth day, in the *Niskevalya* litany, the *Sāmapragātha* of the Vairūpa chant, beginning with "Indra tridhātu," is to be recited. It is prescribed in the Sūtra: "‘Indra tridhātu śaraṇaṃ,’ ‘tvamindra pratittiṣu’" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.3).

O Indra, grant a three-layered, triple-protected, and auspicious refuge—a dwelling provided with shelter—to our generous patrons and to me, Bṛhaduktha. And drive away from them the piercing weapon of the enemy. O Indra, grant a three-layered (*tridhātu*), triple-protected (*trivarūtha*), and auspicious (*svastimat*) refuge (*śaraṇa*)—a dwelling (*chardiḥ*) provided with a roof (*chadiṣmat*)—characterized by such qualities, to our generous patrons (*maghavadbhyaḥ*). "Generous" (*maghavan*) refers to those who possess wealth in the form of oblations; grant it to them and to me, Bṛhaduktha. Furthermore, from among these [patrons], drive away (*yavaya*) the piercing (*dvidhu*) weapon—that is, the shining weapon hurled by the enemy.

Those who, with minds desiring cattle, have brought upon themselves the enemy and strike him down boldly—O bounteous Indra, lover of songs, at that very time, be the closest protector of our bodies. Those people who, with minds intent on obtaining cattle, have brought upon themselves the enemy—that is, the one who destroys or the adversary—and those who, being bold and daring, strike us down and severely harm us: O bounteous Indra, possessor of wealth, lover of songs, at this very moment, being the protector of our bodies, be our closest friend.
1. *jha-ta-nṛsahe* | 2. *kha-jha-na-bha-chardiṣmat* | 3. *ra-yāvaya* |

Like rivers rushing down a slope with swift motion, they have sped forth; if one calls out, the sound follows for a *krośa*. Like birds circling about meat, they are seized by the arms within the enclosure. Like rivers on a downward slope, with swift speed, they have gone forth; if one calls, the sound follows for a *krośa*. Like birds wheeling around for meat, they are held fast by the arms in the lap.
This [verse] is for the purpose of further illustrating the very meaning already stated:

"O Indra, if you should urge [them] on—just as rivers flowing swiftly toward the *pravaṇa*, that is, toward low-lying ground, flow quickly—that is, moving rapidly. When? [The answer follows: "When..."
*Krośanu*.
*Krośa* is a name for fear. When one's own cry of fear (*svani*) arises within oneself (*sve*), it is unobserved.
What kind of paths are these?
Those horses which are grasped—that is, bound by a girth—at the arms or at the armpits, turn back again and again when there is wealth in the form of cattle to be won;
just as birds such as hawks turn back again and again when meat is to be seized, so it is here.
The connection is as follows: when you, being thus terrified, cry out and urge [the enemy], then grant vomiting to our people.

Even though there is no specific mention of the *Ṛgveda* here, there is no contradiction whatsoever, as victory for the king's men is prayed for by virtue of his status as royal priest (*rājapurohita*).
The fourth hymn, consisting of thirty verses beginning with "svāduḥ," has Garga, the son of Bharadvāja, as its seer.

The verse beginning with "prastoka ikṣu" is a Triṣṭubh; "daśāśvān" is an Anuṣṭubh; "daśa rathān" is a Gāyatrī; "mahi rādhaḥ" consists of two Dvipadās of eleven syllables each; "yujāno haritā" is a Bṛhatī; "divaspṛthivyāḥ" is a Jagatī; and the remaining verses are Triṣṭubhs. For the first five verses, Soma is the deity.

In the first quarter-verse of the half-verse beginning with "agavyūti kṣetram," the gods are the deity; in the second [quarter], Ṛkṣid; in the fourth, Bṛhaspati; and in the [subsequent] fourth, Indra.

The four verses beginning with "prastokaḥ" are hymns of praise for the gift of King Sṛñjaya’s son; thus, they have him as their deity. This triplet beginning with "vanaspate vīḍvaḥ" has the chariot as its deity.
The triplet beginning with "upa śvāsaya" has the drum as its deity;
the half-verse beginning with "samaśvaparṇāḥ" belongs to Indra;
the remaining verses have Indra as their deity.

And thus it has been indexed: "In 'svāduḥ kila', there are thirty-one [verses] beginning with five; they have the Soma as their deity; the first half-verse has its deity indicated by its characteristic mark; 'prastoka' is a Triṣṭubh, a Nuṣṭubh, a Gāyatrī, and a Dvipadā; this is a praise of the gift of Prastoka, son of Saṃjaya; the two following triplets have the chariot and the drum as their deities; the other two half-verses are for Yujāna; a Bṛhatī, a Triṣṭubh, a Mahā-dvipadā, and a Jagatī for Heaven and Earth. In the Āgnimāruta [Śastra], the ten verses beginning with 'svāduḥ kila' are to be recited. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'svāduḥ kilāyam'—these four [are recited], and there is an invitation in the middle" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.20).

Truly, this is sweet; indeed, this is honeyed. Truly, this is sharp; indeed, this is full of flavor. And truly, no one at all can withstand his most powerful [Soma] in battles, like Indra. *svāduḥ* | *kila* | *ayam* | *madhumān* | *uta* | *ayam* | *tīvraḥ* | *kila* | *ayam* | *rasavān* | *uta* | *ayam* | *uto* | *nu* | *asya* | *paviṣṭham* | *indram* | *na* | *kaḥ* | *cana* | *sahate* | *āhaveṣu* || 1 ||
"This Soma, being purified, is indeed sweet—that is, worthy of being tasted.
Moreover, this Soma is full of honeyed sweetness.
Likewise, this Soma is indeed sharp—that is, it is truly keen in producing intoxication."
Furthermore, this Soma is both refreshing and substantial.
Through these four statements, the extreme sweetness of the Soma is established. Moreover, of this very Soma...
The genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
No one at all (*na kaścana*) overcomes or surpasses this Indra—who has drunk this most purifying Soma—in battles, that is, in conflicts.
The particle *nu* is a filler.

1. [The suffixes] *kha*, *jha*, *jña*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra* are applied by *preraya*; *śa* is applied by *prerayase*. 2. *kha*... the attachment to Rudra (*rudraprasaktiḥ*). 3. *ta*... it is established (*pratipādyate*). This [Soma], sweet here, was most intoxicating, at whose exhilaration Indra became drunk for the slaying of Vṛtra; he who shattered the many fortresses of Śambara and struck down nine and ninety walls. (2) This one is sweet; here, most intoxicating, it was; at whose [exhilaration] Indra, for the slaying of Vṛtra, became drunk; he who [shattered] the many fortresses of Śambara; he struck down nine and ninety walls. (2)
In this sacrifice, this Soma, having been tasted and drunk, has become most intoxicating, exceedingly exhilarating;
by the drinking of which Soma, Indra rejoiced and was gladdened at the slaying of Vṛtra, during the time of the destruction of Vṛtra;
that Soma which struck down the many, numerous fortresses—the citadels—of the Asura Śambara.

Likewise, he struck down (*vyahan*) those embodied ones—the Asuras who were smeared with poison and had accumulated [strength], or their cities, or their bodies; nine times nine and ninety-nine in number—this is connected with the first quarter-verse: "This Soma."

This one, when drunk by me, stirs up speech; this one has awakened the yearning wisdom. This wise one has measured out the firmaments, like a messenger of Yama, reaching every world without exception. 3. This one, when drunk by me, stirs up speech; this one has awakened the yearning wisdom. This wise one has measured out the firmaments, like a messenger of Yama, reaching every world without exception. 3.
Now, the Soma, having been drunk, raises up—that is, causes to emerge—my speech.
This very Soma has awakened—that is, causes to rise up—the longing and beloved *manīṣā*, the intellect;
he makes it manifest.
This is the form [of the verb] in the luṅ tense with the augment caṅ, derived from the causative (ṇyantā) of the root gṛ in the sense of "swallowing" (nigaraṇe).

Moreover, this wise and intelligent Soma measured out—that is, fashioned—the worlds beginning with heaven and earth, as established in the passage: "May Heaven and Earth, Night and Day, and the Waters and Plants protect us.

From the vast expanses belonging to Yama, he fashioned such worlds where not even the slightest being exists in a remote or distant place; rather, he fashioned those [worlds] wherein every kind of living creature indeed exists.

This is he who made the breadth of the earth and the height of heaven; this is he. This Soma has established the nectar in the three flowing rivers and the wide mid-air. 4. This is he; he who made the breadth of the earth and the height of heaven—this is he. This Soma has established the nectar in the three flowing rivers and the wide mid-air. 4.
Indeed, this Soma is he who made the wide extent, the vastness, and the expansion of the earth;
likewise, this Soma made the density, the compactness, and the firmness of heaven, the celestial world.
This Soma is indeed our protector.
Moreover, this Soma sustains—that is, holds fast—the essence of nectar within these three: the plants, the waters, and the cows that have flowed forth;
likewise, he sustains the vast and expansive mid-air.
Thus says another mantra: "O Soma, you generated for us all the plants, you generated the waters, and you generated the cows."
"You have stretched out the mid-air" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.91.22).
1. Because of the presentation of *gha* and *śa*. 2. Endowed with *kha*, *jha*, *bha*, *ra*, and *sa*; the greatness of *na*.

This one has found the sea of wondrous appearance at the forefront of the dawns that have white wealth. This great one, the bull accompanied by the Maruts, has propped up the sky with a mighty pillar. This one has found the sea of wondrous appearance, the bright wealth at the face of the dawns. This great one, the bull accompanied by the Maruts, has propped up the sky with a mighty pillar.

This Soma finds—that is, causes one to obtain—the ocean, which is of wondrous appearance (*citradṛśīka*), meaning of varied aspect, or rather, marvellously beautiful to behold; it is the solar light that impels all.
At what time?
At the forefront (*anīke*) of those dawns whose common dwelling (*sadha-sadana*) is the bright, pure atmosphere (*śukra*).
The meaning is "at the time of dawn.

Furthermore, this great and fully grown Soma, by means of a great and most massive support—the intermediate space situated between heaven and earth—propped up the sky, the world of heaven, holding it aloft.
The sense is that he made the intermediate space its foundation so that the sky would not fall.
Of what nature is Soma?
He is the bull (*vṛṣabha*), the progenitor of rain;
for it is through the oblation of Soma that rain is produced.
On account of his greatness, he is joined by the Maruts.

O hero, O Indra, you who possess valor, the slayer of Vṛtra—the obstructors and enemies—drink boldly, as is fitting, the Soma situated in the *droṇakalaśa* vessel during the battle, that is, the conflict for the sake of acquiring wealth (*vasu*). Furthermore, at the midday libation (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*), pour it forth;
fill your belly with Soma.
For the midday pressing belongs entirely to Indra;
moreover, you who are the abode of wealth—the source of riches—bestow and maintain wealth within us.

O Indra, look upon us like a leader; lead us forward toward greater prosperity. Be a good deliverer, carry us across; be our excellent guide and our noble leader. (7) O Indra, look upon us like a leader; lead us forward toward greater prosperity. Be a good deliverer, carry us across; be our excellent guide and our noble leader. (7)

O Indra, you, like a leader who goes before us, look out for us; that is to say, look upon us with special care, just as a guardian of the road, going himself at the front, watches the travelers following behind whom he must protect. Likewise, lead us forward toward wealth that is more excellent, more desirable, and most preeminent.
Likewise, be a good deliverer, one who carries us safely across from sufferings;
likewise, carry us, your praisers, across to the other side, making us pass beyond our enemies;
and be a source of excellent guidance for us.
Moreover, be a Vāmanīti— a leader (netṛ) of desirable (vāma) and praiseworthy riches;
or rather,
be one who procures the highest excellence for our sake.
1. Regarding the presence of the *gha* and *śa* [sounds]: in the animal sacrifice dedicated to Indra (*aindra-paśu*), "uruṃ naḥ" is the *yājyā* for the omentum (*vapā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "uruṃ no lokamanu neṣi vidvān pra sasāhiṣe puruhūta śatrūn" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
The *hotṛ* assistants: This [verse] is also to be muttered at the time of the *sadas-prasarpaṇa* (entering the *sadas*).
And it is stated in the *Sūtra*: "Muttering 'Lead us to a wide world, O Knower' (*uruṃ no lokamanu neṣi vidvān*), they enter" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 5.3).

On the second and subsequent days of the multi-day sacrificial sessions (*ahargaṇa*) belonging to the four classes of priests, this [verse] serves as the introductory hymn (*ārambhaṇīyā*) for the Acchāvāka at the midday pressing (*mādhyaṃdina-savana*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'May you, the Knower, lead us to a wide world'—this is the *kadrudra* [verse] to be recited at the commencement" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.4).

O Knower, lead us toward a wide world; [lead us] to all light, to fearlessness, and to well-being. O Indra, lofty and firm are your arms; may we take refuge in them, the great protectors. 8. Lead us toward a wide world, O Knower; [lead us] to all light, to fearlessness, and to well-being. O Indra, lofty and firm are your arms; may we take refuge in them, the great protectors. 8.
O Indra, you who are all-knowing, knowing [the way], lead us toward the wide, expansive world—the station situated in heaven.
Likewise, lead us toward that which is pleasant on every side, fearless, free from danger, and light; lead us toward well-being with security.
O Indra, we would approach as a refuge, for protection, your two arms—your hands—which belong to you, the ancient, the massive, the grown, the lofty, the beautiful, and the great.
Let us serve.

Place us, O Indra, upon the broadest chariot-seat; with your two most swift horses, O Lord of a hundred steeds, bring hither food—the most excellent of all nourishments. O Maghavan, let not the wealth of the enemy overcome us. 9. Place us, O Indra, upon the broadest chariot-seat; with your two most swift horses, O Lord of a hundred steeds, bring hither food—the most excellent of all nourishments. O Maghavan, let not the wealth of the enemy overcome us. 9.
O Indra, place us— hold us— upon your own most excellent, widest, and most expansive chariot-seat (*vandhura*). Furthermore,
O Lord of a hundred steeds, [place us] upon your two most excellent carriers.
The particle *ākāra* signifies conjunction (*samuccaye*). "Of the two horses" means: sustain us with your two horses.
Likewise, among the *iṣas*, that is, the foods, bring hither for our sake the most excellent (*varṣiṣṭhām*), the greatest food.
O Maghavan, O wealthy Śakra, let no other person whatsoever be the master of our wealth; do not let him take away, nor harm, our riches.

O Indra, be gracious to me; desire that I live; impel my prayer like the stream of a suppliant. Whatever I, seeking you, speak here, accept that; make me one who possesses the gods. 10 O Indra, be gracious to me; desire that I live; impel my prayer like the stream of a suppliant. Whatever I, seeking you, speak here, accept that; make me one who possesses the gods. 10

O Indra, be gracious, be merciful! Grant us happiness. Desire to give me the means of life and the medicinal herb that sustains life. Likewise, impel our *dhi*—our intellect; urge it toward the subject of praise or the subject of ritual action; sharpen it. Like the edge of an iron sword or similar weapon, which is exceedingly sharp, so too do you impel our intellect toward subtle objects. This is the meaning.
Furthermore, O Vāyu, whatever I speak now—whether it be correct or incorrect—desiring you as my very self, please accept and favor that;
and make me one who possesses the gods, endowed with the protecting deities.
For those desiring long life, "Trātāram" (The Savior) is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for Indra the Protector.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "Trātāram indram avitāram indram... mā te asyāṃ sahasāvan apariṣṭau" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.10).

I call upon Indra, the protector, Indra, the helper; at every invocation, I call upon the hero Indra, who is easily invoked. I implore Śakra, Indra who is invoked by many; may the bounteous Indra bestow well-being upon us.

I invoke Indra, the protector; Indra, the helper; the hero Indra, who is easily invoked in every battle. I call upon Śakra, Indra, who is invoked by many. May the bounteous Indra bestow well-being upon us. 11.
I invoke Indra, the protector who guards from enemies;
likewise, I invoke Indra, the fulfiller who satisfies with desires.

In every invocation, I invoke such an Indra: the one who is easily invoked, the hero, the powerful one capable in all undertakings, and the one invoked by many for the sake of protection. I call upon him.
Thus invoked, may that Indra, the possessor of wealth and lord of abundance, bestow— grant— to us, to us, well-being, which is non-destruction;
or rather, may he ordain it for us.
May Indra, the good protector, the possessor of wealth, with his aids, be well-disposed toward us—he who possesses all knowledge.
May he drive away our enemies and grant us fearlessness; may we be masters of heroic vigor.

May Indra—the good protector, possessed of his own strength, rich in blessings, and all-knowing—be present with his aids. May he drive away our enemies and grant us fearlessness. May we be masters of heroic power. 12.
May that Indra—*sutrāmā*, the excellent protector; *svavān*, possessed of wealth; and *sumṇākaḥ*, the one who provides great happiness—be present with his *vavobhiḥ*, his protections.
And may that Indra, the *viśvavedāḥ*, possessor of all wealth or all-knowing, drive away (*bādhatām*) the *dveṣaḥ*, the hating enemies, and make us *abhayam*, free from fear.
And by his grace, may we become masters of excellent vigor—that is, of beautiful heroism.
May we abide in the good-will of that one worthy of sacrifice, and also in his auspicious favor. May that Indra, the good protector and possessor of wealth, drive our enemies far away from us.

May we abide in the good-will of that one worthy of sacrifice, and in his auspicious favor. May that Indra, the excellent protector and possessor of noble horses, drive the haters far away from us. 13.
May we abide in the benevolent mind—that is, in the auspicious and gracious disposition—of the one worthy of sacrifice;
may we never be excluded from it.
Likewise, may we abide in his auspicious and kindly state of mind.
"He is not"—
this *ṛc* is prescribed for the occasion when those who have been initiated suffer from illness.

And it is stated in the *Khaṇḍa* section concerning the affliction of those who have been initiated (*dīkṣitānām upatāpe*): "The hymn beginning with *trātāram indram avitāram* [is used] for the son of Tarkṣya and others" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.9).
2. Variant readings *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*: "to restore by means of ease" (*sukhena dhātum*).
3. Variants *sa* and *bha*: the phrase "or else... may he ordain" (*yadvā ... vidadhātu*) is absent.
4. [The letters] *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra* have become the objects [of the rule].
[Maṇḍala 6, Anuvāka 4, Sūtra 47] The fourth Aṣṭaka, 163:
The meaning is that Indra should grant us a mind inclined toward favor and a state of well-being.

Sutrāmā—the excellent protector, possessed of his own power and wealth—may that Indra drive those who hate us far away from us; "ārāccit" means even from a distant place; he shall separate and keep hidden those haters.
"Antarhitām" is the same as "antarhitān": he shall cause them to be concealed. May he set them apart.
O Indra, as waves descend the steep slopes, so do our songs, our prayers, and our teams of horses hasten toward you.
Like a vast bounty, O wielder of the thunderbolt, you gather for yourself many cattle and Soma drops at the libations.

Toward you, O Indra, our prayers speed forth like waves down a slope from a mountain; they rush like harnessed teams. Like a vast gift, you gather for yourself many spoils, waters, and cattle, O wielder of the thunderbolt, along with the Soma drops.
O Indra, the hymns—the words consisting of *ukthas*—and the sacred prayers (*brahmāṇi*) in the form of *sāmans*, as well as the praises, flow toward you and reach you with devotion.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
like a wave born from water [reaching] downward slopes, that is, precipitous places.

Just as one quickly goes from a high place to a low-lying region, so it is here— the word *na* is used for conjunction. Vast, extensive, and abundant *rādhas*— that is, riches characterized by oblations— and many *purūṇi* (many) *savanāni*— that is, numerous pressed *soma* juices— approach you alone.

O Vajrin, you who possess the thunderbolt, you thoroughly mix together the waters known as *vasatīvarī*, the products of the cow such as curd and the like used for cooking, and the *indu*s, the Soma juices;
that is to say, having pressed the Soma with the *vasatīvarī* waters, you have refined it with the cooking ingredients such as milk-curd (*āśira*).

Who can satisfy him by praise? Who can worship him? For when the bountiful Lord, the Mighty One, always protects us, he strikes down one after another like two feet, making the first the last by his powers.

Who shall praise him? Who shall satisfy him? Who shall worship him? Since the bountiful one, the fierce one, always comes forth, striking down one after another like two feet, he makes the former the latter by his powers. 15.
Who is the praiser who might praise this Indra?
Who would be able to praise him? Or who indeed might satisfy him, gladden him?

And who could worship him? Who could offer oblations to him? Because this Maghavan, the wealthy Indra, always—indeed at all times—knows himself as truly fierce (*ugram*); he perceives and knows himself to be eternally fierce. For that reason, the sense is that no one is able to praise, please, or sacrifice to him.
He states further that he is beyond the scope of praise and such.

Because this Indra, by means of his own powers (*śacībhiḥ*)—that is, his own insights (*prajñābhiḥ*)—makes the one who was previously the first-born praiser and the other who is later-born mutually exchange their positions;
he makes that foremost praiser who was first-born the last, and he makes that last-born praiser the foremost.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
It is like striking one's feet;
just as a man striking his feet while walking on a path alternates the front foot with the back and the back foot with the front, so it is here.
For this reason also, the sense is that Indra is not an object of praise and the like.
By this first pentad of verses, Indra’s supreme independence is established.

1. [The manuscripts] śa, °vā, and °vagacchanti; 2. [the manuscripts] kha, jña, na, and ma read °rabhiputam; tara reads °rabhiputyaṃ tam; 3. [the manuscripts] kha, jña, sa, ta, na, and bha read °ryajate.

He is heard of as the Hero, subduing every fierce one, leading each one in turn by his thought; increasing in enmity, the King of both, Indra drives away the people and men. 16. He is heard of... the Hero... every fierce one... subduing... each one in turn... being led by his thought... increasing in enmity... of both... the King... he drives away... the people... Indra... men. 16.
This Indra, the hero, is heard of as being "heroic";
what is he doing?
Subduing every fierce and arrogant enemy.
*Damaḥ* means subduing; desiring to oppress, he *atinenīyamānaḥ*—
leading the singers forward by alternating one who was to be led first with another who was to be led later, and leading back again those who had already come.

Moreover, "Edhamānadviṭ" means the hater of those who are "edhamānānām," that is, of those who are increasing or rising up; he is the "śatā," meaning hundreds—that is, ten thousand or immeasurable—of both the celestial and the terrestrial.
For this reason, having assumed many bodies, he goes simultaneously to the sacrificers who possess the oblation (*haviṣmat*); such is the meaning.
Others think:
because it follows the meaning of the verbal root *id*, namely "supreme sovereignty," Indra is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).
And he, like space, is all-pervading and has the nature of eternal bliss.
That very [Self], being delimited in each body by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is designated as the "living soul" (*jīva*).

That same [Self] manifests as the world-soul (*jagadātman*)—consisting of ether and the rest—through its beginningless power of *māyā*; and the functions of the senses, which have the nature of seizing objects such as sound and are connected with that very [power], likewise manifest.
This indeed is the true nature of that Supreme Self, for the purpose of its manifestation.
This meaning is established by this [verse]:
"Form, form.
Form is that which is formed; it refers to the body and so forth.
The Supreme Self, whose nature is consciousness and who is omnipresent, became present in every body as a corresponding form— that is, as a reflected image— and thus attained them.
And that attained state of being a reflected image serves for the sake of the perception of this Supreme Self, which possesses a specific form at every moment.
And you, O Indra, the Supreme Lord, through your powers of illusion (*māyābhiḥ*),

reveal and make known [the way] to me in the search for cattle— the means of seeking cows. Thus, in this manner, for me, your singer and worshipper who experiences suffering, O Indra, reveal and point out the path.
On the second day, he drove away the one who was easy to see; he repelled the dark one, the offspring of Sarayu.
On that other day, the bull struck down the two Dāsas, Vṛcīna and Śambara, within the enclosure.

Day after day, Sudās drove away one half, the dark [host], while the bull Indra struck down the Dāsa Sarabha and the two who sought to clothe themselves [in armor]. He slew Vṛcīna and Śambara at Udavraja.

This Indra, the slayer, being born from his own seat—the region of the intermediate space—and manifesting himself in the form of the sun, drives away the nights, which are black in color and uniform in appearance, day after day. For what purpose?
To illuminate the other half, the subsequent portion of the day.
For the night is indeed one part of the day, which consists of day and night.
Moreover, Vṛṣabha—the showerer—is Indra; he [overcomes] the two Dāsas, the destroyers who obstruct the sacrificial rites.
*Vasta* refers to wealth that serves as the cause for dwelling.
Desiring them, he slew Varcin and Śambara—those two Asuras known by those names—at Udavraja.
Udavraja is a specific locality so called because "waters flow forth" (*udakāni vrajanti*) there;
it was at that place that he struck them down.
Now indeed, O Indra, from Divodāsa, the son of Tṛṣṭigva, you have bestowed ten chariot-poles and ten prize-winning horses as a gift;
we have received the wealth of Śambara as a reward.
A mere drop indeed of your bounty, O Indra—ten leather bags, ten horses, the wealth of Divodāsa Atithigva, and the Śambara treasure—we have received. 22.
In these first four [verses], there is a praise of the gift of King Prastoka, the son of Sṛñjaya.
He is known as Divodāsa, Atithigva, and Atya.
O Indra, [this is] for you, the bestower of wealth (*rādhasaḥ*), that is, for the one who gratifies, the singer of praises.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the dative.
To me, who was praising you, King Prastāṅka gave—bestowed immediately—ten *kośīs* of gold-filled treasure, ten in number, as well as ten *vājins*, that is, horses;
the particle *it* serves as a filler.
And we, from that Divodāsa, received—that is, accepted—this wealth (*vasu*) known as the Prastokas.
Of what sort was it?
It was the *rādhas* (gift) belonging to that very Prastoka, the son of Atithigva; it was the *śambara*, [the wealth] obtained from Śambara.
The meaning is that it was given by you after you had slain Śambara, as his own [property].
Ten horses, ten chests, ten garments, and ten vessels for food;
ten lumps of gold—these gifts from heaven I have received.
Ten horses, ten buckets, ten garments for wearing, two golden lumps—may I win these from Divodāsa. 23.

Ten horses numbering ten, ten treasure-chests filled with gold—*adhibhojana*; "bhojana" is a name for wealth, meaning those whose value is excessive wealth—and likewise ten garments numbering ten. (1. kha, na, bha: *pracodaya*; ta: *pradeya*. 2. jha, ta, na: *aparādham*; śa: *aharātmakam*).
3. From Divodāsa, I, Prastoka, brought away garments—clothes—and all ten lumps of gold, that is, lumps of refined gold; I obtained them, I shared in them.

Aśvatha gave ten chariots with side-horses and a hundred cows to Pāyu, the descendant of Atharvan. 24. Ten chariots; with side-horses; a hundred; cows; to the descendants of Atharvan; Aśvatha; to Pāyu; gave. 24.
"Ten" refers to those numbering ten. "Praṣṭimat" means having a four-legged support;
those that carry such [a load] are called *praṣṭi*, meaning horses.

Aśvatha, the possessor of horses, and Prastoka gave one hundred chariots yoked thereto and hundreds of cows to the Atharvans—that is, to the sages of the Atharva lineage—to Pāyu, the son of Bharadvāja, and to this one named Saṃjaya, our maternal uncle.

Sāṅkhya sacrificed for the Bharadvājas, who were bestowing great wealth beneficial to all people. 25. *mahi* | *rādhaḥ* | *viśvajanyam* | *dadānān* | *bharadvājān* | *sāṅkhyaḥ* | *abhi* | *ayaṣṭa* || 25 ||
Prastoka, the son of Sañjaya, honored us—the Bharadvājas, sons of Bharadvāja—who bestow and maintain great wealth beneficial to all people. Sāṅkhyas, the son of Sañjaya, has praised us.
The verse beginning with "O Lord of the Forest" (*vanaspate*) is prescribed for the mounting of the sacrificial post.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "With this verse, 'O Lord of the Forest, may you be firm-limbed,' [one mounts] other wooden objects as well" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.6.5).

O Lord of the Forest, may you be firm-limbed; be our friend, a furtherer, and a possessor of noble heroes. You are bound with cow-hides, O firm one; may your rider conquer all that is to be conquered. 26. O Lord of the Forest! Be firm-limbed! Indeed! May you become! Our friend! A furtherer! Possessing noble heroes! You are! Bound with cow-hides! O firm one! Your rider! May he conquer! All things to be conquered! 26.

O Vanaspati, you who are a modification of the Vanaspati (the Lord of the Forest), O chariot, may you have firm limbs—be one whose parts are solid—and be our friend; may you be such that we are your friends. Be a furtherer, a promoter of prosperity, and be endowed with excellent heroes—whether they be brave warriors or sons and other kinsmen.
Moreover, you are bound with cow-products—that is, you are firmly fastened with leathers;
as such, take courage and make us firm.
May your rider, who stands upon you, and the charioteer likewise, conquer the enemy forces that are to be conquered.

The vigor drawn forth from heaven and earth, the conquering strength brought from the lords of the forest, the essence of the waters, encompassed by the rays of light—worship with an oblation the chariot, the thunderbolt of Indra. 27 From heaven and from earth, vigor has been drawn forth; from the lords of the forest, conquering strength has been brought. The essence of the waters, encompassed on all sides by the rays of light—worship with an oblation the chariot, the thunderbolt of Indra. 27.
1. He worshipped *kha*; he worshipped *jha*, *na*, and *bha*; he worshipped *tara*; he worshipped *śa*. 2.

Those which were established by *ya*—that strength (*ojas*) which has arisen from heaven (*divaḥ*), from the sky, and from the earth (*pṛthivyāḥ*), and which has been extracted as its essence—that is his form.
Because the chariot is a modification of the *vanaspati* (the lord of the forest),
and since the *vanaspatis* are indeed the essence of the earth and have grown through well-connected shoots,
it is therefore appropriate that the chariot possesses the essence of both worlds.
The word *pari* restates the sense of the ablative case (*pañcamy-artha*). Furthermore, it means "from the *vanaspatis*, that is, from the trees. *Pari* is as explained previously.
"Unassailable" (ābhūtam) and "invincible" (āhatam); "saha" means strength or form; "ojmānam" is the impeller of waters, or alternatively, "ojmā" means speed.

O Adhvaryu, worship with an oblation such as the *puroḍāśa* cake this chariot, which is distinguished by such qualities: which is like the force of the waters, impetuous, and completely surrounded and enveloped on all sides by "cows"—that is, by products of the cow such as hides; [which is] a portion of Indra’s *vajra*. For it is heard in scripture: "Indra raised his *vajra* against Vṛtra; it became threefold: one-third became the *sphyā*, one-third the chariot, and one-third the sacrificial post. Worship that chariot characterized by these attributes with the oblation.

Surely this [verse] and the following one are to be understood from their indicative marks (*liṅga*) as the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* for the oblation dedicated to the deity of the chariot (*rathadevatya*).
"The thunderbolt of Indra, the vanguard of the Maruts, the offspring of Mitra, the navel of Varuṇa— O divine chariot, enjoying this our offering of oblations, do thou accept these gifts."

O God, you who are Indra’s thunderbolt, the vanguard of the Maruts, the offspring of Mitra, and the navel of Varuṇa—accepting this our offering of oblations, O divine chariot, take up the sacrificial gifts. 28.

The chariot which is Indra’s—the portion of the *vajra* described in the manner stated—and which is the *anīka*, the foremost leader, of the *maruts*, the host of gods so named; it is the *garbha*, existing like an embryo within, of *mitra*, the deity presiding over the day (for the chariot moves about during the day);
and it is the *nābhi*, standing in the place of the navel, of *varuṇa*, the deity presiding over sovereignty.

Just as the navel remains fixed in the center of the body, so too, O radiant *deva*, you who possess the aforementioned qualities, being stationed somewhere during the night, may you— rejoicing in and attending to this *havyadāti* of ours, that is, our sacrificial performance consisting of the offering of oblations— accept (*prati gṛbhāya*) our various *havyā*, our offerings. With the subsequent triplet of verses, the drum is to be touched in battle.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With the triplet beginning, 'Make the earth and the sky resound,' he should touch the drum" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 3.12.17).
"Make the earth and the sky resound; let the world scattered in many places take heed of you.
O drum, sounding together with Indra and the gods, drive away our enemies to a distance."

29 | Resound, O drum! Make the earth and the heaven resound! Let the world, established in many places, take heed of you. O drum, together with Indra and the gods, drive our enemies far away to the furthest distance. || 29 ||
O drum, cause the earth and also the heaven to resound with your own cry of victory;

that is to say, make such a sound that both worlds are filled by your noise. Furthermore, let the world—both the stationary and the moving, the two-fold collection of living beings—standing apart in its various places, perceive your sound in many ways.
Let him know:
O *dundubhi*, you—being in harmony with Indra and the other gods—drive away, that is, remove, our enemies even from a distance, to a place far, far beyond.

Regarding this, the *Nirukta* states: "The word *dundubhi* is an imitation of sound; or, it means 'the drum (*duma*) has been split (*bhinnah*'); or, it may derive from the root *dunbhyati*, which signifies the act of making a sound" (Nirukta 9.12), and so forth.

1. [The syllables] *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha* are excluded (*pari*). 2. [The drum] is established (*viṣṭhita*) in *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*; it is situated (*sthita*) in *ta*. 3. [It is] further removed (*dūratara*), exceedingly further removed (*atiśayena dūratara*) from *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *ya*. 4. Regarding the action of making sound (*śabdakarman*) of *jha*:
"O Drum, cry out! Bestow strength and vigor upon us! Roaring, drive away misfortunes. Snort away ill-fortune from here, O Drum! You are the fist of Indra; be firm!"*
Roar! Bestow strength and vigor upon us! O thundering drum, driving away misfortunes, blow away all calamities from here! You are the fist of Indra; be firm! 30.
O drum, roar aloud; make our enemies weep!
Bestow upon us—grant to us—both *balam*, the strength of the army, and *ojas*, bodily vigor. Place these within us. Give them to us.
Likewise, driving away the *duritāni*—the difficult paths—and destroying them yourself, roar forth; make a great sound. The verbal root is *stan*, meaning "to sound."
O drum (dundubhe), [drive away] the hosts of enemies whose "good fortune" (śunaḥ) consists of happiness that is actually a cause of misery for us; salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa!
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the eighth chapter begins.
In the fourth section (anuvāka) of the sixth maṇḍala, four hymns have been explained.
The fifth hymn, consisting of twenty-two verses beginning with "yajñayajñā," is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Śaṃyu, the son of Bṛhaspati.

Here the sequence is stated: "The *yajñayajñā* [verse] has two more [syllables]; the *śaṃyu*, the *tṛṇapāṇika*, the *pṛbhisūkta*, the two *pragāthas*, the *bṛhatī*, the *mahāsatoṛhatī*, the *mahābṛhatībṛhatī*, the two *pragāthas*—these are impure; the *kākubha* *pragātha*, the *purauṣṇih*, the *bṛhatī*, and the *atijagatī* belong to the Maruts; the other three have deities designated by their indicative marks; the *kākubha* *pragātha*, the *purauṣṇih*, and the *bṛhatī* belong to Pūṣan; the *bṛhatī*, the *mahābṛhatī*, the *yavamadhyā*, and the *anuṣṭubh* belong either to Dyāvāpṛthivī or to Pṛśni. Thus, "O *yajña-yajña* unto you" (*yajñayajñā vaḥ*) is this *bṛhatī*.
"The third [verse] consists of twelve [syllables]"—because its characteristics are present there;
the second is a *satobṛhatī*, because it possesses the characteristics stated as: "The *satobṛhatī* has odd-numbered feet consisting of *jagatī*s."
The third and fourth [verses] are bṛhatī and satobṛhatī; the fifth is bṛhatī;
the sixth is mahāsatobṛhatī—wherein the first foot consists of eight syllables and two feet consist of twelve syllables, that is a mahāsatobṛhatī;
the seventh is mahābṛhatī.
Four feet of eight syllables each and one of twelve syllables—that is the Mahābṛhatī.
The eighth [verse] is a Mahāsatobṛhatī.
Two Jagatī verses with eight syllables each—that is the Mahāsatobṛhatī.
The ninth is the Bṛhatī, the tenth is the Satobṛhatī;
these ten have Agni as their deity.
The eleventh is the Kakubh.

If the middle [foot] consists of twelve syllables and both [the first and third] feet consist of eight syllables each, that is a *kakubh*. If the twelfth [syllable] is present, it is a *sato-bṛhatī*; if the thirteenth [syllable] is present, it is a *purauṣṇih*. If the first foot is *jāgata* (twelve syllables) and the second and third are *gāyatra* (eight syllables), that is a *purauṣṇih*.
The fourteenth [verse] is *bṛhatī*, the fifteenth is *atijagatī* consisting of fifty-two syllables.
Five verses beginning with the eleventh have the Maruts as their deities.
For the three verses beginning with the thirteenth, the deities are Indra and others, as indicated by their respective characteristics (*liṅga*).
The sixteenth is a *kakubh*, the seventeenth a *sato-bṛhatī*, the eighteenth a *purauṣṇih*, and the nineteenth a *bṛhatī*.
Pūṣan is the deity of these four verses beginning with the sixteenth.
The twentieth is a *bṛhatī* and the twenty-first a *mahābṛhatī* of the *yavamadhyā* type.
The first two [verses] have eight syllables each, the third has twelve, and the fourth and fifth have eight; that is the *yavamadhyā* (barley-shaped) *mahābṛhatī*.
Because it is stated in the hymn "With the *pṛ* [verse]" (*pṛbhisūktam*) regarding the twenty-first [verse], the deity is *Pṛ*, the mother of the Maruts.
The twenty-second [verse] is an *anuṣṭubh*.
And that [verse] has either the Maruts as its deity or Heaven and Earth as its deity.
Its application to the *sūkta* is based on its indicative mark (*liṅga*).
"Ābhimāste" and "yajñayajñā vaḥ" constitute this *stotriya-pragātha*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two *pragāthas*, 'yajñayajñā vo agnaye' and 'devo vo draviṇodāḥ', are the *stotriya* and *anurūpa* [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.20).
With every sacrifice and with every song, we shall praise for your sake Agni, so that he may be skillful;
we shall celebrate the immortal Jātavedas, like a beloved friend.
With every sacrifice, with every song of praise, we shall extol Agni for your sake, so that he may grant us skill; we shall laud the immortal Jātavedas as a beloved friend. 1.

O you praisers, at every sacrifice—at all rituals—sing a hymn with every word of praise, with speech in the form of a song, for Agni who has grown strong; this is the ellipsis. The particle *ca* (and), which is displaced in order, should be understood as following the word *vaḥ* (you);
thus, "and you too should sing a hymn."
We too have praised that fire.
The repetition of the word *pra* in *prasamupòdaḥ* is for the purpose of filling the metrical foot (*pādapūraṇa*). The singular number is used by way of grammatical substitution (*vyatyaya*),
and the elision [of the case-ending] is Vedic (*chāndasa*).

Praise! Of what kind? Immortal (*amṛta*), free from death; *jātavedas*, the knower of all that is born, or one whose wisdom is born, or whose wealth is born; like a friend (*mitra*), as if having become a companion; dear. (Note:
Variants *kha-jha-na-bha-ya* read "unmanifested" (*avyākṛtāni*) therein; *jña-ta* read "manifested" (*vyākṛtāni*).)
2. *jña-ta-na-ra-śa* with the *anuṣṭubh* meter; *māharayaḥ* is the final [syllable]. 3. *kha-jha-ta-na-bha* as twelve, and *aṣṭaka* (eight); *jña-ta-ra* as twelve, and *ṇya-a-ra* as eight.
4. *kha-jha-ta-na-ma-ra-śaṃsiṣam*.
Favorable.
Alternatively,
by way of transposition, there is the substitution of *vas* for that which resides in its own [original] master;
and in *agnaye*, the dative case is used in the sense of the accusative.
The inclusion of the term "action" (*kriyā*) must also be made because the object (*karman*) functions as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).
The word *ca* is a particle (*nipāta*) meaning "and" (*ca*), used here in the sense of *cet*.
Furthermore, *dakṣase* is a form derived from the root *dakṣ*, which signifies the action of increasing (*vṛddhi*), with the causative sense (*ṇyartha*) internalized, in the present tense (*laṭ*).
Due to its connection with *ca*, there is a prohibition of the *nighāta* accent according to the rule "nipātairyadyadihanta... [Pāṇini 8.1.30].
The meaning here is as follows:
O singer, at every sacrifice you strengthen and increase this Agni with every song—that is, with every hymn of praise—and we too shall extol him who possesses qualities such as immortality.
We have indeed approached this protector of strength, Yama, for the offering of oblations;
may he be our helper in battles, and may he be the guardian and savior of our bodies.
O Son of Strength, it is indeed so: here I am; let us offer worship for the giving of oblations. May he be our helper in battles for booty, may he be the awakener and the protector of our bodies.
"Of *ūrjaḥ*":
[this refers to] food or strength. "The son (*napātam*), the offspring"—by the force of the context, this means "I have praised.
"Hina" is a combination of two particles used in the sense of "hi" (for/indeed).
Truly, this Agni is *asm-yuḥ*, desiring us;
and we, for the sake of giving oblations—that is, for the giver of the sacrificial offerings to the gods—to that Agni, let us *dāśema*, we shall present the oblations.
And may that Agni be our *avitā*, protector, and *vṛdhaḥ*, increaser, in *vājeṣu*, in battles.
And furthermore, may he be the protector and guardian of our bodies—that is, of our sons—and of our progeny.
For you, O bull, ageless and great, have shone forth with your flame from of old;
blaze brightly with your straight-moving luster, O consumer, and shine intensely with your beautiful splendors.
For you, O bull, ageless and great, shine forth at the beginning with your flame; glowing with your vigorous luster, O pure one, shine brightly with your beautiful rays. 3.

O Agni, you who are a bull (*vṛṣan*), a showerer of desires or a maker of rain, ageless (*ajara*) and free from decay, great (*mahat*) and preeminent in qualities—such as you are, you shine with your flame; indeed, you manifest yourself with special brilliance.

O pure (*śuci*) and blazing Agni, burning intensely (*śośucat*) with your unceasing (*arjasena*) radiance (*śocis*), shine forth well (*su dīndihi*) with your excellent lights (*sudītibhiḥ*); illuminate us thoroughly! Make us radiant!
O Agni, you strive toward the great gods; through sacrifice, through your power, and through your wondrous deeds, bring them hither for our protection. Bestow upon us strength and win it for us.
You sacrifice to the great gods; sacrifice to them in due order. By your wisdom and by your wondrous power, O Agni, turn them hither for our protection. Bestow strength upon us and win it for us. 4.
O Agni, you worship the great gods;
you honor them with oblations at the sacrifice of the sacrificers.
Therefore, in our sacrifice as well, worship those gods continuously and uninterruptedly, so that it may be constant.

For that purpose, by means of your *kratu*—that is, your wisdom—and also by your *damsanā*, your wondrous deed, bring all those gods hitherward toward us (*arvācaḥ*) for our protection (*avase*). The particle *sīm* is used here for the sake of emphasis. Make them all turn toward us for our defense.
Likewise, grant us *vājān*— sacrifices characterized by oblations—
and bestow them upon those gods.
Moreover, you too—enjoy them;
partake of the oblations offered to you.
Him whom the waters, the stones, and the forests nourish as the embryo of Eternal Order—
he who is produced by men with force, born upon the high ridge of the earth.
Him whom the waters, the stones, and the forests nourish as the embryo of Cosmic Order (Ṛta)—he who, produced by force, is born from men upon the high ridge of the earth. 5.

The waters known as *vasatīvarī*, the pressing-stones (*adrayaḥ*), and the woods (*vanā*)—that is, the pieces of wood—all these fill (*piprati*) Agni, who dwells within them like an embryo (*garbham*) of the *ṛta* (the sacrifice or the water).
Or alternatively:

the oceanic waters, the clouds (*adrayaḥ*), and the forests (*vanāni*) fill Agni—who exists in the form of the submarine fire (*vāḍava*), lightning (*vaidyuta*), and forest-fire (*dāva*)—as the embryo of the *ṛta*.

And that Agni who, having been churned by men—the leaders and officiating priests—with force (sahasā), is born, manifesting from above the earth (pṛthivyā adhi) upon the high and excellent ridge (sānavi)—that is, in the place of sacrifice (devayajana)—you, being such, may you win [the prize]; this is the syntactical connection.
Or rather, he connects it with the verse beginning, "He who has filled" (yaḥ paprau).
He who has filled both worlds with his radiance hastens through the sky with smoke;
the ruddy bull has become visible through the darkness in the nights, even in the dark ones.

He who has filled both worlds with his radiance, he hastens through the sky with smoke. He has become visible through the darkness in the nights—reddish-brown among the dark ones, the ruddy bull; the dark ones, the ruddy bull. 6.

That Agni who, by his radiance—that is, his light—fills both *rodasī*, heaven and earth, he courses through the sky, that is, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), by means of smoke. For smoke, having been transformed into the form of clouds, moves through the intermediate space;
yet, because of the intended non-difference between cause and effect, that movement is figuratively attributed to the fire itself.

Moreover, this Agni—red, shining, a bull, and a showerer of desires—possessing such qualities, has been seen, or is seen on all sides, having dispelled the darkness in the dark-colored, black nights; for "ūrmyā" is a name for night. He is visible throughout the nights.
The dark ones—meaning those of a dark color—and the nights he stands upon;
the repetition of "the ruddy bull" is for the sake of showing respect or for the purpose of completing the metrical foot.

O Agni, upon the sacrificial grass with your flames, O God, with your bright radiance, being kindled by Bharadvāja, O youngest one, shine forth richly, O pure one; shine forth with splendor, O purifier.

O Agni, with your flames upon the sacrificial grass, O God, with your bright radiance, being kindled in the dwelling of Bharadvāja, O most youthful one, shine upon us, O radiant one; shine with wealth, O purifier, shine with splendor! 7.
1. When there is a desire to express *kha-jha-bha*, it is *bahumatamamā*; when there is a desire to express *ya*, it is *tadmanamamā*.

O *deva*—endowed with qualities such as generosity—O *yaviṣṭha*—most youthful—O *śuka*—radiant—O *agne*—Agni! Being kindled (*samidhānaḥ*) by the fuel-stick (*samidhā*) in the lineage of Bharadvāja (*bharadvāje*), which is our own, shine (*dīdihi*) for us (*naḥ*) so that it may be *revat*—rich in wealth—with your *śuklena śociṣā*—pure, bright splendor and luster (*tejasā*), accompanied by *bṛhadbhir arcibhiḥ*—great rays of light. Shine forth!
Likewise, O purifier, O Agni, shine and blaze forth so that you are endowed with splendor—that is, with radiance.
O Agni, you are the lord of the people, the master of the human tribes.
O youngest one, protect the kindler from violence for a hundred winters with a hundred fortresses; [protect] those who give to the singers for a hundred winters.

O Agni, you are the lord of the people, the master of the dwellings of men. O most youthful one, protect us from distress with a hundred forts; grant a hundred winters to those who kindle you, and to those who offer praise and give gifts. 8.

O Agni, you are the *gṛhapati*, the master of the house, of all the *viśas*—of all the human communities that have come into being through the desire of Manu. O most youthful (*yaviṣṭha*) Agni, therefore protect me for a hundred winters—a hundred years—with a hundredfold fortresses (*pūrbhiḥ*), from distress, from evil, or from the enemy who strikes us down. Protect me with a hundred means of preservation.
And those who bestow wealth upon your praisers—protect them as well, O you who grant it to the one who performs your kindling.
O Vasu, you who are wondrous, impel our gifts with your aid;
O Agni, you are the charioteer of this wealth; find a firm footing for us and for our offspring.
O Vasu, you who are wondrous, impel toward us riches with your aid; O Agni, you are the charioteer of this wealth, bestowing it threefold; grant a firm footing to our offspring. 9.
O *vaso*, O Agni, you who are the dweller, you who are *citras*, the wonderful and worthy of being seen—do you, together with *ūti*, protection, impel and send forth *rādhas*, riches, unto us.
You are the *rathī*, the swift leader, of this *rāyas*, wealth, which is visible everywhere in the world;
for that reason, impel riches toward us. This is the meaning.
Moreover, for our sake (naḥ), for our offspring (tuce)— this is a name for progeny—
for the son and others who are the cause of our non-falling, do thou quickly (tu) find (vidāḥ) and grant (lambhaya) a firm footing (gādham).
Protect our children and grandchildren with your unerring and countless fortresses; O Agni, ward off from us the divine wrath and carry away our godless sins.
Protect our children and descendants with your forts; O Agni, with your unfailing and tireless [guards], ward off from us the divine wrath and the non-divine hostilities. 10.

1. By the illumination of *jha*: at the *vājapeya* sacrifice, the *pragātha* "tvaṃ naścitra" is the *stotriya*. Furthermore, it is stated in the Sūtra (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.9): "The *stotriya* and *anurūpa* for the *agniṣṭoma-sāman* are [the verses] containing the word 'citra', namely 'stuvīraṃ' and 'tvaṃ naścitra ūtyāme vivasvadupasaḥ'. This is additional [information].
2. [The mantra] beginning with *kha-bha-ra-dṛśyamānasya*: "O Agni, you, with those [powers] that are *adabdhaiḥ* (unassailable, i.e., not harmed by anyone) and *aprayutsvabhiḥ* (not separated);
here the root *yu* has the sense of being separate."
With these non-distinct, united, and protective limbs, protect our offspring—our sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons.
O divine one, separate from us all anger related to the gods;
and separate from us all human-related angers and acts of violence.
O friends, drive forth the cow that yields nectar; bestow upon us human splendor;
release it so that it does not shrink away.
O friends, drive hither the cow that yields milk at all times; bestow upon us human splendor that never falters.
"O friends, of common renown, O Adhvaryus, drive toward—the cow that yields the *sabardugha* milk;
*saba* is a name for milk.
Drive toward the cow who milks the milk that is the cause of immortality."
By what means?
By a most recent, newer, and even more recent "speech"—that is, by a word in the form of a statement.
Immediately after that, [he saw her] "not quivering."
Its function is to cause throbbing and increase.
"Drive that cow near"—
make her approach, made to approach by her calf.
Because she is Marudevatā, [she is] to be milked for the sake of the sacrifice of the Maruts—this is the ellipsis.

Alternatively, the mother of the Maruts, known as Pṛśni, is the cow who is the intermediate Vāc. O friends, the singers: approach with a most recent hymn of praise (narvyasā vacasā) the cow Pṛśni, the "all-yielding" one (sabardughām), who milks forth the milk that is the cause of the birth of the Maruts. Approach her.
Create that which does not quiver and cannot be obstructed;
release it from bondage; let it go free.
Such is this great cow, the mother of the Maruts; what more need be said regarding their majesty? Thus ends the praise of the Maruts.
She who has bestowed immortal glory upon the self-luminous host of Maruts;
she who is in the favor of the swift Maruts, she who moves with graciousness.
She who has bestowed immortal glory upon the Marut host, self-luminous; she who dwells in the favor of the swift Maruts, she who comes hither with gracious blessings. 12.

The cow who is the cause of immortality and freedom from death has yielded for the Marut-host—that is, she has milked for the assembly of the Maruts—fame, which is food characterized by milk. For what kind of host? For one who is habitually powerful and whose own splendor is self-dependent.
And she who abides in the favor—that is, the happiness—of the swift-acting Maruts;

and she who goes with the *sumnaiḥ* (means of happiness), namely with the *evayāvarī* (swift-moving) vehicles or with the mid-region winds; and she who, for the sake of the happiness of others, moves along with the waters of rain—to that cow, bring her near. The connection is as before. Here too, as previously, the praise of the Maruts is to be understood.
For Bharadvāja, you have twice bestowed the steed,
the all-sustaining cow, and nourishment that provides for all.
For Bharadvāja, you have twice milked forth the cow who yields all desires, and food that provides nourishment for all. 13.
O Maruts, for Bṛhaduktha, the son of Bharadvāja, our donor, you have doubly bestowed a double gift.
What is that double gift? A cow and a milch-cow, and nourishment and food.
What kind of cow? "The milker of all," that is, the one who yields everything that is pervasive and abundant. What kind of food?
"Viśvabhojasam" means sufficient for the enjoyment of all.
1. *kha-madhyajana* | 2. *jha-ta-adhukṣata* | 3. *kha-bha-madhyasthānai* | 4. *kha-bha-yāti*; *jha-śa-yānti* | 5. *kha-bha-sahāgacchati*; *jha-śa-sahāgacchanti* | 6. *śa-dhṛkṣata datta*.
I praise for my purpose Viṣṇu, who is like Indra of excellent wisdom, like Varuṇa possessed of magic power, like Aryaman the delightful one, and who possesses abundant wealth.

I praise him for you—him who is like Indra of excellent wisdom, like Varuṇa the possessor of wondrous power, like Aryaman the delightful one, most bountiful, and like Viṣṇu for the sake of attaining my goal. 14.
O Marut host, such as you are, I praise you; I extol you for the sake of your command—
that is,
for the bestowing and granting of riches.

Of what sort are you? Like Indra, you are of good wisdom (*sukratu*), that is, of excellent deeds; like Varuṇa, you are possessed of *māyā*, that is, full of creative power and wisdom; like Aryaman, you are delightful, that is, worthy of praise; and like Viṣṇu, you possess excellent nourishment, that is, abundant wealth.
When, however, the deities are indicated by their characteristic marks (*liṅga*), then the two words *iva* (like) should be understood in the sense of *ca* (and).

Like the brilliant host of the Maruts, roaring aloud, bring together Pūṣan, the unassailable one, so that he may gather hundreds and thousands for the people. Reveal the hidden treasures; do not let the ill-spoken words destroy the lord of the forest. Let not even the sun’s rays seize the neck of the bird. Do not uproot the lord of the forest; let the ill-spoken words perish. And let not the sun’s rays seize the neck of the bird. mā | kākambiram | ut | vṛhaḥ | vanaspatim | aśastīḥ | vi | hi | nīnaśaḥ | mā | uta | sūraḥ | ahaḥ | iti | eva | cana | grīvāḥ | ā | dadhate | veḥ | iti veḥ || 17 ||
The seer, representing himself along with his sons and grandsons as a tree (*vanaspati*) that is the support for many ripe fruits, invokes a blessing upon its imitation:
"O Pūṣan, do not carry away—do not uproot—the *kākaṃbīra* tree, the lord of crows; do not harm it."
The meaning is: "Do not harm me, who am accompanied by sons, grandsons, and others who have become my friends, and who am attended by many others.
The word *vhi* (hi) has the sense of "indeed" (*arthe*).

"O Vaśastī"—those who are to be censured (*aśaṃsanīyā*), or rather, those who proclaim undesirable suffering (*aśaṃsanīyasya duḥkhasya kīrtayitrīḥ*), being enemies; "vi vīnaśaḥ"—destroy them utterly (*vināśaya*).
Furthermore, O hero (*vsūra*), impeller (*preraka*), enemy (*śatru*), and protector (*veva*): O *mā*, carry us; do not abandon us (*mā hāḥ*).
Because of this connection with *evam* and because the verb is accented, the word *yathā*, though unexpressed, is supplied in the sentence.
[O] necks (*grīvāḥ*).
They are called *grīvā* because they swallow, they cause [one] to stay within, and they bind; that is, they are bonds.

Just as hunters (*vyādha*) set down on the ground bonds in the form of nets for the sake of seizing birds (*vvi*), and by means of those laid out they seize the birds, so too the meaning is: "May the enemy not seize us through such means of bondage."
Like a bowl, may your mouth be easy to fill; may it be easy to fill for you who are without flaw, who possess abundance, and who are completely full, possessing abundance. 18.
O Pūṣan, may your friendship— your state of being a friend— which is desirable, free from obstacles, and which exists with constant uniformity toward our object— be ours forever.
Just as the friendship offered by Datri is uninterrupted, so too [may yours be].
Of what sort is it?
It is of that which is "vacchidrasya," meaning without gaps; "saṃśliṣṭasya," meaning well-joined; "dadhanvataḥ," meaning possessing curds; "supūrṇasya," meaning well-filled with curds.
The repetition of "dadhanvataḥ" is for the purpose of emphasizing the abundance of the curds.
Such is he: he is always present upon the chariot of Pūṣan.

Like him, may we too become your friends—thus the seer hopes. For you are indeed before mortals as a benefactor, and with the gods through your splendor. O Pūṣan, you who protect us in battles, come now as you did of old. For you are indeed before mortals as a benefactor, and with the gods through your splendor. O Pūṣan, you who protect us in battles, come now as you did of old. (19)
O Pūṣan, you who stand far beyond— beyond mortals, beyond men—
you are equal in glory and prosperity with all the gods.
Therefore, look upon us with a gracious eye, favoring us in battles.

O Vyatha, just as you have surely protected the men of former times in the manner [described], so now protect us here. 1. kha-jha-na-bha-śa: observing; 2. jha-jha-ta-na-ya-ra-śa: do not; 3. jha: "yathā" is in the subsequent sentence; ta: "yathā" is in the other sentence; 4. gha: by means of afflictions; 5. gha-śa: free from affliction; 6. kha-bha: with a mind intent on favoring; 7. kha-jha-bha-ra: the word "vilokaya" (behold) is absent; 8. śa: humans.

O Maruts, shakers of all, may the guidance of the desirable one be desirable; may it be true and pleasant, whether that of a god or of a mortal who performs sacrifice, O you who are swift to worship. 20. *Vāmī*, *vāmasya*, *dhūtayaḥ*, *praṇītiḥ*, *astu*, *sūnṛtā*, *devasya*, *vā*, *marutaḥ*, *martyasya*, *vā*, *ījānasya*, *prayajyavaḥ*. 20.

O Maruts, you who are shakers (*dhūtayaḥ*), tremblers, and those most worthy of sacrifice (*prayajyavaḥ*), let that *sūnṛtā*—your speech consisting of pleasant truth, belonging to the mid-region—be our guide.
Let it be the leader of riches for our sake.

Whether of a god or of a mortal man, of either kind of person who has sacrificed and offered oblations, that excellent (*vāmī*) and praiseworthy speech which is the leader (*praṇītiḥ*) of desirable (*vāmasya*) wealth—that is *sūnṛtā*; such is the syntactical connection.
May there be guidance for our sake.

Even instantly, whose movement goes around the sky like the divine Sūrya; the Maruts have assumed a brilliant power, a name worthy of sacrifice, a Vṛtra-slaying power, the supreme Vṛtra-slaying power. 21. Even instantly; whose; movement; around; the sky; like; the god; goes; Sūrya; brilliant; power; they have assumed; a name; worthy of sacrifice; the Maruts; Vṛtra-slaying; power; the greatest; Vṛtra-slaying; power. 21.

And the activity of that host of Maruts, even as soon as it is performed, immediately goes around the sky; it moves throughout the celestial atmosphere like the shining god Sūrya. Such hosts of Maruts have assumed and maintained a brilliant, blazing power (*śavas*)—a name that subdues enemies—which is worthy of sacrifice (*yajñiya*).
And that power, the slayer of Vṛtra, becomes the destroyer of the Asura Vṛtra and others.
Furthermore, that Vṛtra-slaying power is the most excellent, being the most highly praised of all.

Once indeed the sky was born; once the earth was born. Once the milk of the speckled cow was milked; that fluid—no other is born after it. 22. Once, indeed, the sky was born; once the earth was born. The milk of the speckled one was milked once; that fluid—no other is born after it. 22.
Once indeed, once only, the sky was born; it arose but once.
It remains as something whose origin is known but once;
for when that sky has perished, no other sky similar to it is born again.
And the earth was born all at once;
and the milk of the speckled cow, the mother of the Maruts, was milked but once—only a single time—from which [the Maruts] were born from that great milk.
"The Maruts were indeed born from the milk of the speckled cow," so says the Taittirīya [Saṃhitā 2.2.11.4].
Just as heaven and earth were produced only once, so too Pṛśni generated the Maruts with milk that was milked only once;
beyond that, no other entity of a similar nature is subsequently born.

1. Kha: "Those very ones possess such qualities"; Śa: "Such is the one whose nature consists of the qualities of the wind. 2. Kha: "And this"; Bha: "Furthermore, in this"; Ya: "The sky is not born from this. Ṛgveda 3.12:

The sixth hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "I praise the people" (*stuṣe janam*), is the seerly work (*ārṣa*) of Bhāradvāja Ṛjiṣvan. It is addressed to the Viśvedevas (*vaiśvadeva*). The final verse is a *śakvarī* meter with fifty-six syllables; the remaining verses are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter.
And thus it has been introduced: "I praise [the hymn] with five verses less; Ṛjiṣvan indeed [performs] the Vaiśvadeva ending in Śakvarī.
In the expanded ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*), this Vaiśvadeva [hymn] contains the *nivid* on the fifth day.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'Ṛbhu, Vibhvan, [and Vāja]—I praise the people' is the Vaiśvadeva" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.8).
The first [verse] is to be recited during the Mahānāmnī vow.
I praise the people of noble vows with human songs, Mitra and Varuṇa, who grant favor.
May they come hither; may they listen here—those of good dominion, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni.

I praise the people of noble vows with human songs—Mitra and Varuṇa, who seek our welfare. May they come hither; may they listen here. Those of excellent sovereignty—Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni—[may they hear us]. 1.
"‘The person of good vows, the one of good deeds,’ [refers to] the divine person, the host of gods— this is not a praise of day and night.
‘The two daughters of the shining Aruṣa’ refers to the two daughters of the Sun."
For it is by the sun that the division of day and night is made;

therefore, because they are dependent upon him and because he is free from blemish, they are called "his two daughters. They are "of different forms," meaning they possess diverse forms due to being white and black respectively.
One [of these two] is the night; it is adorned—meaning it is joined together—by the stars (*stṛbhiḥ*), for the root *piś* means "to form parts.
The other, the daughter of the Sun (*sūraḥ*), is adorned—meaning she is joined together—by the sun.
And the meaning is that they both become adorned by the constellations and by the sun. "Mutually hastening" (mithasturā) means they afflict one another;
day is turned back by night, and night by day—this is their mutual affliction.
Therefore, as they move about— that is, wandering in various ways and separately— and as they purify everything,
while Day and Night are being praised by us in this manner, may they reach— that is, pervade— the *śrutam*, that which is to be heard, and the *manma*, the thought or hymn composed by us.

Toward Vāyu let our lofty hymn go forth—a hymn that fills the chariot, possessing vast wealth and containing all boons—to him who is the lord of the teams of horses, whose path is radiant, the sage who desires the sage, O you who are most worthy of sacrifice. 4. toward Vāyu; let our; lofty; hymn; [go] toward him who possesses vast wealth; who contains all boons; who fills the chariot; whose path is radiant; the lord of the teams of horses; the sage; [desiring] the sage; you seek to win over; O you who are most worthy of sacrifice. 4.
May our vast and great hymn of praise proceed forth toward Vāyu.
Due to the hearing of the prefix (*upasarga*), the action of conjunction (*yoga*) is to be supplied.
Of what kind [is] the wind? *Bṛhadrayim*: possessing great wealth; *viśvavāram*: desirable by all, worthy of being honored by all; *rathaprām*: the filler, the one who fills his own chariot.
Or alternatively:
[he is] the one who fills the chariot of the praisers with wealth. Now follows the direct praise.

O Vāyu, worthy of being sacrificed to preeminently (*prayajya*), shining brilliantly (*dyudyan*) with light, you who are approaching— driving toward and reaching— the *niyuts*, the mares yoked to your own chariot; or rather,
the root *pat* signifies the act of moving swiftly.
O Lord of those mares, you who are a *kavi*—one whose vision has transcended;
being such, you honor with wealth the *kavi*, the wise singer who desires to worship you.

May that chariot of the Aśvins, which is resplendent and yoked by thought, manifest its beauty to me—that chariot wherewith, O Nāsatyas, O Heroes, you come to our aid, providing protection for our offspring and for ourselves. 5. That [chariot]. To me. Beauty. May it manifest. Of the two Aśvins. Which. Chariot. Resplendent. Yoked by mind. Wherewith. O Heroes. O Nāsatyas. To go. Protection. Which. For offspring. And for ourselves. 5.
That chariot belonging to the Aśvins—may that chariot cover my *vapuḥ*, my body;
may it cover it with splendor.
That chariot which is *virukmān*, shining, especially radiant, and which becomes yoked by the mind alone, through the mere operation of the mind, being harnessed with horses.

O *narā*, leaders; O *nāsatyā*, you whose nature is truth, leaders of truth, or those born from the nose—the two Aśvins—with whatever chariot you go (*yāthaḥ*) to the house of the worshiper for the sake of the son (*tanayāya*), for yourselves (*ātmane*), and for the sake of the singer (*tasmin stotre*), in order to fulfill desires (*iṣadhyai*); that chariot is [the subject] connected with the preceding verse.
Regarding the animal sacrifice dedicated to the deities beginning with Vāyu, the *yājyā* for the oblation is as follows: "pra vāyurmiāta...
sritaṃ ca-rāye nu yaṃ jagat rodasī me pra vāyumacchā bṛhatī manīṣā" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8). This is the meaning. [Note 1: It is not joined with the letters *jña*, *ta*, *na*, *ra*, and *sa*.
O Parjanya and Vāta, bulls of the earth, quicken the watery soil-mounds;
O seers who hear the truth, by whose songs you sustain the world, bring the world into being!

O Parjanya and Vāta, you two bulls, quicken the watery soil-mounds of the earth! O seers who hear the truth, by whose songs of praise you bring the world of the moving and the stationary into being, make that world prosper! 6.
O Parjanya and Vāta, you two bulls, the makers of rain for the earth—
[note that *antarikṣa* is a name for the intermediate space]—
from the intermediate space, quicken and impel the watery *purīṣas*, the filling waters, which are to be attained.
The latter half-verse concerns the Maruts:

O Maruts, you who are seers (*kavayaḥ*) and hearers of the truth—that is, listeners to the true hymn of praise—when you are praised by the songs (*gīrbhiḥ*) of that singer, then for that singer you must bring together the entire world (*jagat*), comprising all living beings, both moving and stationary; bring it forth in his presence, O sustainers of the world!

The singular number is used to express the intention of the group (*gaṇābhiprāya*). It should be construed as: "O host of Maruts, you who establish the world consisting of the stationary and the moving."
In the Anvārambhaṇīyā [offering], this verse beginning with “pāvīravī” is the invitatory formula (yājyā) for the oblation to Sarasvatī.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “pāvīravī kanyā citrāyuḥ pīpivāṃsaṃ sarasvataḥ” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.8).
It is also the invitatory formula for the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) in the eleven-animal sacrifice dedicated to Sarasvatī.
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The maiden Pāvīrvī of variegated life; that breast of yours which is inexhaustible and which is blissful" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.7).
This [verse] is also used in the Āgnimāruta Śastra.
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "'I invoke Rākā'—these two [verses], and 'the maiden Pāvīrvī of variegated life'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.20).
May Sarasvatī, the daughter of heaven, of varied life-span, the wife of heroes, bestow wisdom upon us.
May she, being well-pleased, grant to the singer a flawless refuge and invincible protection that cannot be overcome by enemies.

The daughter of the lightning, Sarasvatī, whose life is wondrous, the wife of the hero, shall establish our prayer. May she, in harmony with her companions, grant the singer an unassailable refuge—a flawless shelter. 7.
The maiden is purifying, beautiful, and of wondrous life—meaning she possesses wonderful movement or wonderful wisdom;
she is the wife of a hero, that is, one whose husband is Prajāpati, the Hero.
Or alternatively:
The protectress of heroes—
such as this Sarasvatī, may she sustain (dhāt) our intellect (*dhiyam*), that is, our ritual action called sacrifice;
or, may she grant it.
For an object signified by a word is indeed put into practice.
Moreover, [he is] "sajoṣāḥ," meaning rejoicing together with the village goddesses who are the wives of the gods;
or alternatively:
The *grāḥ* are the meters such as the *gāyatrī* and others, according to the Vedic scripture: "The meters are indeed the *grāḥ*" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.1.7.2).

May she, being pleased with them, grant me—while they chant and praise—a refuge that is flawless, free from defects, unassailable by enemies and by cold, wind, and other elements, a home (*gṛha*), and a source of happiness (*śarma*). May she bestow this upon me.
In the case of the animal sacrifice for the eleven deities dedicated to Pūṣan, "pathaspathaḥ" is the invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for the oblation.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "With devotion [one offers] to the protector of every path; 'O Bṛhaspati, that which is the furthest distance'—these two [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.7).
1. According to the intention of the *kha-jha-na-bha-ya* group, there is one [syllable].
2. The establisher of the world (*jagat*) from *gha-śa-ja*:
"The lord of the path, of every path, through speech, by desire, he has kindled the sun."
