May he, Pūṣan, bestow upon us gifts of nourishment tipped with moonlight; may he bring each and every prayer to fulfillment.
From every path, he who was made by desire has reached the Lord of the Path with eloquent speech; may he grant us riches preceded by splendor, and may Pūṣan further each of our prayers. 8.
May the singer, brought under control by his desire for the desired fruit, reach through his eloquent hymn the protector and sovereign lord of every path,
the adorable Pūṣan. And may that Pūṣan grant us the bright-pointed cows, the obstructors of heat.
"Candram" is a name for gold;
[the word] "rāsat" means "may he give," [referring to one] whose foremost part is gold, or who has golden horns.
The root is *rā* in the sense of "giving";
this is the form in the *leṭ* [subjunctive] mood.
In that manner, may that Pūṣan accomplish and bring to fulfillment every single one of our actions, thought by thought.
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to the Aṣṭrā, "the first sharer" is the invitatory verse for the oblation.
And it is prescribed: "The hymn beginning with 'The first sharer, glorious, bestower of vigor, O Soma and Pūṣan, progenitors of riches' [is used]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).

May the radiant Hotṛ worship Tvaṣṭṛ, who is worthy of sacrifice, easy to invoke, the first sharer of glory, the bestower of vigor, the god with beautiful hands, the one of auspicious birth, the sage, and the protector of the people.

May the Hotṛ worship the first-born, glorious, bestower of vitality, fair-handed god, the well-wombed, the impetuous Tvaṣṭṛ, the worthy of sacrifice among those who prosper, the radiant Agni, who is easily invoked. 9.
The first sharer, who distributes [wealth] to living beings at the very time of their birth—according to the Vedic revelation:
"As long as Tvaṣṭṛ fashions the forms of the emitted seed, so long indeed is it born there" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.9.1).

[We praise him] the glorious, the possessor of fame, the bestower and sustainer of *vayas*—that is, food characterized by the oblation—or rather, the giver of food to his worshippers, the one with beautiful hands.
The region above the wrist of the hand is the *pāṇi*.
The Lord possesses beautiful hands (*śobhanapāṇika*), being endowed with virtues such as generosity (*dāna*) and others, and has beautiful rays (*sugabhasti*).
"Gabhasti" is a term for arms.
[We worship] the one with beautiful, straight arms, the widely shining, the great one among those worthy of sight—
"paśyān" being a name for houses— and the adorable one among those who abide there, the one who is to be sacrificed to.
The meaning is that he should be honored by householders.
"Suhavam" means one who can be invoked with ease. May Agni—the invoker of the gods (*hotā*), the radiant (*vibhāvā*) and shining one—worship such a Tvaṣṭṛ. "Yakṣat" means he should sacrifice.
Let him sacrifice with this oblation.
With these songs, magnify Rudra by day, Rudra by night—the father of the world.
May we, impelled by the sage, praise him who is vast, whose heat is unaging, and whose vigor is overwhelming.
With these songs, magnify Rudra, the father of the world, by day; magnify Rudra by night—the great, lofty, unwasting, and most powerful one. Impelled by the sage, let us invoke him individually. 10.

1. By means of speech, [he is] one who knows and speaks. 2. At the time of dawn, he is one who possesses the sound *gha*, *śa*, and *uṣ*. 3. He whose arms are beautiful, possessing the sounds *jña*, *ta*, *śa*, and *su-gabhasti*. 4. He who possesses the sounds *tha*, *jña*, *ta*, *bha*, and *śa* is the caller.
He is Rudra, the protector (*pitaram*) of the world (*bhuvanasya*), that is, of the multitude of beings (*bhūta-jātasya*).
"Rut" refers to suffering (*duḥkham*).
O singer, magnify with these songs—that is, with praises—the Lord who causes that [world] to flow forth during the day;
and at night, during the darkness, magnify that very Rudra with hymns.

And we, impelled by the wise Rudra, shall invoke him separately—so that there may be abundance—praising Rudra, who is great, lofty, beautiful to behold, ageless (free from decay), and well-sleeping (possessing excellent bliss), endowed with such qualities.
O youthful, wise, and worshipful Maruts, come to the longing of the singer;
for you, increasing in strength, quicken even the dull, O heroes, approaching like the Aṅgirases.
O youthful, wise, and worshipful Maruts, come to the prayer of the singer; for you, increasing [in power], truly quicken even the dull, O heroes, approaching in this manner like the Aṅgirases. 11.
O Maruts, who are young, eternally youthful, sages, wise, and worthy of sacrifice— such as you are, come hither toward the excellent, desirable hymn of the one who praises you.
Moreover, O leaders, O Maruts, increasing in this manner— or rather,
pervading thus in that intermediate space (antarikṣa)— like Aṅgiras.
The *aṅgirasaḥ* are the rays, which have the nature of moving;
just as they swiftly pervade the expanse of the sky, so too [is this].
Or alternatively:
The sages are indeed the Aṅgirases;
they are swift-moving.
Being such as you are, O Citra, you are indeed Citra (the Wondrous).
A region dense with medicinal herbs and forest trees is variegated;
you cause such a region—even one devoid of herbs and the like—to rejoice and be satiated by rain.
The particle *hi* serves as a filler.

Forward to the hero, the powerful, the swift one—like a herdsman driving his cattle home—he shall touch the body of the famous one; he shall reach the firmament, the support of the inspired singer’s word.

Forward to the hero, forward to the powerful and swift one, drive him home like a herdsman driving his flocks! May he touch the body of the famous one with his arrows; as with the stars, the inspired hymns reach the vault of heaven. 12.
O singer, send forth your praise to the host of Maruts—those who are heroic, valorous, and who strike down enemies in various ways;
likewise, send it forth to that host which is powerful and swift-moving.
Herein lies the illustration.

Like a herdsman, a protector of cattle, who drives his herds quickly to their home at sunset—so too, drive our hymn of praise quickly; this is the meaning. And that host of Maruts [is like] the *vipaḥ* (speech) of the *vaktṛ* (speaker), the *vipaḥ* (inspired thought) of the *vipraḥ* (wise one), the singer, and the *śruta* (that which is heard).

Since the word "action" (kriyā) must also be supplied [in the rule], the sixth case ending is used in the sense of the fourth case, because the object (karman) functions as the recipient (saṃpradāna).
May that hymn which has been heard and is worthy of being heard touch—that is, cause to be felt—the slender body;
may it cause it to be embraced.
The meaning is: "May that hymn indeed reach its conclusion."
Regarding the touching, there is an illustration:
"the firmament with the stars.
Just as one touches—that is, brings into contact—the sky, the intermediate space, with the stars, so it is here.

1. Of him who has *jha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ya*, and *ra*. 2. Sent forth and impelled by *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*. 3. *Rudra* consisting of *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *ta*. 4. The expanse of the sky (*nabhasthala*) consisting of *kha*, *gha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*. 5. The variegated region (*deśa*) of *kha*, *gha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *ma*, *ya*, and *śa*. 6. For the sake of strength (*bala*) consisting of *kha*, *gha*, and *bha*; [or] in the powerful one (*śabale*). 7. To the one who moves swiftly (*kṣipragāmin*) consisting of *kha*, *gha*, *bha*, and *śa*.

Viṣṇu, who measured out the earthly realms three times for the sake of the oppressed Manu—under your protection, which is being bestowed upon us, may we rejoice in wealth, in our own bodies, and through our progeny. (13) Viṣṇu—who, for the sake of Manu, that is, Prajāpati, when he was afflicted by the Asuras, thrice measured out the earthly realms (*rajāṃsi pārthivāni*)—meaning the worlds connected to the earth, namely the three worlds; *cit* is used for emphasis—measured them out with just three strides. O Viṣṇu, under such *te* (your)—the genitive used in the sense of the instrumental—such as you, while *śarman* (protection, peace, or a dwelling) is being bestowed upon us, may we rejoice in *rāyā* (wealth), in *tanvā* (our bodies free from disease and the like), and in *tanā* (our offspring, our sons); may we be glad and exultant. (13)

May Ahi Budhnya with the waters, may Parvata, and may Savitṛ grant us that food. May Bhaga, the fulfiller, together with the plants, and the Rātiṣācas, impel us toward wealth. *Ahi Budhnya*: *Budhna* means the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); he who dwells there is *Budhnya*. He goes through the intermediate space, thus he is called *Ahi*. As it is said: "Ahi [goes] through the intermediate space because of his movement" (Nirukta 2.17). The deity denoted by these two terms, being praised with *arkaiḥ*—that is, with hymns (*mantra*) which are the means of worship—shall *dhāt* (grant), bestow, and provide for us (*naḥ*) that (*tat*) well-known food (*canaḥ*) in this world, along with the waters (*adbhiḥ*). *Parvata*: The root *parva* means "to fill. Thus, he is the filler (*pūrayitā*). Alternatively, *parvata* is so called because he possesses the *parvan* (jointed) thunderbolt; or, he is *parvata* because he is the enemy of the mountain (*parvata*). May he too grant that food. Likewise, may *Savitṛ*, the impelling deity, grant that food. Furthermore, the *Rātiṣācas*—the All-Gods (*viśve devāḥ*) who attend upon and enjoy the gift (*rāti*)—may they, together with the *oṣadhībhiḥ* (plants)—so called because ripening (*oṣa*) is placed within them, such as rice and other grains—bestow that food. And may *Bhaga*, the adorable deity, who possesses great wisdom or great power, impel us (*pra jinvatu*) toward wealth (*rāye*).

Now grant us wealth that is effective, filling the people, rich in many heroes, a great guardian of the *ṛta*, a giver of a secure dwelling—by which we may overcome hostile, godless men and stride against the godless tribes, O winner of horses! 15. Now | us | wealth | effective | people-filling | many-heroed | great | of the *ṛta* | guardian | dwelling | giver | by which | people | adversaries | godless | against | and | stride | tribes | against-godless | horse-winning || 15 ||

1. [The letters] kha, jha, and ṭha are connected with the earth; gha is connected with the earth; jha, ta, ra, and pa are connected with the earth; na and ya are connected with the earth; bha is connected with the earth; śa is related to the earth. 2. By means of the sequence of kha, jha, na, bha, ya, and kramaṇa (stepping).
3. May we become [endowed with] kha, jha, ta, bha, ya, ra, and sma; may we attain [the state of] na.
O all you gods, grant us—bestow upon us—wealth, riches, and a dwelling, that is, a house. Of what kind is this wealth? It is *rathyam*, connected with chariots.
The meaning is "yoked to the chariot. Regarding *vcarṣaṇiprām*: *carṣaṇayaḥ* are human beings.
The fulfiller of those [desires], the one possessing many heroes; "heroes" (vīrāḥ) refers to sons and others who are born through valor;
[the one] endowed with many such heroes.
The protector (gopām) of the great sacrifice—that is, its guardian—is he who is the great one;
for the sacrifice is protected by wealth in the form of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), according to the statement:
"A sacrifice without a dakṣiṇā is dead."
What kind of dwelling?
An indestructible one, free from old age.
With such a dwelling and with wealth, may we overcome the people—the enemies—and the contending ones, as well as the divine and non-divine armies belonging to the Asuras. May we surpass them.
Likewise, "ādevīḥ": those goddesses (devyaḥ) in whom the gods have arrived for the purpose of accepting the oblation are called ādevyaḥ;

and such "viśaḥ," meaning subjects who perform the sacrifice—by means of which house (guha) we may enter (vabhyabhavāma), that is, approach—we pray that he may grant such wealth and a home; this is the syntactical connection.
In the fifth Anuvāka, there are twelve hymns.
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "huve vaḥ," is addressed to many deities, belongs to Ṛjiśvan Āptya, and is composed in the Triṣṭubh metre.
It is introduced by the words "huve vaḥ."
The application of the hymn has been completed.
I invoke with salutations the goddess Aditi, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni for the sake of refreshment;
also Aryaman, the gracious one, the protecting gods, Savitṛ, and Bhaga.
We invoke for you with prostrations the goddess Aditi, Mīḷhuṣī Varuṇa, Mitra, Agni, the gracious Aryaman, the protecting gods, Savitṛ, and Bhaga. ||1||
O gods, for the sake of Mīḷaka’s happiness, I invoke with salutations—whether by prostrations or hymns—the goddess Vāc, your mother, who is radiant and inviolable among thoughts;
I praise her.
Likewise, I invoke with salutations Varuṇa, the restrainer, Mitra, the protector from death, and the god Agni—I call upon these gods as well.
Likewise, with prostrations, I invoke Abhīṣṭā, the one whose action is the destruction of enemies— the destroyer of foes— who is most gracious, most blissful, and worthy of praise.
With salutations, I invoke Savitṛ and Bhaga;
why say more? With salutations and hymns of praise, I invoke and laud all the gods, the protectors and guardians.
O Sūrya, you of excellent light, father of Dakṣa, come to the gods who are in your presence, O most mighty one.
Those twice-born ones who are observers of the cosmic order (ṛta), who are truthful, who possess the light of heaven, who are worthy of sacrifice, and whose tongue is Agni.

O Sūrya, son of Dakṣa, come to the gods who possess excellent light, for the sake of our sinlessness; O most mighty one, approach those twice-born ones who are observers of *ṛta*, truthful, luminous, worthy of sacrifice, and whose tongue is Agni. 2.
O most excellent, O Sun of beautiful luster, O impeller of all, [addressing] the Dakṣapitṛs—
those for whom Dakṣa Pitāmaha is the ancestor;
for the word *pitṛ* generally denotes any male ancestor.
As it is said: "I have found the benevolent fathers" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.15.3).
Their status as the fathers of Dakṣa is understood from the mantra: "For Aditi was born" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.72.5).
Seek out—that is, desire—the favor of such gods who possess beautiful light (*sujyotis*), provided they are free from offense (*anāgas*).
The meaning is: "Act in such a way that they do not commit an offense against us.

These twice-born ones (*dvijanmānaḥ*)—so called because they are born and manifest in two worlds—are those who touch *ṛta* (the sacrifice), who are true (*satyāḥ*), meaning non-false or speakers of truth. 1. [Variant readings: kha-gha-jha-na-bha-ra read *ādevīm*.]
2. Their grandfather is Jha-jha-ta-na-ra-pitā.

They are possessed of heaven (*svarvantaḥ*), possessed of wealth (*dhanavantaḥ*), worthy of sacrifice (*yajataḥ*), and to be sacrificed to (*yaṣṭavyāḥ*). They are those for whom Agni is the tongue (*agnijihvāḥ*), meaning they have Agni as their representative tongue.
The grammatical connection is: "O, enter those gods who exist in such a state."
And may Heaven and Earth, the two radiant worlds, grant wide and lofty dominion; O Dhiṣaṇās, provide us with a secure refuge and create ample space for our dwelling, so that we may be free from harm.

And you two, Heaven and Earth—the ruling power, the wide and vast, the two worlds—grant refuge to him who praises you well. O two great bowls of wisdom (Dhiṣaṇās), provide for us ample space and freedom from harm for our dwelling. 3.
Moreover, O Heaven and Earth (dyāvāpṛthivī), you two create vast (uru) and extensive power (kṣatra);
likewise, O Heaven and Earth (rodasī), you two create for us, who praise you well (susuṣṭubhe), a great (bṛhat) refuge and a home.
Create it in such a way that there may be for us great wealth (varivaḥ).
Moreover, O two Dhiṣaṇās, the two sustainers, Heaven and Earth, grant us freedom from harm—the absence of evil—for our dwelling-place.
May the two sons of Rudra bow down to us; may the Vasus, invoked as givers of wealth, be unassailable.
When we are placed in great fear or in the pressure of distress, O Maruts, you gods [are our refuge] day by day.
May the sons of Rudra bow down to us—the Vasus, invincible, who consume the wicked—whether they have been placed in great fear or in the pressure of the day’s distress, O Maruts, O Gods.
May the Maruts, the sons of Rudra, being summoned today at this time, bow down toward us;
may they be inclined, may they come.
Of what nature are they?
The *vasavas* are the dwellers; they are *adhṛṣṭas*, unassailed by others.

Whenever (*yat*) we—having been placed, stationed, or standing together against these *maruts*, the gods, in a small or great, extensive *bādha*, that is, in battle—then we call them with our voices (*ahrāṃ*). Such is the syntactical connection.
They have come together with those between whom the two goddesses, Heaven and Earth, now exert themselves; Puṣan, the one who bestows abundance, accompanies them as they sacrifice.
O Maruts, having heard our call, when you come forth, all beings tremble on the path you have set out upon.

They have come together, those among whom the two divine worlds, Rodasī, take delight; Puṣan, who surpasses all in sacrifice, hears their call. O Maruts, when you set forth upon the earth, all things tremble on your path as it is opened out.
Among those Maruts, Rodasī— the goddess, the radiant wife of Rudra, the voice of the mid-region—
quickly unites; likewise, Pūṣan,
the nourishing god who honors with wealth and causes his worshippers to prosper, serves those great ones.

"‘Abhyardhayajvābhyardhayañjati’ (Nirukta 6.6), so says Yāska. O Maruts, having heard our invocation, when indeed you go— when you arrive— then, on the path that has been prepared for your journey, whatever beings (*bhūma*) are present there [unharmed by others].
2. With *gha*, *ta*, *bha*, and *śa* you go; with *kha*, *jha*, *na*, and *ra* you come.
They tremble and shake.
And so says another mantra: "They cause the mountains to quake and they shatter the lords of the forest" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.39.5).

Sing with a new prayer, O singer, to that hero Indra, the lover of songs; may he, being praised, hear our call and, being lauded, grant us great riches and strength. Sing to that hero, the lover of songs, Indra, with a new prayer, O singer! May he indeed hear our invocation; and being praised, may he grant us strengths, being glorified for great wealth.
O singer, praise with a new and beautiful hymn that well-known hero, Indra—the possessor of valor who especially drives away enemies, the lover of songs (girvaṇas) who is perfected by our speech.
Being thus praised, may he surely hear our invocation;
and being glorified, may Indra grant us great and abundant strengths and foods.
Since this is so, the meaning is: "Therefore, praise."

O Waters, you who belong to humanity, bestow upon us for our children and grandchildren that which is uninjured, health, and well-being; for you indeed are the most motherly physicians, the progenitors of all that is stationary and all that moves. 7. *omānam*, *āpaḥ*, *mānuṣīḥ*, *amṛktam*, *dhātam*, *tokāya*, *tanayāya*, *śam*, *yoḥ*, *yūyam*, *hi*, *stha*, *bhiṣajaḥ*, *mātṛtamāḥ*, *viśvasya*, *sthātuḥ*, *jagataḥ*, *janitrīḥ*. 7.

O you waters, who are human and beneficial to man, bestow upon us for our son (*toka*), our grandson (*tanaya*), and his son as well, that which is unimpaired—meaning uninjured—and *omāna*, which is a protector; for *omā* means that which protects, namely, nourishing food. Grant this!
Grant!
Likewise, bestow and grant *śam*, the pacification of calamities, and *yoḥ*, the warding off and the separation of those things that must be separated.
Why? To this he says:

The syntactical connection is as follows: since you are the "most motherly" (*mātṛtamāḥ*), meaning superior even to mothers, and are "physicians" (*bhiṣajaḥ*), therefore [the Lord] says, "Sustain" (*dhāta*).
To the question, "In what way is there a medicine superior even to that of mothers? he replies:
"You are the progenitors (*janitrīḥ*), the givers of birth, of the entire universe—of everything both stationary (*sthātuḥ*) and moving (*jagataḥ*)."
Therefore, you are physicians.

May the divine Savitṛ, the protector, come to us with his golden hands and his silver [hands], the worshipful one; he who, possessing gifts, discloses desirable things for the donor, as the face of the Dawn. 8. May the divine Savitṛ, the protector, come to us with his golden hands and his silver [hands], the worshipful one; he who, possessing gifts, discloses desirable things for the donor, as the face of the Dawn. 8.

May Savitṛ, the impeller, the god who is *trāyamāṇaḥ* (protecting), *rakṣan* (guarding), *hiraṇyapāṇiḥ* (golden-handed), or one whose hands are beautiful and pleasing, and who is *yajataḥ* (worthy of worship)—may he, being such, *ā jaṅgamyāt* (come) to us. That god who is *datravān* (possessed of wealth). [Note: The commentary fragments provided clarify the following terms: 1. [He] would bestow. 2. [Regarding the word *ahiṃsantam*: some manuscripts read *hiṃsantam*, while others read *ahiṃsantam*. 3. [Regarding *tatsutāya*: some manuscripts read *tatsutāya*. 4. [Regarding *bhayānām*: some manuscripts read *pṛthakartavyānāṃ bhayānām* (of fears that are to be separated). 5. [Regarding *bhiṣajaḥ*: some manuscripts read *bhiṣajaḥ ārogyakartāraḥ* (physicians, those who effect health). 6. [Regarding *bhaiṣajyamāsthityata*: some manuscripts read *bhaiṣajyamāsthityata*.]

Like the face of the Dawn—meaning, as the front of the Dawn does—he reveals, discloses, and makes manifest desirable treasures for the donor, that is, for the sacrificer who has offered oblations; he is Savitṛ—this is the syntactical connection.
And you, O Son of Strength, may you turn the gods toward us today at this sacrifice. May I ever abide in your protection; through your favor, may we be rich in heroic sons.
And so, O Son of Strength, may you turn the gods hither today to this our sacrifice. May I ever abide in your bounty; may I, O Agni, through your protection, be rich in heroic sons. 9.
Moreover, O Agni, son of strength, at this very time, in this our sacrifice and ritual, do thou turn hither— the gods, Indra and the others who are to be worshipped— bring them here.
And may I ever indeed remain present in thy bounty, in the giving of wealth.
Likewise, O Agni, through your protection—that is, by means of your guardianship—may I be endowed with excellent heroes, such as sons, grandsons, and so forth.
And may those two Nāsatyas come to my invocation; O sages, you are truly inspired by our prayers.
Like Atri, deliver us from great darkness; O heroes, protect us from misfortune in the encounter.

And so, O Nāsatyas, come to this my invocation through our prayers; for you two, O sages, indeed delivered Atri from the great darkness, as you did for others—O heroes, rescue us from distress in the hour of need! 10.

Moreover, O wise ones, O Nāsatyas whose very nature is truth or who are the leaders of truth—O Aśvins, do you two, those well-known ones, come quickly with your speed to my invocation, this hymn accompanied by our serviceful rites; indeed, come hither!

And having come, O leaders, O Aśvins, just as you two liberated Atri—the seer who was like Atri—from that great darkness, the gloom created by the Asuras, so too do you two rescue us from misfortune, the suffering caused by our enemies, when we have encountered the conflict in close combat.
May you two become the bestowers of wealth upon us—wealth that is resplendent, full of vigor, abundant, and rich in nourishment.
May the divine, terrestrial, and aquatic gods, born of the light, being gracious, show us mercy.
Be you givers to us of wealth that is brilliant, vigorous, and abundant in food—ye divine, terrestrial, and aquatic gods, born of the cow, who bestow blessings; O gods, have mercy upon us! 11.

O gods, may you— who are resplendent, radiant, possessed of vigor, endowed with strength, accompanied by men such as sons and others, and rich in food— become the bestowers of wealth (*rāyaḥ*) upon us. Furthermore, being bountiful and granting our desires, may the divine Ādityas who dwell in heaven, the Vasus who dwell on earth, and those born of the Cow—
the Cow being the variegated speech of the intermediate region— be present.
Arising from that, you who are the great Āpyas and the Rudras who dwell in the waters and the intermediate space—all of you, grant us mercy; bring us happiness.
1. Wealth is to be enjoyed by those born under the signs beginning with Kha, Jha, Na, Bha, and Sa.
2. [They are served] by attendants born under the signs beginning with Kha, Gha, Bha, and Śa.
3. Those born under the signs beginning with Kha, Gha, Bha, and Śa are like Indra himself.

May they—Rudra, Sarasvatī, and Viṣṇu, being of one accord, together with Vāyu, the bounteous ones—be gracious to us. May Ṛbhukṣan, Vāja, the divine Vidhātṛ, Parjanya, and Vāta cause our nourishment to swell. May they—Rudra, Sarasvatī, and Viṣṇu, being of one accord, together with Vāyu, the bounteous ones—be gracious to us. May Ṛbhukṣan, Vāja, the divine Vidhātṛ, Parjanya, and Vāta cause our nourishment to swell. (12)
May those gods—abounding in nourishment and possessing rain—be gracious toward us; may they show mercy and grant us happiness.
If one asks who they are, it is said: Rudra and Sarasvatī, being in harmony and full of joy, as well as Viṣṇu, Vāyu, and Ṛbhukṣan.
R̥bhu, Vibhvan, and Vāja are the three Saudhanvanas;
among them, the first is R̥bhu and the last is Vāja.
This is an elliptical designation.
And may Vibhvan,
the divine one who is beneficial to the gods, Vidhātṛ, and Prajāpati—
as well as Parjanya and Vāta, both the rain-god and the wind— swell and increase our food for us.

And may that god Savitar, Bhaga, and Apāṃ Napāt, the filler of gifts, protect us; may Tvaṣṭṛ be in harmony with the gods and the wives, and may Dyaus with the gods and Pṛthivī with the oceans [protect us]. 13. And may that god Savitar, Bhaga, and Apāṃ Napāt, the filler of gifts, protect us; may Tvaṣṭṛ be in harmony with the gods and the wives, and may Dyaus with the gods and Pṛthivī with the oceans [protect us]. 13.
Moreover, he who is renowned everywhere as the impeller—Savitṛ the god, Bhaga, and Apāṃ Napāt, the son of the waters (the midday fire situated in the clouds)—may he protect and guard us.
Of what nature is Apāṃ Napāt? He is the giver of *dānu*, that is, wealth to be bestowed, and the fulfiller (*papriḥ*) who bestows it.

From the root *prā* in the sense of "filling," the suffix *kin* is applied according to the rule *ātaśca upasarge*; because this [suffix] functions as a nominal stem (*liṅga*), the prohibition of the genitive case by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām* applies.
Likewise, may Tvaṣṭṛ, rejoicing together with the gods and their wives, and Dyaus, rejoicing with the gods, and Pṛthivī, rejoicing with the oceans—all these deities protect us equally.
In the Āgnimāruta [śastra], this verse "uta no 'hiḥ" is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "uta no 'hirbudhnyaḥ śṛṇotu devānām patnīraśatīrabantu naḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.20).

May Ahi Budhnya hear us; may Aja Ekapād, Pṛthivī, and Samudra hear us. May all the gods, the increasers of *ṛta*, being invoked, and the praised mantras recited by the seers, protect us. 14. May Ahi Budhnya hear us; may Aja Ekapād, Pṛthivī, and Samudra hear us. May all the gods, the augmenters of Truth (*ṛta*), being invoked, and the hymns of praise uttered by the sages, grant us protection. 14.
Moreover, may Ahirbudhnya hear our hymn of praise; he is the Unborn (aja), free from birth,
and the One-footed (ekapāt), so called because he moves alone and without companion.
May this deity denoted by non-duality, as well as the earth and the ocean, protect us—
[the latter] being endowed with mutual affection.

May he hear our hymn. Furthermore, may all the gods—who increase *ṛta* (the cosmic order), whether of sacrifice or of truth; who are being invoked by us; who have been praised with hymns by the ancient seers; who are worthy of praise (*mantra*), to be spoken of, or expressed by mantras; and who are extolled by poets (*kavi*)—that is, by wise seers through their words—may such ones protect and guard us.
Thus do the Bṛhaddivas, the descendants of Bharadvāja, honor him with their prayers and fervent hymns.
O Vasus, may you all, being invoked, unassailable, and worthy of sacrifice, be praised and present here.
Thus, the Bharadvājas, with their prayers, sing praises with hymns for me, his grandson. May all the Vasus, invoked and invincible, being praised, become worthy of sacrifice. 15.

In this very way, those sons of mine, the Bharadvājas—descendants of Ṛjīvan belonging to the Bharadvāja lineage, such as Suhotra and others—worship and praise me with *dhīs*, that is, with hymns (*stotras*), and with *arkas*, the means of adoration.

O worshipful ones (*yajatrāḥ*), gods worthy of sacrifice, you who have been offered to (*hutāsaḥ*) and satisfied by oblations such as the *puroḍāśa* cakes, you Vasus, the dwellers (*vasavaḥ*), who are unassailable (*aṣṭṛṣṭāḥ*) and cannot be harmed by anyone—all you Viśvedevas and the wives of the gods, being thus praised, be pleased;
be gratified by these praises from Suhotra and the others.
The second hymn, consisting of sixteen verses beginning with "udu tyat," is composed by Ṛjīvan and is addressed to the Viśvedevas.
The three verses starting from the thirteenth are in the *uṣṇih* meter; the sixteenth is an *anuṣṭubh*, and the remaining verses are in the *triṣṭubh* meter.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "Udu tyat: sixteen verses; [the meters are] *uṣṇih*, *anuṣṭubh*, and *triṣṭubh*."
The application of the hymns has been concluded.
That eye of Mitra and Varuṇa, worthy of honor, has come forth—the beloved, undeceived, pure, and beautiful face of Cosmic Order (Ṛta). Like a golden disk from the sky at dawn, it has shone brightly.
Up! That great eye of Mitra and Varuṇa comes hither—beloved, undeceived, the pure and most beautiful countenance of Ṛta. Like a golden ornament, it has shone forth from the rising sky. 1.
That which is well-known as the eye, the illuminator, great, vast, and extensive, beloved by Mitra and Varuṇa—
the words "Mitra" and "Varuṇa" here denote both Mitra and Varuṇa through their mutual conjunction—
it is the beloved of Mitra and Varuṇa, undeceived (adabdha), unharmed by demons, pure (śuci), stainless, and beautiful to behold (darśata).
Such is the face—the brilliance—of *ṛta*, the Āditya; it rises up, ascending toward all.
When he has risen, at the rising of the sun, that brilliance, having risen, shines forth like a golden ornament of the sky, the intermediate space;
it blazes, it manifests.
1. In the manuscripts Kha, Jha, Na, and Bha, the word “ṛṣibhiḥ” does not exist. 2. In the manuscript Gha, it says “gotrakāḥ.
3. In the manuscripts Jha, Jña, Ta, Na, Bha, Ya, and Ra, it says “aṣṭṛṣṭāḥ,” meaning the Vasus—the dwellers—are those who have not been harmed by enemies.
4. *kha-bha-mitrāyo*: [refers to] Mitra and Varuṇa; *śa-mitrāyo*: Varuṇa and Mitra; *priya-mitrāyo*. 5. *jha-jña-ta-na-bha-ra-śa* means "exceedingly dear" (*atipriyam*); *ya* means "dear" (*priyam*).
6. *kha-bha* shines forth; *u* is a filler (*pūraṇa*).

The inspired sage who knows the three assemblies of these gods and their births from of old—perceiving both the straight and the crooked among mortals, the Sun beholds the ways of the noble one. veda | yaḥ | trīṇi | vidathāni | eṣām | devānām | janma | sanutaḥ | ā | ca | vipraḥ | ṛju | marteṣu | vṛjinā | ca | paśyan | abhi | caṣṭe | sūraḥ | aryaḥ | evān || 2 ||
The Sun, who knows— the one who understands and perceives— the three *vidathas*, the three stations to be known, the three worlds;
[he knows] from afar (*sanutaḥ*) the unmanifest name of these gods residing in these three worlds, who consist of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas.
The wise and intelligent one, like the Sun, knows that which is hidden and imperceptible—namely, birth and procreation.
The prefix *ā* has the sense of "filling.

That *sūra*, the Sun, beholding and directly perceiving the straight (*ṛju*) and beautiful deeds as well as the crooked (*vṛjina*) and unbeautiful deeds existing among mortals, i.e., human beings, shines forth and illuminates the entire world.

Thus, O noble Lord, being our father in heaven, O mother Earth, O unassailable brothers Vasus, be gracious to us! O all you Ādityas, including Aditi, being of one accord, extend to us manifold protection.
O Heaven, Father; O Earth, Mother; O Agni, Brother; O Vasus, have mercy on us! O all Ādityas, together with Aditi, grant us extensive protection in harmony. 5.

O Father, you who stand in the place of a father, O Heaven; O Mother, you who stand in the place of a mother, O Earth; O Brother, you who stand in the place of a brother, O Agni; O Vasus, the gods who provide dwelling—may you all be gracious to us and grant us happiness. O All-Adityas, all the sons of Aditi, O Goddess Aditi, may you all be of one accord and bestow upon us abundant, superior, and wide-reaching *śarma*—happiness or a spacious home.
O worshipful ones, do not surrender us to the wolf, nor to the she-wolf, nor to any who seeks to harm us;
for you indeed are the charioteers of our bodies.

Homage indeed to the fierce; homage I offer up. Homage has supported the earth and the sky. Homage to the gods; homage is the master of these. Even committed sin I dispel by means of homage. (8) "Homage" (*namaḥ*)—homage alone is "fierce" (*ugram*), that is, powerful and most excellent. For by that everything is obtained. Therefore, "homage"—I offer up (*ā viṃvāse*) and attend to homage. "Homage"—homage alone supports (*dādhāra*) both the earth and the sky (*uta dyām*). When heaven and earth are saluted by living beings, they remain for a long time for their enjoyment. Therefore, I offer homage to the gods. Homage to these gods is the "master" (*īśe*); for by it they are brought under control. "Even committed" (*kṛtaṃ cit*)—even a sin (*enaḥ*) that has been performed or practiced, I dispel (*ā viṃvāse*) by means of homage. *Vivāsaḥ* means avoidance; I avoid it; I destroy it.

O worshipful gods, I bow down with salutations toward you all—you who are the charioteers of *ṛta* (the cosmic order), whose will is pure, who sit within the dwelling-place of *ṛta*, who are inviolable, far-seeing, and leaders among men; I, the great one, bow down before you all with my prostrations. He who is worthy of sacrifice, O worshipful gods, I bow down toward you all with salutations—those who are the charioteers of your *ṛta* (sacrifice), whose power is purified, who dwell in the household of *ṛta* (the sacrificial ground), who are unassailable by demons and other foes, who are far-sighted, and who are the leaders of men; I, the great one, bow down before you all with my prostrations.

For they indeed possess the most excellent luster; may they lead us across all difficulties. Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni, who possess good dominion, whose thoughts are fixed on Truth (Ṛta), and who are true to those who offer hymns—[may they lead us]. For they, those gods whose qualities are about to be described, are indeed possessed of the most excellent luster—that is, they possess praiseworthy radiance. Therefore, "they"—meaning those very ones—"lead" (nayanti)—or rather, "may they lead"—"us," our "all" (viśvāni) "difficulties" (duritā), so that they become "hidden" (tiraḥ). The meaning is: "may they destroy them. Those gods, Varuṇa and the others, who have "good dominion" (sukṣatrāsaḥ)—meaning either beautiful power or beautiful wealth—and whose "thoughts are fixed on Truth" (ṛtadhītayaḥ), meaning whose actions are real, and who are "true to those who offer hymns" (vakmarājasatyāḥ): "hymn" (vakma) means speech or praise; its "kings" (rājānaḥ) are the masters, namely the chanters (stotāraḥ); they are "true" (satyāḥ), meaning not false, toward them. Such are they—this is the syntactical connection. 10.12.

1. Kha-bha, I pay homage. 2. Śa, O evil ones, [ward off] our evils! May Indra, Pṛthivī, Kṣāman, Pūṣan, Bhaga, Aditi, and the five peoples—may they be for us providers of good refuge, possessors of good wealth, excellent leaders, good protectors, and good guardians. 11. May they—Indra, Pṛthivī, Kṣāman, Pūṣan, Bhaga, Aditi, and the five peoples—be for us providers of good refuge, possessors of good wealth, excellent leaders, good protectors, and good guardians. 11. Te naḥ indraḥ pṛthivī kṣāmaṃ vardhan pūṣā bhago aditiḥ pañca janāḥ | suśarmāṇaḥ svarvasaḥ sunīthā bhavantu naḥ sutrātrāsaḥ sugopāḥ || 11 || May they—Indra, Pṛthivī, Kṣāman, Pūṣan, Bhaga, Aditi, and the five peoples—be for us providers of good refuge, possessors of good wealth, excellent leaders, good protectors, and good guardians. 11.

May those gods increase our *kṣāma*, our dwelling place. Who are they? Indra, Pṛthivī, Pūṣan, Bhaga, Aditi—the undepressed mother of the gods—and the Five Peoples (*pañca janāḥ*), namely the gods, humans, Gandharvas, and Apsarases, as mentioned in the Brāhmaṇa (AiB 3.31). May they, for our sake, be providers of good shelter (*suśarmāṇaḥ*), i.e., sources of great happiness; providers of excellent protection (*svavasaḥ*); providers of fine food (*sunīthāḥ*); and providers of easy access (*suprāpaṇāḥ*).
The sense is: "May they grant us beautiful happiness and so forth.
Likewise, may they be *sutratrāsaḥ*—excellent protectors—and *sugopāḥ*—excellent guardians.
Protection from enemies who have approached is *trāṇam*.
By means of their arising and cessation, there is protection and concealment.

Now indeed, O divine lords, the Hotṛ Bhāradvāja goes toward the celestial favor of you all. With the sacrificial offerings placed before him, the sacrificer, seeking wealth, praises the lineage of the gods. 12. Now indeed, O divine lords, the Hotṛ Bhāradvāja goes toward the celestial favor of you all. With the sacrificial offerings placed before him, the sacrificer, seeking wealth, praises the lineage of the gods. 12.
By this verse, the seer describes himself indirectly:
"O gods, may this Bharadvāja—one born of the Bharadvāja lineage—the Hotṛ priest and singer, quickly reach the divine, celestial abode, the seat of the *sattra* sacrifice;
likewise, he seeks from you your benevolent thought and your gracious disposition."
The *yāti* is one whose function is to go.

For that purpose, together with other sacrificers who are *miyedhas*—that is, pure (*medhya*), worthy of sacrifice (*medhārha*), and seated (*āsānebhiḥ*) as they perform the sacrificial session (*satrāsana*)—this sacrificer, performing the sacrifice, being a seeker of wealth (*vasyuḥ*) desiring riches for himself, pays homage (*vavanda*) to the *janma*, the birth or assembly (*saṃgha*) of the gods;
he praises them.
On the fourth day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), in the *prauga-śastra*, there is this triplet dedicated to the Viśvedevas beginning with "apa tyaṃ vṛjinam.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *prauga* [consists] of anuṣṭubh verses beginning with 'apa tyaṃ vṛjinam' and 'asmat ripo nadītamaḥ'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.11).
Drive away that crooked enemy, O Agni, the thief of evil intent; O Lord of Beings, make his path most difficult to travel, and provide an easy way for us. 13.

O Agni, drive away—that is, cast far off—that well-known crooked enemy, the evildoer, the one of evil intent who meditates wicked thoughts; such a thief, a harmful person, most distant and difficult to approach. (The root *asu* is used in the sense of "casting away.")

1. Those such as Kha, Bha, and Te. 2. The ground of Jha, Na, Ra, and Bha. 3. Gods, humans, and others, as well as ancestors and serpents, beginning with Kha, Bha, and Deva-manuṣya. 4. I speak through the invisibility of Kha, Gha, Bha, and Śa. 5. By means of Gha, Jha, Ta, Bha, Ra, and other sacrifices. 6. The assembly of people (janasaṃgham) of Kha, Gha, Bha, and Ja; all birth (jananam) of Śa. Ṛgveda 3.13: Dhātu.
O Vṛṣan, protector of the virtuous, make for us a good path (sugam)—that is, a beautiful way to go—and create happiness.
In this case, because the fire—which consists of all the gods—is praised, it possesses the character of being dedicated to all the gods (vaiśvadevatva).
O Soma, for have not the pressing-stones indeed prepared themselves for our friendship? Slay the niggardly Paṇi, for he is a wolf.
O Soma, the pressing-stones have indeed chosen you for our friendship. Strike down the greedy Pani; for he is a wolf. 14.
O Soma, these stones of ours, intended for the purpose of pressing, desire—through your friendship—that is, for the sake of your companionship—to turn toward you;
"kam" is a filler;
"hi" has the sense of "because."
Since this is so, therefore you must destroy—that is, annihilate—the *paṇi*, the merchant; the *vṛtra*, the devouring one, such as a Rākṣasa or similar being.
For that *paṇi* is indeed a wolf, intent on seizing, intoxicated by all women, and habitually engaged in plundering.
Therefore, the meaning is: "you must abandon [it]."
The verbal root is *kuk*, meaning "to eat," as in *vṛka* (wolf).
For you indeed stand there, O bounteous ones, with Indra as your chief;
may you provide us a fair path on our journey and be our protectors at home.
For you indeed are bounteous givers, with Indra as your chief; you are our protectors on the journey, providing us with a good path and guardians at home. 15.
O bounteous gods, you who give beautiful gifts, for you indeed are most capable;
you are prosperous,
with Indra as your chief.
Those for whom Indra is the eldest and the chief;
you who have attained splendor—being our protectors and guardians together on the path, may you grant us a happy way. (The particle *ā* is used as a conjunction.)
And perform what brings happiness.
Upon returning from a journey, this verse beginning with "api panthām" is to be muttered by the sacrificer.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having returned with fuel in his hand, [he recites] 'api panthāmagammahi' and so forth" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.5).
Moreover, we have come upon the path that leads to well-being and is free from danger,
by which one avoids all enemies and finds wealth.
We have indeed gone upon the path that leads to well-being, free from danger, by which one avoids all enemies and finds wealth. 16.
"Or even (*vāpi*) have we gone (*aganmahi*) upon the path (*panthām*), the way, the road? We have entered it; we have reached it.
Of what kind [is it]?"
One should go by a path that is auspicious (*svasti-gām*), easy to traverse, free from distress, and devoid of evil.
Traveling by such a path, one avoids, shuns, and repels all hostile beings; furthermore, one finds and acquires wealth (*vasu*). This refers to such a path.
1. One should go to a beautiful place [indicated by] kha, jha, na, bha, and ya.
2. One who is intent on non-giving [is indicated by] kha, jha, and bha.
3. One who delights in evil [is indicated by] jha, ta, na, ra, and pa.
The third hymn, consisting of seventeen verses beginning with “na tad divā,” is the work of Ṛjiśvan and is addressed to the Viśvedevas.
Of these, the first six are *triṣṭubh* meters; from the seventh verse, there are six *gāyatrī*s; the thirteenth is a *triṣṭubh*, the fourteenth is a *jagatī*, and the remaining three are *triṣṭubh*s.
Thus it has been stated in the *Anukramaṇī*: “na tat—deficient [in syllables] after the seventh; six *gāyatrī*s; the fourteenth is a *jagatī*.”
The application has been explained.
I do not approve of that [offering] by day, nor on earth, nor by means of sacrifice, nor by the protections of the gods.
May the well-established mountains cast him down; may the performer of the excessive sacrifice fall low.
Not by day, nor upon the earth do I grant him leave; neither by sacrifice nor by these protections. May the well-formed mountains crush him down; let the performer of the *atīyāja* fall. 1.

There was once a certain Atiyāja who, with the thought "May I be superior to another, Ṛjiśvan," desired to sacrifice to the gods. A seer (ṛṣi) rejected his sacrifice, saying: "I do not approve of that sacrifice of the seer Atiyāja; it is not joined with 'heaven'—that is, it is not endowed with the world of heaven and the host of gods residing there."
I do not grant my consent.
Nor do I approve, thinking that it is not fitting even for the earthly king or the host of gods;
nor do I approve, thinking that it is not equal to a sacrifice performed by me.
"Moreover, I do not approve of [the sacrifice] being equal to these *śamī* rites, nor even to other deeds performed by me.
The meaning is that the gods, having been brought under my control, do not accept his sacrifice; and he, due to his ignorance, is not even capable of performing it correctly.
Furthermore, let the 'well-being' (*subhvaḥ*) mountains—meaning the mountains sent by Indra—tear him apart, that is, destroy that seer."
His action was one of humiliation.

Thus, may he who is the sacrificer—the performer of the sacrifice for that seer Ṛjiśvan, who was possessed by the thought "I alone sacrifice to the gods in an excessive manner"—be utterly humbled, let him become completely degraded.

O Maruts, may the burning heats fall upon him who holds us in contempt, or who seeks to revile the sacred prayer (*brahman*) being performed; may his crooked deeds be consumed by fire, and may the sky scorch that hater of sacred prayer.

Or he who, O Maruts, holds us in contempt, or he who seeks to revile the sacred prayer (*brahman*) as it is being performed—for him let his crooked deeds become burning heats; let the sky scorch that hater of sacred prayer! 2.

O Maruts, let those heats—the piercing, obstructive forces—be against that man who thinks beyond us, who considers himself superior by surpassing us, and who perceives himself to be greater than we are; and against him who would wish to revile the sacred hymn (*brahman*) being performed by us. Let both Heaven and the Sun scorch and consume that enemy who hates the sacred word.
May he speak.

O Soma, why do they call you the guardian of the sacred word (*brahman*), and why do they call you our protector against curses? Why, O Guardian, do you look with indifference upon us as we are being reviled? Cast forth your bolt and your weapons against the hater of the sacred word!

What indeed, O Soma, do they call you—the guardian of the sacred word (*brahman*)? What indeed do they say of you—that you are the protector against our slanderers? Why indeed do you look upon us while we are being reviled? Cast forth your weapons and your darts against the hater of the sacred word! 3.
1. I do not approve even of "kha-tad"; I also approve of "jha-ta-na-ra-tad.
The particles *kim* and *aṅga* are well-known indicators [of emphasis].
O Soma, those who know the past indeed call you the protector (*gopām*)—the guardian—of the *brahman*, whether that be the mantra, the ritual action, or the *brahma*-caste.
Likewise, they indeed call you alone our protector from the curses and the revilers—the enemies. Or rather:
"Aṅga" is used here as a term for drawing [the listener's] attention.
O Soma, dear friend, for what reason do they call you the guardian of the sacred word (*brahman*)?
Or for what reason do they call you our protector against curses?
O Soma, why do you look upon us—us who are being constantly reviled and oppressed by others?
Everyone declares you alone to be the protector of the Brahmins and their guardian against enemies; therefore, it is unbecoming of you to remain indifferent while we are being led away by others.
Hence, hurl—that is, cast forth—the burning weapon, the scorching missile, against that hater of Brahmins, the one who hates the Brāhmaṇas.
May those born of life move swiftly for me; may the swelling rivers move swiftly for me;
may the firm mountains move swiftly for me; and may the two parents move swiftly for me at the invocation of the gods.

May the Dawns, as they are born, hasten toward me; may the swelling rivers hasten toward me; may the firm mountains hasten toward me; and may the Fathers hasten toward me at the invocation of the gods.
May the Dawns, as they are being born and manifesting themselves, protect me;
likewise, may the rivers—the flowing streams that swell and increase—protect me;
and likewise, may the mountains—the immovable peaks—protect me.

Likewise, in the *devahūti* [hymn]: the *devahūti* sacrifice is so called because it is the invocation (*hūti*) or calling of the gods (*devānām*). May the fathers (*pitaraḥ*) and the ancestral deities (*pitṛdevatāḥ*) residing therein protect me.
May we always be of good mind as the sun rises;
may the Lord of Wealths, the two gods who bestow riches, grant this, coming with their aid.
May we always be of good mind. Now, toward the rising sun, may the Lord of Wealth, the bestower of riches, acting as the one who carries the gods, come hither with his protection. 5.
O gods, may we always—at all times—be well-disposed, that is, possess auspicious minds.
The word *nu* is used as a conjunction.
And may we always behold the rising sun as it ascends.

May he, the Lord of Wealth (*vasupati*), the supreme master of riches, having been invoked by our oblation (*vasā*)—he who brings and conveys [the gods]—come most swiftly; being distinguished by such qualities, may he act accordingly:
may he make us such as have been described.
May Indra come most near to us; may Sarasvatī, swelling with the rivers, and Parjanya with the joy-bestowing plants, be well-praised and easy to invoke like a father.

May Indra come most near with his protection; may Sarasvatī, swelling with the rivers, and Parjanya, like a father, come to us with joy-bestowing plants—both he who is of goodly praise and he who is easy to invoke. 6.

1. [The lord] of the Brāhmaṇa caste beginning with *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *ya*; or [the lord] of the Brāhmaṇa caste beginning with *jha* and *ta*. 2. The protector of the Brāhmaṇas beginning with *kha*, *bha*, and *ra*; the protector of the Brāhmaṇas beginning with *jha* and *na*. 3. The sovereign of riches beginning with *jha* and *ta*.
May this Indra come most near, as close as possible, together with protection; may he be the one who arrives most readily.
And may Sarasvatī, swelling and increasing with the flowing waters of the rivers, come most swiftly.
And may Parjanya, together with the plants, be the bringer of bliss to us.
And may Agni be like a father to his son, easy to praise, and easy to invoke.
In the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, for the Vaiśvadeva oblation of cooked rice, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) is “O Viśve Devas, come hither” (*viśve devāsa ā gata*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*viśve devāsa ā gata ye ca 'mā mahino ahimāyāḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.9).
O All-Gods, come hither; hear this my invocation;
sit upon this sacred grass.
May all the gods, Indra accompanied by the host of Maruts— the Maruts being his attendants— as well as Tvaṣṭṛ, Mitra, and Aryaman, graciously accept our hymn and these oblations.
O Agni, Hotṛ-priest, knowing the divine folk, offer this sacrifice of ours according to the proper order.
O Agni, Hotṛ-priest who perceives the sacred ordinances, perform this sacrifice for us; being wise, worship the divine host. 12.

He is the Hotṛ, the invoker of the gods. O Agni, being wise and knowing, perform the sacrifice for us—this our unimpaired *adhvara*—in due order according to the sequence of knowledge, so that the gods, present in the intellect, may be worshipped; offer the sacrifice to the divine host (*devyaṃ janaṃ*) who are worthy of worship.
The *yājyā* for the *vaiśvadeva-śastra* is "O Viśve Devās.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having recited [the *śastra*] with 'For the hearing, thee,' he should mutter the *yājyā*: 'O Viśve Devās, hear this invocation of mine'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 5.18).
This very *yājyā* is used in the *vaiśvadeva* animal sacrifice as well.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O All-Gods, hear this my invocation, you who are on earth, great ones of serpent-like power" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 1.7).
O All-Gods, hear this my invocation—ye who are in the mid-air and ye who are in heaven;
ye who have Agni as your tongue and ye who are worthy of worship, sit down upon this sacred grass and rejoice!

O All-Gods, hear this my invocation—ye who dwell in the intermediate space and ye who are in heaven, ye whose tongue is Agni or who are worthy of sacrifice; rejoice this very day upon this sacred grass. 13.
O All-Gods (*viśve devāḥ*), hear this my invocation (*havam*);
you who abide in the atmosphere (*antarikṣe*)— that is, in the world of the intermediate space—
and you who are near, in the world of earth (*bhūloke*).
And those who are in the heavenly world today,
and those whose tongue is Agni—
that is, for whom Agni stands in the place of a tongue.
Alternatively,
they are called "fire-tongued" because they are nourished by that which is the tongue of fire.
Moreover, even those who are worthy of worship—O you all, having sat down upon this strewn sacrificial grass (barhis), rejoice; satisfy yourselves with Soma.
May all the gods worthy of sacrifice hear my heart’s thought, and may both the worlds and the Son of the Waters hear it.
Let me not utter words that should be disregarded by you; being wise, may I rejoice in those who are closest to me.

May all the gods worthy of sacrifice hear my heart’s core; may both the worlds and the Son of the Waters hear my prayer. I shall not speak words of yours that should be disregarded; O wise ones, as your closest kin, may we rejoice together. 14.
May all the gods, worthy of sacrifice and deserving of worship, hear my thought— that is, my hymn of praise— and take it to heart.
Likewise, may both the worlds, heaven and earth, and Apāṃ Napāt, Agni who dwells in the intermediate space, [hear] our [prayer].

1. Those surrounded by *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra* are "supporters of people" (*janabhṛt*). 2. *Kha*, *bha*, and *śa* are the "assembly of people" (*janasaṃgha*); *ta* is the "assembly" (*saṃgha*). 3. *Na* is the "tongue of fire" (*amerjihvā*). 4. *Kha*, *jha*, *na*, and *bha* are called "tongues"; *ta* and *śa* are called "tongues. 5. *Kha*, *gha*, *ma*, and *he* are "sacrificial" (*yajñiya*); *śa* and *ye* are "pertaining to the Maśas" (*maśiya*). 6. *Kha*, *bha*, and *ma* are the "fire situated in the middle" (*madhyasthānāgni*).

Let them hear the hymn. Now, [the verses] addressed directly: O gods, let me not speak words that are to be avoided (*paricakṣyāṇi*)—that is, let me not utter [unfit] hymns unto you (*vaḥ* = *yuṣmabhyam*). Rather, let them be correct. Therefore, being your closest (*antamāḥ* = most proximate) and abiding only in the joys (*sujñeṣpat*) bestowed by you, may we rejoice (*madema* = *modema*). In the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, for the *vaiśvadeva* offering, the invitatory verse (*yājyā*) is "ye ke ca jmā. It is stated in the Sūtra: "O All-Gods, come hither, whoever on earth, the great ones of serpent-like wisdom" (*āśva. śrau. 2.9*). This same verse is the invitatory verse for the *vaiśvadeva* sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). The Sūtra has been cited. **Text:** ye ke ca jmā mahino ahimāyā divo jajñire apāṃ sadhasthe | te asmabhyamiṣaye viśvamāyuḥ kṣapa ustrā varivasyantu devāḥ || 15 || **Translation:** Whoever they may be, the great ones of serpent-like wisdom (*ahimāyāḥ*) who were born upon the earth (*jmā*), or from heaven (*divaḥ*), or in the gathering place of the waters (*apāṃ sadhasthe*), may all those gods (*devāḥ*) grant us full life (*viśvamāyuḥ*) and provide space (*varivasyantu*) for our nourishment (*iṣaye*) through nights (*kṣapaḥ*) and days (*ustrāḥ*). **Notes:** *Mahinaḥ* means "great. *Ahimāyāḥ*: *māyā* is a name for wisdom (*prajñā*); thus, "those whose wisdom is striking" (*āhanuprajñāḥ*). Such gods, whoever they may be, who were born upon the earth—*jmā* is a name for the earth—they appeared on the earth. Whoever they may be who were born from heaven; whoever they may be who were born in the gathering place of the waters, in the intermediate space (*antarīkṣa*): may all those gods, for our nourishment—*iṣaḥ* is derived from *iṣ*, meaning "desired"—for our sons and so forth, grant all life, food, or existence, through all nights and all days, always and without interruption. **Text:** agnīparjanyāvarvataṃ dhiyaṃ me'sminhave suhavā suṣṭutiṃ naḥ | iḷāmanyo janayadgarbhamanyaḥ prajāvatīriṣa ā dhattamesme || 16 || **Translation:** O Agni and Parjanya, protect my thought (*dhiyam*)—that is, the ritual act characterized by sacrifice—at this invocation (*asmin have*). O you who are easily invoked (*suhavā*), protect our beautiful praise (*suṣṭutim*) at this sacrifice. Or rather, the root *ava* is used here in the sense of hearing: "hear us. Between you two, one (*anyaḥ* = Parjanya) generates nourishment (*iḷām* = food) through rain, for by rain plants and trees are born, and from them food is produced. The other (*anyaḥ* = Agni) generates the embryo (*garbham*). Food eaten by man, when cooked by the digestive fire (*jāṭharāgni*), transforms into the form of semen, which becomes the embryo in women. Therefore, bestow upon us (*asme*) food accompanied by progeny (*prajāvatīḥ iṣaḥ*). **Text:** stīrṇe barhiṣi samidhāne agnau suktena mahā namasā vivāse | asminnadya vidathe yajatrā viśve devā haviṣi mādayadhvam || 17 || **Translation:** On the strewn sacred grass (*barhiṣi*), while the fire is kindled (*samidhāne agnau*), with a beautiful hymn (*suktena*) and great reverence (*namasā*), I invite you. O worshipful ones (*yajatrāḥ*), O All-Gods (*viśve devāḥ*), today at this assembly (*vidathe*), rejoice in our oblation (*haviṣi*). 1. kha-prajñānanāma | 2. kha-jña-ta-na-bha-ra- ‘jmāyām’ is not present | 3. kha-1-na-bha- ye ke ca; ja-ṇa- eke ca | 4. ja-ṇa-na | 5. kha-gha-bha-asmākam |

O All-Gods (Viśve Devāḥ), when the sacrificial grass (darbha) has been spread upon the altar (vedi) as a heap, and when the fire has been kindled and fully ignited, I have approached and served you with this hymn of praise and with great reverence.
O all you gods, worthy of sacrifice, on this day, at this our sacrificial assembly (*vidatha*), rejoice in this oblation (*havis*)—
the locative case here having the sense of the instrumental—
be satisfied by the offering given by us.
16 | "vayamu tvā" is the fourth hymn, consisting of ten verses; it is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Bharadvāja and is addressed to Pūṣan.
The verse beginning with "yāṃ pūṣan" is an Anuṣṭubh, while the remaining verses are Gāyatrīs.
And thus it is listed in the Anukramaṇī: "We ten [verses] for Pūṣan; that is in the Gāyatrī meter; 'vai yāṃ pūṣan' is in the Uṣṇih.
This is to be recited by those seeking wealth while traveling abroad.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'vayamu tvā pathaspate'—one who is about to undertake a journey for the sake of wealth [should recite this]" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 3.7.8).
The word "one should mutter" (*japet*) is to be supplied [at the end].

1. O Pūṣan, Lord of the Path, we yoke you for our prayer, like a chariot for the winning of booty. O Pūṣan, Lord of the Path (*pathas-pati*), protector of the way, we yoke you—just as one yokes a chariot in battle—for the sake of our prayer (*dhiye*) and for the acquisition of food (*vājasātaye*). We bring you toward us. The particle *u* is a filler.

Lead us toward manly wealth, toward a hero who bestows liberal gifts; lead us to a desirable householder. O Pūṣan, lead us—to attain—manly wealth beneficial to men, to a hero who specifically drives away poverty, one who has already bestowed wealth upon others (or whose pure sacrificial fee is offered); lead us to such a desirable householder, a master of the home.

O glowing Pūṣan, impel even one who is unwilling to give toward giving; soften even the heart of the usurer. O glowing Pūṣan, urge even a person who is unwilling to give toward the act of giving for our sake. Soften even the mind—the heart—of the usurer, even that of the greedy moneylender, so that he may be inclined to give.

Clear the paths wide for the winning of booty; strike down the adversaries. O Mighty One, may our prayers be fulfilled. O *ugra* (Mighty One), O Pūṣan of fierce power, clear the *pathaḥ* (paths) for *vājasātaye* (the winning of booty)—that is, for the acquisition of food. Make them purified; the meaning is: distinguish such paths by which, having gone, we may obtain wealth. Strike down (*vi jahi*) the *mṛdhaḥ* (adversaries)—the obstructors such as thieves and the like—and drive them away. Likewise, may our *dhiyaḥ* (prayers)—our ritual actions performed for the sake of obtaining food—be *sādhantām* (fulfilled); may they become successful and bear fruit.
1. gha—being kindled;
2. śa—rejoice with Agni;
3. jha—the remainder.

Thus Śaunaka said: "One who, having become pure, constantly recites the hymn beginning with 'vayamu tvā' (RV 6.5.53), which is dedicated to Pūṣan and increases wealth, obtains the desired riches. [Maṇḍala 6, Anuvāka 5, Sūkta 53] End of the Fourth Aṣṭaka, 201.
Pierce through the hearts of the Paṇis with your arrow, O Sage; for our sake, deliver this man to us. || 5 ||
O wise Pūṣan, pierce through the hearts—the hard hearts—of the Paṇis, those greedy traders, with an *ārā*.
An *ārā* is called a goad, a rod with a fine iron point;
with that, pierce them through completely.
The meaning is: "Remove their struck hardness.
Then, immediately after that, subject these Paṇis to us; bring them under our control.

O Pūṣan, pierce with your goad; seek out what is dear in the heart of the stingy one. Deliver this man over to us for our purpose. 6. O Pūṣan, pierce with your goad; seek out what is dear in the heart of the stingy one. Deliver this man over to us for our purpose. 6.

O Pūṣan, pierce through with your goad the heart of the noble merchant and the trader; having pierced it, stir his heart. In that merchant's heart, desire for us—that is, generate the wish—"May wealth favorable to us be given.
Then, immediately after that, subject them to our will; bring them under our control.
Scratch them out, O Sage; rend asunder the hearts of the Paṇis! Deliver this man over to us for our purpose. || 7 ||
O wise Pūṣan, scrape—scratch out—the hearts of the Paṇis, those traders. Having scratched them, rend them apart; make them shattered and scattered. "Mṛdnīhi" means "crush."
The rest is as before.

O Pūṣan, O glowing one, with that goad which you carry, O impeller of prayer, scratch out the heart of this man and tear it to pieces. 8. O Pūṣan, O glowing one, with that goad which you carry, O impeller of prayer, scratch out the heart of this man and tear it to pieces. 8.

O glowing Pūṣan, you who have arrived with brilliance, with that awl which you carry and hold in your hand—the one that impels the sacred word (*brahman*) and incites the priest—scratch, scratch out the hearts of every greedy person!
Rend them asunder, scatter them, and make them utterly shattered!

O Radiant One, that eightfold head-band of thine which wins cattle—that of thee we pray for favor. 9. That of thine, O Radiant One, which is eightfold, a head-band of kine, the winner of cattle—that of thee we pray for favor. 9.
O glowing one, O Pūṣan, those eight spokes of yours which have come to light—
those that lie upon [the nave] are called *upaśas*;
such is that whose *upaśas* are cows.
Therefore, she who brings cattle to completion—that is, she who accomplishes the attainment of cattle—her *sumna*, her happiness which belongs to you, we *īmahe*, we beg for.
1. O you who strike with the whip! 2. O you who impel with the goad!

Furthermore, make our prayer one that wins cattle, wins horses, and wins booty; make it effective for our enjoyment. 10. Furthermore, make our prayer one that wins cattle, wins horses, and wins booty; make it effective for our enjoyment. 10.

Moreover, O Pūṣan, "make" (kṛṇuhi) "our" (naḥ) "thought" (dhīyam)—whether it be the intellect or the ritual action—"for our enjoyment" (vītaye), for consumption; [a thought] which is "winning of cattle" (goṣaṇam), a winner of cows; "winning of horses" (aśvasām), a winner of steeds; "winning of spoils" (vājasām), a winner of prizes or knowledge; and furthermore, "winning of men" (nṛvat), or rather, a giver (vanitrīm) to men. Make it so.
The fifth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "saṃ pūṣan," is the work of Bharadvāja; it is addressed to Pūṣan and is in the Gāyatrī meter.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī entry: "saṃ pūṣan.
It is to be recited by a person seeking lost property.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Pūṣan, [lead] him who knows; [lead] the one who has perished, the one who seeks his kin, or the one who destroys the root" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.7.9).
O Pūṣan, lead us together with one who knows, he who [knows] the unknown.

Whosoever serves him with an oblation, Pūṣan does not neglect him; he is the first to find wealth. (4) Whoever—that sacrificer—who serves him, Pūṣan, with an oblation such as cooked rice or a sacrificial cake (*caru-puroḍāśa*), him Pūṣan does not neglect. The word *api* is used here in the sense of "even slightly"; he does not harm him even in the slightest. And being foremost, he finds and obtains wealth.

May Pūṣan follow after our cows; may Pūṣan protect our horses; may Pūṣan win us strength. (5) May Pūṣan follow after our cows; may Pūṣan protect our horses; may Pūṣan win us strength. (5) Pūṣan, the nourishing deity, shall follow after our cows, going after them for their protection. And that Pūṣan shall protect our horses from harm. Likewise, may Pūṣan win—that is, bestow—strength and food upon us. (5)

O Pūṣan, go forth after the cattle of the sacrificer who presses the Soma, and also after ours who offer praise. (6) O Pūṣan, go forth after the cattle of the sacrificer who presses the Soma; go also after ours who offer praise. O Pūṣan, go forth after the cattle of the sacrificer who performs the pressing of Soma—go in pursuit for the sake of their protection—and also after ours who offer beautiful hymns of praise.

May none of it perish; may none of it be harmed; may none of it be shattered in a pit. Then come with them unharmed. (7) May none of it perish; may none of it be harmed; may none of it be shattered in a pit. Then, with them unharmed, come hither. O Pūṣan, let none of our wealth of cattle perish; let it not be lost. The two words *mākīm* and *mākīm* function merely as prohibitions. May none of it be harmed—let it not be injured by tigers and other predators. And may none of it be shattered in a pit—let it not be destroyed by falling into a well. This being so, come at evening time together with the cattle that are unharmed.

We pray to Pūṣan, who hears us, the active one, whose wealth is never lost, the lord of riches. (8) We pray to Pūṣan, who hears us, the active one, whose wealth is never lost, the lord of riches. (8) We pray for wealth to that god Pūṣan—who listens to our hymns, who drives away poverty, whose possessions are never lost, and who is the sovereign lord of all—such a Pūṣan we implore for riches.
At the Vaiśvadeva parvan during the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the verse "O Pūṣan, in thy ordinance" (*pūṣantava vrate*) is the invitatory verse (*anu-vākyā*) for the oblation to Pūṣan.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "O Savitṛ, what is auspicious today, and what is auspicious tomorrow; O Pūṣan, in thy ordinance we [follow]" (*āśva. śrau. 2. 16*).
1. Kha, jha, ta, na, bha, ra—for the purpose of protection. 2. Kha, jha, na, bha, ya, no—this is ours.
O Pūṣan, within your sacred law, may we never suffer harm;
we here are your praisers.
O Pūṣan, under your protection, may we never suffer harm; we here are your praisers. 9.
O Pūṣan, nourisher, may we who abide in your vow—your ritual act—never at any time suffer harm; may we not be injured.
And being such, may we remain here in this rite as your praisers; we are yours. We become [your praisers].
May Pūṣan place us around from the east; may he bestow upon us the south;
may he cleanse away what has been lost of our wealth.
May Pūṣan place his right hand around us from the front; may he drive back to us what has been lost. 10.

May the nourishing deity Pūṣan place his own right hand around the wealth of cattle belonging to us as we travel toward the distant region—that is, to another place far away, infested by thieves, tigers, and the like—in order to ward it off. May he provide this protection; and may he bring back again our lost cattle-wealth.
May he wait.
20. Fourth Aṣṭaka.

O glowing one, you are a stream of wealth; O possessor of goats for steeds, you are a heap of treasure, the friend of every seeker of wisdom. 3. You are a stream of wealth, O glowing one; a heap of treasure, O you whose steeds are goats; the friend of every seeker of wisdom. 3.
O *āghṛṇi*, you who have arrived with brilliance, O *pūṣan*, you are the stream, the flow of *rāyaḥ*, that is, of wealth;
the meaning is that you bestow abundant wealth continuously upon those who praise you.
O you whose horses are goats!
O Pūṣan, you are one whose horses are indeed goats and sheep, and who possesses the power to perform the tasks of horses; you are a heap and a multitude of *vasu*, that is, of wealth.
The meaning is that the multitude of riches dwells in you alone.
Furthermore, you are the friend and companion of every person who possesses devotion—that is, every man who offers praise.

Now let us praise Pūṣan, the possessor of goat-drawn chariots, the vigorous one; he who is called the lover of his sister. 4. Pūṣan; now; goat-drawn; let us praise; the vigorous one; of the sister; he who; is called; the lover. 4.

He who praises Pūṣan—the one with goats for horses, whose vehicle is the goat, the nourisher, the consumer of *karabhā* (barley-meal mixed with ghee)—he does not praise another person over him; that is, he does not praise any other deity. The meaning is that because Pūṣan alone obtains all the desired wealth, he praises no other god. He praises him by directing [the hymn] toward him, and there is no other to be directed toward or praised. Thus, he praises Pūṣan alone.
And indeed, he, the best of chariot-warriors, Indra, the lord of the virtuous, slays the Vṛtras with his friend as his ally. || 2 ||

With Pūṣan as his companion—meaning joined by Pūṣan acting as a friend—and with him as his ally, Indra, who is renowned for being the slayer of enemies, who is the most excellent of chariot-warriors (*rathītama*), a great warrior (*mahāratha*), and the protector of the virtuous (*satpati*)—smites and kills the *vṛtras*, that is, the enemies.
The meaning is that he is the one who provides assistance even to Indra himself.

And there, upon the speckled ox, the most excellent charioteer, the Sun, set down his golden wheel. 3. And there, upon the speckled ox, the Sun, the most excellent charioteer, set down his golden wheel. 3.

And furthermore, that golden wheel of the chariot— which Pūṣan, the impeller, the best of charioteers, or the supreme leader, set in motion— was made of gold, fashioned from pure gold; it is that wheel of his chariot which he drove forward with great force upon the sun, who is called "Gau" because he moves, and who is "paruṣmat" (possessing joints) or "bhāsvat" (radiant).

O you who are praised by many, O performer of wondrous deeds, O wise one—whatever we shall speak to you today, fulfill that prayer of ours well. 4. Whatever we shall speak to you today, O you who are praised by many, O performer of wondrous deeds, O wise one—fulfill that prayer of ours well. 4.

O you who are praised by many men, celebrated by numerous sacrificers—O Pūṣan, you who are worthy of being seen, you who are most gentle and wise—whatever we may say concerning you today, whatever we may praise you for, and whatever wealth of ours is to be meditated upon, that do you accomplish and bring forth.

And for our gain, O Pūṣan, you are renowned from afar as one who bestows this merit upon us in the search for cattle. 5. And for our gain, O Pūṣan, you are renowned from afar as one who bestows this merit upon us in the search for cattle. 5.
O Pūṣan, lead our journey for the sake of victory and gain; guide this human host toward the search for cattle, O seeker of cattle, and bring it to fulfillment.
O Pūṣan, you are renowned and famous even from afar.
We implore you for well-being, far from evil and bringing us wealth—both today for complete fulfillment, and tomorrow for complete fulfillment. (6)
1. After *kha*, *bha*, and *śa*, [the augment] *at* occurs.

2. After *kha*, *gha*, *jha*, *bha*, and *śa*, [the suffix] *ādi* is used in the sense of "to point out" (*ādiśati*); after *na*, it is used in the sense of "to instruct repeatedly" (*punaḥ-punar-ādiśati*).
3. Also after *gha*, *bha*, and *śa*, [the suffix] *anya* occurs.
4. There is no *jña-ta-ya-‘na*.
5. The meaning is that *kha-na-bha* are the auxiliaries (*sahakārin*).
6. *Kha-jha-ta-na-bha-ra* are for the praise of Indra.
7. Kha, bha, ya, and dyam with reference to [thee]; gha, with reference to thee (tvām); jña, ta, na, ra, and yam with reference to [thee].
O Pūṣan, may there be for thee—belonging to thee and to be granted by thee—a blessed *svasti*, a protection, which has its evil (*agha*) far away;
that is, such that its sin is distant and remote.
I have approached you, one who has attained wealth.
May such prosperity and freedom from evil be ours at this time for the sake of total success (*sarvatāti*).
"Total success" (*sarvatāti*) refers to the sacrifice, for it is protected against all obstacles.
For that purpose;
or rather,
for the expansion of all enjoyments.
And on the following day as well, for the sake of universal welfare—that is, always for the purpose of universal welfare—we entreat and implore [you].
The eighth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “indrā nu pūṣaṇā,” is the seer Bharadvāja’s composition; it is in the Gāyatrī meter and is dedicated to Indra and Pūṣan.
It is announced [in the Anukramaṇī] as: “indrā maindraṃ ca.
Its ritual application has been explained.
Now we call upon Indra and Pūṣan for friendship, for well-being, and for the winning of booty. (1) Now we call upon Indra and Pūṣan for friendship, for well-being, and for the winning of booty. (1)
Because of their mutual conjunction, the dual number is used for both the words *indra* and *pūṣan*:
"We grasp that benevolent favor of Pūṣan and of Indra, as one would grasp the branch of a tree. (5) We grasp that benevolent favor of Pūṣan and of Indra, as one would grasp the branch of a tree. (5)

We grasp—that is, we take hold of, or rely upon—the well-known, auspicious, and benevolent wisdom (sumati) of the nourishing god Pūṣan or of Indra; just as one might grasp the excellent, firm branch of a great tree or a mountain-growth (mahīruha).
This is the meaning.

We draw Pūṣan toward us, as a charioteer draws the reins; we call upon great Indra for our well-being. 6. And we draw Pūṣan toward us, as a charioteer draws the reins; we call upon great Indra for our well-being. 6.
We invoke Pūṣan, the nourishing god, and Indra for great well-being—that is, for the sake of protection. "Invoke" (v yuvāmahe) means we exert ourselves; it implies drawing [them forth].
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Just as a charioteer or driver pulls in the reins— the reins being the cords used for binding the horses— so too [does he].
The fourth hymn, the ninth [of this section], beginning with “śukraṃ te,” is the seerly composition of Bharadvāja; it is dedicated to Pūṣan.
The second verse is a Jagatī, while the remaining verses are Triṣṭubhs.
Thus it has been enumerated: “The [hymn] beginning with ‘śukraṃ’ consists of four [verses]; the second is a Jagatī.”
At the Vaiśvadeva parvan, the *yājyā* for the oblation to Pūṣan is “*śukraṃ te*.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: “*śukraṃ te anyadyajataṃ te anyadideha vaḥ svatavasaḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.16).
This same verse serves as the *yājyā* for the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal sacrifice to Pūṣan belonging to the *ekādaśina* set.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: “One [aspect] of yours is bright, the other is worshipful; Pūṣan was born on the path in the midst of paths” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7). This same verse is also used for the Pravargya sacrifice.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “I beheld one [aspect] of yours as bright, the other as worshipful, the guardian who is never to be approached” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.6).

One of your forms is bright, the other is worthy of sacrifice; you possess two days of different aspects, like the sky. For you, O self-dependent one, protect all wondrous powers. O Pūṣan, may your bounty here be auspicious. *śukram* | *te* | *anyat* | *yajataṃ* | *te* | *anyat* | *vi-rūpe* | *ahanī* | *dyauḥ-iva* | *asi* | *viśvāḥ* | *hi* | *māyāḥ* | *avasi* | *svadhāvaḥ* | *bhadrā* | *te* | *pūṣan* | *iha* | *rātiḥ* | *astu* || 1 ||

O Pūṣan, one day of yours is indeed bright (*śukram*), white in color, consisting of the daytime; likewise, another [day] belonging to you is worthy of worship (*yajatam*). Here, the root *yaj* signifies the act of bringing about union.
One day, called Night, becomes manifestly fit for sacrifice, naturally united [with the other], and black in color; while the other is one [day].
Thus, indeed, by your greatness, two days of different forms—distinguished by their white and black aspects—are produced.
Or rather:

O Pūṣan, one of your forms is bright and stainless, the producer of the day; another of your forms is worshipful, purely worthy of sacrifice, not luminous, the producer of the night. Thus, from these two dissimilar forms of yours, there come to be the two days and nights, which are forms of Viṣṇu.
Since the sun alone is the agent in the creation of day and night, he states how it is that this [agent] is connected to him:
"You are like the sky.
Just as the sky is the illuminator through the sun, so too are you the illuminator.
Why is this? To this he says: O *svadhāvan*, O possessor of food, O *pūṣan*, [protect] all [beings].
(Note: In the variants kha, gha, and bha, the reading is "of Indra and Pūṣan.")
Because you protect all *māyās* (powers of manifestation) through wisdom, for that reason you are like the sun;
such as you are, may your auspicious and beneficial gift (*rāti*) be present here among us.

Yāska says: "One [form] of yours is bright, another is red, one is worthy of sacrifice, and another is worthy of sacrifice"—thus, by your action, you are like the sky with its two days of dissimilar form.
"And all forms of consciousness were established [in him]" (Nirukta 12.17).
Unaging, the guardian of cattle, whose abode is strength, he stirs the prayer; established over all the world, Pūṣan has raised up the eight broad expanses. Surveying all beings, the god moves along.

He whose horses are goats; the guardian of cattle; whose home is strength; the inspirer of the prayer; established throughout the entire world—Pūṣan has sent forth his broad and yielding path. The god, beholding all beings clearly, moves along. 2.
He whose horses are goats, who has goats as his vehicle, the protector of cattle,
whose home abounds in food— such is he who invigorates our prayer.
The *dhiyaḥ* are either the singers or their deeds;
their delighter is *Pūṣan*, who is established by Prajāpati as the nourisher throughout *viśve*—that is, in the entire *bhuvane*, the world.

Being such, the god Pūṣan, the nourisher, *udvarījat*—that is, he raised up—the *aṣṭām* spoke, which was in his own hand and had become *śithirām*, loose.
