Beholding (*saṃcakṣāṇaḥ*) all the worlds (*bhuvanā*), or all created beings, illuminating them through his solar nature, he *īyate*, he moves through the sky.
For the omentum, the iḍā-portion, and the sacrificial cake of the animal dedicated to Pūṣan, the two verses beginning with “yāste pūṣan” are the invitatory verses (anuvākyās).
This is stated in the Sūtra: “‘yāste pūṣannāvo antaḥ samudre’ and ‘pūṣemā āśā anu veda sarvāḥ’” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
O Pūṣan, those golden ships of yours which travel within the ocean in the mid-air—
with those you go on a mission as the messenger of Sūrya, seeking glory out of desire.
O Pūṣan, those golden ships of yours which travel within the ocean, through the mid-air—with those you go on your mission as the messenger of Sūrya, seeking glory, impelled by desire. 3.

O Pūṣan, those golden ships of yours—delightful and made of gold—which travel within the ocean, the great sea, and through the atmosphere in the sky: with those ships you go on the mission of a messenger for Sūrya.

Once, when Sūrya had set out together with the gods for the purpose of slaying the Asuras, his wife became filled with longing for her husband; toward her, Sūrya dispatched Pūṣan, and it is for this reason that Pūṣan is praised here.
Moreover, desiring *śravaḥ*—that is, food characterized by oblations—and being drawn by desire toward the objects of the senses, you have been brought under control by the worshippers.

Pūṣan is the close kinsman of heaven and earth, the lord of nourishment, the dispeller of enemies, possessing resplendent luster— him whom the gods gave to Sūryā, him who was created by desire, powerful and possessed of noble steeds.

Pūṣan, the good kinsman, the lord of heaven and earth, the master of nourishment, who wards off enemies and possesses radiant luster—he whom the gods gave to Sūryā, the strong one fashioned by desire and possessed of noble horses. 4.
1. Kha, jña, ta, na, bha, ra—these are yours; another is for sacrifice to you; another is yours; śa is another; that which is for sacrifice is yours; another is yours. 2.
Jña and bha—there is no "vā" or "īta. 3. Jña—those two days.
Pūṣan, the nourishing god, is the excellent kinsman of both heaven and earth;
likewise, he is the lord of *iḷā* (nourishment/food) and the bountiful one.
*Magha* is a name for wealth;
he possesses that.
Or else:

In the word *magha*, derived from the root *man* in the sense of the act of giving (*bhāvasādhana*), the term signifies "one who possesses gifts. He is "rich in splendor" (*vasuvarcas*). "Splendor" (*varcas*) is a name for form.
He whose splendor is wondrous and beautiful to behold—such [a one], Pūṣan, all the gods gave to Sūryā, the wife of Sūrya—or perhaps to Sāvitrī, she who is named Sūryā, and to the Aśvins and Varuṇa;
for it is heard in scripture: "Pūṣan, as a son, chose his parents" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.85.14).

Of what sort is Pūṣan? He who is *kāmena*—by desire directed toward the future—*kṛtam*, made submissive by the praisers; *tavasam*, powerful or increased; and *svannam*, having good food, or moving well (*su-gacchantam*).
The syntactical connection is that he who gave such a Pūṣan is Pūṣan Subandhu.
The tenth hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "pra nu vocā," is the *ṛṣi*-verse of Bharadvāja and has Indra and Agni as its deities.
The last four verses, beginning with the seventh, are *anuṣṭubh*s; the remaining six are *bṛhatī*s.
Thus it is stated in the *Anukramaṇī*: "Pra nu daśa... [is] for Indra, but it is *bārhata*, ending in four *anuṣṭubh*s."
The application is concluded.
Now, while the juices are pressed, I shall proclaim those heroic deeds which you two have performed:
those enemies, the fathers who were the foes of the gods, have been slain by you; O Indra and Agni, you two still live.
Now proclaim, while the juices are being pressed, those heroic deeds which you two have performed: your fathers, the enemies of the gods, have been slain; O Indra and Agni, you two indeed live on.

O Indra and Agni, you two have performed heroic deeds, deeds of valor, and heroic acts. Regarding those heroic deeds of yours at our sacrifice when the Soma juices have been pressed, I quickly proclaim them to you; I speak them forth.
He demonstrates that very valor:
O Indra and Agni, [you slew] the enemies of the gods.
The gods are those whose kinsmen are enemies;
the Asuras are indeed fathers who are harmful,
for the root *pīy* signifies the act of harming.
This is its form:
such were the Asuras slain by you two;
they were killed, while you two remain alive, possessed of life.
That is to say, "we are not oppressed by the Asuras."
Truly, O Indra and Agni, your greatness is most manifest;
you have a common father, you are brothers, twins born here from the same mother.
Truly, such is your greatness, O Indra and Agni. Your chariot-seat is common; you have a common progenitor; you are twin brothers, born here and there from the same mother.

O Indra and Agni, your greatness—that is, your vastness—is *vat*, truly so, in this very manner; the meaning is that the entire greatness of the sacrifice concerning you is established as being exactly according to reality. Furthermore, Prajāpati, the most excellent (*paniṣṭha*) and most worthy of praise, is the common (*samāna*), indeed singular, progenitor (*janitā*) of both of you.
Therefore, you two monkeys are brothers;
moreover, you are twins born together from the same womb,
such that you have the same mother here and everywhere.
For Aditi is the mother of these two; she alone is the vast earth, as it is heard in the Veda: "O Mother Aditi, here, here."
1. *Śa* = Śobhanabandhu; 2. *Kha*, *Jña*, *Na*, *Bha*—the word ‘enemies’ (*śatravaḥ*) is not present; 3. *Kha*, *Bha* = Jīvavantau; 4. *Kha*, *Jña*, *Jña*, *Ta*, *Na*, *Bha*, *Ra* = is praised.

"Having taken up their abode together at the pressed [juice], like two horses and two chariot-steeds at the feeding-trough, Indra and Agni, the wielders of the thunderbolt, we here invoke you both, the gods, for our protection. (3) Having taken up their abode, at the pressed [juice], together, like two horses, like two chariot-steeds, at the feeding-trough, Indra and Agni, now, with wealth, here, the two wielders of the thunderbolt—we, the gods, invoke. (3)
O Indra and Agni, when the Soma has been pressed and poured out, may you two, being together (*sacā*), united (*sa-ha*), and dwelling together (*okivāṃsau*), come together and meet.
This is a form of the root *uc* meaning "to assemble.
In this regard, there is an illustration.
Like two horses at the time of eating their fodder, like two serpents by nature prone to gliding—
now, therefore, we invoke Indra and Agni here at this sacrifice for the sake of protection.
Due to mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), the dual number is used for both the word *indra* and the word *agni*.
Of what nature are Indra and Agni? They are "vajrins," meaning endowed with weapons; they are "gods" (devau), meaning possessed of qualities such as generosity and the like.

O Indra and Agni, you who increase the sacred order, when one praises you while these Soma juices are pressed—may you, who listen to the words of the speaker who offers the *pajra* oblation, never turn away from us like gods who are indifferent. O Indra and Agni, when one praises you while these [Soma juices] are pressed—O you who increase the sacred order (*ṛtāvṛdhā*), may you two, who listen to the speech of the one offering the *pajra-hoṣin* sacrifice, never fail to be present as gods.

O Indra and Agni, you two who increase the *ṛta*—that is, the truth or the sacrifice—at the pressed-out Soma juices; if that singer were to praise you two in a censurable manner, while you two speak words that are to be relished (*joṣya*)—words that ought to be pleasing as a cause of delight yet are themselves unpleasant—then, O gods, you two would not consume the Soma of that singer, for you two possess the renowned and celebrated sound of praise (*hoṣa*). Thus, O Pajra-hoṣiṇā (you two whose praise is celebrated), you do not partake of it.
*Caná* is a word used for filling out the meter.
Regarding this, the *Nirukta* states: "The term *jāpavāka* is a name whose specific meaning is unknown; it refers to that which is to be recited with approval.
'O Indra and Agni, those who praise you when the soma is pressed and the vessels are joined—you two do not eat of the portion of such a person who increases the sacred rite (*ṛtasya*')."
"Now, as for this woman who speaks ill of us, who has spoken against us, O gods—you two who have been our protectors—do not eat of her [offering]" (Nirukta 5.22).

O Indra and Agni, what mortal man perceives you two gods? One, having yoked his horses that move in different directions, proceeds upon a common chariot. O Indra and Agni, who is this mortal man who perceives you two gods? One, having yoked his horses that move in various directions, proceeds upon a single common chariot.
O you two gods, the radiant Indra and Agni, what mortal man could comprehend this deed of yours?
None at all—this is the meaning. What is that deed?
Yoking to a single chariot—common to both of you for the sake of both purposes—the one Indra, existing as the Sun, having harnessed such horses, moves toward all the world.
Or rather:
yoking to a single, uniform chariot consisting of the year, various-colored, pervasive horses, the one Indra, existing as the Sun, comes to you both.
The meaning is: "Who else could understand this deed of yours as it truly is?"
1. kha-bha-devā devā; 2. kha-jha-bha—there is no ‘vākam’; 3. jha-na—devau; 4. śa—viṣpūcaḥ viṣpak.

O Indra and Agni, footless as she is, this Dawn has come from the former paths; having left behind the heads [of creatures], moving with her tongue, speaking aloud, she has traversed thirty steps. O Indra and Agni! Footless (*apāt*), this Dawn (*iyam*) has come (*āgāt*) from the former paths (*paddhatībhyaḥ*), being the first among the offspring endowed with feet. Thus, as the impeller of living beings—alternatively, having left behind their heads, being herself headless—she moves about, making a loud sound with her tongue, that is, with the organ of speech belonging to living beings. Moving in this way, the Dawn has traversed thirty steps, the thirty constituent *muhūrta*s, passing them over in a single day. This is your work; who would know it?—thus connects with the preceding verse.

O Indra and Agni, for indeed the men stretch their bows in their arms. Do not abandon us in this great contest for wealth, nor in the raids for cattle. O Indra and Agni, the warriors—the men—stretch their bows with their arms; they indeed draw the strings taut. And you two, in this great contest for wealth, which is endowed with much booty to be won, and in the raids for cattle, do not turn away from us; do not forsake us.

O Indra and Agni, the evil, hostile, and inimical forces of the enemy afflict me. Drive them away; remove our enemies and separate them from the sight of the sun. (8) O Indra and Agni, the wicked, daily, and hateful enemies—the hostile armies—afflict me; they oppress me. Drive them away; repel them. Likewise, regarding those who hate us, the haters and enemies, [separate them] from the sun. The particle *adhi* here functions as a marker for the ablative case. Separate them from the sight of the sun; act so that they do not behold the sun. The meaning is: "slay them."

O Indra and Agni, even the treasures of yours—both celestial and terrestrial—are at hand. Bestow upon us here wealth that nourishes all life. (9) O Indra and Agni, even the treasures (*vasu*) belonging to you both—whether celestial (*divyāna*), existing in heaven, or terrestrial (*pārthivā*), existing on earth, pertaining to both worlds—reside indeed with you. For this reason, bestow upon us here in this sacrifice wealth (*rayi*) that provides nourishment for all life (*viśvāyupoṣasam*). (9)

Bestow upon us wealth and a charioteer. Of what sort is this charioteer? One who provides nourishment for all life. *Āyavaḥ* refers to human beings; [it means] sufficient for the nourishment of all men. Or rather, capable of nourishing the entirety of life. There is a Vedic elision of a syllable.
O Indra and Agni, who are borne by hymns and are renowned for your delight in chants,
come hither with all our songs for the drinking of the Soma.
O Indra and Agni, you who are borne by hymns, renowned through invocations, come hither with all our songs for the drinking of this Soma. 10.

O you two who are borne by hymns (*ukthavāhasā*), worthy of being carried by praises and eulogies; O you two who hear the invocation (*havanaśrutā*), listeners to our call—such as you are, O Indra and Agni, come hither with songs of praise (*stomebhiḥ*) and with all our voices (*viśvābhir gīrbhiḥ*), that is, with the words of the scriptures serving as the means.
For what purpose?
For the drinking (*pītaye*) of this our Soma.
The eleventh hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with “śrathadvṛtram,” is the seer’s work of Bharadvāja; it is dedicated to Indra and Agni.
The first three verses each consist of three lines, while the nine verses beginning with the fourth are Gāyatrīs.
The thirteenth is a Triṣṭubh, the fourteenth is a Bṛhatī, and the fifteenth is an Anuṣṭubh.

And thus it has been listed: “*Śrathat pañconā*, [then] the *gāyatrī*; [then] three [verses] beginning with *triṣṭubh*, ending with *anuṣṭubh* after the *bṛhatī*. The application (*viniyoga*) of the hymns has been explained.
In the Varuṇapraghāsa rites, this verse beginning with “*śrathat*” is the *yājyā* for the oblation dedicated to Indra and Agni.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Indra and Agni, come with your aid; you loosen Vṛtra and he wins the prize" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.17).
He who honors Indra and Agni, the two victorious ones, shall indeed slay Vṛtra and win booty;
for they rule over abundant wealth, most powerful through their might, and striving for victory.
He loosens Vṛtra and wins the prize, he who worships Indra and Agni, the two victorious ones, who rule over abundant wealth, most powerful, prevailing by their might, and seeking booty.
That man *shatters*—that is, strikes down—*Vṛtra*, the obstructing enemy;
moreover, he *wins*—that is, obtains—*vāja*, meaning food or strength.
That man who *worships*—that is, serves—*Sahurī*, Indra and Agni, the two who overcome their enemies.
Because they are joined together, the dual number is used in both instances as before.
Of what nature are Indra and Agni?
[They are the lords] of *bhūreḥ*, that is, abundant, and of *vasavyasya*, a collection of wealth (*vasu*).
Alternatively,
the suffix *yat* is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). Thus, "masters of wealth" means the two lords or owners of wealth.

*Irājyati* means "to exercise sovereignty. *Sahasā* means "by force. *Sahastamā* means "the two who are most preeminent conquerors of enemies. *Vājayantā* means "desiring for themselves *vāja*, that is, food characterized by the oblation.
Or else: [it may mean]...
Desiring food, they both wish to bestow strength—vāja—upon their worshippers.
O Indra, now come toward those waters and the sun; they have been brought hither by thee.
O Indra, thou possessor of teams, thou art joined with the radiant waters and the kine of the quarters.

O Indra, now indeed drive hither the kine, the waters, the sun, and the dawns; O Agni, thou hast brought together the quarters and the sun. O Indra, thou art joined with the bright waters, the kine, the dawns, and the teams of horses, O Agni. 2.
1. [The verses] are in the form of praises to Śa.
2. Regarding that which is to be caused to dwell in *kha*, *jha*, *bha*, *ra*, and *va*:

O *indra*, O *agne*, you two—*tā* (those two)—*gāḥ* (cows), *apaḥ* (waters), *udakāni* (waters), *svaḥ* (the sun), *uṣasaḥ* (the dawns, i.e., the times of dawn)—having been carried off by the Paṇis, fight for the sake of these cows and other things. *Yodhiṣṭam*.
With those suns, you two have joined them together.
The word *nūnam* is for the purpose of completing the meter.

O Indra, you have united with this world the quarters—the east and so forth—Svar (the sun), the dawns, the wondrous (*citrah*) and admirable waters, and the cows that had been carried off by the Paṇis. You have brought these together.
Or rather,
the meaning is that you removed the obstruction and separated the quarters and other regions which had been enveloped by the Asuras by slaying those Asuras;
O Agni, being joined with your teams of horses (niyutvān), you likewise performed this very act.
For the omentum of the animal dedicated to Indra and Agni, the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) is "ā vṛtrahaṇā.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "ā vṛtrahaṇā vṛtrahabhiḥ śumbhairā bharataṃ ścatrabāhū" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).

O slayers of Vṛtra, come hither with your Vṛtra-slaying splendors, O Indra and Agni, through our prostrations. O Indra and Agni, be present with us with your most excellent gifts for those who sing your praises.

O slayers of Vṛtra, come hither with your Vṛtra-slaying, beautiful aids, O Indra; with your adorations, O Agni, come toward us. With your gifts and your songs of praise, O Indra and Agni, be present for us with your most excellent [helps]. 3.

O you two slayers of Vṛtra, the destroyers of the Asura Vṛtra—O Indra and O Agni—with your Vṛtra-slaying splendors (śumbhaiḥ), that is, with the powers resulting from the destruction of Vṛtra, and with honors (namobhiḥ) and the riches to be bestowed upon us, come hither toward us;
come both of you, O Indra and O Agni, together with unblemished, great, and most excellent gifts (rādhobhiḥ), and manifest yourselves among us.

On the twenty-fourth day, at the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*), during the *acchāvāka* recitation, the triplet beginning with “*tā huve*” serves as the *stotriya* for the verses by feet (*padahastotriya*).
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: “‘*tā huve*, *yayor idam*, *imam vāmasya manmanaḥ*’” (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.2).
Furthermore, when there is an increase in the *stoma* during the *pṛṣṭhya* and *abhiplava* six-day periods, the nine verses beginning with “*tā huve*” are to be inserted as the *āvāpa*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "‘tā huve yayor idam’ and ‘narā vīryasya manmanaḥ’—these eleven [verses]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.5).
I invoke those two by whom this entire universe was fashioned of old; Indra and Agni do not neglect us.
I invoke those two by whom this entire world was fashioned in the past; Indra and Agni do not neglect us. 4.
I invoke those two such Indras and Agnis;
I call upon them, those two for whom this entire world was fashioned in former times, whose heroic power has been celebrated in the ancient hymns and praised by the seers.
Such is the syntactical connection: "I invoke those two Indras and Agnis."
And those two, Indra and Agni, do not "mardhataḥ"—that is, they do not harm—the worshippers;
therefore, being invoked, let them protect us as well—this is the sense.
The root *mṛdh* has the meaning of harming.
We invoke Indra and Agni, the fierce destroyers of adversaries;
may they be gracious to us in such circumstances.
Fierce, with lightning bolts, we invoke Indra and Agni, the destroyers of enemies; may they both show us mercy for our sake in such times as these.
We invoke Indra and Agni, the two fierce ones, who possess fierce strength and color, the two destroyers who have specifically struck down the enemies;
may those two, Indra and Agni, be gracious to us in this such battle.
Or rather:
The root *mṛḍ* has the sense of compassion;
may they two, being compassionate, show us mercy.
He has slain the Vṛtras of the Āryas; he has slain the Dāsas as he goes forth. [RV 1.33.11] Fourth Aṣṭaka, 215. 1. kha-bha-tā tau | ma. 6 a. 5. sū. 60.
Strike away all our enemies.
He has struck down the noble Vṛtras; he has struck down the Dāsa hosts. He has struck them down as they were rushing forward; he has struck down all our enemies. 6.
Indra and Agni, those two, strike down (*hataḥ*) the *vṛtrāṇi*—the multitudes of calamities—caused by the *āryāḥ*, those who perform their duties for the sake of the noble purpose.
Likewise, Indra and Agni, the *satpatī*, the protectors of the virtuous, [strike down] the *dāsāni*.
The *dāsāḥ* are enemies devoid of ritual action.
And you have struck down the various calamities caused by them;
moreover, you strike down—that is, you destroy—all (viśvāḥ) the hostile (dviṣaḥ) beings who have become our enemies.
Therefore, the sense is: "Act for us in exactly this same way."

On the twenty-fourth day, at the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), during the *acchāvāka* recitation, the triplet for the *ṛtuyājñas* is "O Indra and Agni, you two... This is the *ṛtuyājña* triplet of the six-day period. It is also set forth in the Sūtra: "O Indra and Agni, you two are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) of this sacrifice; O Acchāvāka, the mortal who, with kindled [fire], desires to win favor from Indra, crosses the waters most easily for his welfare. [The verse: *indrāgnī yuvāmime yajñasya hi stha ṛtvijelacchāvāka ya iddha āvivāsati sumnaminrdrasya martya: | chumnāya sutarāṃ apa: || 11 ||* [The word-for-word analysis: *ya:* who; *iddhe* [for *iddhe*] in the kindled [fire]; *āvivāsati* desires to win over; *sumnam* favor; *indrasya* of Indra; *martyaḥ* the mortal; *chumnāya* for his welfare; *sutaraḥ* crossing easily; *apaḥ* the waters. || 11 ||

That mortal man who, when the fire is kindled, offers to Indra a pleasing oblation that brings happiness— [the word for Indra is in the dative sense used with a genitive]— for the sake of that mortal’s splendor, that is, for his radiant food, Indra makes the waters, consisting of rain, exceedingly easy to cross. (The verb "makes" is to be supplied.)

As such, O Aśvins, quickly grant us food accompanied by strength and swift horses, so that we may bring Indra and Agni hither. 12. As such, for us, food accompanied by strength, O Aśvins, quickly grant; [grant] swift horses, so that we may bring Indra and Agni hither. 12.
O Indra and Agni, you two—Indra and Agni—hear the invocation of the sacrificer who presses the Soma.
Enjoy the offerings; come hither and drink the Soma-mead. 15. O Indra and Agni, hear! The invocation of the sacrificer who presses [the Soma]. Enjoy the offerings; come; drink the Soma-mead. 15.
O Indra and Agni, hear the invocation and the hymn of the sacrificer who presses the Soma;
having heard it, enjoy his oblations,
and having enjoyed them, come hither!
And having come, O gentle ones, drink this honey which has Soma as its essence.
This hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with "iyaṃ adadāt," has fourteen verses in total; it is the seer's work of Bharadvāja, and Sarasvatī is its deity.
Of these, the first three are Jagatī meters, the thirteenth is also Jagatī, the fourteenth is Triṣṭubh, and the remaining verses are Gāyatrī.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "This [hymn] of six verses addressed to Sarasvatī begins with a Jagatī and ends with a Jagatī and a Triṣṭubh."
Regarding this, Śaunaka states: “Having become pure in the morning, a twice-born man should mutter this first hymn dedicated to Sarasvatī; he becomes eloquent and wise” (Ṛgvidhāna 2.295).
In the *prauga* litany on the sixth day of the *ṣaḍaha* sacrifice, there is the triplet dedicated to Sarasvatī beginning with “iyamadadāt.”
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "This [verse] beginning with 'iyamadadādrabhasamacyutam' is for the Prauga-śastra" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.1).

This [Sarasvatī] bestowed upon the worshipper Vadhryaśva the impetuous Divodāsa, who was free from debt; she who granted constant nourishment at Ākhvada—those are thy mighty gifts, O Sarasvatī. 1. This one gave to the donor Vadhryaśva the impetuous Divodāsa, who was free from debt; she who gave constant nourishment at Ākhvada—those are thy powerful gifts, O Sarasvatī.

This Sarasvatī gave—bestowed upon Vadhryaśva, the seer of that name who had offered oblations—to her son named Divodāsa, one who violently and swiftly causes the discharge of debts, that is, the remover of debts pertaining to the Vedas, the gods, the ancestors, and the mundane world. She, who from the beginning struck down the insatiable merchant who was constantly haggling and seeking only his own gratification, is the one who gave; such is the connection of the words. Now, she is praised by addressing her directly.
O Goddess Sarasvatī, those various gifts of yours, such as the granting of sons and other boons, are yours; they are *taviṣā*, that is, exceedingly powerful and great.

This one, like a boar with its bristling tusks, has shattered the ridges of the mountains with her powerful waves. With well-fashioned hymns and inspired thoughts, let us invoke Sarasvatī, the slayer of Pārāvata, for our protection. *iyam* (this one), *śuṣmebhiḥ* (with her powers), *bisakhāḥ-iva* (like a boar), *arujat* (has broken), *sānu* (the ridges), *girīṇām* (of the mountains), *taviṣebhiḥ* (with mighty), *ūrmi-bhiḥ* (waves). [We invoke] *pārāvat-ghnīm* (the slayer of Pārāvata), *avase* (for aid), *suvṛkti-bhiḥ* (with well-fashioned hymns), *sarasvatīm* (Sarasvatī), *ā* (hither), *vivāsema* (let us worship), *dhīti-bhiḥ* (with inspired thoughts). 2.
Sarasvatī exists both in the form of a deity and in the form of a river. She has been praised in her form as a deity;
now he praises another Sarasvatī, who is in the form of a river.

This Sarasvatī, in the form of a river, with her drying powers—her own mighty forces—and with her powerful, great waves, shatters (arajat) the ridges (sānu) of the mountains—that is, the mountain peaks bordering her banks—as one who digs for lotus stalks [cleanses the ground]. (Note: 1. *gha-śa-śuṣmebhiḥ* is a variant reading for *śuṣmaiḥ*. 1. *bhanakti* is the root meaning "to break" or "shatter.")
"Bisakhāḥ" means "one who digs up lotus stalks"; just as such a person breaks through the mud for the sake of the lotus stalks, so too [is Sarasvatī].

We would, with well-fashioned hymns (*suvṛktibhiḥ*), with praises, and with mental offerings (*dhītibhiḥ*)—that is, with ritual acts—invite and serve that *Sarasvatī*, the slayer of the *pārāvata* (the distant one), who destroys even trees and other things existing in the distance (*parāvati*), for the sake of protection (*avase*).
Or alternatively:
*pārāvataghnīm* means "killing on both banks," that is, killing those who speak from afar upon the two shores.
*Tayor ghatitīm* means "the slayer of those two."
And it has been said: "The slayer of the pigeon, the destroyer of both banks" (Nirukta 2.24).

O Sarasvatī, strike down the god-haters, the offspring of every deceitful sorcerer. And for the sake of the settlements, you found the waters; you have released them for those who are hostile, O lady rich in steeds.

O Sarasvatī, strike down those who revile the gods; destroy the progeny of every deceitful sorcerer. Furthermore, you found the flowing waters for the settlements; O possessor of the prize, you caused the poison to flow away from them.
O Sarasvatī, you struck down the revilers of the gods— the Asuras— and you slew them; likewise,
[you struck down] the deceptive Vṛṣaya,
the master of all illusions.
"Vṛṣaya" is a name for Tvaṣṭṛ.
You struck down the offspring of Tvaṣṭṛ, namely his son Vṛtra the Asura;
the meaning is that Indra slew him solely through your assistance.
Moreover, O Sarasvatī, rich in food, you found—the waters, that is, the lands seized by the Asuras—for the sake of the *kṣitayas*, the human beings;
and for these men, you caused the poison and the water to flow forth.
Or [alternatively]: [the same].

The *kṣitayas* are the asura folk; from them you obtained—meaning you acquired—the *avanīs*, the earths. Having slain them, you poured forth poison, a venom that became the cause of their death, upon those asuras.
May the goddess Sarasvatī, rich in spoils, protect us with her strengths as the guardian of our inspired thoughts.
May the divine Sarasvatī, rich in spoils through her bounties, protect us—she who is the promoter of inspired thoughts. 4.

The goddess is endowed with virtues such as generosity; she is "possessing strength" (vājinīvatī). That action in which there is *vāja*—that is, food—is "strength-endowed" (vājinī); she is possessed of that.
May Sarasvatī, the protectress and guardian of those who possess inspired thoughts— that is, of the worshippers—
favor us with strength, that is, with foods, and satisfy us preeminently.
O Goddess Sarasvatī, he who invokes you when wealth is at stake is like Indra in the conquest of Vṛtra.
O Goddess Sarasvatī, whoever addresses you when the prize is set, like Indra in the struggle against Vṛtra. ||5||
O Goddess Sarasvatī, that singer who praises you like Indra—when the battle for Vṛtra has occurred and wealth is at stake—he protects him; this is the remainder of the sense.
O Goddess Sarasvatī, you who are swift in the contests for booty, grant us gain like Pūṣan.
O Goddess Sarasvatī, swift one, winner of prizes in contests for booty, bestow upon us gain even as Pūṣan does. 6.
O Goddess, endowed with virtues such as generosity; O Vājini—
*vāja* meaning strength or food—
O Sarasvatī, possessed of that, protect us (*ava*) in battles (*vājeṣu*).
Moreover, like Pūṣan, the nourisher, O God, "rada"—that is, scratch out or bestow—upon us a "sanim," a desirable wealth worthy of being honored. This is to say: grant it to us.

1. *Kha*, *bha*: the example is "he splits" (*bhinatti*); *ta*, *bhu*: "he enjoys" (*bhunakti*). 2. *Kha*, *bha*: "O King, Indra is your companion. 3. *Śa*: "of whom" (*yasyāḥ*). 4. *Jña*, *ta*, *ra*, *śa*: the term "in action" (*kriyāyām*) is not present. 5. *Kha*, *gha*, *bha*, *śa*, *ta*: "that you [are]. 6. *Gha*: "she protects" (*rakṣati*).

And may that Sarasvatī, the terrible one whose path is golden, the slayer of Vṛtra, desire our fair praise. (7) And may that well-known Sarasvatī—the terrible one who strikes fear into her enemies, she whose path is golden (the *vartanī* is that by which one moves, namely a chariot; she is so called because her path consists of gold), the slayer of Vṛtras (the destroyers of enemies)—desire, that is, long for, our beautiful hymn of praise.

Of whom [Sarasvatī], this infinite, unimpelled, trembling, moving ocean, the impetuous force, moves along, resounding loudly. (8) Of this Sarasvatī, the infinite—unmeasured, limitless, unimpeded, or not crooked; the trembling—shining; the moving—having the nature of movement, with a steadiness of motion unobstructed everywhere; the ocean—possessing water, meaning the giver of water; being such, and moving—proceeding while making a loud sound—he exists. This connects with the following verse: "May she [grant] us all... (9).

May she carry us across all enemies, she who flows with her sisters, the observer of *ṛta*, as the sun extends the days. (9) May she—Sarasvatī—carry us, us, across all, across every hostile people; may she lead us beyond them. Likewise, may she, flowing by herself (*svasṛ*), born together [with her sisters], the observer of *ṛta*—*ṛta* being a name for water, and thus "she who possesses it"—may she, along with the other rivers, carry us across. Or rather, [the form] is like *jasya*; by the rule "optionally in the Veda" (*vā chandasi*), there is a long vowel of the same quality as the preceding. May the sisters who possess water, and the other rivers such as the Gaṅgā and so forth, carry us across our enemies. Therein is the illustration: as the sun, the impeller of all, the Āditya, constantly moving, [crosses] as it were the days; just as he carries the days swiftly across, even so [may she].
On the third day of the *daśarātra*, in the *prauga* [śastra], there is the triplet dedicated to Sarasvatī beginning with "uta naḥ priyā.
This is set forth in the Sūtra: "uta naḥ priyā priyāsvivoṣṇīha praugam" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.10).
In the *pavitreṣṭi*, "uta naḥ priyā" serves as the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the oblation to Sarasvatī.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Moreover, these our dear ones among the dear ones, offering with obeisances unto you... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.12).

And may Sarasvatī, who is dear among our dears, the one with seven sisters, and well-beloved, become worthy of praise for us. (10) And moreover, may she who is dear among our dears—dearer than the dear—the one with seven sisters (*saptasvasā*), whose sisters are the seven meters beginning with Gāyatrī; or, in her form as a river, whose sisters are the seven rivers such as the Gaṅgā; she who is well-beloved (*sujuṣṭā*), having been served excellently by the ancient seers—may such a goddess Sarasvatī become worthy of praise (*stomyā*), that is, she shall be praised. (31)

Having filled the earthly realms, the wide atmosphere, and the intermediate space, may Sarasvatī protect us from revilers. (11) *Āpapruṣī*—having filled; *pārthivāni*—the things pertaining to the earth; *uru*—wide; *rajaḥ*—the regions; *antarikṣam*—the intermediate space, the sky situated between [heaven and earth]; *sarasvatī*—the goddess Sarasvatī; *nidaḥ*—from revilers; *pātu*—may she protect us. The goddess Sarasvatī, having filled with her own splendor the earthly realms (*pārthivāni*) belonging to the earth, the vast (*uru*) and extensive (*vrajaḥ*) worlds (*rajaḥ*), and the intermediate space (*antarikṣam*) that lies between, may she protect us from revilers (*nidaḥ*)—that is, from enemies who speak ill of us. May she guard us.
1. [The suffix] *rā* occurs after [stems ending in] *jha*, *ta*, and *ṛt* when they signify "possessing water" (*udakavatī*).
2. [The suffixes] *kha*, *jha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra* are Vedic (*chāndasa*).
3. [The suffixes] *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *ya* occur after [stems ending in] *nadī* and others.

Abiding in three stations, consisting of seven elements, nourishing the five born ones—she has become worthy of invocation in every battle. (12) *Triṣadhasthā*, *saptadhātuḥ*, *pañca*, *jātāḥ*, *vardhayantī*, *vāje-vāje*, *havyā*, *bhūt*. "Abiding in three stations" (*triṣadhasthā*) means dwelling together in the three worlds, pervading the three worlds. "Consisting of seven elements" (*saptadhātuḥ*) means she whose constituent parts (*dhātavaḥ*) are seven—either the meters beginning with *gāyatrī* or the rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā. "Nourishing the five born ones" (*pañca jātā vardhayantī*) means she who causes the five classes of beings to flourish—the four castes with the Niṣādas as the fifth, or the Gandharvas and others. Sarasvatī, being such as this, has become "worthy of invocation" (*havyā*) in "every battle" (*vāje-vāje*), that is, in all battles. She is to be offered as a sacrifice.

She who is distinguished among these rivers by her greatness, who excels others in beauty and is the most skillful of workers; vast as a chariot, fashioned for all, she is Sarasvatī, who is to be praised and is ever manifest. 13. *Obeisance to Śrī Gaṇeśa.* She who is distinguished among these [rivers] by her greatness, who [surpasses] others in splendors, who is the most skillful of workers; vast like a chariot, fashioned for all, she is to be praised—she is known as Sarasvatī.
13. *Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.*
I bow to that elephant-faced one, by saluting whom at the commencement of all undertakings, Vāgīśa and the other wise ones become successful in their aims.
I salute that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose very breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now begins the first chapter of the fifth Aṣṭaka. In the sixth Anuvāka of the sixth Maṇḍala, there are fourteen Sūktas.
Among them, the first Sūkta, consisting of eleven Ṛcas, begins with "stuṣe narā."
In this regard, the *Mantramaṇikā* states: “The stūpa, however, belongs to the eleven Aśvins.
The seer (*ṛṣi*) is Bharadvāja, the descendant of Bṛhaspati;
the meters are *anuṣṭubh* and *triṣṭubh*.
The Aśvins are the deities.
These two hymns beginning with "idam" are used in the Prātaranuvāka of the Āśvina ritual,
and they are also used in the Āśvina Śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "In the hymn beginning with 'I praise the Hero' (stuṣe nara...), [one should perform the rite]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.15).

I praise the two heroes; awakening with hymns of praise, I call upon the Aśvins, the dispensers of this heaven—those who at the dawning of the dawn instantly traverse the ends of the earth and across the wide expanses. I praise the two heroes; awakening with hymns of praise, I call upon the Aśvins, the dispensers of this heaven—those who at the dawning of the dawn instantly traverse the ends of the earth and across the wide expanses.

I praise with hymns (*arkaiḥ*)—accomplished by non-chanted mantras—and with chants (*stotraiḥ*)—accomplished by chanted mantras—the two Aśvins, who are the leaders of heaven, the masters of this world, the bestowers, the protectors, and the lords, accompanied by their horses; praising them, I invoke them. To the question of what they are like: [the following description follows].

Those two, who are indeed bountiful and warders-off of enemies, at the dawning—the end of the night—separate on all sides the vast expanses of the earth’s boundaries and the wide, concealing darknesses of form;
or rather, they spread abroad their splendors by warding off the darkness.

Moving toward the sacrifice with your swift movements, you have caused the splendor of your chariot to shine through the mid-air. Measuring out many immeasurable expanses, you pass over the waters and the desert wastes on your course. 2. Moving toward the sacrifice with your swift movements, you have caused the splendor of your chariot to shine through the mid-air. Measuring out many immeasurable expanses, you pass over the waters and the desert wastes on your course.
Furthermore, those two well-known Aśvins, coming toward our sacrifice—that is, approaching our ritual—with their own pure rays of light;
for it is said, “*rajas* is called dust, *rajas* is light, *rajas* is splendor” (Nirukta 4.19). (Gha, Ta, Bhāradvāja)
2. The deities of *gha*, *jha*, *na*, and *bha*; the deity of *kha*. 3.

In the *prātaranuvāka* and *āśvina* sacrifice of *ga*, *jha*, *na*, and *bha*; in the *prātaranuvāka* and *āśvina* sacrifice of *jha* and *śa*; in the *prātaranuvāka* and *āśvina* sacrifice of *ta* and *ya*.
4. *Jha*: *abhicakramāṇī*.
Yāska has said:
"They have caused the *bhānu*, the brilliance, of their own chariot to shine;

moreover, measuring out many (*puru*) and immeasurable (*amitā*) rays of light (*varāṃsi*) which dispel darkness, you two pass over the waters, the desert regions, and the food—namely, your own horses."

O you two fierce ones, with your horses swift as thought, vigorous and capable of enduring the journey, you have always carried away that firm and narrow path for the mortal who offers oblations, so that he may find rest.

Then indeed was that protection, when you two, O fierce ones, truly brought hither your thoughts for the sake of the one who has offered, with horses swift as thought, vigorous and ever-present, to ward off the distress of the mortal donor.

O powerful ones, O mighty Aśvins, you two indeed go to that house of the sacrificer which is deficient, unsuccessful, or obstructed, in order to restore it. Moreover, with these swift, desirable, and mind-swift horses—horses as fleet as thought—you have always carried the worshippers, those who possess devotion, to heaven. Let the affliction of the mortal man, the sacrificer who offers oblations—the one who causes harm—be made into a state of rest for you both, a long sleep.

Let him, yoking his steeds, come to the prayer of the newest singer who adorns it; bringing splendor, nourishment, and strength, may the two Hotṛ-priests, striving together, worship you in your forms.

To the prayer of the newest singer who praises you, come near as you attend to it. Having yoked your seven horses, bringing splendor, nourishment, refreshment, and strength, let the ancient, guileless Hotar-priest worship the two youthful ones.
Those two Aśvins, having yoked their seven-horsed chariot— horses being harnessed to the vehicle— bringing beautiful splendor (*śubham*), nourishing food (*pṛkṣam*)—

for "milk is *pṛkṣa*" is read among the names for food— and bringing refreshment (*iṣam*), prosperity (*puṣṭim*), and strengthening sap (*ūrjam*), attend upon and approach the hymn (*manma*), the object of thought, of the newest one who is chanting praise.
Or rather:
they are present near the hymn of praise.
Furthermore, let those two—young, eternally youthful—the invoker who calls upon the gods, the guileless, the benevolent, the beloved, the ancient Agni, perform the sacrifice.
I invoke with a new hymn those two ancient, beautiful, and most bountiful Dasyūs,
who have become the greatest bringers of bliss to the one who recites and praises them, bestowing wonderful gifts even upon the singer.

Those two who are called "the Lovely Ones," the destroyers of enemies, most bountiful to many, ancient yet renewed by our newest speech—I invoke them with my song. They have become the most beneficent to him who recites and praises; they, whose gifts are wondrous, are ever ready for the singer. 5.
1. kha-atikrāmathaḥ; 2. kha-ca-a-na-bha-pariśayanārtham; ta-pariśayanārthyai; 3. kha-gha-jha-na-bha-kriyate; 4. tara-śravaḥ; 5. kha-to vā haṃtā; ta-hotā; bha-tau vā hotā; 6. ya-sarvapriyaḥ.
[Maṇḍala 6, Adhyāya 6, Sūkta 62] Fifth Aṣṭaka 223.

To the person who praises with *śakha* hymns, who offers praise, and who lauds with *stotra* chants—to that person they have become most beneficent (*śambhaviṣṭhā*), being the greatest bringers of happiness or the very essence of bliss; to the one who sings, praising with worldly hymns distinct from the *stotra* and *śastra*, they have become givers of manifold gifts (*citrarātī*), possessing wonderful bounty. They two are *valgū*, moving gracefully or beautiful; they are most full of deeds (*puruṣākrtamā*) or possess many helpers; they are *pratnā*, ancient and primordial.

Because "pratnaṃ pradiptaḥ" (the ancient, the kindled) occurs among the names for the Purāṇa, I worship with a newer, more recent hymn—the two Aśvins, who are *dastrā*, meaning beautiful to behold. I attend upon them with praise.
You two carried Bhujyu out from the ocean, the son of Tugra, through the mists;
traversing leagues with dustless, winged steeds, he emerged from the waters for us.
You two carried Bhujyu, the son of Tugra, out from the ocean across these three spaces by means of dustless, winged steeds that traverse a league, delivering him from the lap of the waters. 6.

O Aśvins, you two indeed rescued Bhujyu—the son of Tugra—whose ship was submerged in the midst of the ocean, protecting him; with dustless, aerial paths, with leagues traversed by yoked chariots, and with winged horses that fly like birds, you brought him out from the lap of the waters, from the womb of the sea.
The expression "from the sea, O Aṅgas" is used in the same manner as the phrase "going to his mother's house."
Come hither with your life-giving chariot, O famous ones; O bulls, answer the call of Vadhryamati.
Let yourselves be seen by Śayu; you made the cow swell with milk for Gharma—O Cyavānas, you who are swift and full of benevolence.

With your life-sustaining power, O chariot-borne ones, come to the mountain; hear the call of Vadhryamatī, O bulls! You made the cow swell for Śayu; thus, O Cyavānas, you who are ever-active, you brought forth favor.
O Aśvins, with your swift and victorious chariot, you two drove apart—that is, you shattered—the mountain situated in your path;
here the root *yā* signifies the act of striking.
Thus, another Vedic verse says: “O Nāsatyas, undecaying ones, you went through the mountains with your piercing chariot” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.20).

O you two showerers of desires, hear the invocation—the call—of Vadhrimatī, who desired a son. Bestowing boons upon those worthy of honor, you two caused the cow of Śayu, who was praising you, to swell with milk—that is, you restored her fertility.
Thus says another Vedic passage: “O Nāsatyas, by your powers, you caused the cow of Jaṃsuri, though barren, to swell for Śayu” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.22).
Thus, being of good mind and receiving excellent praise, you two who move swiftly—going everywhere or supporting the sacrifice—come hither.

Whatever abundance of wrath there is from the two worlds, from of old, whether among the gods or among mortals—O Ādityas, Vasus, and Rudriyas, destroy that which seeks to harm us; bestow upon us what is strengthening.

Whatever offense against the gods or against mortals exists from of old upon the two worlds and throughout the earth—that, O Ādityas, Vasus, and sons of Rudra, destroy; deprive the one allied with the Rākṣasa of his food. 8.

O *rodasī*, Heaven and Earth; O Ādityas; O Vasus; O Rudriyas, the Maruts, sons of Rudra—whatever great wrath (*heḷaḥ*) exists among mortals, toward the attendants of the Aśvins, that wrath, burning and tormenting, do you cast down upon the one who delights in Rākṣasas, or upon the lord or instigator of the Rākṣasas; strike him down, make him low!
Or else, against the sacrificer who is joined with Rākṣasas, cast down that wrath and strike him low.
He who, like a king, has established these [laws] unerringly in the mid-air—he is Mitra and Varuṇa, the mindful one.
Against the deep-seated demon, he hurls his weapon; against the deceitful one of wondrous luster who dwells in the ocean.

May he who knows Mitra and Varuṇa, the two kings who maintain the regions in their proper order according to the seasons—may he direct his missile against the deep-seated demon, even against the deceitful one who seeks to harm the splendor of the ocean.

The two Aśvins, who are the sovereign rulers of all the *rajas*— for Yāska has stated that "the worlds are called *rajāṃsi*"— and who he serves by attending upon them at the proper times (*ṛtuthā*), may Mitra and Varuṇa take notice of him; may they know him.

The meaning is that the gods, such as Mitra, Varuṇa, and others, know him. Furthermore, this attendant hurls— that is, casts— a *heti*, a weapon that slays, at the *rakṣas*, the demon of profound and great power.
There is an exchange of the third person for the second person.
"Against the treacherous one"—that is, against one whose nature is malice—"against the speech of man," that is, even against mere human speech, he hurls his weapon;
he attacks him for the sake of harming human beings.
With your inner wheels and with smoke, come to the son of Stanayitnu on your swift-moving chariot;
with your destructive power against the mortal, strike off the heads of those who seek to harm us.

With your inner wheels, with your circles, for the sake of our offspring, come hither with your protective, resplendent, and well-furnished chariot. Cast down the heads of the mortal who seeks to harm us and those who desire to do us injury. 10.
He [goes] with the Aśvins, joined with inner, non-rugged wheels, and with a bright, glowing, and resonant leader-charioteer;
or rather,
with one yoked with horses.
Because "pataṅgāḥ naraḥ" is listed among the names for horses (Nirukta 1.14.22),
[come] by chariot to our dwelling, to our *vartir*, in order to grant a son to our offspring.
Moreover, [come] with your hidden *sarṇutya*— that is, with your *tyajas* or wrath.

Because "haṇiḥ tyajaḥ" is listed among the names for anger; and because Yāska has stated that "vanuṣyati" is a verb meaning "to strike," [it refers to] "martyasya," i.e., of the mortal man, and "vanuṣyatām," i.e., of those who assail or oppress.
You have even torn away their heads;
come with your supreme, your middle, and your lowest teams of horses.
Break open the doors of the firm enclosure for the one who praises you, O you of wondrous bounty.

Come hither with your supreme teams, with your middle ones, and even with your lowest teams! Open wide the doors of the stall, however firm it may be, that is rich in cattle, for the singer who bestows wonderful gifts, O you who grant wealth from your dwelling! 11.

1. *gha-jña-ta-na-śa-bhūma*; 2. *kha-a-na-bha-ahantu*; 3. *kha-aghamahanta*; *jña-ta-na-śa-aghamahantu*; 4. *kha-jña-na-bha-paricaran*; *gha-paricaran*; 5. *tha-mitrāvaruṇa*; 6. *kha-bha-śara-na tu manuṣyāṇāmabhi*; *jña-ta-na-nanu manuṣyāṇāmabhi*; 7. *ta-evam*; 8. *kha-jña-na-bha-śara-āskandatīti*; 9. *kha-jña-bha-ya-śa-pravaktam*; *gha-chinatam*.
O Aśvins, come hither toward us with your teams of horses—whether they be the most excellent and superior, or even those that are middling and not superior, or the lowest and inferior.
Open wide the doors of the cow-stall, even though it be firm and firmly closed, and filled with cattle.
Furthermore, O you of wondrous bounty, be providers of manifold gifts for me who praises you.
2. The second hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with “Ka tyā,” is the seerly composition of Bharadvāja.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “Ka tyā... ending with a single-footed verse; [the meter] is Triṣṭubh.”
The eleventh verse, “ā vāṃ sumne,” is a one-footed *triṣṭubh*; the remaining verses are *triṣṭubhs*.
Having stated, “But [this] belongs to the Aśvins,” the two Aśvins are also the deities of this hymn.
Its application (*viniyoga*) has been stated for the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra* in the *triṣṭubh* meter.

Who, O much-invoked one, has praised those two beautiful ones for you like a messenger? For your sake, the praise has been offered; the pressing of Soma has been performed. That which was to be done has been accomplished.
The sacrificial grass (*barhis*), most easy of access and most gentle, has been spread out and strewn.

With hands extended and palms joined in reverence, the Hotṛ priest, desiring you both, pays homage and praises you. "Seeking you"— that is, pervading you— [using] the verbal root *nakṣ* (as in *tṛkṣ*, *pṛkṣ*, *nakṣ*), meaning "to go" or "to pervade."
The pressing-stones, indeed, have manifested the Soma juice on all sides for Bhadra.
Your flame has stood upright at the sacrifices; the offering goes toward the glowing, butter-dripping ladle.
The Hotṛ-priest, with a mind full of praise, choosing [the gods], has yoked those who possess the Nāsatyas as his sacrificial food.

Agni has stood erect at the sacrifices; the glowing, butter-dripping ladle goes forth as an offering. The Hotṛ-priest, chosen with a well-disposed mind, has yoked those two Nāsatyas who possess the sacrificial oblation. 4.
O Agni, for the sake of your sacrifice, you have risen up;
in the sacrificial rites (*vadhvareṣu*), being well-kindled, you proceed and go toward the *āhavanīya* fire.
O observer of vows (*vrati*), you are the wealth, the oblation, and the one who moves forward.
As Yāska has stated [in Nirukta 6.4], "jūrṇiḥ is from the root *ju* (to hasten).
*Ghṛtācī* means "anointed with ghee," that is to say, spread out and sprinkled with ghee.

Furthermore, the Hotṛ priest—who makes wide space (*urūṇaḥ*), who is one whose mind is intensely engaged (*pragūtamanaḥ*)—yokes the two Aśvins, the Nāsatyas, to the invocation (*havīrman*) or to the hymn of praise (*āhlāne*).
For the sake of glory, the daughter of Sūrya mounted the chariot, O you of many enjoyments, for a hundredfold protection.
By means of your wondrous powers, O masters of illusion, you two became manifest, O heroes, dancers among men, the progenitors of those worthy of sacrifice.

For the sake of glory, the daughter of Sūrya mounted the chariot of the two who enjoy many blessings, she of a hundred aids. By means of your wondrous powers, O masters of magic, you became manifest here, O heroes, the dancers among those worthy of sacrifice. 5.

O Aśvins, you two of many arms— meaning you who possess full arms or are the protectors of many— the daughter of Sūrya, Sūryā, for the sake of beauty (śriye), mounted (tasthau) upon your chariot (ratham), which possesses a hundred protections (śatāvitim) or many movements (bahugamanam).
Furthermore, at this birth (janini)— that is, in this manifestation among the gods worthy of sacrifice (yajñiyānām devānām)— she stood there by means of your wondrous powers (māyābhiḥ),
for "śacī" and "māyā" are listed among the synonyms for wisdom (prajñā).
O two masters of illusion (*māyin*), wise ones, leaders, men, dancers, you have become possessed of great power.
Or rather:

O two masters of illusion, wise ones, leaders, men, dancers—the Aśvins—you have, through your powers of illusion (*māyābhiḥ*), whether understood as insights or skills, conquered the most wise god, Agni and the others, at the birth, the manifestation, of the gods worthy of sacrifice. This is the meaning.
The meaning of this is made clear by such passages as: "Prajāpati gave his daughter Sūryā Sāvitrī to King Soma" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 4.7).
With these glorious, visible splendors, you two brought auspicious nourishment to Sūryā;
our well-praised song has flown forth toward you two for the sake of beauty, O ye who are worthy of hymns, O ye who possess divine wisdom.

With these visible splendors, O auspicious ones, you two brought nourishment for Sūryā. Our song of praise has followed after your beauty; O wise ones, worthy of hymns, the well-praised Akṣadrāṇī honors you both. 6.

O Aśvins, you two, by means of these beautiful and visible splendors, fortunes, or radiances, brought about nourishment and fulfillment for the sake of the beauty of Sūryā, your wife. Moreover, your horses followed after you with great speed for the sake of your majesty. Furthermore, O worthy ones, O Aśvins deserving of praise, the well-uttered speech—the hymn of the seers—reaches unto you both.
May your winged horses, the best at carrying, bring you toward the offerings, O Nāsatyas;
your chariot, swift as thought, has been let loose, following the many ancient nourishments.

O Nāsatyas, may your birds and your most swift horses carry you toward the offerings. Your mind-swift chariot has been sent forth; it follows many refreshments, winged foods, and strengthening draughts. 7.
O Nāsatyas, may your two steeds—swift-moving, most excellent carriers—bring toward you the *praya*, the food consisting of Soma.
Your chariot, swift as thought, has been released; your wings, your desirable offerings, and your many, abundant foods, the Soma-libations, have been set forth.
For many indeed are the gifts for you two, O possessors of much wealth; make our cows swell with inexhaustible nourishment.
Both praise and fair hymn belong to you, O lovers of sweetness, as do the juices that have followed your bounty.

O you who enjoy many things, indeed, your gift is manifold; make our cow swell with nourishing food that never fails. O lovers of sweetness, may our hymns of praise and our well-spoken eulogies reach you, as do the juices that follow your bounty. 8.
O you two of many enjoyments—meaning, O you who possess full enjoyment or are the protectors of many—the wealth (*deṣṇam*) to be given by you both is indeed abundant (*puru*).
For this reason, grant us a cow that provides nourishment, one that does not fail (*asrakām*), and one that does not wander elsewhere than to me;
for Yāska has stated, "‘Asrakā’ means ‘not wandering elsewhere’" (Nirukta 6.29).
Make food swell; that is, bestow it. Or rather, the construction is: "Make the cow, which is to be sought as food (iṣa), swell."
Furthermore, "praised" (*stutaḥ*): those who praise are the "praisers" (*stotāraḥ*);
they exist.
The sweet intoxicating sound of the Aśvins and the beautiful praise exist among the worshippers;
and there are the juices— the juices of Soma—
which have come forth toward the place of sacrifice, directed toward your gift, O you two.
The meaning is this:
having heard the excellent praise, [the two gods] should drink the Soma juices at the place of sacrifice for the gods and grant desires to the worshippers; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
And for me, the skillful one, Puraya gave a hundred [cows] at Sumīḷha and Pukā;
Ṣāṇḍa gave two golden [ornaments], Sphiṣṭin ten heifers, and Abhisāca the tall ones.

Moreover, for my sake, Puraya gave two swift mares, well-fed, along with Śata, Paruka, and Puka; and Śāṇḍa gave golden-horned oxen, well-directed, conspicuous, powerful, and accompanied by female cattle. ||9||
Moreover, when the city named Pura was being attacked, two swift-moving mares, moving straight forward, became my [means of escape] as I offered praise to the Aśvins.
While Suram̐has was ruling, the cows were mine;
while Peruka was king, the cooked sacrificial offerings were mine.

May the Aśvins grant to their worshippers ten chariots—each with seven yokes, made of gold, golden-hued, with seven horses, excellent in appearance, swift as horses, obedient, overcoming enemies, lofty, and beautiful to behold.
O Nāsatyas, may he who has many paths grant you hundreds and thousands of horses for my song;
O heroes, grant them now to Bharadvāja for his song! May the demons be destroyed, O performers of many wonders.

O Hero, Purupanthas has given you hundreds and thousands of horses for your song; he has given them to Bharadvāja for his hymn. He slays the demons and makes the paths easy to traverse, well-marked, and pleasant to travel.
Furthermore, the wealthy Dawn has become a source of riches, a praiseworthy and capable sacrificial gift.
The auspicious one has been seen; you shine far and wide, and your flame spreads out as it follows the path of the sun.
Making your chest manifest, O Goddess Dawn, you shine brightly with your great splendors.

O auspicious one, you are seen; you shine far and wide. Your flames and rays have ascended to their station. Making your breast manifest, you make it beautiful as you shine upward, O Goddess, with your great splendors.
O Goddess Uṣas, you have appeared—you are seen—as auspicious and beautiful;
you shine forth widely and extensively. Of your radiance, of your light...
There is elision (*luk*) of the *jas* [suffix].
The shining rays of light rise up into the sky;
moreover, O Goddess Uṣas, shining, gleaming, and blazing with great splendors, you reveal—that is, you make manifest—your own form, your breast-like appearance.
The ruddy, radiant bulls draw him as he spreads far and wide toward the auspicious earth;
like a hero with a bow, he drives away his enemies, and like a swift steed, he presses on through the darkness.

The ruddy, radiant rays of light carry her forth; she who is auspiciously blessed, spreading herself far and wide. Like a hero shooting at his enemies with a bow, she drives away the darkness; she is like a swift steed that carries its rider.
The ruddy ones—red-colored, shining, and swift—are the rays;
for "rays" are listed among the names for "cows. They carry this goddess Uṣas, who is auspiciously radiant, far-extending, and wide-spreading.
This very Uṣas, like a hero at dawn and like a brave warrior at sunset, drives away the darkness as a hunter [drives away] his enemies;
she, the bearer of the army, like one who moves swiftly, dispels the darkness just as she repels the foes.
O well-guided one, lead us by good paths through the mountains; O self-luminous one, bring us across the waters.
O daughter of heaven, you who travel on broad paths, bring to us, O noble one, wealth sufficient for our sustenance.

O Goddess of fair countenance, easy indeed are your paths across the mountains and through the windless air; you cross over the waters, O self-luminous one. As such, O daughter of Heaven, bring us wealth from the vast realm for our nourishment, O exalted lady upon your wide-reaching path.
O Goddess Uṣas, even on the mountains and even in difficult places—a region devoid of means of travel—your paths become fair paths, easy to traverse, and pleasant to walk upon.
O you of self-luminous splendor, *āpaḥ* refers to the intermediate space, the sky; for "āpaḥ" is listed among the names for the intermediate space.

O Daughter of Heaven, born from the mid-air, O lofty and beautiful Dawn, you who cross over the waters of the ocean with your broad path and wide chariot— O Goddess, bring to us that desirable wealth for our enjoyment.
1. In manuscripts Kha, Jha, Ta, and Śa, it is seen.
2. In manuscripts Kha, Gha, Jha, Ta, Na, Bha, and Śa, the word "śatrūn" (enemies) is absent.
3. In manuscripts Kha, Gha, Jha, Ta, Na, Bha, and Śa, it is "iva" (like).
O River, you flow with bulls; you carry the waters according to your own choice and pleasure.
O Goddess, Daughter of Heaven, you have appeared in greatness at the first invocation.

She—O Dawn, who with thy bulls hast brought us hither, and according to thy pleasure bringest what we desire; thou, O Daughter of Heaven, who as a Goddess hast appeared with greatness at the first invocation! 5.
O Dawn, as such, bring to me that excellent wealth— you who, unassailed and unopposed, according to your pleasure, bring what is desirable to the worshippers by means of bulls, oxen, or horses;

furthermore, O Daughter of Heaven, O Daughter of the Mid-region, you who, as a radiant goddess, are worthy of honor with great praise at the first invocation, the morning litany (prātaranuvāka)—you are she who has become visible, the one to be beheld. Such is the construction.

If that which was shown [as the subject] were *bhūḥ* by virtue of its co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word *yad-vṛtta*, then the *bhūḥ* would not be subject to the *nighāta* (anudātta) accent.
Even the birds have flown up at dawn, as have the men who share in the portion of the fathers;
O Goddess Dawn, you bring much that is desirable to the mortal who gives offerings and dwells at home.

Even the birds have flown forth from their dwelling; and the men who share in the portion of the Fathers at the break of dawn—O Goddess Uṣas, you bring abundant wealth to the mortal who dwells at home and offers oblations.
O Goddess Uṣas, at your true dawning, even the birds (vayaḥ) fly up from their dwelling places (vasateḥ).
And those who partake of the ancestral offerings (pitṛbhājaḥ)—that is, sharers of the oblations or earners of food—[also rise];
for "pitu" is listed among the names for food.
And those men also fly up.
Moreover, O Goddess Uṣas, you bring abundant desirable wealth to the mortal who offers oblations and dwells near you.
"This would be hers" (*eṣā syā*): this fourth hymn consists of five verses; it is the seer Bharadvāja’s *ṛṣi*-hymn in the *triṣṭubh* meter. It is enumerated as "This would be hers.
Since it was stated in the preceding hymn that "the lap" (*upasthaṃ tu*) [is the deity], this hymn also has the same deities.
The application of [the verses] for the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra has been stated.
This daughter of ours, born of heaven, shining upon the dwellings, has awakened the human races—
she who, with her radiant glow, has illumined the lovely nights across even the thick darkness.
This is our daughter, born of heaven; shining forth, she has awakened the human settlements. She who, with her radiant beam, has become manifest through the nights, even across the veils of darkness.

This is she, born of heaven, produced from heaven; thus she is the daughter of heaven, the daughter of the sky. Dawn, shining forth for our sake and driving away the darkness, has awakened the human settlements, that is, the people—she causes them to rise.
Regarding this, Yāska says: "'Jigarti' is a root meaning 'to swallow' or 'to devour'" (Nirukta 6.8);
that is to say, she illuminates them.
She who, with her radiant, blazing [form], ...
1. (kha, jha, ta, na, bha, śa: prati) 2. (kha, gha, jha, ta, na, bha, śa: vahasi).
Joined with the sun during the lovely nights of the southern course—
here there is a transposition of the letters *ra* and *ya*—
she is perceived, that is, she is seen, as she overshadows the *aktūn*, the lights of the stars and so forth, as well as the *tamasaḥ*, the very depths of darkness.

They have driven apart that [darkness] with their ruddy-yoked horses; the Dawns shine forth wondrously on their radiant chariots. O Agni, leading forward the great sacrifice, they drive away that [darkness] of the night. vi | tat | yuyuḥ | aruṇayugbhiḥ | aśvaiḥ | citram | bhānti | uṣasaḥ | candrarathāḥ | agne | yajñasya | bṛhataḥ | nayantīḥ | vi | tāḥ | bādhante | tam | ūrmyāyāḥ || 2 ||

The Dawns— whose chariots are bright (*candrarathāḥ*), for Yāska states [Nirukta 11.5] that "the moon (*candra*) is from the root *cand*, meaning 'to shine' with beauty"— at that time, at dawn, leading the face of the great, expansive sacrifice of Agni, they have spread forth, traveling far with their horses yoked with ruddy-colored mares.
And they shine in a manifold manner;
[they shine] "of the night," for *ūrmyā* is listed among the names for night in the passage: "The night-watch is *ūrmyā*."
They drive away and completely dispel the darkness;

carrying glory, booty, food, and vigor, the Dawns bestow these upon the mortal who offers oblations. Wealthy, ruling over heroic sons, grant protection and treasure today to the one who serves you. *śravaḥ*, *vājam*, *iṣam*, *ūrjam*, *vahantīḥ*, *ni*, *dāśuṣe*, *uṣasaḥ*, *martyāya*, *maghonīḥ*, *vīravat*, *patyamānāḥ*, *avaḥ*, *dhāta*, *vidhate*, *ratnam*, *adya*.

O Dawns, carrying to the mortal donor who offers oblations fame (*śravaḥ*), renown (*kīrtim*), booty (*vājam*), strength (*balam*), food (*iṣam*), and nourishing essence (*ūrjam*), you who are wealthy (*maghonīḥ*) and moving forth (*patyamānāḥ*), grant today to me, your worshipper, protection (*avaḥ*) consisting of heroic offspring— sons, grandsons, and the like— as well as food (*avah*); for *sinam* and *avaḥ* are listed among the names for food— and treasure (*ratnam*).

“*Śvātraṃ ratnam*” (a brilliant treasure) is read among the names for wealth. “*Ni dhāta*”: bestow it fully. For now, O Dawns, there is treasure for him who honors you; now, for the heroic patron who offers oblations. Now, for the inspired singer who chants hymns, you truly bring [wealth] even to one such as I, even as of old. For now, O Dawns, there is treasure for him who honors you; now, for the heroic patron who offers oblations. Now, for the inspired singer who chants hymns, you truly bring [wealth] even to one such as I, even as of old. 4.
"O Dawns, now indeed—at this very moment—there is treasure, wealth, for you to give to the one who serves you.
For now indeed there is treasure for you to give to the sacrificer who offers oblations and impels [the rite].
For now indeed there is treasure for you to give to the wise one who praises you."

"In which sage (*vipra*) hymns (*ukthā*)—so-called praises—are fixed, for a sacrificer such as I, you bring that treasure down. Even in former times, treasure was given to me. 1. [In the variants] *kha-gha-jha-ta-na-bha-śa*, it was seen (*adṛśyata*). 2. [In the variants] *kha-jha-na-bha-śa*, [the reading is] *bṛhaṇasya*. 3. [In the variants] *kha-jha-na-bha*, the word "of the sacrifice" (*yajñasya*) is absent. 4. [In the variants] *kha-gha-jha-ta-na-bha-śa*, [the reading is] "to the giver of oblations" (*havīṃṣi pradātre*). 5. [In the variants] *sva-gha-jha-na-bha*, the word "to the one who praises" (*stuvate*) is absent. 6. [In the variant] *śa*, [the reading is] *janāya* ("for the people").

Now indeed, O Dawn, you who are seated upon the mountain peaks, the Aṅgirases sing forth to your herds of cattle; with their hymn and their prayer they have shattered the darkness, and the invocation of the gods by these men has become true. Now indeed, O Dawn, you who are seated upon the mountain peaks (*adrisāna*), by your grace, the Aṅgirases immediately (*idā*) sing forth to your herds (*gotrā*) of cattle and release them. Thus another Vedic passage says: "When the Aṅgirases drove out the herd of cattle" (*Ṛgveda* 2.23.18). With their hymn (*arka*), that which is worthy of praise, and with their prayer (*brahman*) or song of praise, they have shattered the darkness and torn it asunder. The invocation of the gods (*devahūti*) by those leaders, the Aṅgirases, has become true—that is, its fruit has become realized.

Shine forth, O Daughter of Heaven, for us as of old; O Bounteous One, increase [us] like Bharadvāja. Grant wealth with noble heroes to the one who praises you; bestow upon us far-reaching fame. Shine forth, O Daughter of Heaven! As of old, shine for us; O Bounteous One, for the one who serves like Bharadvāja. By the mention of "like Bharadvāja," it is implied that there is another Bharadvāja as well; thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "Bharadvāja is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa). To me, who praises you, grant wealth accompanied by excellent sons, grandsons, and so forth. Furthermore, bestow upon us food worthy of being sung of by many; give it abundantly.
The fifth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with “vapuḥ nu tat,” is the seerly composition of Bharadvāja; it is in the Triṣṭubh meter and addressed to the Maruts.
Accordingly, it is enumerated thus: “vapuḥ, eleven verses; [it is] Māruta.
In the Daśarātra sacrifice, on the sixth day, during the Ābhimāruta śastra, this hymn serves as the indicator for the Maruts.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*haviṣpāntaṃ vapurnu tat*” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.8).
At the Vaiśvadeva Parvan, the *yājyā* for the seven-pot-sherd offering to the Maruts is “*pra citramarkam*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*pra citramarkaṃ gṛṇate turāya*—these are the nine after-offerings” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.16).
In the case of the eleven-animal offering to the Maruts, the *yājyā* verse is precisely “*pra citram arkam*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*pra citram arkam gṛṇate turāyārā ived acaramā aheva*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).

May that wondrous form indeed be known even to the wise; it bears the common name of "the Cow" among mortals. Yet she swells for another purpose to be milked; the speckled one has once yielded her pure milk from her udder. *Vapuḥ* | *nu* | *tat* | *cikituṣe* | *cit* | *astu* | *samānam* | *nāma* | *dhenu* | *patyamānam* | *martyeṣu* | *anyat* | *dohase* | *pīpāya* | *sakṛt* | *śukram* | *duduhe* | *pṛśniḥ* | *ūdhaḥ* || 1 || That well-known, uniform, and single-formed [form] belongs to the Maruts, who are always of identical appearance. Thus, there is another Vedic citation: "Among them there is no eldest and no youngest" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.60.5). This "name" is the designator of those who are otherwise stable; it is the "Cow."
1. [The consonants] kha, jha, ta, na, bha, and śa are *upadhmānīya*.
2. [The consonants] kha, jha, na, bha, and sa have the same result [as the following vowel].
[Mbh. 6.1.66] Fifth Aṣṭaka, Chapter 6, Sūtra 66. 233.
May that great form (*vapuḥ*), which is always being cherished as the object of delight, quickly manifest for the wise singer who knows it.
The word *cit* is a filler.
Furthermore, that reality (*tattvam*) nourishes (*pīpāya*) other things among mortals in the world of men—such as plants and trees—in order to milk out their desires.

Moreover, because it is described as belonging to the great ones alone, the Earth has milked—i.e., pours forth—the bright, white-colored water (ūdhah) from the atmosphere once in the rains of the year.
Those fires which, like flames, have shone forth from their enclosures, have increased to their full extent;
they have become free from dust, golden-hued, and endowed with manly vigor and heroic powers all at once.
Those fires which, being kindled, did not burn out—since the Maruts grew strong twice and thrice—their chariots became dustless and golden, together with their manly powers and heroic deeds.
Those Maruts who, like kindled fires, blaze forth like fires being enkindled;
those Maruts who have grown twice, thrice, and even more, increasing according to their desire.
The long vowel in the *saṃhitā* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) feature.
The chariots of these great ones are dustless and adorned with gold ornaments.
Those Maruts manifest together with manly wealth and heroic powers;
as it is said in another Vedic verse: "Those who [come] with spotted spears" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.37.2).
Those who are the sons of the bounteous Rudra—whom indeed Pṛśni bore to sustain them—the Great Mother knows them as great; she, the protector, has placed the embryo within her fair udder.

Those who are the sons of the bounteous Rudra, whom Dādhṛvi indeed brought forth to bear—verily, that great Mother is known as the vast one; she, Pṛśni, has placed the embryo within her beautiful womb.
The sons of Rudra, the Maruts, who are the offspring of the bounteous shedder [of rain]—the earth, the supporter, and the mid-air are capable of bearing them now and hereafter.
For she, the mother of these great ones, is indeed all-knowing and vast;
moreover, that Pṛśni, for the well-being of men, places within her womb the water.
They do not shrink from their birth even now, purifying themselves while remaining within the depths; the pure ones have emerged according to their pleasure, sprinkling their bodies with splendor.

No; those who from birth even now shrink back, being within the depths and purifying themselves, when the bright ones have milked forth according to their pleasure, sprinkling their own bodies with splendor.
Those Maruts who are well-known do not fail to go toward the people who are their worshippers by means of that very movement which is their vehicle.
Is it because they have no one to protect that they do not go? No, he says;
for they, being within—dwelling in the hearts of all—purify and cleanse away sins.
And likewise, another scriptural passage states: “The vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are indeed the Maruts, the sleepers” (Ai. Brā. 3.16). [Note: 1.

In the variants kha, gha, jha, na, bha, śa, the word ‘rūpa’ is absent; 2. in the variants kha, gha, jha, ta, na, bha, śa, the word ‘viduṣe’ is absent; 3. in the variant gha, it says ‘manuṣyaloke’; in ta, ya, śa, it says ‘martyalokeṣu’; 4. in the variants kha, gha, jha, ta, na, bha, śa, it says ‘te'mī’.]
Therefore, because they abide in the hearts of all living beings, it is shown that there is no movement for them when they exist internally in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
However, their quality of moving swiftly should be understood as pertaining to their form as deities (*adhidaivata*).
Whenever the pure, blazing Maruts milk forth water abundantly in accordance with the desire (*joṣman*) of the worshippers.
Thus, accompanied by splendor and radiance, they illuminate their own bodies; moreover, they become those who sprinkle the earth,
or rather,
the meaning is that they sprinkle the earth so as to make it extensive.

Swift are they, upon whom even the milking of the udders is performed; they who assume the bold name of the Maruts—those who are not to be praised as mere common folk, but are mighty and truly bountiful—may those fierce ones come hither.
Swiftly—nay, even before the milking of those [cows] has begun—they have come, boldly assuming their Marut-name. They who are not sluggish, who are tireless—that chariot impels them;

though without horses, without fodder, and without reins, it moves through the mid-air, driving forth the waters, fulfilling the desires of the singers, and traversing in various ways the two worlds, heaven and earth, along the paths of the atmosphere.
There is no one to withstand him, nor any to overcome him, O Maruts, whom you protect in the struggle for booty;
whether for offspring, cattle, progeny, or waters, he is the breaker of the enclosure at the final hour of the contest.

No one is his restrainer, nor is there any overcomer of him, O Maruts, whom you protect in the contest for booty, or for offspring, cattle, progeny, or waters; he shall break open the stall at the decisive hour of the day.
O Maruts, that man whom you protect and guard in the battle for booty finds no one to turn him back;
indeed, there is no one to harm him.

Moreover, whether it be for his son, his grandson, his wealth, or for cattle and waters as the occasion arises—whomsoever you protect, he shall be the breaker of the stall, the destroyer of the herd of cattle belonging even to a glowing or victorious enemy in the decisive battle.
Bring forth a brilliant hymn for the swift Marut host, who possess their own inherent strength, for they who by force overcome all powers;
at their onset, the earth trembles before the mighty ones.

Bring forth a brilliant hymn for the swift Marut host, who possess their own inherent strength, for they who by force overcome all powers; at their onset, the earth trembles before the mighty ones. 9.
Bring forth the wonderful, visible *arka*—that is, food or oblation—for the swift, self-strong host of Maruts who are praised by us as they utter sound;
for "food" (*arka*) is listed among the names for nourishment.
Bring it forward!
"O you who have become my companions, O priests, and you yourself—all of you together, bring forth [the offering].

Just as in the world, when many are performing a single task, one addresses the principal person, saying 'you all do this,' so too here, address the principal one alone and say 'bring it forth'; thus the plural form is used.

Those Maruts who by their force (*sahasa*) overcome (*sahante*) the forces (*sahāṃsi*) of their enemies—the earth trembles out of fear of those Maruts, who are worthy of honor (*makhebhyas*) for their greatness."

In the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita-vṛtti*) such as *mārutāya*, there is a reflective reference (*pratyavamarśa*) using the word "those" (*ye*), because even though the great [elements] are included within it, they are mentally distinguished;
just as in the *Mahābhāṣya*: "Now begins the instruction of words (*atha śabdānuśāsanam*).
Of which words? (Pā. Ma. 1.1.1).
Or as in common worldly usage, when one says "the king's man," [the question arises] "of which king?"
Radiant like the flashes of a sacrifice, like the ladles of Agni,
the Maruts— praising, roaring like heroes, shining as they are born— are unassailable.
Radiant like the flash of a sacrifice, they move swiftly with triple energy like the ladles of Agni; singing their praises, like roaring heroes, the Maruts appear with gleaming forms, invincible. 10.

The Maruts, shining like the lightning of a sacrifice, swift-moving, radiant as the flames of Agni’s ladle, brilliant, worthy of praise, shaking their enemies like whips, heroes, born of splendor, and invincible by others—thus they are.

1. ta-a-śayāmaḥ | 2. In the manuscripts kha, jha, ta, na, bha, and śa, the word "saḥ" is not present. 3. In manuscript kha: dīptasya; in jha, ta, na, bha, and śa: dīptasyāya. 4. In kha, jha, ta, na, bha, and tvatsahāyaprabhūtāḥ.
I invoke with my call that increasing host of Maruts, the sons of Rudra, who possess straight-glancing spears.
For the army of heaven, the bright-minded ones have contended like mountains, as fierce as bulls.

I seek to win over with my invocation that increasing host of Maruts, whose spears are straight, the sons of Rudra. For the host of Heaven, the zealous ones have offered their inspired thoughts; like mountains, the fierce ones have vied with one another to flow forth. 11.

I honor with my invocation—that is, I serve—the famous, increasing, and ever-growing son of Rudra, the host of Maruts, who possesses sharp-pointed spears and wields arrows; I honor him with my praise or service.
Furthermore, the pure and stainless hymns of the praising worshipper, uplifted and powerful, [are offered] to the forceful host of Maruts;
for "tukṣaḥ śardhaḥ" (the forceful host) is read among the names for strength.
Like mountains that receive rain, like clouds;
for "giri" (mountain) is listed among the names of clouds in the *Nighaṇṭu* as "giri vrajaḥ. They contended, they vied with one another.
The sixth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with "viśveṣāṃ vaḥ," is the *ārṣa* of Bharadvāja; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and is addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa (*maitrāvaruṇa*).
