Thus it is enumerated: "viśveṣāṃ maitrāvaruṇam. The application (*viniyoga*) of this hymn is determined by its internal characteristics (*laiṅgika*).

In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa, "Come hither, O Mitra and Varuṇa" (*ā yātaṃ mitrāvaruṇā*) is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the sacrificial cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*). This is stated in the Sūtra: "‘Come hither, O Mitra and Varuṇa’ with our fair praise; O Mitra and Varuṇa, [accept] our enjoyment of the oblation" (*āśvalāyana-śrautasūtra* 3.8). In the *vyūḍha-daśarātra* sacrifice, on the seventh day, the third triplet of verses in the *prauga-śastra* is "pra yad vām" (*pra yad vām*), dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.
And thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Nāsatyas, Mitra and Varuṇa, when you two hasten forward with your chariot rich in cattle" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.9).
O Mitra and Varuṇa, may I strengthen you with songs— you who are the most eminent among all existing beings,
you who, like reins, have best restrained the two peoples, being peerless in your own arms.

To you all, the most excellent among the virtuous, O Mitra and Varuṇa, may our songs of praise cause you to awaken. You two, who are peerless, have drawn together the two peoples with your own arms, like reins that best restrain.
Among all existing beings, you two, Mitra and Varuṇa, are the most preeminent; I have begun with hymns and praises to exalt you both.

As for those two who are joined together, they are unequal, as shown by another Vedic citation: "Indra slays three, and the chariot [slays] even four" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.152.2). Thus their inequality is demonstrated.

"Those who are most eager to sacrifice, who are most inclined to bow with their own arms—they have restrained, they have controlled the people, as one restrains horses with a bridle. The plural number in "with arms" (*bāhubhiḥ*) is used for the sake of honor.
This prayer is spread forth toward the beloved sacrificial grass with reverence;
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who are invincible and bounteous givers, grant us a secure and protective dwelling.

This prayer of mine is spread forth for you both; with reverence, it approaches the dear sacred grass. Come to us, O Mitra and Varuṇa, for our protection, granting that shelter which is yours to bestow, O bounteous givers. 2.
1. *Gha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, and *śa* do not compete; *jha*, *ya*, and *spa* compete. 2. *Kha* belongs to all the gods (*viśveṣāṃ devānām*).
3. *Kha*, *gha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*, and *sa* come together.
O Mitra and Varuna, this my prayer— this hymn of praise— covers you both; O beloved ones,
it approaches you with reverence and with the oblation of clarified butter,
and it reaches your sacred grass at the sacrifice.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, grant us an invincible dwelling—a home that extends its protection. O you of noble gifts, that house which belongs to you both, which is to be given by you, is a shelter that wards off cold, wind, and rain.
Come hither, O Mitra and Varuṇa, with fair praise, being invoked with beloved homage;
you who encompass all people like craftsmen, hear us with your greatness.

Come, O Mitra and Varuṇa, to this fair praise, being invoked with beloved homage! You two who, like workers, have united all people together by your greatness, even those who are far away and hear you. 3.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, being invoked with beautiful praise, with homage, with oblation, or with a hymn—being praised and beloved by all—come hither!
You two, endowed with greatness, [protect] the people who desire for themselves fame worthy of hearing; [you protect] the man appointed to his task, for "apām" is read among the names for action.
"By means of action alone, as it were, you two restrain [him] together."
Like horses that are swift and of pure lineage, when Aditi bore the embryo according to the Eternal Law (ṛta);
they who, being great and increasing in greatness, have established themselves as terrible for the mortal enemy.

The two mares who are swift, whose kinsmen are pure, who, as Aditi, brought forth the embryo according to the Eternal Law; they who, being great and mighty, were manifested, and who, terrible in their intent, have established themselves against the enemy. 4.
Those two who are like two horses, powerful like two prize-winning steeds, whose kinship is pure, whose praise is purified, and who are true to the Eternal Law (Ṛta);
those two whom the goddess Aditi bore while still in the womb;

and those two, Mitra and Varuṇa, who as they were being born, great and most mighty, Aditi placed within her own belly for the sake of the mortal who intends harm, as terrible destroyers of the enemy.
When you all, O gods, rejoicing in your abundance, bestowed dominion together in harmony;
when you encompassed even the two wide worlds, your spies stand around, unerring and watchful.

When all the gods, exhilarated by your bounty, bestowed sovereign power upon you with great delight; when you encompassed even the two wide worlds, O vast ones—your spies are unfailing and they do not miss their mark.
All the gods, acting in harmony with one another, being delighted by the greatness of you two, have bestowed sovereign power and strength upon you.
Furthermore, since you two encompass the two vast worlds, heaven and earth, your spies—or rays—are inviolable and undeluded.

1. Being invoked, they are summoned. For you two uphold the sovereign power (*kṣatra*) day after day; you fashion its ridge as if reaching toward the highest heaven. Firm is the constellation, and it belongs to all the gods; it has stretched out the earth and the sky with the nourishment of the living one. 6. For you two uphold the sovereign power day after day; you fashion its ridge as if reaching toward the highest heaven. Firm is the constellation, and it belongs to all the gods; it has stretched out the earth and the sky with the nourishment of the living one.
O Mitra and Varuna, you two uphold sovereignty and power day after day; for you strengthen the ridge of heaven—
the exalted region of the intermediate space, the cloud, or the sun—
just as if from a comparison.
It is called *upamāt* because it is measured or placed near; thus, the pillar (*sthūṇā*) is so named.
The meaning is that just as it supports a calf, so too [does this cloud].

The cloud, made firm and strengthened by you both, reaches across the atmosphere (*nakṣatra*). Furthermore, the sun, who belongs to all the gods (*viśvadeva*), [reaches] the earth and the heaven of the living mortal (*āyoḥ*, i.e., of man).
Because "duhavaḥ āyavaḥ" is listed among the names of humans; and [the word] "dhāsinā" means with food or oblation,
because "dhūna dhāsiḥ" is listed among the names of food.
Having been nourished, he stretches out his webs; indeed, it has been made firm by you two.

You two fill your wide belly to be filled, when they, gathered together in unison, fill it for you. The young maidens do not tire as they bring the all-inspiring milk, which flows forth without fail. tā vigraṃ dhaithe jaṭharaṃ puṇadhyā ā yatsabre sabhṛtayaḥ puṇanti | na mṛṣyante yuvatayo'vātā vi yatpayo viśvajinvā bharante || 7 || You two fill your wide belly to be filled, when they, gathered together in unison, fill it for you. The young maidens do not tire as they bring the all-inspiring milk, which flows forth without fail.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two sustain the wise sacrificer—
*vipra* being listed among the names for the intelligent—
as you hold him within your belly (*jaṭhara*) in order to fill it with soma.
When the officiating priests, gathered together with their equipment, occupy the sacrificial seat and fill it,
O you two who enliven all, when the water— your bestowed wealth— is sent forth, then the youthful rivers or the quarters do not fail; they are not overcome by the dust, and being windless and bright,
they bear and maintain great splendor.

With your tongue, O wise ones, you have always partaken of this; since the true steward has appeared for you in accordance with the Eternal Law (*ṛta*), let that be your greatness, O you whose food is ghee! May you two dispel the darkness for the donor. 8. With your tongue, always, this—O wise one, since the true steward has come for you in accordance with the *ṛta*, let that be your majesty, O you who feed on ghee! May you two dispel the day [of distress] for the giver. 8.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two, the wise one—possessed of excellent intelligence—constantly entreats this water with his tongue, that is, with his speech.
Because of the observation of the prefix *ā*, the verb *yācati* (he entreats) is supplied as the appropriate action;
for since water was the subject in the preceding ṛc, it is referred to by the pronoun *idam* (this) as it remains present in the mind.
Whenever your messenger, true and free from illusion, comes to you in the sacrifice, O you whose food is ghee, let that greatness of yours—characterized by the granting of what is desired—be yours.
Moreover, may you two [grant it] to the donor, to the sacrificing patron.
The dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
"Drive away the evil"—the meaning is "destroy it."

1. O wise ones, when they strive against you, O Mitra and Varuṇa, and violate the dear ordinances established by you—those who are neither gods through their power nor mortals, who do not attend the sacrifice, like waters without sons. When they strive against you, O Mitra and Varuṇa, and violate the dear ordinances established by you—those who are neither gods through their power nor mortals, who do not attend the sacrifice, like waters without sons.
O Mitra and Varuna, these are your dear and beloved domains—your deeds ordained by you both. Those people who do not sacrifice, who vie with one another, indeed transgress and cause harm.
And those gods who are not joined with *ohas*—the means of carrying, namely, praise—and those mortals who are not joined with *ohas*.
And those who perform water-related rites, who do not attend the sacrifice, who do not associate with the sacrifice— meaning those who perform useless actions—
and those who are not sons.
They are called "sons" (putrāḥ) because they satisfy (pṛṇanti);
the meaning is that sons do not fail to satisfy.
The phrase "you should search out all of them" is supplied [from the preceding context].

When they bring forth their speech, having prepared it, and some recite the *nivids* with devotion, then we shall proclaim to you two true hymns; for by no other gods do you strive in greatness. When they bring forth their speech, having prepared it, and some recite the *nivids* with devotion, then we shall proclaim to you two true hymns; for by no other gods do you strive in greatness. 10.
When the wise *udgātṛ*s—

referred to as "the eager ones" (*uśijaḥ*) because they are listed among the names for the wise— are assigned their tasks, they distribute the speech, that is, they utter the hymns of praise separately; at that time, some of the *Bahvṛcas*, being mindful and praising the *adya*-verses and so forth, recite the *nivid*s.
Therefore, being so, we shall speak true hymns of praise (*ukthāni*) to you two;
with your greatness, along with the other gods, you two do not fail—that is, you do not go astray.

Thus have you both granted protection for our aid; O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who are free from stinginess. When the cows followed the bold, darting, and vigorous bull as he was born in battle. 11. avaḥ (protection); itthā (thus); vām (of you two); chardiṣaḥ (from the shelter); abhiṣṭau (in the aid); yuvaḥ (you two); mitrāvaruṇau (O Mitra and Varuṇa); askṛdhoyu (free from stinginess); anu (along); yat (when); gāvaḥ (the cows); spurān (darted); ṛjipyam (the darting one); dhṛṣṇum (the bold one); yat (when); raṇe (in battle); vṛṣaṇam (the bull); yunarjana (was born). 11.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, in your protection— that is, in your assistance or in your approach— [we seek] for our shelter, home, or comfort (the genitive case is used in the sense of the dative). When you have approached the worshippers, that which belongs to you both, which is to be given by you both, such as wealth and the like, becomes *askṛdhoyu*, meaning uninterrupted.
And thus Yāska says: "Askṛdhoyuḥ means ṛkudhāyuḥ;
for the word *kṛdhi* is a name for 'short,' as it is cut down" (Nirukta 6.3).
This is indeed the truth.
Regarding when the approach of Mitra and Varuṇa occurs, he says:
whenever the cows—that is, the hymns of praise—should throb in accordance [with them];
and whenever the sacrificers should yoke at the delightful sacrifice, for the sake of sport, the Soma who moves straight, who is bold, the subduer of enemies, the bull, and the showerer of desires.

1. In *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *bha*, and *ya*, [the suffix] *yaj* [is applied]; in *na* and *ya*, *yajña*; and in *śa* and *ya*, *yajamāna*. 2. In *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*, and *ya*, they are not joined with *yajña*.
3. In *kha*, *ta*, *na*, and *śa*, the meaning is "they perform"; in *jha* and *bha*, the meaning is "they are performing."
4. There is no connection with *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, or *sa*.
5. At that time, *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, [and *sa*].

The seventh hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with “*śruṣṭī vām*,” is the seerly composition (*ārṣa*) of Bharadvāja; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and is addressed to Indra and Varuṇa (*aindrāvaruṇa*).
And thus it is enumerated: “*śruṣṭī vām*, *indrāvaruṇaṃ*, and the two final [verses] are *jagatī*s.
The two *jagatī*s are “*pra saṃnāje*” and “*indrāvaruṇā sutapā*” (Indra and Varuṇa, drinkers of the pressed juice); the remaining verses are *triṣṭubh*s.
Indra and Varuṇa are the deities.
In the *ābhilvika* hymns at the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*), during the recitations of the *hotraka* priests when the *stoma* is increased, this hymn serves as the *āvāpa* for the Maitrāvaruṇa.
It is prescribed in the Sūtra: “*śruṣṭī vāṃ yajño yuvāṃ narā*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.9).
At the third pressing, the *prasthitayājyā* for the Praśāstṛ is: “*indrāvaruṇā sutapāv imaṃ sutam*.”
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “O Indra and Varuṇa, drinkers of the pressed [juice], drink this pressed [Soma]; O Indra and Bṛhaspati, drink the Soma” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.5).
At the third pressing of the Ukthya sacrifice, the verse beginning with “O Indra and Varuṇa, of the most honey-sweet [Soma]” is the Yājyā for the recitation of the Maitrāvaruṇa.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘O Indra and Varuṇa, of the most honey-sweet [Soma]’ is the Yājyā” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 6.1).

May the sacrifice, uplifted with readiness and shared by you both, be offered like that of Manu upon the strewn sacrificial grass. O Indra and Varuṇa, may he who turns toward you today for food and for great, abundant favor, come hither. śruṣṭī | vām | yajñaḥ | ut'yataḥ | sa'joṣaḥ | manuṣ'vat | vṛkta'barhiṣaḥ | yajadhyai | ā | yaḥ | indrāvaruṇau | iṣe | adya | mahe | sumnāya | mahe | ā'vivartat || 1 ||
O ye two, Indra and Varuṇa, who are most worthy of honor; for you both, let there be swift obedience (*śruṣṭī*).
Thus says Yāska: “*Śruṣṭī* is a name for 'swift'; *aṣṭī* is also [a name for] eight” (Nirukta 6.12).
*Yajñaḥ* refers to Soma.
Accordant with the officiating priests,
he who is today engaged and active on all sides—
that Soma, like Manu, for the food and great bliss of the sacrificer who has strewn the sacrificial grass— turns you both hither so that you may worship.

For they are the most excellent in the divine assembly, impetuous and most powerful among heroes; for they have become the most liberal among the wealthy patrons, possessing great vigor, overcoming Vṛtra by the Eternal Law, and accompanied by all their hosts. 2. They—for they are the most excellent in the divine assembly, impetuous and most powerful among heroes; for they have become the most liberal among the wealthy patrons, possessing great vigor, overcoming Vṛtra by the Eternal Law, and accompanied by all their hosts. 2.
O Indra and Varuṇa, you two who are well-known, be the most excellent of the gods at the sacrifice;
for "devatātā" is listed among the names of the sacrifice in the sense of "the place of the deities. Indeed, be the impellers of riches through your vigor.
Furthermore, O you two, among heroes you have indeed become the most powerful, preeminent in strength;

moreover, among the generous givers you are the most munificent, possessed of great vigor and abundant power; by means of *ṛta* (truth), you are the slayers of Vṛtra—the destroyers of enemies—and you possess complete armies.

Praise those two, Indra and Varuṇa, who are eager for our beautiful and worshipful blessings. One of them, by his might, slays Vṛtra with the thunderbolt; the other, the sage, glides through the assemblies. 3. Praise those two. With worshipful. Beautiful. Blessings. O Indra and Varuṇa. Being eager. With the thunderbolt. The one. By his strength. Slays. Vṛtra. Glides. The other. Through the assemblies. The sage. 3.
2. Of the gods Kha, Jña, Na, Bha, and Maghon;
O Bharadvāja, with praises worthy of homage (namasyebhiḥ) and with powers (śūyaiḥ)—for "śūya" is listed among the names for strength.
"By all those who are well-praising and well-extolling," *cakānāḥ* means "delighting in praise.
The root *kāyati* has the sense of sound;
this is a form of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) with the suffix *kānac*.
Praise, extol those two, Indra and Varuṇa!
Of them, one is Indra, who slays Vṛtra—the Asura named Vṛtra—with his thunderbolt;
the other is Varuṇa, the wise one, who with his power (*śavas*) unites with strength to protect the singers within their enclosures (*vrajaneṣu*).
Both the Ādityas and the Maruts have all grown strong; the gods, praised by men, are seekers of heaven.
O Indra and Varuṇa, you two have surpassed them in greatness; O Heaven and Earth, you have become vast.

Āḥ! And when all the gods, including Vṛtra-slayers and men, who are the self-guiding protectors of men, [are present], O Indra and Varuṇa, you two have become great through your majesty, as has the heaven and the broad earth. 4.
Among men—that is, among human beings—both women and men;
for Yāska states, “*menā ā* refers to women” (Nirukta 3.21).
And all the gods—the *nara*s, meaning males, and the *viśve devāsaḥ*, meaning all the praising deities.

Regarding the word *devāḥ* here, because of the grammatical rule *pumān striyā* (Pāṇini 1.2.67), which effects a single-remainder compound (*ekaśeṣa*), the reference *devāsaḥ*—meaning both goddesses and gods—is a masculine designation.

When they are *svagūrtāḥ*, meaning self-exalted, and *vāvṛdhanta*, meaning they cause themselves to grow through hymns of praise, then, O Indra and Varuṇa, endowed with greatness (*mahitvā*), *pra bhūtam*, i.e., be preeminent for these singers.
O Heaven (*dyauḥ*) and Earth (*pṛthivī*), both of you who are wide (*urvī*), the phrase “be preeminent for them” is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
He indeed is bountiful, self-reliant, and devoted to the cosmic order (*ṛta*), O Indra and Varuṇa, who worships you both with his own person.
May he, possessing food, overcome his enemies; may he obtain horses and possess wealth along with wealthy people.

He indeed is the one who gives good gifts, possessing noble horses, upholder of the cosmic order—O Indra and Varuṇa, he who serves you both with his own self. With nourishment, that liberal giver shall overcome his enemies; he shall win wealth and the men who possess riches. 5.
"O you two Indras," "O you two Varuṇas"—
the dual number is used in both cases due to mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).
In the word *varuṇā*, the short vowel in the *saṃhitā* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) feature.
The sacrificer who offers oblations to you two by himself—he alone becomes a "good giver" (sudānu), one who gives beautifully;

he becomes possessed of wealth (*svavān*) and possessed of sacrifice (*ṛtāvā*). Furthermore, being a generous giver (*dāsvān*), he shall overcome his enemies along with the food obtained through victory.
Moreover, may he enjoy wealth and riches, and may he possess sons from men who are wealthy.
O Gods, you bestow upon the worshiper who offers oblations that wealth which is full of treasures and abundant in food.
O Indra and Varuṇa, may he be with us who, through your favor, shatters Vṛtra and the curses.
O Gods, bestow upon the donor that wealth which is full of treasures and abundant in food; may he be with us, O Indra and Varuṇa, who shatters Vṛtra and the curses.
O divine Indra and Varuṇa, being praised as gods, you two bestow upon the donor who has offered oblations such wealth— consisting of riches, abundant cattle, or full glory—
as well as the ill-repute of the harmful ones;
that is to say, the disgrace caused by enemies.
That such wealth (rayiḥ) may belong to us (asme), it shall be ours; it bestows and imparts [it]. 1.
Those who increase by means of praise (ya-stulā) cause [others] to increase.
2. Kha, jha, bha, and sa read "he partakes" (saṃbhajate); na and śa read "he should partake" (saṃbhajeta).
Ṛgveda 3.16

And may there be for us, O Indra and Varuṇa, wealth that is well-protecting and guarded by the gods, for the sake of our patrons—wealth belonging to those whose brilliant strength is victorious in battles, and who, as swift conquerors, immediately spread their glory far and wide. And furthermore, O Indra and Varuṇa, may there be for us—for us, the patrons and singers—wealth that is well-protecting and has the gods as its guardians. Moreover, may the brilliant strength of these [patrons], which is victorious over enemies in battles and destructive, immediately and fully extend their glories.

Now, O Indra and Varuṇa, being praised, O Gods, bestow upon us wealth for the sake of glorious renown. Thus extolling the power of the Great One, may we cross over difficulties as one crosses waters with a boat. O Indra and Varuṇa, you two who are being praised—grant us, for the sake of glorious renown (*sauśravasāya*), wealth quickly; O Gods, praising thus the strength (*śardhaḥ*) of the Great One, may we cross over misfortunes as if crossing waters with a boat.

Now sing forth a dear hymn, O wide-extending one, to the sovereign Varuṇa, the great god. He who, by his greatness, is the lord of mighty laws, shines with wisdom like one undecaying with his radiance. O singer, now proclaim today the pleasing hymn to the sovereign, the ruler by command, the great, the radiant god Varuṇa, which is wide-reaching on all sides. And thus Yāska says: "Saprathas means wide on all sides" (Nighaṇṭu 6.7). Proclaim the hymn now; for this Varuṇa, endowed with greatness, possessing mighty laws and great deeds, joined with wisdom and free from decay, illumines the two vast expanses of heaven and earth with his light.

O Indra and Varuṇa, drinkers of the pressed juice, drink this pressed Soma, which intoxicates, you whose vows are firm. Your chariot comes toward the sacrifice for the feast of the gods, to the dwelling place, for the sake of drinking. 10. O Indra and Varuṇa, drinkers of the pressed juice, drink this pressed Soma, which intoxicates, you whose vows are firm. Your chariot comes toward the sacrifice for the feast of the gods, to the dwelling place, for the sake of drinking. 10. 1. kha-bha-sauśravasāya; jha-na-suyaśasthāya; śa-suyaśastvāya | 2. kha-jha-na-bha-mahivrato mahāvrataḥ |
O Indra and Varuṇa, you two who drink the pressed juice—drinkers of the pressed Soma—this most beloved, pressed, and effused Soma which produces exhilaration.
Furthermore, O performers of the pressing rite, your chariot, for the sake of the feast of the gods and for your own drinking of the Soma, has sped forth toward the path of the sun.
O Indra and Varuṇa, you two bulls, drink of this most honeyed, potent Soma. This exhilarating juice has been poured out for you; having sat down upon this sacred grass (barhis), rejoice in it.
O Indra and Varuṇa, you two bulls, drink of this most honeyed, potent Soma. This juice has been poured out for you among us; having sat down upon this sacred grass (barhis), may you both rejoice. 11.
O Indra and Varuṇa, O you two bulls, you two who are the showerers of desires, [come] to the most honey-sweet, exceedingly sweet, and delightful bull.

O Indra and Viṣṇu, you who are the generators of all thoughts and the vessels that hold the Soma; may our recited hymns favor you, and may our praises being sung with chants come forth to you. O Indra and Viṣṇu, those two well-known ones, the generators of all thoughts—that is, of all praises—the word *janitārā* is derived from the root *jan* (to beget) with the suffix *tṛc*, or alternatively from the root *jan* (to appear) with the same suffix, following the Vedic rule *janitā mantre*. You two are the vessels, the repositories of the Soma. Now follows the direct praise: O Indra and Viṣṇu, may the *giraḥ*—the words in the form of hymns being recited (*śasyamānāḥ*)—favor (*pravantu*) you both. And may the *stomāsaḥ*—the hymns (*stotrāṇi*) being sung (*gīyamānāsaḥ*) by the singers (*arkaiḥ*)—also favor you both.

O Indra and Viṣṇu, lords of exhilaration, come toward the Soma, bestowing riches. May the praises of the wise adorn you with splendors; may the hymns being recited together with the *ukthas* [strengthen] you both. (3) O Indra and Viṣṇu, lords of exhilaration—that is, masters of the intoxicating Soma juices—come hither toward the Soma, granting us wealth (*draviṇa*). May the hymns (*stomāsaḥ*) of the worshippers, being recited along with the *uktha* liturgies, adorn you both with their luster (*aktubhiḥ*). The repetition of "together" (*saṃ... saṃ*) is for the sake of emphasis.

May your horses, the overcomers of adversaries, O Indra and Viṣṇu, bring you both to the joint revelry. May you enjoy all the invocations of our thoughts; listen to my prayers and my songs. O Indra and Viṣṇu, may your horses—the conquerors of those who seek to harm us—bring you both to the shared feast. Enjoy all the invocations of the singers; for that purpose, listen to my prayers and my words in the form of hymns.
1. The sound *drama* [is formed] from *jha*, *na*, *śa*, and *da*. 2. *Kha* and *bha* are the opposites. 3. *Jha*, *ta*, *na*, *ya*, *śa*, and *sa* are the consonants (*jantu*).

O Indra and Viṣṇu, that deed of yours is praiseworthy; in the exhilaration of Soma, you strode out widely. You made the mid-region more spacious and you expanded the worlds for our life. (5) O Indra and Viṣṇu, that deed of yours (*vām*) is praiseworthy (*panyāyyam*). What is that deed? To this he says: when there was the exhilaration of Soma, that which you strode out widely (*uru cakramāthe*), you traversed extensively. Although the stride belongs to Viṣṇu alone, nevertheless, because they share a single purpose, it is spoken of as belonging to both. And that which you made the mid-region (*antarikṣam*) more spacious (*varīyaḥ*), you made it wider. And also the worlds (*rajāṃsi*); Yāska says, "The worlds are called *rajāṃsi*. You expanded (*aprathatam*) them for our life (*jīvase*). (5)

O Indra and Viṣṇu, increasing through the oblation, eating the first portion, with reverence, having been granted the offering, and drinking the clarified butter—bestow wealth upon us! You two are the ocean, you are the jar that holds the Soma. O Indra and Viṣṇu, who drink the clarified butter, you two, increasing through the oblation of Soma, eating the first portion—the bright essence of the Soma—with reverence, and having been granted the offering by the sacrificers, bestow wealth and riches upon us. Furthermore, you two are like the ocean; for you are the jar that contains the Soma, the repository of the Soma.

O Indra and Viṣṇu, drink of this honeyed Soma; O destroyers of foes, fill your bellies! May the intoxicating draughts come to you both; hear my prayers and my invocation. (7) "O Indra and Viṣṇu," [it is said]. "Drink! "Of this honeyed Soma. "O destroyers of foes," "fill your bellies"—that is, fill your stomachs with Soma. "O Indra and Viṣṇu, may the intoxicating draughts"—the food consisting of Soma which causes exhilaration—"come to you both. And "hear my prayers"—my hymns of praise—and "my invocation. (7)
1. In the manuscripts kha, gha, jha, na, bha, and śa, the word *vicakramāthe* is absent. 2. In the manuscripts kha, gha, jha, na, bha, and śa, [the reading] is *somasya*. 3.

In the manuscripts kha, gha, jha, na, bha, and śa, the phrase *madhvo...yuvām* is absent; however, in manuscript gha, it reads: *madhvo madhurasya madhuramasya somasya imaṃ somaṃ pibantaṃ jaṭharaṃ pṛṇethāṃ pūrayethām* ("of the sweet, of the most sweet Soma—fill your bellies with this Soma as you drink it").

O you two, Indra and Viṣṇu—*vām* means "you two"—drink this *soma*, this sweet (*madhvaḥ*) soma; and with that soma, fill (*pṛṇethām*) your bellies (*jaṭharam*). O Indra and Viṣṇu, *vām* means "you two."
Both of you have conquered; you are not defeated, nor has either of you been vanquished. O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you two strove together, you divided the thousandfold [booty] into three parts.
Both of you have conquered; you are not defeated. Neither of these two has been defeated. O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you two contended, you divided the thousandfold [booty] into three parts. 8.

O Indra and Viṣṇu, both of you have conquered your enemies; we too have conquered. You two are never defeated, nor are you ever vanquished again. Between these two of you, not even one has been defeated, nor has either ever suffered defeat.

O Viṣṇu and you, O Indra, whatever object you two contended for—that is, you contended with the Asuras—over that which exists in a threefold state (as the worlds, the Vedas, and speech), you two have pervaded the thousandfold and the immeasurable; the meaning is that you two strode across it.

And thus says the Brāhmaṇa: “‘Both of you have conquered,’ [is the verse] for the Ācchāvāka; for both of them indeed conquered, neither was defeated, nor was either vanquished. ‘O Indra and Viṣṇu, when you two contended, you divided the thousandfold [booty] three ways. Indeed, Indra and Viṣṇu fought with the Asuras; having conquered them, they said, ‘Let us divide [the booty]. The Asuras replied accordingly. Then Indra said, ‘As far as this Viṣṇu strides, that much shall be ours, and the rest yours. He strode across these worlds, then the Vedas, and then speech. Regarding this, they ask: ‘What is that thousandfold? One should say: ‘These worlds, these Vedas, and speech. ‘We have divided, we have divided’ (aireyāmaireyām). (Ai. Brā. 6.15)
Or rather, the meaning is: "That thousand of cows—that thousand—should be divided into three parts.

The ninth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “ghṛtavatī bhuvanānām,” is the seerly composition of Bharadvāja; it is in the Jagatī meter and has Heaven and Earth (Dyāvāpṛthivī) as its deities.
Thus it is enumerated: “ghṛtavatī: six [verses], addressed to Heaven and Earth, in the Jagatī meter.
On the fifth day of the Ābhiplavika rite, during the Vaiśvadeva Śastra, the first triplet of this hymn is used for the insertion of the Nivid dedicated to Heaven and Earth.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “The two triplets beginning with ‘ghṛtavatī bhuvanānām abhiśrīḥ’ and ‘indra ṛbhubhir vājavat’ [are used]” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.7).
This triplet is also used in the Vaiśvadeva-śastra at the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice;
and it is stated in the Sūtra (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.5).

On the third day of the *ābhiplavika* [six-day period], in the *vaiśvadeva* *śastra*, there are three verses beginning with "With ghee, Heaven and Earth" (*ghṛtena dyāvāpṛthivī*) intended for insertion into the *nivids* addressed to Heaven and Earth.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'With ghee, Heaven and Earth'—these three; 'Not born as a horse'... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.7).
Rich in ghee, the glory of all beings, vast and wide, yielding honey, well-formed—
Heaven and Earth are propped apart by the ordinance of Varuṇa, ageless and abounding in seed.

The two butter-rich ones, the glory of all beings, the wide and broad, the honey-yielding, the well-adorned, Heaven and Earth, by the law of Varuṇa, are propped apart, ageless, and possessing abundant seed. || 1 ||
1. *kha-jha-ta-śa* with *indra*; *gha* with *indra*. 2. *kha-jha-na-bha* with *dyāvāpṛthivī*.

*dyāvāpṛthivī* (the two, heaven and earth); *dyāvāpṛthivyau* (the two, heaven and earth). [They are] possessed of clarified butter (*ghṛtavatī*), radiant (*dīptimatī*), or possessed of water (*udakavatī*).

Because "vana" is listed among the names for water in the sense of "clarified butter" (ghṛta), the word "you two" (bhavataḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. In every instance, it should be understood that "you two are the ones to be resorted to" (abhiśriyā) by the worlds (bhuvanānām), that is, by living beings (bhūtānām).

The two vast and wide expanses, the Earth and Heaven, renowned for their manifold forms of activity, yielding honey—that is, water—and beautifully adorned with fair forms, are supported by the law (*dharman*) of Varuṇa, the controller of all; they are held apart and sustained individually, ageless and eternal, possessing abundant seed or, alternatively, having many functions. Here, while there is a direct praise of Heaven and Earth, it should be understood that by extension, Varuṇa is also being praised.
Unfailing, with many streams, full of nourishment, they milk out ghee for the doer of good deeds, O ye of pure vows;
ruling over this world, O Heaven and Earth, pour upon us that seed which is beneficial to man.

"Unfailing," "abounding in streams," "rich in milk," "they both yield ghee for the well-doer," "of pure vows," "shining over this world," O Heaven and Earth, "pour into us that seed which was established by Manu. 2.
Not resting, not being anointed, casting away [impurities], with many streams, with abundant flows—
the showers of rain from heaven and the streams of milk from the earth have both been invoked;
thus, both possess the quality of having many streams.
The two [worlds] are full of milk and full of water;
thus Yāska says: "They are either 'not being obstructed' or 'casting away,' possessing many streams and full of water" (Nirukta 5.2).

O you two of pure vows, of pure actions, Heaven and Earth, for the sacrificer who performs beautiful deeds, you two milk forth *ghṛta*—water that is the cause of the abundance of crops and other things.

Now follows the direct praise: O *rodasī*, Heaven and Earth, you two who rule as sovereigns over this world, the multitude of living beings, pour forth upon us *retas*— the generative vigor capable of procreation—
that *retas* which is beneficial for human beings (*manu-hita*).
O Heaven and Earth, O two Dhiṣaṇās, he who has beheld you with a mind directed toward upright action succeeds;
he is born again through offspring from the sacred law (dharman). From your union, beings of diverse forms are produced in every way.

O Rodasī, O two Dhiṣaṇās, he who has perceived you both for the sake of the upright man through his ritual action—that man succeeds; he is born forth with offspring from the divine law (*dharman*). From your union, beings of diverse forms are poured forth, yet they share a common vow.

O *Dhiṣaṇā*, you two who are created as the dwelling places of the entire world, O *Rodasī* (Heaven and Earth), that mortal who gives oblations to you both for the sake of upright action—that is, for your easy approach—attains his desires;
furthermore, he is propagated through offspring, such as sons and grandsons, and thus prospers.
From the dharma of your action, from above, the seeds poured forth by you two—beings of diverse forms, of various colors, yet possessing common vows and identical actions—are born.

1. By means of the suffixes *kha*, *gha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* [the sense of] "relying upon" (*abhiśrayaṇāya*) is expressed. 2. [The suffix] *ya* expresses the sense of "bearing" (*dhāraka*). 3. [The suffix] *ya* expresses the sense of "having much work" (*bahukārya*); such is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). 4. [The suffixes] *kha*, *jha*, *na*, and *bha* express "many streams" (*bahudhāra*); [the suffix] *śa* expresses "you are one who has many streams" (*bahudhāraṃ tvam*). 5. [The suffixes] *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa* express "he accomplishes" (*sādhati*).

Enveloped by clarified butter, Heaven and Earth are adorned with clarified butter, touched by clarified butter, and increased by clarified butter. Wide and expansive, these two, placed in front for the choosing of the Hotṛ-priest, the wise ones indeed praise for the sake of well-offered sacrifice. Heaven and Earth (dyāvāpṛthivī) are enveloped (abhīvṛte) by clarified butter (ghṛtena), that is, by water. They are those who rest upon (ghṛtaśriyāṃ) water, who are touched by (ghṛtapṛcā) clarified butter, who increase (ghṛtāvṛdhā) clarified butter, who are wide (urvī) and expansive (pṛthivī). Placed in front (purohite) at the choosing of the Hotṛ (hotṛvūryai)—that is, honored by the sacrificers—the wise (viprāḥ), the singers of praise, indeed (it) praise (īḷate) them, Heaven and Earth alone, for the sake of sacrifice (iṣṭaye); for "sacrifice" (iṣṭiḥ) is listed among the names of the rite. They pray for (īḷate) bliss (sumnaṃ), that is, happiness; for when there is happiness, sacrifices proceed.

May Heaven and Earth sprinkle us with sweetness—those who distill sweetness, who yield sweetness, whose ordinances are sweet, who, as deities, bestow upon us the sacrifice, wealth, great renown, food, and heroic vigor. (5) *madhuśrutā*: pouring forth water; *madhudughe*: milking out water; *madhuvrate*: whose ritual acts are directed toward water; *devatā*: having become deities; *asme*: upon us; *yajñam*: the sacrifice; *draviṇam*: wealth; *ca*: and; *mahi*: great; *śravaḥ*: renown; *vājam*: food; *suvīryam*: heroic vigor; *dadhāne*: bestowing; *dyāvāpṛthivī*: Heaven and Earth; *naḥ*: us; *madhu*: with sweetness; [the third case singular ending is elided]; *mimikṣatām*: may they sprinkle.

May Heaven and Earth swell strength for us—Father and Mother, all-knowing and of wondrous deeds. May the two worlds, rejoicing together and bringing welfare to all, bestow upon us gain, booty, and wealth. ūrjam | naḥ | dyauḥ | ca | pṛthivī | ca | pinvatām | pitā | mātā | viśvavidā | sudaṃsasā | saṃrarāṇe | rodasī | viśvaśaṃbhuvā | sanim | vājam | rayim | asme | sam | invatām || 6 ||
1. Kha, gha, jña, na, bha, śa, apavṛte. 2. Kha, jha, ta, na, bha, śa, ghṛtadhṛt. 3. Jha, hotṛvūrye, hotābhirvarṇanīye. 4. Kha, jha, na, bha, prajāḥ.

May the Father, Heaven, who is like a father by virtue of being the sprinkler of rain, and the Mother, Earth, who is like a mother by virtue of being the sustainer—may both of them swell and grant us nourishing food (*ūrj*).

Furthermore, may the two *Rodasī*—Heaven and Earth—who know all (*viśvavidā*), who make all known (*viśvasya vedayitrī*), who perform noble deeds (*sudaṃsasā*), who take delight together (*saṃrāṇe*) in a state of mutual assistance, and who nourish everything (*viśvabhuvā*), bestow upon us (*arama*) desirable offspring and the like (*sanim*), as well as strength (*vājam*) and wealth (*rayim*). May they grant these abundantly.
The tenth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “udu tyad deva,” is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Bharadvāja and has Savitṛ as its deity.
The first three verses are Jagatī, and the next three, beginning with the fourth, are Triṣṭubh.
Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: “udu tyad is addressed to Savitṛ; it consists of three [Jagatīs] and ends with Triṣṭubhs.”
The application (*viniyoga*) of the hymn (*sūkta*) is based on its internal characteristics (*laiṅgika*).
On the twenty-fourth day, the first triplet (*tṛca*) from the *Sāvitra-sūkta* is to be inserted (*āvapanīya*) into the *Vaiśvadeva-śastra*.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "‘ud u tyad devaḥ savitā hiraṇyayā’—these three [verses]... for these two are heaven and earth" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 7.4).
In the Bṛhaspatisava sacrifice as well, this triplet [of verses] is used in place of the Sāvitra hymn within the Vaiśvadeva Śastra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “One should rise with the words, ‘Upward now rises the god Savitṛ, the golden one... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.5).

On the fifth day of the Nūḷaha festival, in the Vaiśvadeva Śastra, the triplet beginning with “Upward now rises the god Savitṛ, the friend of the house... is for the purpose of inserting the Nivid into the Sāvitra hymn.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “The three verses beginning with ‘ud u tyam devaḥ savitā damūnāḥ’” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 8.8).
In the Vaiśvadeva section, the *yājyā* for the twelve-potherd oblation to Savitṛ is “vāmam adya.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “vāmam adya savitar vāmaṃ śvo bhuvā pūṣan tava vrate vayam” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.16).
The divine Savitṛ, the wise one, has extended his golden arms for the sake of impelling all things;
he anoints his hands with ghee, he who is youthful, most skillful, and the upholder of the firmament.

And: Om! This god Savitṛ has extended his two golden arms for the sake of impelling [the world] or for bestowing gifts; he of noble will. With clarified butter (ghṛta), he fills his hands; he is youthful, most skillful, and established in the sustaining support of the mid-world (rajas). The radiant god, of noble will and good deeds—this well-known Savitṛ—has raised up his own two golden arms for the sake of impelling or for bestowing. Furthermore, he who is worthy of honor, eternally youthful, most skillful, and possessed of excellent wisdom, standing in the sustaining support of the mid-world (rajas)—he fills and extends his own hands, which are full of clarified butter (water).
May we abide within the most excellent impulsion of the God Savitṛ, that we may be recipients of his wealth-giving;
you who are the master of all that is biped and quadruped, both in their resting place and in their coming forth from the world.

May we be among those who, at the impulse (*savīman*) of the divine Savitṛ, may be capable of receiving the most excellent gift of wealth. For you are independent in the settling and the procreation of all bipeds and quadrupeds, and indeed of the multitude of beings. At the impulse—that is, the impelling, the granting of permission—of that god Savitṛ, the prompter; and likewise Yāska says: "In the impulse, in the procreation" (*Nirukta* 6.7). In the most excellent, pre-eminently praised, giving—that is, the bestowing—of wealth (*vasu*), may we be capable. You, O Vaya, are independent in the settling and the procreation of every biped, and you are independent in the settling and the procreation of the many quadrupeds.
1. [The reading] "of the year kha-jha-na-bha-śa" [is found] in kha, jha, na, bha, and śa.
2. [The phrase] "kha-jha-ta-na-bha-śa 'Viśvabhuvā...bhāvayitrī'" does not exist.
3. [The reading] "ending in triṣṭubh" [is found] in kha, jha, na, bha, and śa.

O Savitṛ, with your unfailing, auspicious, and protecting arms, guard our household today. O golden-tongued one, protect us for the sake of new-found prosperity; let not the malevolent one have power over us. *adabdhebhiḥ*—with those that are unfailing; *savitari*—O Savitṛ; *pāyubhiḥ*—with protecting [arms]; *tvam*—you; *śivebhiḥ*—with those that are auspicious; *adya*—today; *pari pāhi*—protect completely; *naḥ*—our; *gayam*—household; *hiraṇyajihvaḥ*—O golden-tongued one; *suvitāya*—for prosperity; *navyase*—new; *rakṣa*—protect; *mākinaḥ*—let him not; *aghaśaṃsaḥ*—the malevolent one; *īśata*—have power.

O Savitṛ, with your undeceived, unharmed, and protective rays— or rather, with your auspicious, bliss-bestowing powers— protect today our *gaya*, that is, our home or wealth (for *gaya* is listed among the names for "house" in the phrase *gayaḥ kudaraḥ*, and among the names for "wealth" in the phrase *mīḷahaṃ gayaḥ*). Guard it completely.
Hiraṇyajihvaḥ—one whose speech is pleasant and delightful;
thus Yāska says, beginning with "From what is *hiraṇyam*?"—"Or because it is a delight that is beneficial" (*Nirukta* 2.10).
Be for our new, most recent, and happy welfare.
Protect us and guard us;
let no enemy who intends us harm have power over us, nor prevail against us.

This very god Savitṛ, the friend of the home, with golden hands, has risen at every twilight; he of the iron jaws, the holy one with the pleasant tongue, bestows abundant wealth upon the donor. 4. He, that god Savitṛ, the friend of the home, with golden hands, has risen at every twilight; he of the iron jaws, the holy one with the pleasant tongue, bestows abundant wealth upon the donor. 4.
The god is the shining one, the *damūnā*—meaning either "one whose mind is self-controlled" (*damamanāḥ*) or "one whose mind is disposed toward giving" (*dānamanāḥ*).

Thus Yāska says: "The *damūnā* is one whose mind is self-controlled (*damamanāḥ*), or one whose mind is disposed toward giving (*dānamanāḥ*), or one whose mind is subdued (*dāntamanāḥ*)" (Nirukta 4.4). He is *hiraṇyapāṇiḥ*, having golden hands; *ayohanuḥ*, having golden jaws.

Because "rukma" is listed among the names for gold, it means golden. Worthy of worship (*yajataḥ*), meaning he who is to be sacrificed to; with a pleasant tongue (*mandrajihvaḥ*), meaning one whose speech is delightful—may that Savitṛ rise up every evening, at the end of every night. He who, for the donor, the sacrificer, [bestows] "mahaṃ"—that is, much, abundant—"vāmaṃ," that which is desirable and worthy of being honored—a golden ornament (*rukmam*).
"Vāma means that which is desirable," says Yāska (Nirukta 6.31).
It impels or urges forward.

Like an invoking priest, Savitar, the golden-hued one of beautiful countenance, has stretched forth his two arms. He has ascended the heights of heaven from the earth; he has brought to rest whatever moves upon it. ut | ūm iti | ayān | upavaktā'iva | bāhū iti | hiraṇyayā | savitā | supratīkā | divaḥ | rohāṃsi | aruhat | pṛthivyāḥ | arīramata | patayat | kat | cit | bhuvam || 5 ||
Like an Upavaktṛ priest, may Savitṛ, like an Adhivaktṛ priest, extend his two golden, golden-hued arms of beautiful form.
He who has ascended, ascends from the earth—that is, from the limits of the earth—to the heights of heaven, the elevated regions of the intermediate space;
and as he moves, he causes everything that exists, even the great and hidden, to rest and find delight.
1. kha-jha: *rakṣṇesmān*; gha: *asmān rakṣa*; na-bha: *rakṣaṇena*; śa: *rakṣaṇāsmān*. 2. kha-bha: *aghamā°*; jha-na: *arthamā°*. 3. kha-jha-ta-na-bha-śa: *śatruḥ no'smākam*.

4. [The syllables] *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, or *dānamanā* do not exist. O God, grant us today that which is desirable, and grant it day by day; grant us that which is desirable. For with this prayer, O God, may we become partakers of abundant desirable wealth.

O Savitṛ, bestow upon us today what is desirable; Oṃ! Bestow it upon us tomorrow, and day after day, what is desirable. For you, O God, are the master of abundant desirable wealth; through this prayer, may we be partakers of that which is desirable. 6.
O Savitṛ, impel for us today desirable wealth; impel it also tomorrow.
What is the use of speaking much?
Day by day, or every single day, bestow desirable wealth!

O God, since you are indeed the giver of abundant and desirable wealth that serves as a dwelling place for our prosperity, may we therefore, through this prayer of praise, become possessors of the desirable—that is, may we become wealthy.

The hymn beginning with “indrāsomā mahi” is the eleventh in the fifth [maṇḍala]; it is the seer’s own composition (ārṣa) by Bharadvāja, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter, and has Indra and Soma as its deities.
It is enumerated thus: “indrāsomā pañca; indrāsoma.
The application of this hymn is determined by its internal characteristics (laiṅgika).
O Indra and Soma, great indeed is that majesty of yours; you two performed the first great deeds.
You two found the sun, you two found the light of heaven, and you struck down all darknesses and reproaches.

O Indra and Soma, great indeed is that majesty of yours; you two performed the first great deeds. You two found the sun, you two found the light of heaven, and you struck down all darknesses and reproaches. 1.
O Indra and Soma—indeed, O Indra and Soma—great is that majesty, that greatness, of you two; how so? It is said:
you two [have created] the great, the vast, the primary, or the foremost beings.

‘*Prathama* is a primary name; it means *pratamaḥ* (the foremost),' says Yāska (Nirukta 2.22). *Cakrathuḥ* means you two performed (*akārṣṭam*). Furthermore, you two, *yuvām*, found (*vividathuḥ*) the sun and caused the people to obtain it.
You two have found the light and the water—
since "light" (*svaḥ*) is listed among the names for water—
and moreover, you have struck down all darknesses, as well as the revilers and the Asuras. You have slain the serpent.
O Indra and Soma, you two cause the dawn to shine; you lead forth the sun together with its light.
You have propped up the sky with a support and have spread out the mother earth.

O Indra and Soma, you two cause the dawn to appear; you lead forth the sun together with its light. You have propped up the sky with a support and have spread out the earth, the mother, far and wide. 2.

O Indra and Soma—indeed, O Indra and Soma—you cause the dawn to shine; you cause her to dawn, meaning you cause the dawning dawn to appear. Furthermore, you raise up the sun along with light and splendor.

Moreover, enough with this prolixity. With the sky as the support—that is, by means of the atmosphere which serves as the support and was established in the middle—they propped it up; they supported it. 1. kha, jha, ta, na, bha, ya, śa, kiñca: "bahuktyā" (enough with prolixity); gha, kiñca. 2. kha, gha, jha, na, bha, śa: "adhanaṃ" (wealth) is not present. 3. kha, jha, ta, na, bha, śa: "pratatāni" (extended). 4. jha, na, śa: "prathamo" (first). *Note: The text contains various manuscript variants regarding the reading and placement of certain words.*
You two caused the Earth—the mother of the universe, who has become the mother—to expand wide.
O Indra and Soma, you drove away the obstructing waters; you slew Vṛtra, and the cow yielded to you.
You sent forth the breaths of the rivers and filled the many oceans.

O Indra and Soma, you two slew the serpent Ahi and Vṛtra who encompassed the waters; the heaven rejoiced in you both, and you set free the floods of the rivers. You have filled the many oceans to the full.

O Indra and Soma, you two slew Vṛtra, the Asura who lay encompassing the waters—the waters situated in the clouds—and who was the slayer of the moving world; at that time, Heaven approved of you both. Furthermore, you two set in motion the floods, the waters of the rivers.
*Purūṇi* means many; this is because *tuvi* and *puru* are listed among the names for "much" (*bahunāmasu*).
*Samudrāṇi* refers to reservoirs of water; you two have *ā paprathuḥ*, that is, you have filled them with water.
Alternatively, they are called *samudrāṇi* because they swell (*samundanti*) with waters;
the meaning is that you two should fill them with sap.

And thus says Yāska: "Why 'samudra'? Because from it the waters flow out (*samudravanti*), or the waters rush toward it (*samabhidravanti*), or beings rejoice in it (*saṃmodante*), or it is a place where water has gathered (*samudraka*), or it swells up (*samunnatti*)" (Nirukta 2.10).
10) Thus.
O Indra and Soma, you placed the cooked [milk] within the raw cows; you seized it within those trees that were bound up—within those bright and variegated moving creatures.
O Indra and Soma, you placed the cooked [milk] within the raw cows; you seized it within the trees. You have taken that bright, unbound [milk] within these variegated moving creatures. 4.

O Indra and Soma— ye two, Indra and Soma— within the udders (*vakṣaṇāsu*) of these cows, that is, within their teats (*ūdhas*), ye have deposited the cooked milk. Moreover, within these *jagatīs* (cows)— for "Iḷā" and "jagatī" are listed among the names for cows— their colors are variegated (*citrasu*).
"You two have sung [of] the white-colored milk, unbound within—that is, not tied by anyone—within [the udder].
The meaning is that you two have supported it in such a way that it does not flow out on its own upon the earth.
The word *it* is a filler.
O Indra and Soma, you two indeed have granted a protective, never-failing, and famous [gift] to the one who honors you;
you two, O fierce ones, bestow manly vigor upon the people, conquering in battle.
O Indra and Soma, you two indeed have granted a watery chariot that is worthy of hearing; you two have bestowed manly vigor upon the peoples, O fierce ones, for the conquest of armies.

O Indra and Soma—O you two, Indra and Soma—you have quickly bestowed upon us a chariot that is victorious, accompanied by a continuous flow [of wealth], worthy of being heard of, and a treasure of riches.
Furthermore, O fierce ones—O you two, Indra and Soma—you have granted to the people a force that is beneficial to men, capable of withstanding armies, and overpowering the hosts of enemies;
for "carṣaṇī" is listed among the names for humans.
You two have joined together; you have spread it out, or rather, you encircle it.
1. By means of the cause of the suppression of *kha*, *gha*, *jña*, *ta*, *na*, and *bha*; by means of the cause of the support of *ya*.
2. *Ya* caused [them] to be suppressed. 3. It is fully understood through *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*.
4. [The hymn] is to be heard with the syllables *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*.
5. [The hymn] containing *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa* is not "conquering the enemy's army.

The twelfth hymn, beginning with "He who is the mountain-splitter" (*yo adribhit*), consists of three verses; it belongs to Bṛhaspati, is the seerly composition of Bharadvāja, and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.

And it is recited in sequence as follows: “*Yo adribhit... bārhaspatyam*. This hymn is for the purpose of the *stomātiśaṃsana* (additional praise of the *stoma*) by the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin during the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*) at the *ābhiplavika* sacrifices.
For it is prescribed: “In the hymn *yo adribhid divaḥ...*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.9).
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, at the oblation for Bṛhaspati, [he recites]: "Bṛhaspati won all treasures... and "...thee, the swift one, he praises for the sake of the Dūlī" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.9).

He who is the mountain-shatterer, the first-born, the observer of Truth, Bṛhaspati, the descendant of Aṅgiras, rich in oblations, the doubly-mighty one, the father who dwells in the heat of the sacrifice— he, the bull, roars aloud to us across the two worlds.

He who is the mountain-shatterer, the first-born, the upholder of cosmic order, Bṛhaspati, the son of Aṅgiras, possessed of oblations, doubly mighty, the partaker of the Gharma offering, our father—he, the bull, bellows loudly unto the two worlds, heaven and earth.
He who is Bṛhaspati, the breaker of mountain peaks fashioned by the Paṇis with stones, or the piercer of clouds.
Because "adriḥ prāvaḥ" is listed among the names for the cloud;
he is the first-born, born first from the creative power (*vīrya*) of Prajāpati;
he is the possessor of truth (*ṛtāvā*), or the possessor of water.

Āṅgirasa was born later. And thus there is a Vedic citation: "Those who were Āṅgirasas became the Āṅgirasas; the descendants of Aṅgiras, having won [the prize], played at dice, and from that Bṛhaspati arose" (AiB 3.34). Haviṣmān means possessing a share in the sacrifice.
With a double path, he who moves for the benefit of rain in both worlds;
dwelling pre-eminently in the high place of heat,
may that Bṛhaspati be our father and protector.
Being the showerer, the bull bellows loudly toward the two worlds, heaven and earth, making them resound.
Bṛhaspati has created wide space even for the people who invoke the gods;
he shatters the fortresses that are not protected by the Ṛbhus, conquering the enemies and overcoming the adversary in battles.
For the people indeed, Bṛhaspati has made wide space when invoked by the gods; slaying the Vṛtras, he shatters the fortresses, conquering his enemies and foes, prevailing in battles.
Moreover,
Bṛhaspati creates— that is, he makes— a world, a place, for the person who offers praise, who approaches and praises him at the invocation of the gods when the sacrifice is underway.
The word *cit* is a filler.
He, striking down—that is, warding off—the *vṛtrāṇi*, the obstructing darknesses;
conquering his enemies in battles (*pṛtsu*); overcoming his adversaries; [and shattering] the *purah*, the fortresses of the Asuras.
"Vi dardarīti" means he tears it apart violently.
Bṛhaspati has won all treasures; this god has seized the great pens full of cattle.
Desiring to win the waters, Bṛhaspati glides forward with his swift steeds; with his hymns, he slays the enemy.
Bṛhaspati has won all treasures; this god, irresistible, desiring to win the waters and the light, has conquered the great stalls full of cattle. With his hymns, Bṛhaspati slays the enemy. 3.

The radiant god, this well-known Bṛhaspati, conquered the great riches—the wealth of the Paṇis, the Asuras, or of Vala—as well as the cow-filled enclosures. Thus, there are two Vedic citations: "Bṛhaspati stripped away the cattle-bodied Vala, as one might tear apart the joints of a limb" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.68.9); and "Far away let the Paṇis go, even further, fleeing from the truth;
those whom Bṛhaspati found hidden, Soma, the pressing-stones, and the wise sages [recovered]" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.108.11).

Furthermore, Bṛhaspati—unassailable, meaning not overcome by anyone—desiring to win (*sipāsan*), that is, wishing to conquer, slays his enemy, the Asura, with *arkas*, which are mantras serving as means of worship.
Yāska states: "The *arka* is a mantra, because they worship (*arcanti*) with it" (Nirukta 5.4).
The thirteenth hymn, consisting of four verses beginning with "somārudrā," is the seerly composition of Bharadvāja and has Soma and Rudra as its deities.
It is enumerated thus: "The [hymn] beginning with 'somārudrā' consists of four verses; it is addressed to Soma and Rudra.
Its application is indicated by the internal evidence of the hymn itself.
O Soma and Rudra, uphold your divine power; may your gracious favors reach us fully.
Bestowing jewels upon this dwelling, be a source of well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds.

O Soma and Rudra, uphold your divine power! May our offerings reach you sufficiently. Bestowing jewels in every dwelling, be auspicious to us—be a source of well-being for our bipeds and well-being for our quadrupeds.

O Soma and Rudra, O Soma and Rudra, bestow upon us the *asurya*—the power belonging to the Asuras. Furthermore, in every house, in every dwelling, may our sacrifices reach you both sufficiently and pervade you completely. Moreover, holding and bestowing treasures, become for us sources of well-being, bringers of happiness, or embodiments of bliss.
May you both be auspicious for our two-footed son and for our four-footed livestock.
O Soma and Rudra, tear asunder this affliction that has entered our home;
drive away Destruction to a distance, and may auspicious glories of renown attend us.
O Soma and Rudra, drive away in all directions the hostility that has entered our home; cast far away destruction to a distance, and may auspicious glories attend us.

O Soma and Rudra, O Soma and Rudra, whatever disease or enemy has entered our house or the living beings within it—that three-jointed one which spreads in every direction—tear it apart and separate it from us. Furthermore, drive away misfortune and ill-fortune so that they go far off; keep them at a distance and repel them.
May auspicious things, excellent renown, food, and glory belong to us.
The state of being well-renowned is *sauśravasa*; "renown" (*śrava*) refers both to fame and to glory.
O Soma and Rudra, place all these healing medicines within our bodies.
Cast away and release whatever sin has been committed and is bound within our bodies.
O Soma and Rudra, bestow upon us all these remedies within our bodies. Untie and release whatever sin has been committed and remains bound within our bodies; let it go away from us. 3.
1. [The *kha-jha-na-bha-śa* recension] lacks the word "ratnā.
[Ma. 6.6.75] The Fifth Aṣṭaka, 255:
O Soma and Rudra, O Soma and Rudra, you two—place (*dhattam*), that is, bestow, all these well-known medicinal herbs (*bheṣajāni*) within our bodies (*tanūṣu*), that is, upon our limbs.
Furthermore, whatever sin or evil (*enaḥ*) has been committed or bound by us within our bodies (*tanūṣu*), that sin you two must cast down, exhaust, and loosen— meaning,
make its bonds slack.
And bestow favor (*sumna*) upon us.
O Rudra and Soma, you who possess sharp weapons and sharp missiles, and who are most gracious—be merciful to us here!
Release us from the noose of Varuṇa and favor us with a well-disposed mind.

O you two with sharp weapons, with sharp missiles, most gracious ones, O Soma and Rudra, be well-disposed toward us here; show us mercy. Release us from the noose of Varuṇa, and protect us with a benevolent mind. 4.

O Soma and Rudra, you two who possess sharp weapons, blazing bows, keen missiles, and sharp-edged tools; who are most gracious, bestowing beautiful happiness; who are well-disposed, desiring our hymns with beautiful minds—or being well-disposed as you are praised, or being of noble mind—do you both here in this world exceedingly favor us and grant us happiness. Release us from the noose of Varuṇa.
Protect us and guard us from calamities.
The fourteenth hymn, consisting of nineteen verses beginning with "jīmūtasya," is the seerly composition (*ārṣam*) of Pāyu Bhāradvāja.

It is enumerated as follows: "In the hymn beginning with *jīmūtasya*, Pāyu Bhāradvāja praised the battles. He praised the armor, the bow, the quiver, the arrows, and half a verse the charioteer; half a verse the reins, the stones, the chariot, and the chariot-fenders. In the *jagatī* [verse], the deities are indicated by their characteristics (*liṅgodevatā*). With two [verses], the arrow, the thrower, and the hand-guard; with two [more], the arrow. The remaining [verses] beginning with the *paṅkti* have deities indicated by their characteristics; they are blessings for battle. The others are in the *anuṣṭubh* meter. And the two [verses] beginning with *ālāktā* are each in pairs."

"Standing on the chariot" (*rathe tiṣṭhan*) and "The Brahmins" (*brāhmaṇāsaḥ*) are two *jagatī* verses in the sixth and tenth meters; the final verse, "Who [is] our own" (*yo naḥ svaḥ*), is an *anuṣṭubh*. "In the joints" (*arjāne*), "They struck down" (*ā jaṅghnanta*), "Smeared with poison" (*ālāktā*), "Released" (*avasṛṣṭā*), and "Who [is] our own" (*yo naḥ svaḥ*)—these five are *anuṣṭubhs*. "Where the arrows" (*yatra bāṇāḥ*) is a *paṅkti*; the remaining verses are *triṣṭubhs*. By the first [verse], the armor (*varman*) is praised; by the second, the bow; by the third, the bowstring (*jyā*); by the fourth, the leather thong (*āttnī*); by the fifth, the quiver (*iṣudhi*). Therefore, the deities of these five are the armor and the others.
The charioteer is praised with the first half of the sixth [verse];
therefore, that half has him as its deity.
The reins are praised with the second half.
The horses belong to the seventh [verse], the chariot to the eighth, and the chariot-protectors to the ninth;
these are their respective deities.
In the verse beginning with "brāhmaṇāsaḥ," the deities indicated by the marks of the text (liṅgadevatāḥ) are the Brahmins, the Pitṛs, Māyava, Heaven and Earth, and Pūṣan.
The eleventh and twelfth [days] have the arrow as their deity because they consist of the praise of the arrow;
the thirteenth has the goad;
the fourteenth has the hand-striker.
The fifteenth and sixteenth [verses] have the arrow as their deity.
The seventeenth has as its deities, indicated by their characteristic marks (*liṅga*), the battlefield, Brahmanaspati, and the day.
The eighteenth has the armor, Soma, and Varuṇa as its deities.
For the final [verse], the deities are the gods and Brahman.
With this hymn, one should cause the king to don his armor for battle.

And likewise Āśvalāyana says: "When a battle is imminent, he should cause the king to put on his armor with [the verse], 'I have brought thee hither, O thou who art within'; having stood behind the horse, he should give him the breastplate with [the verse], 'Like a cloud is thy appearance'; with the next [verse] he should give him the bow; he should cause him to recite the next [verse]; he himself should conquer the fourth [verse]; with the fifth he should give him the quiver; with the sixth and the seventh and eighth [verses], while looking at the arrows, he should cause him to recite, 'As one looks upon a sacrificial oblation with enjoyments, so he looks upon the arm'; [this is for] the hand being bound with a leather guard" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 3.12).

And likewise: "When [the teacher] says, 'Let the arrow fly forth,' he should dismiss them where the arrows fall together; while they are fighting, he should mutter [the mantra] 'May you strike down the enemy' (āśva. gṛ. 3.12).
At the commencement and the dismissal of the term of study, this verse "He who is our own" (āśva. gṛ. 3.5.7) is recited within the circle.
1. In manuscripts Kha, Gha, Jha, Ta, Na, Bha, and Śa, the word "akṣapayataṃ" (destroy) is absent.

2. In manuscript Ya, it reads "mṛḷayataṃ"; in manuscript Śa, it reads "mṛḷataṃ mṛḷayatam. 3. In manuscript Kha, it says "jagatyādyā liṅgoktaḥ"; in manuscript Śa, it says "jagatyādyā liṅgoktā devatāḥ" (the deities beginning with Jagatī are indicated by their gender).

4. *Araṇā* (the absence of conflict) is [indicated by] the syllables *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*. 5. *Ardhastha* (standing on half) is [indicated by] the syllables *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *sa*. 6. The deity is [indicated by] the syllables *kha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*.
Like a cloud, his appearance becomes such when he goes into the lap of the contending hosts;
with an unpierced body, may you be victorious, and may that greatness protect you with its armor.
Like the front of a cloud, it becomes manifest when you go forth among the joyful ones. With an unassailable body, may you be victorious; may that armor and its greatness protect you. 1.

When there is the presence of the onset of battles, whenever this king goes forth clad in armor (*varman*), then the appearance of the king, equipped with his iron armor, becomes like that of a cloud (*jīmūta*);
the meaning is that it becomes like the form of a cloud.
O King, conquer the enemies with a body (*tanu*) that is unpierced by them.
May such greatness of Varman protect you, may it preserve you.
With the bow may we win cattle, with the bow may we conquer in battle; with the bow may we overcome fierce assailants.
The bow frustrates the enemy’s purpose; with the bow may we conquer all the quarters.

With the bow may we win cattle; with the bow may we conquer in battle; with the bow may we overcome the fierce, intoxicating [foes]. The bow frustrates the desire of the enemy; with the bow may we conquer all the quarters. 2.
With the bow, with the archer’s weapon, may we conquer and bring under our control the cattle of our enemies;
with the bow may we conquer the battle, the conflict;
and with the bow may we conquer the fierce, arrogant, and exceedingly intoxicated armies of our foes.
And thus says Yāska: “*Samadaḥ* means either *samadaḥ* [from the root *ad*, 'to eat'] or *saṃmadaḥ* [from the root *mad*, 'to rejoice']" (Nirukta 9.17).
The bow (*dhanuḥ*) effects the removal of the enemy's desire—that is, it brings about the departure of his longing.
Furthermore, with the bow (*dhanvanā*), may we conquer all enemies existing in all directions (*pradiśaḥ*).
The word *pradiś* (direction) refers by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to those persons [who are situated] within it, just as in the expression "the submerged ones are crying out.
The repetition of the words *dhanvan* (desert) and *jayati* (he conquers) is for the sake of emphasis.
As if about to speak, she comes close to the ear, embracing her dear friend;
like a woman, this bowstring clings to the wide-stretched back of the bow, carrying us across in the encounter.

As if about to speak, she comes again and again to the ear; embracing her dear friend, she whispers like a woman. This bowstring, stretched upon the bow, crackles like a woman at the assembly, carrying [the warrior] across.
In the preceding section, the armor and the bow were praised with two verses;
here, the praise is for the bowstring.
This bowstring [is] upon the bow in every battle.

*Adhi* is a restatement of the locative sense (*saptamy-artha*). *Vitata* means spread out; *pārayantī* means leading to the further shore (*pāraṃ nayan-tī*). *Priyam* means a pleasant word that brings delight. *Vakṣyantī-iva* means as if about to speak. *Karṇe* refers to the region of the ear of the archer king. *Ā ganīganti* means she comes toward [him]. *It* is a filler particle (*pūraṇaḥ*).
Like a young woman embracing her friend, her husband, so the arrow, embracing [the bow], hisses and makes a sound.

Thus Yāska says: “As if about to speak, she comes to the ear; embracing the arrow as if it were a dear friend, like a woman she hisses—that is, she makes a sound—stretched upon the bow, with the string, in the encounter, in battle, bringing across, leading to the further shore” (Nirukta 9.18).
1. Like a cloud [is the sound of] *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*.
2. *Kha*, *gha*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, and *bha* are utterly [silent].
They move together like a woman; as a mother bears her son in her lap, so do they bear him.
May these two, acting in concert and darting forth, pierce the enemies and strike down the foes.

These two, acting together—like two women moving in harmony, like a mother carrying her son upon her lap—may they drive away our enemies; may these two, acting in concert, drawing their bows, and discharging them, strike down our adversaries. 4.
Here is the praise of the two ends of the bow (*dhanuṣkoṭi*):

"Those two" ends of the bow, "like a woman with a mind" (*samaneva*), like a wife who does not abandon her husband, "moving about" (*ācarantī*) on both sides; "in the lap" (*upasthe*), "like a mother" (*mātā iva*), may they "bear" (*vibhṛtām*) the king, just as a mother supports her son.
Furthermore, "these two" ends of the bow, "being in agreement" (*saṃvidāne*), being of one mind and free from discord, "go toward" (*ātnī*) [the target].
From the root *ṛ* meaning "to go," [the word *ṛju* is derived].
In this verse, the first half is a praise of the charioteer and the second half is a praise of the reins.
A "good charioteer" (*susārathi*), standing on the chariot, leads the "horses" (*vājinaḥ*) that are positioned in front toward whatever place he desires to lead them.

Those reins which, having extended from the necks of the horses, exist as cords at the rear of the chariot on its back part—those which restrain and guide the horses according to the mind of the charioteer—hearken to the greatness and majesty of those *abhīśu* reins; O people, praise them!

And thus Yāska says: “The spirited horses stand on the chariot in front; wherever the good charioteer, the auspicious driver, desires, there they go. Admire the greatness of the reins! The mind is behind, while the reins, being present, restrain [the horses] from behind” (Nirukta 9.16).
The bull-like, swift-footed horses produce a piercing sound along with the chariots.

*Śaktimantaḥ*: those possessing *śakti*, which is a particular weapon; that is to say, those with spears in their hands. Alternatively, *śakti* means strength; those possessing it. *Gabhīrāḥ*: profound, unassailable. *Citrasenāḥ*: having beautiful armies. *Iṣubalāḥ*: having the power of arrows. *Amṛdhāḥ*: incapable of being harmed. *Satovīrāḥ*: those who have attained heroic vigor. Thus says Yāska: "Regarding *tiraḥ sataḥ*, [it refers to] what has been attained; *tiras* means spread out, and *sataḥ* means that which is gathered together" (*Nirukta* 3.20). *Uravaḥ*: great. *Vrātasāhāḥ*: they are the subduers of hosts. Brāhmaṇas, Fathers, worthy of Soma—may Heaven and Earth be auspicious to us, the faultless ones. May Pūṣan protect us from misfortune, O increasers of *ṛta*. Guard us; let not the malevolent one have power over us. *Brāhmaṇāsaḥ*, *pitaraḥ*, *somyāsaḥ*, *śive*, *naḥ*, *dyāvāpṛthivī*, *anehasāṃ*, *pūṣā*, *naḥ*, *pātu*, *duritāt*, *ṛtavṛdhaḥ*, *rakṣa*, *mākiḥ*, *naḥ*, *aghaśaṃsaḥ*, *īśata*. 10. *Brāhmaṇa...* Brāhmaṇas, Fathers, worthy of Soma—may Heaven and Earth be auspicious to us, the faultless ones. May Pūṣan protect us from misfortune, O increasers of *ṛta*. Guard us; let not the malevolent one have power over us. 10. Brāhmaṇa...

O straight-flying one, spare us! May our bodies be as stone. May Soma speak for us; may Aditi grant us protection. (12) O straight-flying one (*ṛjīti*), spare (*pari-vṛṅdhi*) us. May our body (*tanūḥ*) be like stone (*aśmā*). May Soma speak in our favor (*adhi-bravītu*); may Aditi grant us security (*śarma*). O straight-flying one: that which goes straight is the "straight-flying" (*ṛjīti*), namely the arrow. O arrow, spare us—protect us on all sides. May our body be like stone; let it be firm and unbreakable like a rock. Furthermore, may Soma speak for us, speaking with partiality toward us; and may Aditi also grant us happiness.

They strike upon their backs; they beat upon their haunches. O wise horse-whip, urge the horses on in the battles! They strike upon their backs (*sānu*); they beat upon their haunches (*jaghana*). O wise horse-whip (*aśvājani*), urge the horses on in the battles (*samatsu*). O horse-whip, as you are the healer (*kṣetri*) of the horses, so by you the riders or charioteers, being highly intelligent (*pracetas*), strike upon their backs—their haunches or thighs—and they beat upon their haunches. Therefore, urge the horses forward in the battles, the encounters. Thus says Yāska: “They strike their backs—their running thighs. ‘Thigh’ (*sakthi*) comes from the root *sac*, for the body is attached to it. And they beat upon their haunches. ‘Haunch’ (*jaghana*) means that which is struck. O wise horse-whip, one whose consciousness is expanded, urge the horses on in the battles, the encounters, the conflicts” (Nighaṇṭu 9.20).

Like a serpent with its coils, it encircles the arm, warding off the strike of the bowstring. The hand-guard (*hastaghna*), knowing all ways, may he, a man himself, protect the man from every side. (14) Here is the praise of the *hastaghna* (hand-guard), which is to be bound upon the forearm of the archer. "Hand-guard" (*hastaghna*): being situated on the *hasta*—that is, near the hand, on the forearm—it guards against the *hasta*; thus it is called *hastaghna*. [The suffix] *ka* is applied according to the rule: "The suffix *ka* is prescribed in the sense of 'one who destroys'. Warding off—that is, preventing—the "strike of the bowstring" (*jyāyā hetiḥ*), which means injury caused by the bowstring; with its "coils" (*bhogaiḥ*), meaning its body (there is a change in grammatical number); like a serpent (*ahiḥ*)—meaning a snake—it "encircles" (*paryaiti*), that is, wraps around, the "arm" (*bāhum*). By metonymy, the word "arm" (*bāhu*) refers here to the forearm. Furthermore, "knowing all ways" (*viśvā vayunāni vidvān*)—since "ways" (*vayuna*) is listed among the names for "knowledge" (*māyā*) and "wisdom"—it is "knowing," that is, perceiving, all things to be known. Being a "man" (*pumān*) endowed with virility himself, may he protect the "man" (*pumāṃsam*), the archer, "from every side" (*viśvataḥ*). Thus says Yāska: "Like a serpent, it encircles the arm with its coils, protecting it from the blow of the bowstring; the hand-guard, perceiving all forms of knowledge, becomes a man (*pumān*) through the root *puṃs* (to nourish/grow)" (Nirukta 9.15).

1. *kha* is to be excluded; *jha*, *na*, *bha*, and *na* undergo *vṛddhi*. 2. *kha*, *gha*, *sa*, *ta*, *na*, *ma*, and *śa* are present. 3. A wise man who knows [the etymology]—*kha*, *jha*, *sa*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*—becomes *puman* from the root *puṃsati*; thus says Yāska.

May the one who possesses a great mind protect and guard the man from every side, from all directions. That which is smeared with poison, whose head is that of a deer, and whose mouth is of iron—to this arrow, the offspring of Parjanya, the divine weapon, be great homage! 15 Smeared with poison; that which; has the head of a deer; and also; whose; mouth is; of iron; to this; offspring of Parjanya; to the arrow; to the goddess; be great; homage. 15.
The arrow which is smeared with poison, anointed with venom, and tipped with the head of a ruru deer—may it strike down the heads of the slayers.
For the word *ruha* arises from the root *at*, which has the meaning "to injure."
Or with a horn-tip.
Furthermore,
that arrow whose point is made of iron belongs to Parjanya as its seed.
She whose seed is Parjanya is "Parjanyaretas";
[the offering is] for her,
who has become the effect of Parjanya, because the stalk of reed (śarakāṇḍa) is produced by Parjanya.
"To the Great One, to the Great, to her, to the Arrow, to the Divine—one pays this homage."

O arrow, discharged, fly away, sharpened by prayer, into the refuge! Go toward the enemies; fall upon them; let not one of them remain. 16. O arrow, discharged, fly away, sharpened by prayer, into the refuge! Go toward the enemies; fall upon them; let not one of them remain. 16.
O arrow, sharpened by the mantra consecrated by Brahmā, you who are a refuge and skilled in slaying—being released and shot, fly away!
Go far away from this place;
go forth and strike down our enemies, those who do us harm.
Among these enemies, do not leave even one behind; do not let anyone remain.

Where arrows fly together like boys with their toy bows, there may Brahmaṇaspati and Aditi grant us protection; may they grant us protection for all days. 17. Where | arrows | fly together | like boys | with their toy bows | there | for us | the Lord of Prayer | and Aditi | protection | may they grant | for all days | protection | may they grant. 17.
In whatever battle the arrows fall like young princes with shorn hair, there may Brahmaṇaspati grant us protection and happiness at all times;
and Aditi too shall grant us protection.
The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.

I cover your vital organs with armor; may King Soma clothe you with immortality. May Varuṇa make for you a space wider than the wide; may the gods rejoice after you as you conquer. 18. Your vital organs. With armor. I cover. Soma. You. The king. With immortality. Along. May he clothe. From the wide. A wider space. Varuṇa. For you. May he make. You, conquering. After you. May the gods. Rejoice. 18.
O King, these are your vital points (*marmāṇi*);
those places in which one pierced dies instantly are the vital points.
I cover them with armor (*varmaṇā*), that is, with a coat of mail (*kavacena*).
May King Soma clothe you with immortality immediately after the covering of your vital organs.
1. [The reading] "ateḥ" is absent in manuscripts kha, jha, na, bha, and dā. 2. [The reading] "tasyaiva" is in manuscripts kha, jha, na, and ma.
3. Because of the nature of the syllables kha, gha, jha, na, and bha, like Parjanya, may he cover [us].
Furthermore, may Varuṇa also create and grant you (*te*) a wider, more excellent, and higher happiness (*vuror varīyaḥ uttaram sukham*).
Having struck you down, let all the gods indeed rejoice and exult in you.
Whoever—whether our own kinsman, a stranger, or one from afar—seeks to harm us, may all the gods strike him down; may the sacred word (*brahman*) be my inner armor.
Whoever seeks to harm us—whether he be our own kin or a stranger, whether he be a neighbor or a foreigner—O gods, may you all strike him down. May the sacred word (*brahman*) be my inner armor. 19.
O gods, let all the gods strike down—that is, destroy—that kinsman who, though our own, is hostile, unyielding, spreading abroad, base-born, hidden, and standing afar off, and who seeks to slay us;
for my *brahman*—the sacred mantra—is my armor that wards off arrows.
Thus ends the sixth Anuvāka in the sixth Maṇḍala of the Dākṣāyaṇī hymns, composed by Sāyaṇācārya; and the Maṇḍala is also completed.
1. sa-dha-sa-na-bha-svaḥ | 2.
In the Vedārthaprakāśa composed by Śa [Śaṅkarācārya].
